choices: In the production account's vault, protected by tagging every resource backup=daily
In the production account, but taken every hour so that more recovery points exist
In a vault in a separate, dedicated backup account, ideally in a different Region
In a second vault inside the same production account, in the same Region
questions.why: Isolation means storing copies in a separate account and a second Region, so a compromised production login cannot reach both production and its backups. More frequent copies or extra vaults in the same account stay within the attacker's reach.

questions.prompt: A media company backs up encrypted databases nightly and copies each recovery point to a central backup account. It has never run a restore test. During a real outage it tries to restore from the backup account, and the restore fails. Based on the risks of untested backups, what is the most likely cause?
choices: The vault in the backup account was not in the same Region as production
The backup plan ran too often, so the recovery points overwrote each other
The backup account could not use the encryption key that protects the copies
The organization backup policy only applies to resources that have tags
questions.why: Encrypted copies can fail to restore when the destination account cannot use the encryption key. Regular restore tests exist to find this problem before an outage, not during one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design backups for 200 AWS accounts so that an auditor is satisfied and a stolen admin login cannot wipe out the copies. Name at least one tradeoff or limit of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd use AWS Backup, which is a managed backup service. I'd drive it centrally with an Organizations backup policy, so every account gets the same plan and coverage depends on tags rather than people remembering. The plan sets frequency, which fixes our worst-case data loss (RPO), and it sets retention. Each recovery point gets copied to a vault in a separate backup account in a second Region. That way a compromised production login or a regional outage can't touch both. I'd turn on Vault Lock on that vault, so copies are write-once and can't be deleted early, even by admins. That's what the auditor and our ransomware defense need. Finally, I'd schedule restore tests so we prove the copies work. Tradeoffs: more frequent copies and cross-Region storage cost more money. A locked vault means mistakes in retention settings can't be undone. Restoring big databases can be slow. Cross-account copies also need the encryption keys shared correctly, or the restore fails.
rubricPoints: Defines a backup plan as frequency plus retention, and links frequency to RPO.
Applies plans centrally across accounts using an Organizations backup policy and tags.
Isolates copies in a separate account and Region.
Uses Vault Lock or WORM immutability so copies cannot be deleted early.
Includes regular restore testing as proof the backups work.
Names a tradeoff such as cost, irreversible retention, slow restores or encryption key access.

suggested.rationale: Backup design at this level is about matching each requirement (coverage, frequency, isolation, immutability, proof) to a mechanism, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style enterprise scenarios.

lessons.plain: An AWS account is a sealed container for cloud resources, permissions and a bill. Large companies use many accounts instead of one, so a mistake or breach in one team's space cannot spill into another's. AWS Organizations groups those accounts under one parent and sorts them into folders. It can then apply rules to a whole folder at once. AWS Control Tower is a ready-made setup built on top of Organizations. It creates a recommended starting layout, standard logging and security accounts, and preset rules. Think of an apartment building: separate flats, one building manager, and house rules that can differ per floor.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants its developers to experiment freely but never touch the systems that handle customer payments. Would you give everyone one shared cloud account with careful permissions, or separate accounts? Why?
lessons.teach:
An account structure is how you split workloads into separate AWS accounts and group those accounts so that rules and billing follow the grouping. AWS Organizations is the service that does the grouping. One account is the management account. It creates or invites member accounts and pays the combined bill, called consolidated billing.

Accounts sit inside organizational units (OUs), which are folders that can nest inside each other. A service control policy (SCP) is a guardrail attached to the root, an OU or a single account. It caps the maximum permissions any identity in those accounts can use, and it never grants permission on its own. Policies inherit downward, so design OUs around which accounts need the same rules, not around the company org chart.

AWS Control Tower automates a well-arranged starting point called a landing zone. A landing zone includes a Security OU that holds two accounts. The log archive account keeps central, protected copies of audit logs. The audit account gives security staff read access across accounts. Control Tower also adds controls, which are prepackaged rules that either prevent actions (often using SCPs) or detect drift from the intended setup. Its Account Factory creates new accounts already wired into this setup.

Worked example. A bank needs three things: production isolated from developers, card-payment data under a stricter audit regime, and sandboxes limited to two approved Regions.
Step 1: create OUs named Security, Prod, NonProd, PCI and Sandbox.
Step 2: put the payment workload in its own account under the PCI OU, so the auditor's scope is just that account.
Step 3: attach an SCP to the Sandbox OU that denies actions outside the two Regions. Every sandbox account inherits it.
Step 4: use Control Tower so logs from all accounts land in the log archive account, which developers cannot modify.

Common mistake: running workloads in the management account. SCPs do not restrict the management account, so anything running there escapes your guardrails. A compromise there can reach the whole organization. Keep it nearly empty and use it only for billing and organization administration.

questions.prompt:
A university research institute has three needs. Student lab accounts must only use one approved Region, eu-west-1. Research teams need audit logs from every account kept centrally where researchers cannot change them. New accounts should arrive already wired into the setup. The cloud team's plan is below, with one step missing.
Step 1: Create OUs named Security, Research and StudentLabs.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Use AWS Control Tower so logs from all accounts land in the log archive account, which researchers cannot modify.
Step 4: Create new accounts through Control Tower's Account Factory so they are already wired into this setup.
Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Attach an SCP to the StudentLabs OU that denies actions outside eu-west-1, so every lab account in that OU inherits the limit.
Attach an SCP to the management account that denies actions outside eu-west-1, because the management account controls all member accounts.
Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies actions outside eu-west-1, so every account in the organization inherits the Region limit.
Attach an SCP to the StudentLabs OU that grants students permission to use eu-west-1, so they need no other permission policies.
questions.why: Policies inherit downward, so a deny SCP on the StudentLabs OU limits every lab account without affecting research accounts, while the root option is too broad, SCPs never restrict the management account, and SCPs never grant permissions.

questions.prompt: In AWS Organizations, which statement best describes what a service control policy (SCP) does?
choices: It sets the maximum permissions any identity in the attached accounts can use, without granting any permission itself.
It restricts the management account first, then passes those limits down to member accounts.
It only records which actions users took, so auditors can review them later.
It gives users in the attached accounts the permissions they need to do their work.
questions.why: An SCP is a guardrail that caps the most an identity can do in the accounts it covers; it never grants permission on its own, and it does not restrict the management account.

questions.prompt: A logistics company created OUs that mirror its departments: Finance, Marketing and Engineering. Each department has both production and test accounts. The company now wants stricter rules on all production accounts and looser rules on all test accounts. What is the better OU design?
choices: Keep the department OUs and attach the strict SCP directly to the management account so it covers production everywhere.
Regroup accounts into OUs by which ones need the same rules, such as a Prod OU and a NonProd OU, and attach SCPs there.
Move every account into one single OU so that one SCP can be maintained in one place.
Keep the department OUs and attach both the strict and loose SCPs to the root, letting each account pick one.
questions.why: Because policies inherit downward, OUs should group accounts that need the same rules, not follow the org chart, so Prod and NonProd OUs let each set of rules apply cleanly.

questions.prompt: A startup attached an SCP at the organization root that denies deleting its central log storage. Later, an engineer working in the management account, where the company also runs its data pipeline, deletes that storage successfully. Why did the SCP not stop this?
choices: Only AWS Control Tower controls can block deletion; SCPs can only detect drift after it happens.
SCPs do not restrict the management account, so workloads and users there escape the guardrail.
SCPs attached at the root only apply to OUs created after the policy was attached.
The SCP needed a second policy that granted the deny before it could take effect.
questions.why: The management account is not restricted by SCPs, which is why it should be kept nearly empty and used only for billing and organization administration, not for running workloads.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose OUs and accounts for a company with production, development, sandboxes and a regulated workload, and name one limit of SCPs or of the management account that affects the design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd give each workload and environment its own account, because an account is the strongest isolation boundary: separate permissions, separate blast radius and a separate line on the bill. Then I'd group the accounts into OUs by the rules they share. I'd have Security, Prod, NonProd, Sandbox, and a separate OU for the regulated workload so the auditor's scope stays small. SCPs attached to an OU flow down to every account inside it, which lets me do things like restrict sandboxes to approved Regions. Control Tower gives me that layout fast. It sets up a landing zone with a log archive account and an audit account, preset controls, and Account Factory for consistent new accounts. There are two limits to keep in mind. SCPs only cap permissions and never grant them. They also don't apply to the management account, so I keep that account free of workloads.
rubricPoints: Uses separate accounts as the isolation and billing boundary for workloads and environments.
Groups accounts into OUs by shared policy needs, not by org chart.
Explains that SCPs inherit downward and cap permissions without granting them.
Describes Control Tower's landing zone with log archive and audit accounts, controls and Account Factory.
Notes that the management account is not restricted by SCPs and should hold no workloads.
Ties a regulated workload to its own account or OU to narrow audit scope.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an account and OU layout is a design judgement best practised by reasoning through exam-style enterprise scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine builds an organization structure.

lessons.plain: Central logging means every account in a company sends its records of what happened (who logged in, which settings changed, what errors an application threw) to one protected place, instead of leaving them scattered across dozens of accounts. Multi-account event notifications means that when something important happens in any account, a message about it travels to one central spot where people or automation can react. Think of a hotel chain: each hotel keeps a front-desk logbook, but head office receives copies of every logbook in a locked archive, and gets an immediate phone call whenever an alarm goes off at any branch.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an attacker gains administrator rights in one AWS account, where would you rather the logs of their actions be stored: in that same account, or in a separate account they cannot reach? Why?
lessons.teach:
A central logging strategy collects logs from many accounts into one dedicated log archive account, a separate AWS account used only to store logs, with very few people allowed in. Logs are records of activity. AWS CloudTrail records API calls (actions taken against AWS). An organization trail is one CloudTrail setting, created from the management account of AWS Organizations (the service that groups accounts), that captures activity from every member account and writes it to an Amazon S3 bucket (object storage) in the archive account. Application logs live in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. A subscription filter streams matching log lines onward, typically through Amazon Data Firehose (a managed delivery stream) into that central bucket.

Why it works: the people who run a workload account cannot delete or alter copies held elsewhere. A bucket policy (a permission document on the bucket) that allows writes only from principals in your organization, S3 Object Lock (write-once storage that blocks deletion for a set period) and encryption with AWS KMS keys make the archive tamper-resistant.

For notifications, Amazon EventBridge is an event router. Each account has an event bus; a rule matches events and sends them to a target, which can be an event bus in another account. A central bus with a resource policy allowing your organization ID receives events from all accounts, then forwards them to Amazon SNS (a managed publish-and-subscribe notification service) or to an automated fix.

Worked example: a developer in account Dev deletes a security group. CloudTrail in Dev records the call; the organization trail writes it to the archive bucket. A rule on Dev's default bus matches the deletion event and sends it to the central bus in the operations account. The central rule routes it to an SNS topic, and the security team gets an email within seconds.

Common mistake: EventBridge rules are regional, so forwarding only in one Region silently misses events from others. The consequence is a blind spot exactly where an intruder chose to act. Deploy forwarding rules in every Region you use, often with CloudFormation StackSets.

questions.prompt:
A retailer runs AWS Organizations with an organization trail and a central event bus in its Security account. That bus's resource policy allows the retailer's organization ID. All its workloads run in one Region, eu-west-1, and forwarding rules are deployed there. An engineer in the Payments account changes an S3 bucket policy so the bucket becomes publicly readable. Trace the response.

Step 1: CloudTrail in Payments records the API call that changed the bucket policy.
Step 2: The organization trail writes that record to the S3 bucket in the log archive account.
Step 3: A rule on the Payments account's default event bus in eu-west-1 matches the bucket-policy-change event.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: A rule on the Security account's bus routes the event to an automated fix that restores the private policy, and also to an SNS topic that pages the on-call engineer.

What is Step 4?
choices: The Security account's event bus regularly polls the Payments bus and pulls in any new matching events.
The Payments rule sends the event to the central event bus in the Security account, which accepts it because its resource policy allows the organization ID.
The Payments rule publishes straight to an SNS topic in Payments, and that topic runs the automated fix.
The Payments rule writes the event into the log archive bucket, and the Security account reads it from there.
questions.why: A rule's target can be an event bus in another account, so the Payments rule pushes the event to the central bus, whose resource policy allows the organization, and the central rule then routes it onward.

questions.prompt: An auditor requires that administrators of a company's workload accounts must not be able to delete or alter the API activity logs from their own accounts. Which design best meets this requirement?
choices: Use an organization trail that writes to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account. Protect the bucket with a policy allowing writes only from the organization, with S3 Object Lock, and with AWS KMS encryption.
Send every account's CloudTrail events to a central EventBridge bus, and treat the bus as the long-term record.
Turn on CloudTrail in each workload account and store its logs in a bucket inside that same account, encrypted with a KMS key.
Keep the logs in CloudWatch Logs in each workload account and limit access with IAM so that only senior administrators can read them.
questions.why: Copies held in a separate, tightly restricted archive account, protected by write-once Object Lock, an organization-only bucket policy and encryption, are out of reach of the people who run the workload accounts.

questions.prompt: A media company's applications write their logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs in 40 member accounts. The company wants only the lines containing "ERROR" copied into the central S3 bucket in its log archive account. What is the usual way to do this?
choices: Attach a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter that matches "ERROR" and streams those lines through Amazon Data Firehose into the central bucket.
Create an organization trail, because it captures application log lines from every member account.
Add a rule on each account's EventBridge default bus that matches "ERROR" text and targets the S3 bucket.
Turn on S3 Object Lock on the central bucket so that it pulls matching lines from each account.
questions.why: A subscription filter streams matching CloudWatch Logs lines onward, typically through Firehose, a managed delivery stream, into the central bucket; CloudTrail only records API calls.

questions.prompt: A bank uses us-east-1 and ap-southeast-2. Its EventBridge rules that forward security events to a central bus exist only in us-east-1. An attacker deletes a network firewall rule in ap-southeast-2. The organization trail still captures the call, but no alert ever fires. What explains the gap, and what fixes it?
choices: The organization trail captures only us-east-1 activity, so the fix is to create a second trail for ap-southeast-2.
SNS cannot send email for events that come from Asia Pacific Regions, so the fix is to create a separate SNS topic for each Region.
The central bus's resource policy blocks events that come from other Regions, so the fix is to add the Region name to the policy.
EventBridge rules are regional, so the fix is to deploy the forwarding rules in every Region the bank uses, for example with CloudFormation StackSets.
questions.why: Each Region has its own event buses and rules, so with forwarding set up only in us-east-1, events in ap-southeast-2 never reach the central bus; deploying the rules in every Region used closes that blind spot.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would centralize logs and event notifications for 50 AWS accounts, and name one tradeoff or limit of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd create a dedicated log archive account that almost nobody can log into. An organization trail from the management account sends CloudTrail activity from all 50 accounts to an S3 bucket there, and CloudWatch Logs subscription filters stream application logs through Firehose to the same place. The bucket policy only accepts writes from our organization, Object Lock prevents deletion for the retention period, and KMS encrypts everything, so even an admin in a workload account can't erase evidence. For notifications, each account's EventBridge rules forward important events to a central event bus in an operations account, whose resource policy trusts our organization ID; central rules then publish to SNS or trigger automation. The limit: EventBridge rules are per Region, so I have to deploy forwarding everywhere with StackSets, and central storage and streaming add cost that grows with log volume.
rubricPoints: Logs go to a separate, tightly restricted log archive account rather than staying in each workload account.
An organization trail captures CloudTrail activity from all member accounts in one setting.
The archive is protected with an organization-scoped bucket policy, Object Lock and encryption.
Events are forwarded from each account's EventBridge bus to a central bus that permits the organization, then routed to SNS or automation.
Names a limit such as EventBridge rules being regional or cost growing with log volume.

suggested.rationale: This is a design objective best learned by reasoning through exam-style multi-account scenarios and choosing where logs and events should flow, which no current mission or planned engine fully exercises.

lessons.plain: A multi-account governance model is the rulebook for a company that runs many separate cloud accounts. Each account is like a separate apartment in one building: tenants can arrange their own rooms, but the building owner sets rules nobody can break, such as no open flames, and installs smoke detectors that report problems. In AWS, the owner groups accounts into folders, sets hard limits that apply to every account in a folder, and adds automatic checks that flag rule breaking. The goal is to let teams move quickly inside their own accounts while the company keeps security, compliance and cost under control from one central place.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a developer has full administrator rights inside their own account, but the company has a central rule saying no one may create resources outside Europe. If the developer tries to launch a server in the United States, which do you think wins, their admin rights or the central rule, and why?
lessons.teach:
A multi-account governance model is the set of central controls that decides what every account in an organization may do, who manages those controls, and how violations are detected. In AWS it is built from a few parts. AWS Organizations is the service that links many accounts under one management account, which is the single payer and owner account. Accounts are grouped into organizational units (OUs), folders such as Security, Production and Sandbox, so one rule can cover a whole group. Service control policies (SCPs) are permission ceilings attached to the organization root, an OU or an account. They never grant anything; they only cap what identity policies, the permission documents attached to users and roles inside the account, are allowed to grant. AWS Control Tower adds ready-made guardrails: preventive ones, usually SCPs that block an action, and detective ones, usually AWS Config rules, which are automated checks that report noncompliant resources after the fact.

This works because an action succeeds only if every layer allows it: effective permission is the overlap of the SCP and the identity policy. Worked example: the Production OU has an SCP denying all actions outside eu-west-1 and eu-central-1. A developer in a production account holds AdministratorAccess. Step one, they request a server in us-east-1. Step two, the identity policy allows it. Step three, the SCP inherited from the OU denies it. Step four, an explicit deny always wins, so the request fails.

Good models also keep the management account nearly empty and hand day-to-day tools to delegated administrator accounts, member accounts trusted to run a security or audit service for everyone.

A common mistake is assuming SCPs protect the management account; they do not apply to it, so workloads placed there escape every guardrail. Another is writing an overly broad deny: in a running system, an SCP that blocks a needed action, such as a global service that only lives in us-east-1, can instantly break deployments across every account in the OU.

questions.prompt: A retail company called Northwind Outlets has an Analytics OU. Its SCP is an allow-list that permits only Amazon S3, Amazon Athena and AWS Glue actions. An analyst in an analytics account uses a role whose identity policy grants Athena actions only. The analyst tries to download a file directly from an S3 bucket. Step one: check the SCP, which allows S3 actions. Step two: check the identity policy, which grants no S3 actions. Step three is missing. What is step three?
choices: The request succeeds, because the SCP explicitly allows S3 and that permission is passed down to every role in the account.
The request fails, because an allow-list SCP automatically denies every action that a role's identity policy has not already granted.
The request fails, because effective permission is the overlap of both layers, and an SCP never grants anything on its own.
The request succeeds, because Athena already has access to S3, so the analyst inherits that access through the Athena grant.
questions.why: An action works only if both the SCP and the identity policy allow it, and an SCP only sets a ceiling, so S3 permitted by the SCP but not granted by the identity policy is still refused.

questions.prompt: A bank's security team wants to know, within hours, whenever any account in its organization creates a storage bucket that is open to the public. They do not want to block the action itself, only to have it reported. Which kind of control fits this requirement?
choices: A delegated administrator account that holds the payer role for the whole organization.
A detective guardrail, such as an AWS Config rule that checks resources and reports noncompliant ones after they exist.
A preventive guardrail, such as an SCP that blocks the bucket from being made public in the first place.
An identity policy attached to each user that grants permission to read bucket settings.
questions.why: Detective guardrails, usually AWS Config rules, find and report noncompliant resources after the fact, which matches a requirement to report rather than block.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm attaches an SCP to its organization root that denies turning off audit logging. Its finance team then runs a billing-reporting application directly in the management account. An engineer with full admin rights in the management account turns off audit logging there. What happens, and why?
choices: It fails, because an SCP attached to the root applies to every account, including the management account.
It succeeds only if a delegated administrator account approves the change first.
It fails, because full admin rights in the management account are themselves capped by the identity policy of the root.
It succeeds, because SCPs do not apply to the management account, so workloads there escape every guardrail.
questions.why: SCPs never apply to the management account, which is why good models keep it nearly empty and run workloads in member accounts.

questions.prompt: A media company attaches an SCP to its Workloads OU, which holds 40 accounts, denying every action outside the ap-southeast-2 Region. The next morning, deployments in all 40 accounts start failing at a step that calls a global service that only runs in us-east-1. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The SCP's deny is too broad: it also blocks a needed global service in us-east-1, and because it is inherited from the OU it breaks every account at once.
An AWS Config rule detected noncompliant resources and automatically deleted the deployment pipelines.
The SCP removed the AdministratorAccess grant from each role, so the roles now have no permissions in any Region.
The identity policies in the 40 accounts expired overnight and must be reissued.
questions.why: An overly broad deny that catches a needed action, such as a global service living only in us-east-1, instantly breaks deployments in every account under that OU.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how SCPs, OUs and detective guardrails work together to govern many accounts, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on SCPs.
lessons.modelAnswer: We group accounts into organizational units by purpose, like Production, Sandbox and Security, and attach service control policies to those OUs. An SCP is a ceiling, not a grant: a person still needs an IAM policy allowing an action, and the action only works if the SCP also allows it. An explicit deny in either place wins. That gives us preventive control, things like blocking unapproved regions or stopping anyone from turning off logging. Because preventive rules cannot catch everything, we add detective guardrails such as Config rules that flag misconfigured resources after they exist. One limit is that SCPs do not apply to the management account, so we keep workloads out of it and delegate security tooling to member accounts. The tradeoff is blast radius: a badly scoped deny on an OU can break every workload in it at once, so we test SCPs on a sandbox OU first.
rubricPoints: Accounts are grouped into OUs so controls apply to whole groups.
SCPs set maximum permissions and never grant access on their own.
Effective permission is the overlap of SCP and identity policy, and explicit deny wins.
Preventive guardrails block actions while detective guardrails report violations afterward.
SCPs do not restrict the management account, so it should hold no workloads and admin duties should be delegated.
A broad deny can break many workloads at once, so SCPs need careful testing.

suggested.rationale: Tracing how an organization-level ceiling and an account-level policy combine to allow or deny a request is exactly what an authorization policy evaluator would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: Sharing resources across environments means letting several separate accounts use one thing that a single account owns and pays for, instead of each account building its own copy. Think of an apartment building: the landlord owns the plumbing and hallways, and tenants use them every day, but tenants cannot rip out pipes. In AWS, a company with many accounts (dev, test, prod, each team) often keeps networks, connection hubs and similar shared plumbing in one central account. It then lends access to the others. Each account stays separate for billing and safety, while the expensive or tightly controlled parts are built once and governed in one place.
lessons.guessPrompt: A central networking team owns a network and lets an application team's separate account launch servers into one of its subnets. Should the application team be able to change that subnet's routing rules? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) is the managed sharing service. It lets one account, the owner, offer specific resources to other accounts, called participants, without copying them. A share names the resources, which are things like subnets, transit gateways (a central hub that connects many virtual networks) and DNS forwarding rules. It also names the principals who receive them: individual account IDs, an organizational unit (OU, a folder of accounts in AWS Organizations), or the whole organization. If you turn on sharing with your organization, accounts inside it receive shares automatically. An account outside the organization must accept an invitation first.

This works because ownership and use are separated. The owner keeps control of how the resource is configured and pays for the resource itself. Participants pay for what they run on it.

Worked example: a networking account owns a VPC (virtual private cloud, a private virtual network). First, it creates a RAM share containing two private subnets. Second, it names the Workloads OU as the principal. Third, the dev and prod accounts in that OU now see those subnets. Fourth, the dev account launches servers and databases into them. Those servers belong to and are billed to dev. Fifth, dev cannot edit the subnet, its route tables or its network ACLs (subnet-level traffic filters). Dev can still manage its own security groups (per-resource firewalls). The result is one network design, one set of IP ranges and central inspection, with many tenants.

Not everything goes through RAM. Some resources are shared through their own permissions instead. Machine images and disk snapshots carry launch or copy permissions. Encryption keys, storage buckets and queues use resource-based policies, which are rules attached to the resource saying who may use it.

A common mistake is assuming that sharing hands over control or makes a copy. A participant cannot fix a broken route, and deleting the share cuts off access. If the owner removes a shared subnet while participants' resources still live in it, those workloads lose their network path. Removal and changes need coordination.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Retail keeps a central connectivity account that owns a transit gateway (a hub that links many virtual networks). Larkspur has just bought a smaller company whose AWS account is not yet part of Larkspur's organization in AWS Organizations. The goal is for the acquired account to connect its own VPC (virtual private cloud, a private virtual network) to the hub without building a second hub. Step 1: the connectivity account creates an AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) share containing the transit gateway. Step 2: it names the acquired company's account ID as the principal (the receiver of the share). Step 3: ??? Step 4: the acquired account attaches its VPC to the shared transit gateway, and that attachment is billed to the acquired account. Step 5: the acquired account still cannot change the hub's own configuration, which stays with the connectivity account. What is Step 3?
choices: The acquired account writes a resource-based policy on the transit gateway granting itself access
The connectivity account copies the transit gateway into the acquired account so it has its own editable version
Nothing is needed, because every account named in a RAM share receives it automatically
The acquired account accepts the RAM invitation, because it sits outside the organization
questions.why: Automatic receipt only applies to accounts inside an organization that has turned on organization sharing, so an outside account must accept the invitation before it can use the shared resource.

questions.prompt: At Halden Insurance, a central network account uses AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM, the managed sharing service) to share three private subnets with the claims-analytics account. The analytics team launches a large database server into one of those subnets. Which account owns and pays for that database server?
choices: The network account, because it owns the subnet the server runs in
The claims-analytics account, because it launched the server
Neither account until the share is accepted by the whole organization
Both accounts, split evenly, because the subnet is shared between them
questions.why: Sharing separates ownership from use: the owner keeps and pays for the shared resource itself, while each participant (the receiving account) owns and pays for what it runs on it.

questions.prompt: A media company wants its security account to let a separate rendering account use one specific encryption key. Based on how AWS sharing works, which mechanism fits this resource?
choices: Attach a resource-based policy to the key that names the rendering account
Grant launch permission on the key, as is done with machine images
Copy the key into the rendering account so it holds its own version
Add the key to a RAM share and name the rendering account as principal
questions.why: Encryption keys are not shared through RAM; they use a resource-based policy, which is a rule attached to the resource itself saying who may use it.

questions.prompt: Orvik Logistics shares subnets from a networking account to its billing-service account using AWS Resource Access Manager. One morning the billing team finds that a route in their shared subnet's route table points to the wrong place, and their servers cannot reach an internal service. What can the billing-service account do?
choices: Ask the networking account to fix the route, while it can still adjust its own security groups (per-resource firewalls)
Change the subnet's network ACLs (subnet-level traffic filters) to bypass the bad route
Edit the shared subnet's route table directly, since its servers live in that subnet
Delete the share and recreate the subnet in its own account to regain control
questions.why: A participant cannot edit a shared subnet, its route tables or its network ACLs because the owner keeps configuration control, but the participant can still manage its own security groups.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how one central networking account can let many workload accounts use the same network, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of doing it that way.
lessons.modelAnswer: We keep the VPC in a networking account and use AWS Resource Access Manager to share specific subnets with the workload accounts, usually by targeting an OU so new accounts get access automatically. Nothing is copied. The workload accounts launch their own servers into those subnets, and those servers belong to and are billed to them. The networking account still owns the subnets, route tables and network ACLs, so routing and inspection stay consistent and IP ranges don't overlap. The tradeoff is that teams lose autonomy. A participant can't change routes or ACLs, only its own security groups, so every network change goes through the central team. We are also coupled to the owner: if the share is removed or the subnet is changed carelessly, workloads in several accounts break at once. Some things, like images, snapshots, keys and buckets, are shared through their own permissions or resource policies rather than RAM.
rubricPoints: Names AWS RAM (or a managed sharing service) as the way an owner account shares resources with participant accounts without copying them.
Distinguishes owner control (subnet, route tables, ACLs) from participant use (own instances, own security groups).
Mentions sharing to accounts, an OU or the whole organization, with invitations needed outside the organization.
States a limit: participants cannot change shared configuration, so changes are centralized and outages can spread to many accounts.
Notes that some resources are shared through their own permissions or resource-based policies instead of RAM.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing who owns and who uses a shared resource in a multi-account scenario, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations rather than by any existing mission.

lessons.plain: Four AWS tools help you see and control what the cloud costs. Think of household money. The Pricing Calculator is planning a renovation on paper before spending anything. Cost Explorer is your bank statement with charts, showing where the money already went. Budgets is the alert your bank texts you when spending nears a limit you chose. Trusted Advisor is a home inspector who walks through and points out waste, like lights left on in empty rooms. Each one answers a different question: what will it cost, what did it cost, warn me when, and where am I wasting money.
lessons.guessPrompt: You want to be warned before one team's monthly cloud bill passes a limit. Do you need a tool that estimates a design that is not built yet, a tool that charts past spending, or a tool that compares spending to a limit you set and alerts you?
lessons.teach:
AWS Pricing Calculator is a free web tool that estimates the monthly cost of an architecture before you build it. You describe the planned resources, such as server size, hours of use and storage, and it returns an estimate. It needs no running resources and shows nothing about real bills.

AWS Cost Explorer shows actual past spend and usage as charts and tables. You can filter and group by service, by member account in AWS Organizations (the service that groups many accounts under one management account), or by cost allocation tag (a label on resources that billing can group costs by). It also forecasts future spend from past trends and suggests purchase commitments such as Savings Plans.

AWS Budgets lets you set a threshold for cost, usage, or commitment coverage, and sends an alert when actual or forecasted spend crosses it. Budget actions can also automatically apply a restrictive policy or stop chosen instances.

AWS Trusted Advisor runs automated checks against best practices, including cost checks that flag idle load balancers or underused servers, plus security, resilience, performance and service-limit checks. How many checks you get depends on your AWS support plan.

Worked example. A company plans a migration and uses the Pricing Calculator: about $40,000 a month. After go-live, finance sets a $45,000 monthly budget with an alert at 80% of forecast. On day 12 the alert fires. An engineer opens Cost Explorer, groups by account and then by service, and finds a data-transfer spike in the development account. Trusted Advisor then lists three idle load balancers and several barely used instances in that account, which the team removes.

Common mistake: treating Budgets as a hard spending cap. Billing data arrives with a delay of hours, and by default a budget only alerts. A running system can still overspend between alerts unless you configure budget actions or other guardrails. Each tool answers one question, so a full cost-visibility design uses all four together.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a separate testing account in AWS Organizations. Its engineers sometimes forget to shut down large rendering servers, and the bill jumps. The company wants spend in that account to be held back automatically, not just reported. Step 1: In AWS Cost Explorer, the cloud lead filters by the testing account and sees normal spend of about $7,000 a month. Step 2: She creates an AWS Budgets cost budget of $9,000 a month for that account, with a threshold based on forecasted spend. Step 3: ??? Step 4: She tells the team that billing data arrives hours late, so some overspend can still slip through before the automatic response runs. What is Step 3?
choices: Attach a budget action that applies a restrictive policy or stops the chosen rendering instances when the threshold is crossed.
Enter the $9,000 limit into AWS Pricing Calculator so the testing account cannot be billed beyond that figure.
Turn on AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks so that Trusted Advisor stops any underused rendering servers it flags.
Rely on the Cost Explorer forecast, which blocks new resources once forecast spend passes the budget amount.
questions.why: A budget alerts by default and only takes automatic action, such as applying a restrictive policy or stopping instances, when you configure a budget action. Trusted Advisor only flags waste, the Pricing Calculator only estimates, and Cost Explorer only reports and forecasts.

questions.prompt: A hospital group is designing a new patient-records platform that will not be built for six months. The board wants a monthly cost figure for the proposed server sizes, hours of use and storage before approving the project. Which tool fits this request?
choices: AWS Cost Explorer, because it forecasts future spend from the platform's past usage trends.
AWS Trusted Advisor, because its cost checks calculate the price of a proposed design.
AWS Budgets, because it sets a threshold that defines how much the new platform will cost.
AWS Pricing Calculator, because it estimates the monthly cost of planned resources without needing anything running.
questions.why: Only the Pricing Calculator estimates cost from a description of planned resources. Cost Explorer needs past usage to forecast, and this platform has none yet.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's monthly spend is steady and has no surprise spikes, but the CFO suspects it is paying for resources nobody uses. She wants an automated best-practice review that names specific idle load balancers and barely used servers. Which tool gives this?
choices: AWS Budgets, by sending an alert when usage of a load balancer drops below a threshold.
AWS Cost Explorer, by grouping last month's spend by cost allocation tag.
AWS Trusted Advisor, whose cost checks flag idle and underused resources.
AWS Pricing Calculator, by comparing the planned architecture with the current one.
questions.why: Trusted Advisor runs automated best-practice checks, and its cost checks flag specific idle load balancers and underused servers. How many checks you get depends on your support plan.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's bill last month was $18,000 higher than usual. An analyst opens AWS Pricing Calculator to find out which account and service caused the rise, but cannot find the answer. Why, and what should the analyst use instead?
choices: The Pricing Calculator only estimates planned resources and shows nothing about real bills, so the analyst should group actual spend by account and service in AWS Cost Explorer.
The Pricing Calculator shows past spend only after a budget alert fires, so the analyst should first create a budget in AWS Budgets.
The Pricing Calculator only shows spend for the management account, so the analyst should open AWS Budgets for each member account.
The Pricing Calculator needs cost allocation tags to show past spend, so the analyst should add tags and then rerun the estimate.
questions.why: The Pricing Calculator works only from a description of planned resources and never reads actual billing data. Cost Explorer shows real past spend and can group it by member account and by service.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which of the four tools you would use before a project starts, during monthly operations, and when investigating a cost spike, and name one limit of relying on Budgets alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before building, I use the Pricing Calculator to estimate what the planned design should cost. It works on assumptions only, so it never reflects real usage. Once workloads run, I set up Budgets per account or team with alerts on actual and forecasted spend, so someone hears about overspending before the invoice arrives. When an alert fires, I go to Cost Explorer, which shows real historical spend that I can group by account, service, or cost allocation tag to find what grew. Trusted Advisor runs alongside as an ongoing check that flags waste such as idle load balancers or underused instances. The limit of Budgets alone is that billing data lags by hours and, by default, a budget only alerts. It does not stop spending unless I configure budget actions, and it tells me that I overspent, not why.
rubricPoints: Pricing Calculator estimates planned designs before anything runs.
Cost Explorer analyzes actual historical spend, grouped by account, service, or tag, and can forecast.
Budgets alerts on thresholds for actual or forecasted spend and can trigger actions.
Trusted Advisor runs best-practice checks that flag waste such as idle or underused resources.
Budgets is not a real-time hard cap because data lags and it alerts by default.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is choosing the right tool for a stated cost question, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios like the spike investigation above.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers sell the same computer time at different prices depending on what you promise in return. If you pay as you go, you pay full price and can stop any time. If you promise to keep spending for one or three years, you get a large discount. If you are willing to use spare capacity that can be taken back at short notice, you get the deepest discount of all. Think of a gym: a day pass costs the most, a yearly membership costs less per visit, and standby slots are cheap but you may get bumped.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs 20 servers around the clock every day, adds 40 more during business hours, and runs a nightly batch job that can safely restart if interrupted. Which of those three kinds of work would you lock into a long-term discount, and which would you run on cheap capacity that might be taken away?
lessons.teach:
On-Demand is the baseline: you pay a per-second or per-hour rate with no commitment. Every other option trades flexibility for a lower price.

Reserved Instances (RIs) are a one- or three-year commitment to a specific instance type in a Region. Standard RIs give the bigger discount; Convertible RIs let you exchange for other instance types at a smaller discount. A zonal RI, tied to one Availability Zone (an isolated data center group), also reserves capacity there; a regional RI does not reserve capacity but applies across zones. You can pay all upfront, partly upfront, or nothing upfront; more upfront means a bigger discount.

Savings Plans are a commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour for one or three years. Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, Regions, and container and function services; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are locked to one instance family in one Region for a deeper discount. Savings Plans never reserve capacity; pair them with On-Demand Capacity Reservations if you must guarantee it.

Spot Instances use the provider's spare capacity at up to roughly 90 percent off, but can be reclaimed with about two minutes' warning. They suit stateless, restartable, or fault-tolerant work.

With AWS Organizations consolidated billing, unused RI and Savings Plan discounts can be shared across accounts, which is why many enterprises buy commitments centrally.

Worked example: the guess scenario. Step 1, the 20 always-on servers are steady, so cover them with a Compute Savings Plan sized to that baseline. Step 2, the 40 daytime servers run about a third of the day, so a commitment would sit idle overnight; leave them On-Demand, or mix in Spot if the tier is stateless. Step 3, the restartable batch job goes on Spot, spread across several instance types to reduce interruption risk.

Common mistake: committing to peak usage. You then pay for unused commitment every hour of the term. A related trap is assuming a Savings Plan guarantees capacity during a zone shortage; it does not. None of these options change how fast an instance runs; they change price and, for Spot, availability.

questions.prompt:
A media company in one Region runs three kinds of compute. It is choosing a purchasing option for each. Purchasing option means how it pays: On-Demand with no commitment, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, or Spot. Spot is spare capacity sold at a deep discount that can be reclaimed with about two minutes' warning.

Step 1: 12 database servers run around the clock. They will stay in the same instance family and the same Region for three years. The company covers them with an EC2 Instance Savings Plan sized to those 12 servers. That plan is an hourly spend commitment locked to one instance family in one Region, and it gives a deeper discount than a Compute Savings Plan.

Step 2: 50 video-rendering workers process frames from a queue. If a worker stops, its frame is simply re-queued and rendered again. [missing step]

Step 3: A reporting tier runs about 4 hours each weekday. A commitment would sit idle most of the week, so it stays On-Demand.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Run the workers on Spot and spread them across several instance types, because restartable work tolerates reclaims.
Run the workers on Spot using one identical instance type, so every worker behaves the same and is easier to manage.
Cover the workers with a Compute Savings Plan, because the plan guarantees capacity if spare capacity runs short.
Buy a Standard Reserved Instance for all 50 workers, so the rendering tier gets the biggest discount available.
questions.why: The rendering work is restartable, so it suits Spot's deep discount, and spreading it across several instance types reduces the risk of many workers being reclaimed at once.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a steady workload that must keep running for three years. They want a discount, and they also need capacity reserved in one specific Availability Zone (an isolated data center group within a Region). Which single purchasing option meets both needs on its own?
choices: A regional Reserved Instance, because it applies its discount across every zone in the Region.
A Compute Savings Plan, because it is the most flexible commitment across families and Regions.
Spot Instances, because they offer the largest discount of any purchasing option.
A zonal Reserved Instance, because it is tied to one zone and reserves capacity there.
questions.why: Only a zonal Reserved Instance both discounts the usage and reserves capacity in its zone. Regional RIs and Savings Plans do not reserve capacity, and Spot can be reclaimed.

questions.prompt: A retailer has 15 AWS accounts. One account bought a Savings Plan but is using only part of it. Meanwhile, another account runs similar servers at full On-Demand price. What lets the unused discount apply to the second account?
choices: Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations, which shares unused commitment discounts across accounts
Moving the second account's servers to Spot so that they match the plan
Converting the Savings Plan into a Convertible Reserved Instance in the second account
Buying On-Demand Capacity Reservations in the second account to receive the discount
questions.why: With consolidated billing in AWS Organizations, unused Reserved Instance and Savings Plan discounts can be shared across the organization's accounts. This is why enterprises often buy commitments centrally.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company normally runs 60 servers. It reaches 200 only during a two-week holiday rush each year. It buys a three-year Savings Plan sized to cover all 200 servers. What is the main consequence for the running system and the bill?
choices: It pays for unused commitment every hour of the three years, because most of the year usage sits far below 200.
It is protected from capacity shortages during the rush, because the plan holds 200 servers' worth of capacity.
It pays nothing extra, because unused Savings Plan commitment is refunded at the end of each month.
Its servers run faster during the rush, because committed capacity gets better performance than On-Demand.
questions.why: Committing to peak usage means paying for the full commitment every hour, even when usage is lower. A Savings Plan neither reserves capacity nor changes how fast an instance runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose among Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Spot, and On-Demand for a mixed workload, and name at least one tradeoff or limit of each discounted option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by splitting usage into a steady baseline, predictable peaks, and interruptible work. The baseline gets a commitment: a Compute Savings Plan if we want flexibility to change instance families, Regions, or move to containers, or an EC2 Instance Savings Plan or Standard RI for a deeper discount if the instance family will not change. The tradeoff is lock-in for one or three years, and if we size it to peak we pay for idle commitment. Savings Plans and regional RIs do not reserve capacity, so if a workload must be guaranteed space in a zone I add a zonal RI or a Capacity Reservation. Peaks stay On-Demand because they would waste a commitment. Restartable or stateless work goes on Spot for the biggest discount, accepting a two-minute interruption notice, so I never put a stateful database there. Buying centrally under consolidated billing lets unused discounts flow to other accounts.
rubricPoints: Separates steady baseline, variable peaks, and interruptible work before choosing.
Explains that RIs and Savings Plans trade a one- or three-year commitment for a discount, and over-committing wastes money.
Distinguishes Compute Savings Plans' flexibility from the deeper but narrower EC2 Instance Savings Plans or Standard RIs.
States that Savings Plans and regional RIs do not reserve capacity, while zonal RIs or Capacity Reservations do.
Describes Spot as cheapest but interruptible with short notice, suited only to fault-tolerant work.
Notes that consolidated billing shares commitment discounts across accounts.

suggested.rationale: Sizing commitments against a usage curve and seeing the cost of over-committing or interruptions is best learned by building and adjusting a cost model.

lessons.plain: Rightsizing means matching what you pay for to what you actually use, like trading a half-empty delivery truck for a van. In a large organization with hundreds of accounts, nobody can check every server or storage bucket by hand, so you need tools that watch usage and point out waste. AWS Compute Optimizer studies how hard your servers and functions really work and suggests bigger or smaller sizes. Amazon S3 Storage Lens gives one dashboard of how much object storage you hold, where it sits, and which habits waste money. Both only show you the problem. People still decide and make the change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual server has used less than 10% of its CPU for the last two weeks. Before you shrink it to a smaller size, what else would you want to know about it?
lessons.teach:
AWS Compute Optimizer is a recommendation service. It reads utilization metrics, meaning measured usage of CPU, network and disk, from Amazon CloudWatch, the AWS metrics service. It does this for virtual servers (EC2 instances), Auto Scaling groups, block storage volumes (EBS), serverless functions (Lambda) and some container and database resources. It labels each resource Over-provisioned (too big), Under-provisioned (too small) or Optimized, and it estimates a performance risk for each suggested size. It looks back 14 days by default. A paid option called enhanced infrastructure metrics extends this to about three months, which catches monthly peaks. You turn it on from the organization's management account or a delegated administrator account, an account the organization trusts to manage the service. It then covers every member account.

Amazon S3 Storage Lens does the same job for object storage. It gathers metrics across all buckets and accounts, such as bytes per storage class, old object versions and incomplete multipart uploads (abandoned upload fragments that still cost money). The free tier keeps 14 days of data. Paid advanced metrics add activity data, prefix-level detail and 15 months of history. It can also export a daily report to a bucket so other tools can analyze it.

Worked example. An m5.2xlarge instance averages 8% CPU and peaks at 20% over 14 days. Compute Optimizer marks it Over-provisioned and suggests m5.large with low risk. You check memory first. Memory is not measured unless the CloudWatch agent, a small program that reports from inside the server, is installed. The agent shows memory at 85%. Downsizing would starve the application, so you pick a size with less CPU but enough memory.

The common mistake is to act on recommendations blindly. Without memory data, or with a lookback window too short to include a month-end batch job, a resize can cause an outage. Neither tool changes anything on its own. Savings appear only when teams resize resources or add lifecycle rules, which move or delete storage automatically.

questions.prompt:
A logistics firm runs a c5.4xlarge invoicing server. Over the default 14-day window it averages 12% CPU, and Compute Optimizer marks it Over-provisioned, suggesting c5.xlarge with low risk. The finance lead mentions that the big invoice run happens only on the 1st of each month, and the last 14 days did not include the 1st.

Step 1: Confirm the CloudWatch agent is installed so memory is measured. Memory peaks at 40%, so memory is not the limit.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: With the longer data, the recommendation now shows CPU jumping to 70% on the 1st of each month, so the team chooses c5.2xlarge instead of c5.xlarge.
Step 4: The team resizes the instance during a quiet period.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Turn on Compute Optimizer's paid enhanced infrastructure metrics so the lookback extends to about three months and includes the month-end runs.
Reinstall the CloudWatch agent so Compute Optimizer begins measuring CPU, which it cannot see without the agent.
Wait for Compute Optimizer to resize the instance to c5.xlarge automatically, then watch the next month-end run for problems.
Turn on S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics so the server's history extends to 15 months.
questions.why: Enhanced infrastructure metrics stretch Compute Optimizer's lookback from 14 days to about three months, so it can see the monthly peak that the short window missed.

questions.prompt: A media company has 300 AWS accounts with thousands of S3 buckets (object storage). Finance suspects it is paying for abandoned upload fragments left behind by failed large-file uploads. Which approach finds them across all accounts and then actually reduces the cost?
choices: Use S3 Storage Lens to find incomplete multipart uploads across buckets and accounts, then have teams add lifecycle rules to clean them up.
Use Compute Optimizer's block storage (EBS) recommendations to find the fragments, then resize the volumes.
Install the CloudWatch agent on each bucket so it reports upload fragments to CloudWatch.
Turn on S3 Storage Lens, which deletes incomplete multipart uploads by itself once it finds them.
questions.why: Storage Lens reports incomplete multipart uploads across buckets and accounts, but it changes nothing by itself, so savings come only when teams add lifecycle rules that remove the fragments.

questions.prompt: A central cost team at a bank wants Compute Optimizer recommendations for all 80 member accounts in its AWS organization. It does not want to sign in to each account separately. How should it set this up?
choices: Install the CloudWatch agent in every member account, because Compute Optimizer only works where the agent runs.
Enable Compute Optimizer separately inside each of the 80 member accounts, since it cannot span accounts.
Enable S3 Storage Lens organization-wide and read the compute recommendations from its daily export report.
Enable Compute Optimizer from the organization's management account or a delegated administrator account so it covers every member account.
questions.why: Turning Compute Optimizer on from the management account or a trusted delegated administrator account extends it to all member accounts in the organization.

questions.prompt: A compliance auditor asks a healthcare company to show how its S3 storage-class mix has changed over the past year, broken down by prefix (the folder-like part of an object's name), directly in S3 Storage Lens. Which option meets this?
choices: Compute Optimizer with enhanced infrastructure metrics, which keeps about three months of storage history.
The CloudWatch agent installed on the buckets, which reports prefix-level history to Storage Lens.
The S3 Storage Lens free tier, which keeps 15 months of bucket and prefix history at no charge.
S3 Storage Lens paid advanced metrics, which add prefix-level detail and keep 15 months of history.
questions.why: Only Storage Lens advanced metrics provide prefix-level detail and 15 months of history; the free tier keeps just 14 days.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Compute Optimizer and S3 Storage Lens give rightsizing visibility across many accounts, and name one limit that could make a recommendation wrong.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are visibility tools, not fixers. Compute Optimizer reads CloudWatch usage for servers, Auto Scaling groups, volumes and functions. It labels each one over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimized and suggests a size with a risk rating. S3 Storage Lens summarizes object storage across all buckets. It shows bytes per storage class, old versions and incomplete multipart uploads, so we can see where lifecycle rules would save money. We enable both through the management account or a delegated admin, so one view covers every account in the organization. The catch is the input data. Compute Optimizer cannot see memory unless the CloudWatch agent reports it. Its default 14-day window can also miss monthly peaks unless we pay for the longer lookback. So a memory-heavy server can look oversized. We confirm each recommendation, then a person resizes the resource or writes the lifecycle rule.
rubricPoints: Compute Optimizer uses measured utilization to label resources over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimized and suggest sizes.
S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide storage usage metrics such as storage class mix, old versions and incomplete uploads.
Both can cover all accounts through the management account or a delegated administrator.
Missing memory metrics or a short lookback window can produce a wrong recommendation.
The tools only recommend, so people must make the change to save money.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present an enterprise scenario and ask which visibility tool fits and what its blind spots are, so reasoning through a situation teaches more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A tagging strategy is an agreed set of labels you attach to every cloud resource, such as a server, a database or a storage bucket, so the monthly bill can be sorted by who owns what. Each label is a tag: a name and a value, like CostCenter = Retail. Think of colored stickers on office equipment. If every department puts its own sticker on its printers and laptops, finance can count each department's share. If people skip stickers or invent their own colors, the count falls apart. The strategy is the rulebook that keeps the stickers consistent.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a team starts labeling its servers with its department name today, do you think last month's bill will suddenly show that department's costs? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A tag is a key-value label on a resource, for example CostCenter=Retail. A cost allocation tag is a tag key that you switch on in the billing settings of the AWS Organizations management account, the account that pays for all member accounts. Only activated keys appear as columns in billing reports and in Cost Explorer, the console tool that charts spending. AWS also offers some AWS-generated tags, such as who created a resource, but business-unit mapping comes from user-defined tags you design.

It works because billing records carry each resource's tags, so spend can be grouped by tag value. Accounts give the coarsest split, one account per business unit or workload. Tags give finer splits inside an account. Cost Categories are rules that combine accounts and tags into business-friendly groups.

Consistency needs enforcement. A tag policy, a type of AWS Organizations policy, standardizes allowed keys, capitalization and values. A service control policy (SCP), an organization-wide guardrail on what actions accounts may take, can deny creating a resource when a required tag is missing from the request.

Worked example: a company has Retail, Logistics and Finance units. It chooses the keys CostCenter, Owner and Environment. Step one, a tag policy allows only the three CostCenter values with exact capitalization. Step two, an SCP refuses to launch servers without CostCenter. Step three, the management account activates CostCenter as a cost allocation tag. Step four, after the data catches up, Cost Explorer grouped by CostCenter shows three bars plus a bucket for untagged spend.

The common mistake is expecting tags to rewrite history. Tag data appears in billing only from activation onward, so last month stays unattributed. Inconsistent spelling such as costcenter versus CostCenter also splits one unit into two lines. Some costs, like shared networking or support fees, cannot be tagged at all and need an agreed split rule. In a running organization, a large untagged bucket means chargeback reports are disputed and nobody owns the waste.

questions.prompt: A university cloud team must show spending for three departments: Physics, Biology and Library. Here is their plan, traced step by step. Step 1: each department gets its own AWS account, which gives the coarsest split. Step 2: a shared research account holds jointly used resources, and each one there is tagged with the key Dept and a value such as Dept=Biology. Step 3: a tag policy allows only the three Dept values, with exact capitalization. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: a few weeks later, Cost Explorer grouped by Dept shows one bar per department plus a bucket for untagged spend. Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Attach a service control policy that denies creating resources without a Dept tag, which makes Dept appear in billing reports
Re-run last semester's billing reports so the new Dept tags are applied to past spending
Turn on Dept as a cost allocation tag in the billing settings of each department's member account
In the billing settings of the AWS Organizations management account, turn on Dept as a cost allocation tag
questions.why: Only tag keys that are turned on as cost allocation tags in the management account, the account that pays for all member accounts, appear as columns in billing reports and Cost Explorer.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm switched on the tag key Team as a cost allocation tag (a tag key enabled for billing reports) on 12 May. On 20 June, finance asks for April spending grouped by Team. All the relevant resources were already carrying Team tags in April. What will they find?
choices: April spending is fully grouped by Team, because the resources already had the tags in April
April spending is grouped by Team only after the tag policy is reapplied to April's resources
April spending stays unattributed, because tag data appears in billing only from the date the key was switched on
April spending is grouped by Team only for accounts that a service control policy covered
questions.why: Activating a cost allocation tag does not rewrite history, so spending from before 12 May stays unattributed to Team.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's Cost Explorer report, grouped by the tag key Unit, shows separate lines for Claims, claims and CLAIMS. All three really belong to one business unit. Which control best prevents this split from happening again?
choices: A service control policy that denies all actions in accounts belonging to the Claims unit
Moving the Claims resources into the AWS Organizations management account
Switching on a second cost allocation tag key named unit in lowercase
A tag policy, an AWS Organizations policy that standardizes allowed tag keys, values and capitalization
questions.why: Different spellings are treated as different tag values, and a tag policy enforces one allowed spelling and capitalization.

questions.prompt: A retail group has tagged every taggable resource by business unit. Yet a monthly support fee and the cost of a shared network connection used by every unit still land in the untagged bucket. What is the right way to handle these costs?
choices: Tag the support fee directly with each business unit's value
Agree on a split rule, for example by share of usage, and group the costs with Cost Categories, which are rules that combine accounts and tags into business-friendly groups
Write a service control policy that blocks the support fee until it has a tag
Leave them in the untagged bucket, since untagged spend has no effect on chargeback reports
questions.why: Some costs, such as support fees and shared networking, cannot be tagged at all, so they need an agreed split rule rather than tags.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure every business unit's cloud costs show up correctly on the bill, and name at least one limit of relying on tags.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with account structure, giving each business unit its own accounts, because that split is automatic and cannot be forgotten. Inside accounts I would require a small set of tag keys, such as CostCenter, Owner and Environment. A tag policy in AWS Organizations fixes the exact spelling and allowed values, and an SCP denies creating resources that arrive without CostCenter. Then the management account activates CostCenter as a cost allocation tag so it shows up in Cost Explorer, and Cost Categories can roll accounts and tags into the groups finance recognizes. The limits: tags only count from activation forward, so old spend stays unattributed. Some charges, like shared networking or support, cannot carry tags and need an agreed split rule. Enforcement also adds friction for teams, and anything created before the rules existed must be retagged.
rubricPoints: Defines a tag as a key-value label and a cost allocation tag as one activated in the management account for billing.
Uses accounts as the coarse cost boundary and tags for finer attribution.
Enforces consistency with tag policies and blocks untagged creation with an SCP.
States that tag data is not retroactive and only appears from activation onward.
Notes that some shared costs cannot be tagged and need a split rule.

suggested.rationale: Attributing a fictional bill to business units, then seeing how untagged and misspelled resources distort the result, teaches the strategy better than reading about it.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means writing down your cloud setup (networks, servers, databases, permissions) in a text file that a tool reads and builds for you, instead of clicking it together by hand. AWS CloudFormation is Amazon's tool for this. Think of it like an architect's blueprint handed to a builder: the same blueprint produces the same building every time, in any city. Change management means the blueprint is edited carefully. You preview what an edit will knock down or rebuild before anyone touches the real building, and you lock the rooms that must never be demolished by accident.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you edit a blueprint file that describes a live production database and apply it, what could go wrong that would not go wrong when editing a description of a stateless web server, and how would you want to find out before it happens?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing infrastructure in text files that a tool builds, rather than creating it by hand. AWS CloudFormation is AWS's IaC service. You write a template, which is a JSON or YAML file declaring the resources you want and their settings. CloudFormation turns a template into a stack, which is the live group of resources it creates and tracks as one unit. The template is declarative: it states the end result, not the steps. So CloudFormation works out the build order. If any resource fails during a create or update, it rolls the stack back to its last working state.

Change management is controlling how a running stack changes. A change set is a preview. You submit an edited template, and CloudFormation lists every resource it would add, modify or delete. For each modification it also says whether replacement is needed, meaning the old resource is destroyed and a new one is built.

Three safeguards help. A stack policy is a JSON rule attached to a stack that blocks chosen update actions on chosen resources. A DeletionPolicy is a resource setting that decides what happens when the resource leaves the stack: Delete, Retain (keep it), or Snapshot (take a final backup first). Drift detection compares the live resources with the template and reports anything changed outside CloudFormation. Separately, StackSets deploy one template across many accounts and Regions.

Worked example: a team renames the database identifier in its template. First, they create a change set instead of updating directly. Second, the change set shows the database as Modify with Replacement True. Third, they realise that replacement means a new, empty database. Fourth, they revert the rename. As a guard, they add a stack policy that denies replacing the database and set its DeletionPolicy to Snapshot.

A common mistake is fixing production by hand in the console. The template no longer matches reality, so drift appears. The next update may then overwrite the manual fix or fail. In a running system, that means outages caused by the very tool meant to make change safe.

questions.prompt: During a late-night incident at a ticketing company, an on-call engineer opened the console and raised the idle timeout on a production load balancer from 60 to 300 seconds. That load balancer is managed by a CloudFormation stack, the live group of resources CloudFormation builds from a template and tracks as one unit. The fix worked. The next morning the team cleans up. Step 1: they run drift detection, which compares live resources with the template, and it reports that the load balancer's idle timeout differs from the template. Step 2: ??? Step 3: before applying anything, they create a change set, a preview of what an update would add, modify or delete, and confirm it lists no change to the load balancer. Step 4: they apply the update. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Delete the stack and recreate it from the original template so the live resources and the template start fresh together.
Edit the template to set the idle timeout to 300 seconds, so the template once again matches what is actually running.
Add a DeletionPolicy of Retain to the load balancer so the manual timeout value is kept during the next update.
Leave the template alone, because once drift has been detected CloudFormation keeps the manually changed value on future updates.
questions.why: The safe way to keep a manual fix is to write it into the template, so the template matches reality again and the next update does not reset the timeout to 60 or fail.

questions.prompt: A media company's CloudFormation template includes a block storage volume with its DeletionPolicy set to Snapshot. A DeletionPolicy is the resource setting that decides what happens when the resource leaves the stack. An engineer removes the volume from the template and updates the stack. What happens to the volume?
choices: A final backup of it is taken, and then the volume is deleted.
The update is blocked until someone removes the DeletionPolicy from the template.
It is deleted immediately with no backup, because Snapshot only applies when the whole stack is deleted.
It is kept running exactly as it is, and CloudFormation simply stops tracking it.
questions.why: Snapshot means CloudFormation takes a final backup first and then removes the resource, unlike Retain, which keeps it.

questions.prompt: A bank runs 40 AWS accounts across 3 Regions. Its security team has written one CloudFormation template that sets up a standard audit-logging configuration, and it needs that same configuration deployed in every account and Region. Which CloudFormation feature fits this need?
choices: A stack policy attached to one stack in the main account.
