StackSets, which deploy one template across many accounts and Regions.
A change set created once and reused in every Region.
Drift detection run against each of the 40 accounts.
questions.why: StackSets exist to roll out a single template to many accounts and Regions, while stack policies, drift detection and change sets each work on an individual stack.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm updates a CloudFormation stack to add four new resources: two message queues, a function and a database table. The two queues are created successfully, but creating the function fails because of a bad setting. What does CloudFormation do with the stack?
choices: It retries the function repeatedly until it succeeds, without touching the queues.
It rolls the stack back to its last working state, removing the two new queues so the stack is as it was before the update.
It keeps the two new queues, skips the function, and goes on to create the database table.
It stops where it is and leaves the two queues in place until an engineer finishes the update by hand.
questions.why: When any resource fails during a create or update, CloudFormation rolls the whole stack back to its last working state rather than leaving a half-finished change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CloudFormation templates, stacks and change sets work together to make infrastructure changes safe, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We describe our infrastructure in a template, a YAML or JSON file. CloudFormation builds it as a stack, which it tracks as one unit and rolls back if something fails partway. Because the template is the source of truth, we can rebuild the same environment in another account or Region, and with StackSets we can push it to many accounts at once. To change production, we never apply an edit blind. We create a change set first and read it, especially the replacement column, because replacing a database means a new, empty one. For resources that must survive, we add a stack policy that blocks replacement and a DeletionPolicy of Retain or Snapshot. The tradeoff is discipline. If anyone changes things by hand, the stack drifts from the template, and the next update can undo their fix or fail. So drift detection and a no-console-edits rule are part of the deal. Changes also become slower than a quick click.
rubricPoints: A template declares resources and CloudFormation creates and tracks them as a stack.
Failed creates or updates roll back to the last working state.
A change set previews additions, modifications and deletions, including whether a resource will be replaced.
Stack policies and DeletionPolicy (Retain or Snapshot) protect critical stateful resources.
Manual changes cause drift, which drift detection reveals, and a later update can overwrite or conflict with them.
Names a tradeoff, such as slower changes or needing team discipline to keep the template as the only path to change.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs CloudFormation stacks, and the exam tests this through scenarios about choosing change sets, stack policies, DeletionPolicy, drift detection or StackSets, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Continuous integration and delivery, usually shortened to CI/CD, is an automated assembly line for software changes. Every time an engineer saves a change to the shared code, a machine builds it, runs the tests, and packages the result. Delivery then carries that same package through test environments toward production, stopping wherever a person or a check must approve it. Think of a car factory: every car goes down the same line with the same inspections, instead of each mechanic building cars in their own garage. In a solution design, CI/CD decides how safely and how often the system can change.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team builds the application once for the test environment and then builds it again from the same code for production. Why might a bug appear in production that never showed up in testing?
lessons.teach:
Continuous integration (CI) means every change merged into the shared code repository is automatically built and tested, so problems surface within minutes. Continuous delivery (CD) means the tested output, called an artifact (a packaged, versioned build such as a zip file or container image), is automatically moved toward production, usually with a human approval before the final step. Continuous deployment removes that approval entirely. A pipeline is the ordered chain of stages that does this work.

On AWS, CodePipeline is the managed orchestrator that runs the stages. CodeBuild is a managed build service that compiles code and runs tests on temporary machines, so you never patch a build server. CodeDeploy is a managed deployment service that pushes an artifact onto servers, containers, or functions. Artifacts sit between stages in an S3 bucket (object storage).

Why it works: building once and promoting the identical artifact means what you tested is exactly what ships. Small, frequent changes are easier to find faults in and to undo.

Worked example for a multi-account organization. First, a developer merges a change; the source stage in a central tooling account detects it. Second, CodeBuild compiles, runs unit tests, and writes artifact version 42 to S3, encrypted with a KMS customer managed key (an encryption key whose access policy you write). Third, the deploy stage assumes an IAM role (a set of permissions that can be borrowed temporarily) in the test account and deploys version 42. Fourth, integration tests pass and a manual approval stage waits for a release manager. Fifth, the pipeline assumes a role in the production account and deploys the same version 42.

A common mistake is encrypting artifacts with the default AWS managed key, whose policy cannot be edited to let other accounts read it, so cross-account deploys fail. The related mistake is rebuilding per environment, which lets untested differences reach production. In a running system, a well-designed pipeline turns releases into routine, auditable events instead of risky nights.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its release pipeline in a shared-services account and deploys to separate staging and production accounts. Its policy says no change may reach production without a human sign-off, and production must run exactly what was tested. Trace the release of a fix. Step 1: an engineer merges the fix, and the pipeline's source stage in the shared-services account picks it up. Step 2: CodeBuild (a managed build service) compiles the code, runs unit tests and writes artifact build 318 (a packaged, versioned output) to an S3 bucket (object storage), encrypted with a KMS customer managed key whose policy lets the staging and production deployment roles read it. Step 3: the pipeline assumes an IAM role (temporarily borrowed permissions) in the staging account and deploys build 318, and the end-to-end tests pass. Step 4: an approval stage waits, and the on-call lead approves. Step 5: ______. Which choice correctly fills Step 5?
choices: The pipeline assumes a role in the production account and deploys build 318 again, now re-encrypted with the default AWS managed key so production can read it.
The pipeline runs CodeBuild again against the same source commit inside the production account, producing build 319, and deploys build 319 there.
The pipeline skips any further stage, because the approval in Step 4 already counts as the production deployment.
The pipeline assumes a role in the production account and deploys the identical build 318 from the S3 artifact store.
questions.why: Promoting the same tested build 318 through an assumed production role, with the customer managed key already allowing access, ships exactly what was tested and meets the sign-off policy.

questions.prompt: An online grocery company wants every change that passes all automated tests to go live in production immediately, with no person approving any release. Which practice describes this goal?
choices: Continuous delivery, because artifacts move toward production with a final manual approval
A manual release process, because production changes still need a release window
Continuous integration, because each merged change is automatically built and tested
Continuous deployment, because tested changes reach production with no human approval step
questions.why: Continuous deployment is continuous delivery with the human approval removed, so every passing change goes straight to production.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's pipeline lives in a tooling account. Builds succeed and artifacts land in S3, but every deploy into the firm's analytics account fails with an access-denied error when the deploy role tries to read the artifact. The artifacts are encrypted with the default AWS managed key for S3. What is the most appropriate fix?
choices: Give the deploy role in the analytics account full administrator permissions in that account
Encrypt artifacts with a KMS customer managed key whose policy grants the analytics account's deploy role access
Rebuild the artifact inside the analytics account so it never needs to be read across accounts
Turn off encryption on the artifact bucket so any account can read the artifacts
questions.why: The AWS managed key's policy cannot be edited to admit other accounts, while a customer managed key's policy can be written to let the target account's role decrypt the artifact.

questions.prompt: An insurance team's pipeline compiles the application separately for staging and again for production from the same branch. A defect appears in production that never showed up in staging. What is the most likely design cause, and the correct change?
choices: Rebuilding per environment let untested differences reach production; build once and promote the identical versioned artifact
Staging lacked enough unit tests; keep the per-environment builds but add more tests to the staging build
The approval stage was too slow; remove it so releases happen faster and defects are found sooner
The build machines were not patched; move compilation to a long-lived build server the team maintains
questions.why: Building once and promoting the same artifact guarantees production runs exactly what was tested, while separate builds can differ in ways staging never checked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why our design builds the artifact once in a central tooling account and promotes it across test and production accounts, and name one tradeoff or limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: CI means every merged change is built and tested automatically; CD means the resulting artifact is moved toward production, usually pausing for an approval. We run CodePipeline in a central tooling account: CodeBuild creates one versioned artifact and stores it in S3 encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. The pipeline then assumes narrowly scoped IAM roles in the test and production accounts and deploys that same artifact, so production runs exactly what we tested, and workload accounts never hold build tooling. The tradeoff is setup complexity: the KMS key policy, bucket policy, and cross-account roles must all grant the right access, and the tooling account becomes a high-value target, so it needs tight access control. A manual approval also adds a delay that we accept in exchange for a human check before production.
rubricPoints: Defines CI as automatic build and test on every merged change and CD as automated promotion of the artifact toward production.
States that one artifact is built once and promoted unchanged so tested code equals shipped code.
Explains cross-account deployment through assumed IAM roles from a central tooling account.
Notes the artifact store needs a customer managed KMS key whose policy allows the other accounts.
Names a real tradeoff such as setup complexity, approval delay, or the tooling account as a sensitive target.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing and justifying a multi-account pipeline design under constraints, which is best practised by reasoning through a scenario alongside the hands-on pipeline repair in devops-01-broken-pipeline.

lessons.plain: AWS Systems Manager is a managed service for configuring and running a fleet of servers from one place, without logging into each machine. You describe the setup a server should have, choose which servers it applies to, and the service pushes it out and keeps checking that it is still true. It also stores shared settings centrally, so programs read them instead of hard-coding them. Think of a building manager with a master checklist who walks every floor on a schedule and resets any thermostat someone fiddled with. It works for cloud servers and for machines in your own data center.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run 300 servers that should all have the same logging setup, but people keep changing it by hand on a few of them. What would you want a tool to do automatically so the fleet stays consistent?
lessons.teach:
AWS Systems Manager is a managed service for configuring and operating managed nodes. A managed node is any server it controls: an EC2 instance, an on-premises machine, or a virtual machine elsewhere. Each node runs the SSM Agent, a small program that calls out to the service over HTTPS, so no inbound port is opened. The agent needs an IAM role granting it permission to talk to the service, plus network reach to the service endpoint. On EC2 that role is attached as an instance profile. Instructions are written as SSM documents, which are JSON or YAML files listing steps.

Run Command executes a document once across many nodes, usually chosen by tag. State Manager creates an association, which binds a document to target nodes on a schedule. Because the association re-applies the desired setup repeatedly and reports compliance, it corrects drift. Drift is a server slowly diverging from its intended configuration. Parameter Store holds configuration values, including encrypted SecureString values, in paths like /app/prod/db-host, so settings are read at runtime rather than baked in. Automation runs multi-step runbooks. Inventory records what software each node has. Session Manager gives an audited shell without SSH keys or a bastion host.

Worked example: 300 web servers must keep a log agent configured. First, tag them Role=web. Second, store the agent config in Parameter Store at /web/prod/logconfig. Third, create a State Manager association that installs the agent and reads that parameter, targeting Role=web every 30 minutes. Fourth, someone removes the agent by hand on one server. At the next run it is reinstalled, and compliance shows non-compliant, then compliant. Fifth, a newly auto-scaled server carrying the tag is picked up automatically.

Common mistake: assuming an installed agent means a managed node. Without the IAM role, or without a route to the endpoints, the node never registers. That route can be the internet, a NAT gateway, or VPC interface endpoints in a private subnet. Associations then skip that node silently, and its drift stays uncorrected.

questions.prompt:
A payroll company runs 80 report servers on EC2 in a private subnet. The subnet has no internet route and no NAT gateway. The servers must keep a time-sync setting that admins sometimes change by mistake. The team's plan is below, with one step missing.
Step 1: Attach an instance profile to every server. An instance profile is how an IAM role is given to an EC2 instance, and this role lets the SSM Agent talk to Systems Manager.
Step 2: (missing)
Step 3: Tag the servers Team=reports and store the setting in Parameter Store at /reports/prod/timesync.
Step 4: Create a State Manager association that applies the setting to Team=reports every 60 minutes, so any drift is corrected and reported as compliance.
Which step 2 is needed for the servers to become managed nodes?
choices: Open inbound port 443 on the servers' security group so Systems Manager can connect to each agent
Put SSH keys on each server and add a bastion host so Systems Manager can log in to apply settings
Replace the association with a single Run Command execution, because associations need internet access
Create VPC interface endpoints for Systems Manager in the private subnet so the agent can reach the service
questions.why: The agent makes outbound calls to the service endpoint, so a private subnet with no internet or NAT route needs VPC interface endpoints before the nodes can register.

questions.prompt: At a logistics firm, a host firewall rule must stay enabled on 200 servers tagged Tier=app. Administrators keep switching it off during troubleshooting and forget to switch it back on. The team wants the rule put back automatically and wants a report of which servers drifted. Which Systems Manager feature fits best?
choices: Inventory, recording the software installed on each server
Session Manager, so administrators use an audited shell instead of SSH
Run Command, executing a document once across all Tier=app servers
A State Manager association that applies the rule to Tier=app on a schedule
questions.why: A State Manager association reapplies the desired configuration on a schedule and reports compliance, which corrects drift. A one-time Run Command does not.

questions.prompt: An engineer installs the SSM Agent on an on-premises virtual machine that has internet access. The machine is tagged correctly. A State Manager association targeting that tag has run many times, but the machine's settings are never applied and no error appears for it. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The machine has no IAM role permission to talk to Systems Manager, so it never registered as a managed node
Systems Manager can only manage EC2 instances, so on-premises machines are always ignored
The association must target machines by name rather than by tag to include on-premises machines
An inbound port must be opened on the machine before the agent can receive instructions
questions.why: An installed agent alone does not make a managed node. Without IAM permission the machine never registers, and associations skip it silently.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company builds its server images with the database password written into a config file. It wants to change the password without rebuilding images, and it wants the value stored encrypted. Which approach fits Systems Manager's intended use?
choices: Put the password in the SSM document's steps so the association applies it
Store it as a SecureString in Parameter Store, for example at /tickets/prod/db-password, and have the app read it at runtime
Use Run Command once to write the password into every image
Use Inventory to record the password on each node and read it back from there
questions.why: Parameter Store holds configuration values, including encrypted SecureString values, so the app reads them at runtime instead of having them baked into images.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how Systems Manager keeps a large fleet configured consistently, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every server runs the SSM Agent, which reaches out to Systems Manager using an IAM role, so we never open inbound ports. We write the desired setup as an SSM document. A State Manager association applies that document to every server with a given tag, on a schedule. Because it keeps re-applying the document, it fixes drift when someone changes a box by hand, and it shows us compliance. Settings live in Parameter Store under paths like /app/prod, so we change them once instead of rebuilding servers. New tagged servers are picked up automatically. The limit is that this only works for nodes that actually register. A server without the role, or without a route to the endpoints, is silently skipped. Private subnets therefore need NAT or VPC interface endpoints. Also, scheduled correction is not instant, so drift can exist between runs.
rubricPoints: States that the SSM Agent plus an IAM role makes a server a managed node, using outbound calls only.
Explains that State Manager associations re-apply a document on a schedule to correct drift and report compliance.
Mentions targeting by tags so new servers are covered automatically.
Describes Parameter Store as central, runtime-read configuration.
Names a limit, such as missing role or endpoint access leaving nodes unmanaged, or the gap between scheduled runs.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises Systems Manager directly, so the most value comes from reasoning through exam-style fleet scenarios: choosing between Run Command, State Manager and Parameter Store, and spotting missing roles or endpoints.

lessons.plain: A deployment strategy is the plan for swapping an old version of software for a new one while people are still using it. A rollback mechanism is the plan for getting the old version back quickly if the new one misbehaves. Think of replacing a bridge. You can close it and rebuild it all at once. You can rebuild one lane at a time. You can build a second bridge beside it and switch traffic over. Or you can let a few cars cross first and watch. Each choice trades speed, cost, and risk differently. A good architect picks the plan, and the tools that carry it out, to match how much downtime and risk the business can accept.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run a payment service that must never be fully down, and you can afford to briefly run twice as many servers. If a new release might be broken, would you rather update servers one at a time, or start a complete second copy and switch users over? Why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment strategy decides how traffic moves from the old version to the new one. A rollback mechanism decides how traffic moves back. All-at-once replaces everything together: cheapest and fastest, but it causes an outage and rollback means redeploying. Rolling updates a few servers per batch, so capacity dips and two versions serve users simultaneously. Immutable launches brand-new servers and discards the old only after the new pass health checks. Blue/green runs a full new environment (green) beside the current one (blue) and switches traffic over; rollback is switching back. Canary sends a small slice, say 10 percent, to the new version first; linear raises the share in equal steps over time.

On AWS, AWS CodeDeploy (a managed deployment orchestrator) runs in-place or blue/green deployments to EC2 servers, and canary or linear shifts for AWS Lambda (serverless functions) and Amazon ECS (managed containers). It can roll back automatically when an Amazon CloudWatch alarm (a metric threshold watcher) fires. Lambda aliases (named pointers to a version) can split traffic by weight. An Application Load Balancer can weight two target groups. AWS Elastic Beanstalk (a managed application platform) offers rolling, immutable, and blue/green environment swaps.

Worked example: a Lambda checkout function, requirement "limit blast radius, recover in minutes." Choose CodeDeploy with a canary of 10 percent for five minutes. Step one: the alias sends 10 percent to version 8, 90 percent to version 7. Step two: an error-rate alarm crosses its threshold. Step three: CodeDeploy points the alias fully back to version 7. Only a tenth of users saw errors, for minutes.

Common mistake: assuming blue/green makes rollback free. If the new version changed the database schema in a way the old code cannot read, switching back breaks blue too. Make schema changes backward compatible. Also, DNS-based switching via Amazon Route 53 weighted records is slowed by cached DNS answers, so clients keep reaching the old side for a while; load balancer weighting switches faster.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company ships a new container image to an Amazon ECS service (managed containers). It uses AWS CodeDeploy (a managed deployment orchestrator) with a linear shift of 25 percent every 4 minutes. An Amazon CloudWatch alarm (a metric threshold watcher) is attached to request latency. Step 1: 25 percent of traffic goes to the new version and 75 percent stays on the old one. Step 2: after 4 minutes, the split becomes 50/50. Step 3: the latency alarm crosses its threshold. Step 4: ______. Result: at most half of requests were affected, for under ten minutes. What belongs in Step 4?
choices: CodeDeploy automatically sends all traffic back to the old version, because the alarm fired
An engineer changes a Route 53 weighted DNS record so new clients reach the old version
CodeDeploy keeps moving to 75 percent, because a linear shift always finishes its scheduled steps
CodeDeploy holds the split at 50/50 and waits for an engineer to redeploy the old image by hand
questions.why: CodeDeploy can roll back automatically when a CloudWatch alarm fires, moving all traffic back to the old version within minutes, which matches the stated result.

questions.prompt: A small analytics firm runs its web app on AWS Elastic Beanstalk (a managed application platform). For its next release it wants the existing servers left untouched. New servers should be launched, and the old ones removed only after the new ones pass health checks. Which deployment policy matches this?
choices: Rolling
Immutable
All-at-once
Canary
questions.why: Immutable launches brand-new servers and discards the old ones only after the new ones pass health checks, so existing servers are never modified.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore runs a blue/green deployment. The green version renames a database column, and the old blue code still expects the old name. Green starts failing, so the team switches traffic back to blue, but blue fails too. What practice would have kept the switch back safe?
choices: Switch traffic with Route 53 weighted records instead of a load balancer
Use a canary of 5 percent instead of blue/green so fewer users see the change
Make the schema change backward compatible so the old code can still read the data
Run the switch back during a low-traffic window so fewer users notice
questions.why: Blue/green rollback only works if blue can still read the data, so schema changes must stay backward compatible with the old code.

questions.prompt: A logistics company shifts traffic between two EC2 server fleets using Amazon Route 53 weighted DNS records. After a bad release, it sets the new fleet's weight to zero, yet many clients keep reaching the new fleet for some time. What explains this, and what would switch traffic faster?
choices: Route 53 drains connections in batches like a rolling update; shrink the batch size
The new fleet is still passing health checks; fail its health checks on purpose so DNS drops it
Clients are using cached DNS answers; weighting two target groups on an Application Load Balancer switches faster
The weighted records need a CloudWatch alarm attached before they take effect; add one to each record
questions.why: DNS-based switching is slowed by cached DNS answers, while an Application Load Balancer weighting two target groups changes where traffic goes almost at once.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments for a new service on AWS, which services would carry each out, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you prefer.
lessons.modelAnswer: I match the strategy to downtime tolerance, budget, and blast radius. Rolling updates servers in batches; it is cheap but reduces capacity and runs mixed versions, and rollback means redeploying the old version. Blue/green stands up a full second environment and flips traffic, so rollback is just flipping back, but you pay for double capacity during the switch. Canary sends a small share first and widens it only if metrics stay healthy, which limits how many users a bad release hurts. CodeDeploy handles blue/green for EC2 and canary or linear shifts for Lambda and ECS, and it can roll back automatically on a CloudWatch alarm; Beanstalk offers rolling and immutable options. I prefer canary with alarm-driven rollback, but its limit is that rollback only restores code: if the release made a database change old code cannot handle, switching back fails, so schema changes must stay backward compatible.
rubricPoints: Defines at least rolling, blue/green, and canary and how traffic moves in each.
Links strategies to AWS services such as CodeDeploy, Lambda aliases, load balancer weighting, or Elastic Beanstalk.
Describes an automated rollback trigger such as a CloudWatch alarm.
Names a tradeoff such as double cost, reduced capacity, or mixed versions.
Notes that data or schema changes can make rollback unsafe, or that DNS caching slows switching.

suggested.rationale: Shifting traffic between versions and watching a rollback fire under different strategies is the core skill, which the planned deployment-strategies engine would let the learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: An upgrade path is a planned route for moving an application from what it runs on today to something newer, such as a newer database version, a new cloud service, or a new feature of a service you already use. Cloud providers release new things constantly and retire old ones on a schedule. Choosing a path means deciding whether a change is worth adopting, when to adopt it, and how to move over safely with a way back. It is like moving house. You check that the new place fits your needs and lease dates, move one room at a time, and keep the old keys until you are settled.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database version reaches its end-of-support date in six months, and a newer major version is available. Would you upgrade the live database directly in one step, or first build a copy on the new version and test it? What could go wrong with the first option?
lessons.teach:
Determining an upgrade path means deciding whether, when, and how to move a workload onto a new service, feature, or version. On AWS this happens all the time. Managed databases such as Amazon RDS (a managed relational database service) publish end-of-support dates for engine versions. AWS Lambda (a run-your-code-without-servers service) retires old language runtimes. New offerings, such as Graviton (AWS's own processor family for virtual machines), can lower cost.

A sound decision checks six things. First, does the change meet a real requirement? Second, is it available in every Region (geographic area) you use? Third, does it work with your infrastructure-as-code templates and pipelines? Fourth, is it eligible under your compliance rules? Fifth, what is its support lifecycle, meaning how long the version will be maintained? Sixth, can you reverse it? This works because it turns a vague "should we use the new thing?" into checks you can verify, and it puts reversibility before commitment.

Worked example. A team runs PostgreSQL on RDS, and its major version reaches end of standard support in six months. Step 1: read the release notes for incompatible changes, such as removed functions or extensions. Step 2: restore a snapshot (a point-in-time copy) onto the new version and run the application's tests against it. Step 3: use RDS Blue/Green Deployments. This feature builds a staging copy on the new version and keeps it in sync with production through replication (continuous copying of changes). Step 4: switch over in a low-traffic window, with only a short interruption. Step 5: keep the old environment briefly as a fallback, then retire it.

A common mistake is to ignore deprecation notices until the provider acts. A version can then be upgraded automatically during a maintenance window, without testing. Some services instead charge extra fees for extended support. Another mistake is the opposite: adopting a brand-new feature across every account at once, before checking Region coverage and quotas. In a running system, either mistake turns a planned, reversible change into unplanned downtime or surprise cost.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs 40 virtual machines for its route-planning service in two AWS Regions. One Region opened only recently. The firm wants to move these machines to Graviton, AWS's own processor family, to cut its compute bill. Here is the plan so far. (a) Requirement: finance has asked for a 20% cut in compute cost, so the change serves a real goal. (b) [MISSING STEP] (c) Pipelines: the team confirms that its infrastructure-as-code templates accept the new instance type as a parameter. (d) Compliance: the security team confirms that the new processor family is allowed under the firm's rules. (e) Lifecycle: the instance family is current and will be maintained for years. (f) Reversibility: the old launch configuration is kept, so the fleet can be switched back. Which step best fills (b)?
choices: Move all 40 machines in both Regions at once, so the savings start immediately and the rollout is done in one pass.
Skip any separate check, because step (f) already means any problem can be undone after the move.
Confirm that the new instance type is offered in both Regions, including the newer one, and that the account quotas allow 40 of them.
Wait for AWS to move the machines automatically during a maintenance window, which avoids planning the change by hand.
questions.why: Checking that the change is available in every Region you use, and that quotas allow it, is the check missing from the plan. Leaving it out is exactly the mistake of adopting a new offering before confirming Region coverage and quotas.

questions.prompt: An architect is reviewing a proposed engine-version upgrade for a managed database. She asks about its 'support lifecycle.' What is she asking?
choices: How long the provider will keep maintaining that version before it reaches end of support.
Whether the version is permitted under the company's compliance and audit rules.
Whether the change can be undone quickly if problems appear after the switch.
Whether the new version is offered in every geographic Region the company uses.
questions.why: Support lifecycle means how long a version will be maintained. Region coverage, reversibility and compliance are separate checks in the same decision.

questions.prompt: An insurance company runs its claims system on a managed relational database. Months ago it received a notice that its engine version would reach end of standard support. Nobody acted on it. What is the most likely result once that date passes?
choices: Nothing changes, because a managed service keeps every older version running indefinitely at no cost.
The provider rolls the database back to an earlier version that is still supported.
The database may be upgraded automatically in a maintenance window without testing, or the company may pay extra extended-support fees.
The database is deleted on the end-of-support date unless a support ticket is opened.
questions.why: Ignoring deprecation notices can lead to an untested automatic upgrade or to extra extended-support charges. Either way, a planned and reversible change becomes unplanned downtime or surprise cost.

questions.prompt: A retailer upgrades the managed PostgreSQL database behind its loyalty app. It uses a blue/green approach: a staging copy runs on the new version and stays in sync with production through replication, and traffic is switched over at 3 a.m. What should the team do with the old environment right after the switchover?
choices: Delete it at once, because replication has already copied all the data to the new version.
Upgrade it in place to the same new version, so both environments match.
Keep it for a short period as a fallback in case problems appear, then retire it.
Keep it running permanently alongside the new one as a second production database.
questions.why: Keeping the old environment briefly keeps the change reversible until the new version is proven. Retiring it afterwards avoids paying for two environments with no end date.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide on an upgrade path for a database engine nearing end of support. Name one tradeoff between upgrading early and waiting.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the requirement and the deadline. The engine's support ends on a known date, so doing nothing is not really an option. If we wait, we risk a forced upgrade or extra support fees. I would check the release notes for breaking changes and confirm the new version is available in our Regions. I would also confirm that our templates, pipelines, and compliance rules accept it. Then I would restore a snapshot on the new version and run our tests. For the cutover, I would use a blue/green approach: a synced copy on the new version, a switchover in a quiet window, and the old copy kept briefly as a fallback. The tradeoff is timing. Upgrading early gives us time to fix surprises, but we take on newer, less proven software. Waiting lets others find the bugs first, but it shrinks our margin before the deadline.
rubricPoints: Ties the upgrade decision to a requirement and a support-lifecycle deadline.
Checks Region availability, tooling compatibility, and compliance before committing.
Tests on a copy before touching production.
Uses a reversible cutover with a fallback, such as blue/green.
Names a timing tradeoff: early adoption risk versus a shrinking deadline, forced upgrades, or extra fees.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an upgrade path is a judgment call that weighs deadlines, compatibility, and reversibility, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the skill better than any single existing mission.

lessons.plain: A managed service is one where the cloud provider runs the machinery for you. You ask for a database, a queue or a container platform, and the provider handles buying hardware, installing software, applying security fixes and replacing broken parts. Your team keeps responsibility for its data, its settings and who is allowed in. Think of renting a furnished, serviced apartment instead of buying a house: you still choose who gets a key and what you store there, but someone else fixes the boiler at 3 a.m. The trade is less control over exactly how and when things happen, in exchange for far less routine work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team runs its own database on a rented virtual server and spends two days a month applying security updates and checking backups. If you switched to a database the cloud provider runs for you, which of those chores would you guess disappear, and which do you suspect you would still own?
lessons.teach:
Adopting managed services means choosing services where the provider operates the undifferentiated layers: hardware, operating system, engine installation, patching, and failure replacement. Provisioning means creating and sizing the resources a workload needs. Patching means applying vendor fixes to the operating system and software. Both are toil, meaning repetitive work that adds no business value. AWS describes the split of duties as the shared responsibility model: the further up the managed scale you go, the more of the stack AWS owns.

The scale runs roughly like this. Self-managed on Amazon EC2 (rented virtual servers): you patch everything. Amazon RDS (a managed relational database): AWS patches the operating system and database engine inside a maintenance window you choose, takes automated backups and can fail over to a standby. Serverless options such as AWS Lambda (run code with no servers to see), Amazon DynamoDB (a managed key-value database) or AWS Fargate (run containers without managing hosts): no instances exist for you to patch at all.

Worked example. A requirement says: small ops team, PostgreSQL app, must stay patched for compliance, 99.9 percent availability. Step one, list the toil: OS updates, engine minor versions, backups, failover. Step two, map each item to a service: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ (a standby copy in a second data center) covers backups and failover, and automatic minor version upgrades cover the engine. Step three, name what remains: schema design, query tuning, access permissions, encryption choices, and approving major version upgrades. Step four, check the cost: the managed price is higher per hour than a bare server, but it removes engineer hours.

A common mistake is assuming managed means no responsibility. You still own identity and access, network exposure, data protection, and testing that your app survives a maintenance restart. Another limit: managed services restrict access to the underlying host, so a workload needing a custom engine plugin or operating system tweak may not fit.

In a running system, the payoff is fewer outages caused by missed patches or failed homemade backups. The price is scheduled maintenance events your application must tolerate, often with a brief reconnect.

questions.prompt: A three-person team at a photo-printing startup runs an image-resizing service as containers on four self-managed EC2 hosts. An audit requires every host to stay patched. The team applies the managed-services approach. Step 1, list the toil: patching the host operating systems, updating the container runtime on each host, replacing failed hosts, and adding hosts when traffic grows. Step 2, map it to a service: move the containers to AWS Fargate (run containers without managing hosts), so no hosts exist for the team to patch, replace or size. Step 3 is MISSING. Step 4, check the cost: Fargate can cost more per unit of compute than bare EC2, but it removes the engineer hours spent on host upkeep. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Step 3: The team still patches the Fargate host operating systems, but now does it inside a maintenance window it chooses.
Step 3: Nothing remains for the team, because with Fargate AWS owns every layer, including access rules and data protection.
Step 3: The team still installs custom kernel modules on the Fargate hosts so the resizing library performs well.
Step 3: The team still owns task permissions, network exposure, encryption of stored images, and testing that the service survives task restarts.
questions.why: Managed services remove the host layers, but identity and access, network exposure, data protection and restart tolerance stay with the customer.

questions.prompt: An engineer says, "Moving our database to a managed service cuts our toil." In this context, what does toil mean?
choices: The extra hourly charge a managed service adds on top of a bare virtual server
The duties AWS takes on under the shared responsibility model
Repetitive operational work, such as patching and provisioning, that adds no business value
Any work an engineer does on a database, including schema design and query tuning
questions.why: Toil is repetitive work like patching and provisioning that keeps systems running but adds no business value.

questions.prompt: A research lab wants a managed relational database to cut patching work, but its analytics code depends on a custom database engine plugin and a specific operating system kernel setting. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Use Amazon DynamoDB, because a key-value database supports any relational engine plugin
A managed database may not fit, because it limits host access; self-managed EC2 may be needed
Use AWS Lambda, because serverless options allow full control of the operating system
Use Amazon RDS anyway, since AWS will install any plugin during the maintenance window
questions.why: Managed services restrict access to the underlying host, so workloads needing custom plugins or OS tweaks may have to stay self-managed on EC2.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company moved its database from EC2 to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ. Weeks later, during the chosen maintenance window, users saw errors for about a minute and the app needed a manual restart to recover. What is the most likely gap?
choices: RDS failed to patch the engine, so the team must now patch the operating system itself
Multi-AZ removes all maintenance events, so the outage must be an AWS billing issue
The application was never tested to reconnect after a maintenance restart or failover
The team should have chosen a larger instance size, which avoids maintenance restarts
questions.why: Managed services bring scheduled maintenance with brief reconnects, and testing that the app survives them remains the customer's job.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would move a self-run database or app server onto a managed service, what work really goes away, what work stays with the team, and one tradeoff or limit they should weigh before switching.
lessons.modelAnswer: A managed service hands the routine operational layers to AWS. If we move our PostgreSQL from an EC2 instance to Amazon RDS, we stop installing OS and engine patches by hand, stop scripting backups, and get standby failover with Multi-AZ. That frees the team from toil that keeps us compliant but never improves the product. Going further, Lambda, Fargate or DynamoDB leave no servers for us to patch at all. What stays with us: who can access the data, network exposure, encryption choices, schema and query performance, and approving major upgrades. The tradeoffs are less control and a different bill. We cannot log into the host or install a custom extension that the service does not support. Patches arrive in maintenance windows, so the app must handle a brief restart or failover. The hourly price is higher than a bare server, but it usually costs less once you count engineer time.
rubricPoints: Defines a managed service as the provider operating hardware, OS, patching and failure replacement.
Places options on a scale from self-managed EC2 through RDS to serverless.
States which responsibilities remain with the customer, such as access, network, data protection and schema.
Names a limit, such as reduced host control or unsupported customizations.
Notes that maintenance windows mean the application must tolerate restarts or failover.
Weighs a higher service price against saved engineering effort.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios where you must weigh operational overhead against control and cost, so reasoning through a design situation teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Disaster recovery is your plan for keeping a business running when a whole location fails, such as a flood, a power loss or a regional outage. You keep a second copy of your data, and sometimes your servers, somewhere far away, and you agree in advance how much recent data you can afford to lose and how quickly you must be back. Think of keeping a spare house key at a friend's place across town. A spare that is ready and current costs more effort than one you would have to cut later, but it gets you inside much faster.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a bank copies every new transaction to a second city one second after saving it locally, and the first city suddenly goes dark, what could the bank lose, and roughly how much?
lessons.teach:
Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan and standby setup that restores a workload in another location, usually another AWS Region (a separate geographic group of data centers), when the primary is lost. Two targets drive every choice. Recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time. Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may be down.

Four strategies trade cost against those targets. Backup and restore copies backups to a second Region and rebuilds after a disaster. It is the cheapest option, with an RTO of hours. Pilot light keeps only the data layer replicating, with servers defined but off, giving an RTO of tens of minutes. Warm standby runs a small complete copy that is scaled up on failover, recovering in minutes. Active/active multi-site serves live traffic from both Regions, giving near-zero RTO at the highest cost.

Replication sets your RPO. Synchronous replication confirms a write only once both copies hold it, so nothing is lost. Because every write waits for the far copy, it is used within a Region. Asynchronous replication confirms locally and ships changes afterward, so the lag, often about a second, is data you could lose. Cross-Region options are asynchronous. Aurora Global Database is a managed relational database with promotable read-only secondary Regions. DynamoDB global tables is a key-value store writable in several Regions. S3 Cross-Region Replication copies stored objects. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously copies server disks.

Worked example: a payments app needs an RPO of one minute and an RTO of fifteen minutes on a modest budget. Step one: a one-minute RPO rules out nightly backups, so the data must replicate continuously, and Aurora Global Database fits. Step two: fifteen minutes is too tight to build servers from scratch but does not justify active/active, so pick pilot light or a small warm standby. Step three: on failover, promote the secondary database, scale the app servers, and switch DNS.

Common mistake: treating replication as backup. An accidental delete or a corrupt write replicates within seconds, so the standby holds the same damage. You still need separate point-in-time backups.

questions.prompt: A small museum runs a ticket-booking site in one AWS Region (a separate geographic group of data centres). It can afford to lose up to 12 hours of booking data and to be offline for up to a day, and its budget is very tight. Step one: a 12-hour recovery point objective (RPO, how much recent data you can afford to lose) means continuous replication is not required, so copying backups to a second Region every few hours is enough. Step two: ____. Step three: after a disaster, restore the latest backups in the second Region, rebuild the servers, and point DNS at the new copy. Which choice completes step two?
choices: Choose backup and restore, because a one-day RTO allows hours of rebuilding at the lowest cost
Choose active/active multi-site, serving live traffic from both Regions
Choose pilot light, keeping the database replicating with servers defined but switched off
Choose warm standby, running a small full copy to scale up on failover
questions.why: A recovery time objective (RTO, allowed downtime) of a day easily allows the hours that backup and restore needs, and it is the cheapest strategy, which fits the tight budget.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm states: "Our claims portal may be unavailable for up to 2 hours after a disaster, but we must not lose more than 10 minutes of submitted claims." Which statement correctly names these targets?
choices: The RPO is 10 minutes and the RTO is 2 hours
The RTO is 10 minutes and the RPO is 2 hours
Both figures are RTOs, one for the database and one for the app
Both figures are RPOs, one for data and one for servers
questions.why: RPO measures how much recent data can be lost (10 minutes of claims) and RTO measures how long the service can be down (2 hours).

questions.prompt: A mobile game company wants players in two Regions to keep saving scores to their nearest Region at all times, with near-zero downtime if one Region fails, and it accepts a high cost. Which design fits best?
choices: Backup and restore with nightly backup copies sent to the second Region
Pilot light with Aurora Global Database and app servers switched off
Warm standby with a small app copy and read-only secondary database
Active/active multi-site using DynamoDB global tables, a key-value store writable in several Regions
questions.why: Only active/active serves live traffic from both Regions for near-zero RTO, and DynamoDB global tables accepts writes in several Regions.

questions.prompt: A retailer replicates its order database from its primary Region to a second Region with Aurora Global Database, with lag of about a second. A faulty release overwrites thousands of order prices with zero. When the team checks the second Region a minute later, the prices are zero there too. What should the team have also had in place?
choices: A larger warm standby so the second Region could take traffic faster
DNS failover so customers switch to the second Region automatically
Synchronous replication across Regions so no write could be lost
Separate point-in-time backups they could restore from a moment before the bad write
questions.why: Replication copies bad writes as faithfully as good ones, so only independent point-in-time backups let you return to data from before the damage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a disaster recovery strategy and a database replication method for a new workload, and name one tradeoff or limit they must accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by getting two numbers from the business. RPO is how much recent data we can lose, and RTO is how long we can be down. RPO picks the replication method. If losing hours is fine, cross-Region backups are enough. If it must be seconds, we need continuous asynchronous replication, such as Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables or S3 Cross-Region Replication. RTO picks how much runs in the second Region. Backup and restore takes hours. Pilot light keeps the data replicating with servers off. Warm standby runs a small full copy. Active/active serves traffic from both Regions. The tradeoff is cost: a shorter RTO and RPO means paying for more standby capacity. Cross-Region replication is asynchronous, so a little data can still be lost. Replication also copies mistakes and corruption, so we keep separate point-in-time backups.
rubricPoints: Defines RPO as acceptable data loss and RTO as acceptable downtime.
Ties RPO to the replication or backup method chosen.
Ties RTO to the strategy tier, from backup and restore through pilot light and warm standby to active/active.
Names cost rising as RTO and RPO shrink as the core tradeoff.
Notes that cross-Region replication is asynchronous, so some lag-sized data loss remains possible.
States that replication is not a backup because deletes and corruption replicate too.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner pick strategies and replication methods against stated RPO, RTO and budget targets and see the tradeoffs play out, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Disaster recovery testing means deliberately rehearsing your plan for losing a whole site, Region or database, instead of trusting that the plan on paper will work. A disaster recovery plan is the set of steps and standby resources you would use to bring a system back after a major failure. Think of a fire drill. Everyone believes they know the exit until the drill shows a locked door. Recovery plans fail in the same quiet ways: an expired credential, a backup nobody can restore, a step only one person knows. Testing finds those gaps on a calm day instead of during a real outage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has backed up its production database every night for a year but has never tried restoring one. What do you think they actually know about whether they could recover, and what could go wrong when they first try?
lessons.teach:
Disaster recovery (DR) testing is the planned practice of running your recovery procedure for real, against real backups and standby infrastructure, and measuring the result. Two targets anchor every test. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest outage the business accepts. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data loss it accepts, measured as time. A test is only meaningful if it measures actual recovery time and actual data loss against those numbers.

Testing works because recovery paths are rarely used, so they drift. Configuration changes, rotated secrets, new dependencies and service quotas (account limits on how many resources you may run) all change in production while the standby copy sits untouched. Only executing the plan exposes the drift.

Tests range in depth. A tabletop exercise is a walk-through discussion. A component test restores one backup into an isolated account. A full failover test shifts real or mirrored traffic to the recovery Region. Fault injection deliberately breaks things to see how the system reacts. On AWS, Fault Injection Service is a managed fault-injection tool, and Elastic Disaster Recovery, a managed server-replication service, can launch non-disruptive drill instances.

Worked example: the RTO is 1 hour and the RPO is 15 minutes. The team snapshots the database and replicates it to a second Region. In the drill, they first restore the latest replicated snapshot, which takes 40 minutes. Next they launch the application from infrastructure templates and hit a quota on instances in the second Region, which costs 25 minutes. The newest snapshot was 22 minutes old. The measured result is 65 minutes of outage and 22 minutes of lost data, so both targets are missed. The fixes are to raise the quota ahead of time and to replicate more often. The team then re-tests to confirm the fixes worked.

A common mistake is counting a successful backup job as proof of recovery. A green backup status says nothing about restore time, missing permissions, or DNS cutover. The consequence in a running system is an outage that lasts far beyond the promised RTO, discovered at the worst moment. Regular, scheduled tests with recorded results turn the plan from an assumption into evidence.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company sets an RTO of 90 minutes and an RPO of 10 minutes for its payments database. In a scheduled drill, the team restores the newest replicated copy in the recovery Region, which takes 30 minutes. Switching DNS to the recovery endpoint takes another 15 minutes. The application then fails because a role in the recovery account lacks a permission, and fixing it costs 20 minutes. The newest replicated copy was 18 minutes old when the drill began. Total measured outage: 30 + 15 + 20 = 65 minutes. Measured data loss: 18 minutes. Missing step: what is the correct verdict and next action?
choices: Both targets are missed, because the permission error alone counts as a failed drill regardless of the timings.
The RPO is met because 18 minutes of loss is well inside the 90-minute RTO, so no change is needed.
The RTO is met (65 is under 90) but the RPO is missed (18 is over 10), so replicate more often, pre-fix the role permission, and re-test.
Both targets are met, because the replication job reported success and 65 minutes is under 90.
questions.why: Each measured value is compared with its own target: 65 minutes of outage against the 90-minute RTO passes, and 18 minutes of lost data against the 10-minute RPO fails, so replication must be made more frequent and the fix confirmed by re-testing.

questions.prompt: A grocery delivery firm tells its architects: "If our order system fails, we can afford to lose at most the last 5 minutes of orders." Which DR target does this statement define?
choices: Recovery time objective (RTO), the longest outage the business accepts
Recovery point objective (RPO), the most data loss the business accepts, measured as time
A service quota, an account limit on how many resources may run
A tabletop exercise, a walk-through discussion of the plan
questions.why: Accepted data loss expressed as a span of time is the RPO; the RTO is about how long the outage lasts.

questions.prompt: An insurance team wants to check that last night's backup of its claims database can actually be restored and how long that takes, without touching production traffic or running a full Region switch. Which kind of DR test fits best?
choices: A tabletop exercise where the team talks through the runbook
A component test that restores that one backup into an isolated account
A full failover test that shifts real traffic to the recovery Region
Fault injection that deliberately breaks the production database
questions.why: A component test restores a single backup in isolation, giving a real measured restore time without affecting production.

questions.prompt: A media company's backup dashboard has shown every nightly job as successful for a year, and its DR plan has never been executed. Leadership says recovery is proven. What is the main risk in that belief?
choices: Successful backups say nothing about restore time, missing permissions, or DNS cutover, so a real outage could run far past the RTO
The only risk is storage cost, since a year of successful backups is valid recovery evidence
Backups that succeed every night prevent configuration drift in the standby environment
Successful backups guarantee the RTO is met but may not guarantee the RPO
questions.why: A green backup status only proves data was copied; only running the recovery and measuring it shows whether restore time, permissions and cutover meet the targets.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why your team should schedule disaster recovery tests instead of trusting nightly backups, and name one tradeoff or limit of testing.
lessons.modelAnswer: A backup succeeding only proves data was copied. It doesn't prove we can bring the service back within our RTO, the outage the business tolerates, or within our RPO, the data loss it tolerates. Recovery paths rot because production keeps changing. Secrets rotate, dependencies get added, and quotas in the standby Region stay low. A test means actually restoring and failing over, timing it, and checking how old the recovered data is. If we miss a target, we fix the gap and test again. Tests also train people, so recovery doesn't depend on one person's memory. The tradeoff is cost and risk. A full failover test uses extra resources and staff time, and if done carelessly it can cause the outage it's meant to prevent. So we mix cheap tabletop and isolated restore tests with less frequent full drills, scheduled at low-risk times.
rubricPoints: Defines DR testing as actually executing recovery, not just taking backups.
Ties the test to measured RTO and RPO targets.
Explains that recovery paths drift as production changes.
Gives an example of a hidden failure such as quotas, credentials, or a slow restore.
Names a tradeoff such as cost, effort, or risk of disruption from full tests.
Mentions re-testing after fixing gaps or testing on a regular schedule.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner that lets learners run a simulated drill and compare measured recovery time and data loss against RTO and RPO directly practises this objective.

lessons.plain: A backup is a separate, point-in-time copy of your data that you can restore if the original is deleted, corrupted, or lost with the place it lived. In the cloud you automate this: a schedule takes copies, keeps them for a set time, and copies some of them to another data center group or another geographic area. Think of photocopying important papers every night, keeping recent copies in a desk drawer, moving older ones to a cheap storage unit, and mailing the most important ones to a relative in another city. The design skill is deciding how often, how long, and how far away each copy goes, without paying for more than the business needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your database is copied live to a second location every second, and someone accidentally runs a command that deletes half the rows, does that live copy save you? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Automated backup across Availability Zones and Regions means a policy, not a person, creates restorable point-in-time copies and stores them far enough away to survive the failures the business cares about. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more isolated data centers; a Region is a geographic area containing several AZs. AWS Backup is the managed service that does this: a backup plan holds rules (schedule, retention, lifecycle, copy destinations), and resources are assigned by tag. Copies land in a backup vault, an encrypted container whose access policy you control.

Why it works: many AWS backups, such as EBS snapshots (block-level, incremental copies of a disk), are stored at Region level, so one copy already survives an AZ loss. Surviving a Region loss needs a cross-Region copy rule. Surviving a compromised account needs a cross-account copy, and Vault Lock makes recovery points undeletable for their retention period. Cost is controlled by retention length, incremental storage, and lifecycle rules that move long-lived copies to a cheaper cold tier, which has a minimum stay of roughly 90 days.

Worked example: requirement is a 24-hour recovery point objective (RPO, the maximum data loss allowed), 35 days of daily restores, monthly copies for one year, and Region-loss protection for monthly data only. Step 1: daily rule, 35-day retention, warm storage. Step 2: monthly rule, 365-day retention, move to cold after 30 days. Step 3: monthly rule copies to a vault in a second Region and second account. Step 4: tag production resources so they join automatically. Daily copies never cross Regions, avoiding transfer and duplicate storage charges.

Common mistake: treating replication as backup. Replication copies deletions and corruption within seconds; only point-in-time copies let you go back. In a running system, the team that relied on replicas discovers during a ransomware event that every copy is encrypted too. Backups that are never test-restored are only a hope.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain runs its appointment database on AWS. The requirements are a 12-hour RPO (recovery point objective, the maximum data loss allowed), the ability to restore any point from the last 14 days, weekly copies kept for 180 days, and protection for the weekly copies only against both a full Region outage and a compromised AWS account. The architect builds one AWS Backup plan. Step 1: a rule runs every 12 hours with 14-day retention in warm storage. Step 2: a weekly rule keeps copies for 180 days and moves them to cold storage after 60 days. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the database is tagged so the plan picks it up automatically. Which choice completes Step 3?
choices: Add a copy action to the 12-hour rule that sends every recovery point to a vault in a second Region.
Create a cross-Region read replica of the database in a second Region and second account.
Add a copy action to the weekly rule that sends copies to a vault in a second Region owned by a second account, with Vault Lock on that vault.
Add a copy action to the weekly rule that sends copies to a second vault in the same Region and same account.
questions.why: Only the weekly data needs Region-loss and account-compromise protection, so copying weekly recovery points to a locked vault in another Region and account meets both needs without paying to move and store the frequent 12-hour copies twice.

questions.prompt: A team takes one EBS snapshot (a block-level, incremental copy of a disk) of a server's volume each night and adds no copy rules. Which failure does that single snapshot already let them recover from?
choices: Loss of the Availability Zone the server runs in
Corruption that was written to the disk an hour before the snapshot
An attacker who gains admin rights in the account
Loss of the whole Region the server runs in
questions.why: EBS snapshots are stored at Region level, so they survive an Availability Zone loss, but surviving a Region loss or account compromise needs extra cross-Region or cross-account copies, and a snapshot taken after corruption contains that corruption.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps its order data in a primary database with continuous replication to a standby in another Region, and has no other copies. Ransomware encrypts the primary database. What is the most likely result, and what would have prevented it?
choices: The standby is unaffected because replication only copies inserts; no change needed.
The standby is encrypted too; adding a second replica in a third Region would have prevented this.
The standby is encrypted too; scheduled point-in-time backups in a separate account with Vault Lock would have allowed recovery.
The standby is unaffected because it is in another Region; adding a third replica would add even more safety.
questions.why: Replication copies harmful changes within seconds, so only point-in-time copies stored where the attacker cannot delete them, such as a locked vault in another account, let you go back to a clean state.

questions.prompt: An architect wants to cut backup costs for a dataset whose recovery points are kept for only 45 days in total. Someone suggests a lifecycle rule that moves each copy to the cold tier after 7 days. What is the best response?
choices: Accept the rule, because cold storage is always cheaper no matter how long copies are kept.
Reject the rule and instead extend retention to 365 days so the cold tier pays off.
Keep these copies in warm storage, because the cold tier has a minimum stay of roughly 90 days, longer than these copies exist.
Accept the rule, but copy each recovery point to a second Region first to offset the cost.
questions.why: Copies that live only 45 days cannot meet the cold tier's roughly 90-day minimum stay, so moving them saves nothing and may cost more; cold storage suits long-lived copies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design automated backups that survive both an Availability Zone failure and a Region failure, and name the main cost tradeoff you made.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd use AWS Backup with one backup plan, assigning resources by tag so new production resources are protected automatically. Many backups such as EBS snapshots are stored at Region level, so a normal daily backup already survives losing one AZ. For a Region failure I add a copy rule that sends recovery points to a vault in a second Region, ideally in a separate account with Vault Lock so an attacker or a mistake in the main account cannot delete them. The cost tradeoff is that cross-Region copies mean transfer charges plus duplicate storage, so I only copy what the business needs off-Region, for example monthly or weekly points, and keep frequent daily points local with short retention. Long-retention copies move to cold storage, but only if they stay past its minimum period. Replication is not a substitute, because it copies corruption, and I'd schedule test restores.
rubricPoints: Defines a backup as a point-in-time copy distinct from live replication.
Uses a policy-driven service such as AWS Backup with tag-based assignment so protection is automatic.
Distinguishes AZ protection (Region-level storage) from Region protection (cross-Region copy).
Mentions cross-account copy or Vault Lock to protect against deletion or compromise.
Names a cost lever: retention, selective cross-Region copying, or cold-tier lifecycle with its minimum stay.
Notes that backups must be test-restored to be trusted.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner set RPO, retention, and copy destinations and see the protection and cost consequences of each choice, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Designing for availability through a disruption means building a system so that it keeps serving users while some piece of it breaks: a server dies, a data center loses power, or a dependency slows down. The idea is to have no single part whose failure takes everything down, and to have enough spare capacity already running that losing a part does not overload the rest. Think of a bridge held up by several cables: engineers size it so that if one cable snaps, the others already carry the load, and nobody has to rush in and add a new cable while traffic is still crossing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web tier runs on two independent groups of servers, and each group alone is up 99% of the time. Users can be served by either group. Roughly how often would both groups be down at the same moment, and is the result better or worse than 99%?
lessons.teach:
Availability is the share of time a system does its job for users. A disruption is any event that removes part of the system, such as an instance crash, an Availability Zone outage (an AZ is an isolated data center group inside an AWS Region), or a slow downstream service. A single point of failure is any component with no backup, so its failure stops the whole service.

Two rules of availability math drive the design. Components in series, where a request needs all of them, multiply: two 99.9% parts give about 99.8%, worse than either. Redundant components in parallel, where any one can serve, combine as 1 minus the chance all fail together. That only holds if their failures are independent, which is why copies are spread across AZs.

Worked example: a web tier runs in two AZs behind a load balancer (a service that spreads requests across healthy targets). Each AZ is 99% available, so the tier is 1 minus 0.01 times 0.01, or 99.99%. But every request also reads one database in one AZ at 99.9%. In series, the total is 0.9999 times 0.999, about 99.89%. The single database caps the whole system, so it needs a standby copy in another AZ too.

Static stability means the system survives a disruption without needing to create or change anything during it. If you need four instances of capacity across two AZs, run four in each, so losing one AZ leaves full capacity already running. Graceful degradation means turning off nonessential features, such as recommendations, so the core path keeps working.

A common mistake is counting on scaling up during the event. Auto scaling and other control-plane actions (the APIs that create and change resources) may be slow or impaired in exactly the outage you are surviving, and capacity in the surviving AZ may be contested by everyone else. In a running system, that mistake turns a one-AZ outage into overload, timeouts, and a full outage. Design so the surviving parts can already carry the load.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs its API on instances in three Availability Zones (AZs, isolated data center groups inside a Region) behind a load balancer, so any one AZ's copy can serve a request. Each AZ copy is 98% available, and their failures are independent. Every request must also write to a single message queue hosted in one AZ that is 99.5% available. Step 1: The API copies are redundant in parallel, so the tier fails only if all three fail at once. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The queue is in series with the tier, so the total is about 0.999992 x 0.995, or roughly 99.5%. Step 4: The single queue caps the whole system, so it needs a copy in another AZ. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Multiply the three copies: 0.98 x 0.98 x 0.98, or about 94.1%
Combine them as 1 minus the chance all fail: 1 - (0.02 x 0.02 x 0.02), or 99.9992%
Average the three copies, which gives 98% for the tier
Subtract each failure chance once: 1 - (0.02 x 3), or 94%
questions.why: Parallel redundant parts with independent failures combine as 1 minus the product of their failure chances, so 1 - 0.02^3 gives 99.9992%.

questions.prompt: A payroll service needs 6 running instances to carry its peak load. It spreads instances evenly across three AZs and must be statically stable, meaning it keeps full capacity through the loss of any one AZ without creating or changing anything during the event. What is the minimum number of instances it should run in each AZ?
choices: 3 per AZ (9 total), so the two surviving AZs still hold 6
6 per AZ (18 total), so every single AZ can carry peak alone
2 per AZ, plus an auto scaling rule to add more in the surviving AZs
2 per AZ (6 total), because that already matches peak load
questions.why: After losing one AZ, two remain, and they must already run 6 instances between them, so each AZ needs 3; 6 per AZ also works but is more than the minimum.

questions.prompt: An online form submission passes through three components, and every request needs all three: a login service at 99.95%, an application server at 99.9%, and a database at 99.9%. None has a backup. About how available is the whole path?
choices: 99.9%, the availability of the weakest component
About 99.98%, because three components add protection
About 99.75%, lower than any single component
99.95%, the availability of the best component
questions.why: Components in series multiply, so 0.9995 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 0.9975, which is worse than any one of them.

questions.prompt: A video platform runs 5 instances in each of two AZs, and its peak load needs 8 instances. Its plan for an AZ outage is to let auto scaling launch 3 more instances in the surviving AZ. During a real AZ outage, what is the most likely problem with this plan?
choices: The load balancer will double the speed of the remaining instances
Launches may be slow or fail, so 5 instances face peak load and time out
None; auto scaling launches replacements instantly in any outage
Graceful degradation will switch off the core path to protect capacity
questions.why: Control-plane actions like auto scaling can be impaired and surviving-AZ capacity contested during the outage, so the 5 running instances get overloaded, which can escalate into a full outage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep an application available when one Availability Zone fails, including how you would check the availability math and what tradeoff static stability forces on you.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I remove single points of failure: every tier a request passes through, including the database, gets a copy in a second Availability Zone, so failures are independent. Then I check the math. Redundant copies in parallel improve availability, since both must fail at once, but tiers in series multiply, so one unreplicated dependency caps the total no matter how redundant the rest is. Next, I make the design statically stable: I run enough capacity in each zone that losing one zone leaves the rest able to carry full load without launching anything, because control-plane actions and spare capacity may be unreliable during the outage. I also plan graceful degradation, shedding optional features to protect the core path. The tradeoff is cost: static stability means paying for idle headroom, for example double the capacity across two zones, or about 50% extra across three.
rubricPoints: Identifies and removes single points of failure across every tier, including data.
States that series components multiply while independent parallel copies reduce joint failure.
Notes redundancy only helps when copies fail independently, for example in separate AZs.
Defines static stability as pre-provisioned capacity that needs no changes during the disruption.
Warns against relying on scaling or control-plane actions mid-outage.
Names the cost tradeoff of idle headroom and mentions graceful degradation.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about reasoning through exam-style scenarios that weigh redundancy, availability math, and headroom cost, and no listed mission or planned engine directly exercises that tradeoff.

lessons.plain: Centralized monitoring means gathering health signals from every system you run into one place, so problems are seen quickly and in context. Proactive recovery goes one step further: when a signal crosses a line you set, the system fixes itself before a person has to act. Think of a building's fire panel. Detectors on every floor report to one panel. When smoke is sensed, sprinklers start automatically, and the fire service is called at the same moment. The automatic part buys time and limits damage. The call means humans still learn what happened and can deal with whatever the sprinklers could not fix.
