lessons.guessPrompt: A server's underlying hardware fails at 3 a.m. and nobody is awake. List, in order, what would have to happen for it to be back in service before anyone opens a laptop.
lessons.teach:
Centralized monitoring means sending three kinds of signal from every account and Region into one place. Metrics are numbers measured over time, such as CPU percent or error count. Logs are timestamped text records. Events are notices that something changed. On AWS, Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics and logs. Cross-account observability lets one central monitoring account view data from many member accounts.

Proactive recovery means a detected problem triggers a fix automatically. The chain is signal, alarm, route, action. A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric against a threshold over a set number of evaluation periods, then changes state to ALARM. Amazon EventBridge, a managed event bus, matches that state change or a service event and sends it to a target. The target can be a Lambda function, a Systems Manager Automation runbook (a scripted sequence of repair steps), or an SNS topic, which is a managed notification channel. This works because machines react in seconds and repeat the same steps every time.

Worked example: a host under an EC2 instance breaks. Step 1: the system status check metric reports a failure. Step 2: an alarm requiring two failing one-minute periods enters ALARM. Step 3: the alarm's action is EC2 recover, which moves the instance to healthy hardware and keeps its ID and private IP. Step 4: EventBridge also sends the state change to SNS, so the on-call engineer gets a record rather than a task. Step 5: the alarm returns to OK.

A composite alarm combines several alarms with AND or OR logic, so one root cause raises one page instead of twenty.

Common mistake: auto-remediating symptoms with no limits and trusting default missing-data handling. A restart loop can hide a bad deploy. An agent that stops reporting may leave its alarm stuck showing healthy. The result is an outage that the dashboards call fine. Cap automatic retries, escalate to humans when automation fails, and treat missing heartbeat data as a failure.

questions.prompt:
A video-streaming company runs transcoding workers in 12 member accounts and wants stalled workers fixed without waiting for a human. Fill in the missing step.

Step 1: Every worker publishes a custom heartbeat metric to Amazon CloudWatch once a minute. A heartbeat is a regular 'I am alive' signal. The central monitoring account sees all 12 accounts through cross-account observability.
Step 2: A CloudWatch alarm watches the heartbeat. If the count falls below 1 for three consecutive one-minute evaluation periods, it enters ALARM. Missing data is treated as a failure.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The Systems Manager Automation runbook restarts the worker service. It is capped at two attempts.
Step 5: If the runbook still fails, an SNS topic pages the on-call engineer.
choices: An EventBridge rule holds the alarm until it returns to OK, then invokes the runbook to confirm the fix
An EventBridge rule matches the alarm's change to ALARM and sends it to the Automation runbook as its target
An engineer reads the worker logs on the central dashboard and starts the runbook by hand
An SNS topic receives the alarm and sends a restart command directly to the worker instance
questions.why: The chain runs signal, alarm, route, action: EventBridge is the routing step that matches the alarm state change and delivers it to the runbook, which then carries out the repair.

questions.prompt: A retail company's shared database fails. Within a minute, 18 separate CloudWatch alarms fire across the checkout, search, cart and API services, and the on-call engineer receives 18 pages for one root cause. Which change best reduces this to a single page while keeping the individual alarms?
choices: Raise every alarm's threshold so fewer of them cross it during an incident
Increase the number of evaluation periods on each alarm from one to ten
Delete the service alarms and keep only one alarm on the database CPU metric
Create a composite alarm that combines the related alarms with AND/OR logic and page only on that
questions.why: A composite alarm combines several alarms with AND or OR logic so one root cause raises one page, while the underlying alarms still exist for diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A bank's batch servers each run a monitoring agent that sends a heartbeat metric to CloudWatch. One night an agent crashes. Its server stops processing jobs, but the heartbeat alarm stays in OK and the dashboard shows green. What is the most likely cause, and what fixes it?
choices: The metric is stored as a log rather than a metric; convert the heartbeat into an event
The alarm uses too many evaluation periods; shortening them to one period will make it fire
The alarm relies on default missing-data handling; configure it to treat missing heartbeat data as a failure
Cross-account observability hides member-account alarms; move the alarm into the member account
questions.why: When an agent stops reporting there is no data to breach the threshold, so default handling can leave the alarm showing healthy; treating missing heartbeat data as a failure makes the silence trigger ALARM.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking firm wired an alarm on its API's error count to a Lambda function that restarts the API containers. After a faulty deploy, the function restarted the containers 45 times overnight. Each restart briefly cleared the errors, so the dashboards looked fine, but customers saw failures all night. Which design change best addresses this?
choices: Cap automatic restart attempts and escalate to a human through SNS once the cap is reached
Lower the error-count threshold so the alarm fires before any errors are recorded
Replace the Lambda function with an SNS topic so no automatic action is ever taken
Remove the evaluation periods so the Lambda function restarts the containers even faster
questions.why: Unlimited auto-remediation of a symptom can hide a bad deploy in a restart loop; capping retries and escalating to humans when automation fails surfaces the real problem while still keeping fast automatic recovery.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design centralized monitoring that recovers from failures automatically across many accounts, and name one limit or risk of automatic remediation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd send metrics, logs and events from every member account into a central monitoring account using CloudWatch cross-account observability. That gives us one view. For each failure we know how to fix, I'd build a chain: a CloudWatch alarm on the right metric, with enough evaluation periods to avoid flapping. EventBridge routes the alarm state change to a remediation target. That could be EC2 recover for a host failure, or a Systems Manager Automation runbook or Lambda for application fixes. SNS notifies people either way. Composite alarms group related alarms so one root cause raises one page. The risk is that automation can mask a real problem. Restarting a crashing service forever hides a bad release. So I'd cap retries and escalate to a human when remediation fails. I'd also treat missing heartbeat data as breaching, so a silent agent can't look healthy.
rubricPoints: Signals from many accounts and Regions are aggregated into one central view.
An alarm evaluates a metric against a threshold over set periods.
An event bus routes the alarm or event to an automated remediation target.
Humans are still notified, and they are escalated to when automation fails.
Automation has limits: retry caps, and missing data treated as failure where relevant.
Composite alarms reduce duplicate pages from a single root cause.

suggested.rationale: Building alarms with thresholds, evaluation periods, missing-data handling and remediation actions is the core hands-on skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Least privilege means every person or program gets exactly the permissions it needs to do its job, and nothing more. In AWS, an IAM user is a long-lived identity for one person or tool, and an IAM role is an identity that someone or something temporarily steps into, receiving short-lived credentials. Think of a hotel: a role is like a key card that opens only your room and expires at checkout, while handing out a master key that never expires is the opposite. Designing with least privilege means limiting how much damage any single mistake or stolen credential can cause.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server only needs to read files from one storage bucket. If you gave it permission to read, write, and delete everything in the account instead, what could go wrong if an attacker took over that server?
lessons.teach:
Least privilege is the design rule that each identity receives only the actions it needs, only on the resources it needs, for only as long as it needs them. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), its authorization policy service, gives you several pieces. An IAM user is a permanent identity with long-term credentials, such as a password or an access key. An IAM role is an identity with no permanent credentials of its own. A trusted party assumes it, meaning it requests temporary credentials that expire on their own. A policy is a JSON document listing allowed or denied actions on resources, optionally with conditions such as source network or required multi-factor sign-in. A trust policy is attached to a role and states who may assume it.

This works because IAM denies everything by default. An action succeeds only if some policy explicitly allows it and no policy explicitly denies it. So what you leave out of a policy is a protection in its own right.

Worked example: an application on a virtual server must read objects under the reports/ prefix of one bucket. First, create a role whose trust policy allows only the compute service to assume it. Second, attach a policy that allows only the read action, and only on that bucket and prefix. Third, attach the role to the server through an instance profile, which is the container that delivers role credentials to the machine. Fourth, the server's software fetches temporary credentials that rotate automatically. If an attacker steals them, they can read reports for a few hours and can do nothing else.

A common mistake is creating an IAM user with an access key for an application, or granting wildcard actions to get past an error quickly. Long-lived keys leak through code repositories and logs, and wildcards turn a small breach into control of the whole account. In a running system, prefer roles for workloads and for human access, keep permanent users rare, and tighten policies over time using access logs that show which permissions are actually used.

questions.prompt: A hospital's analytics team uses an IAM role (an identity with no permanent credentials that trusted parties assume to get temporary ones) with exactly two policies attached. Policy 1 allows reading objects in the bucket scans-archive. Policy 2 explicitly denies deleting objects in every bucket. No other policies apply. We trace three requests made with this role. Request 1, reading an object in scans-archive: an allow matches and no deny matches, so it succeeds. Request 2, deleting an object in scans-archive: the explicit deny in Policy 2 matches, so it fails, because an explicit deny always wins. Request 3, uploading a new object to scans-archive: ______. Which choice correctly completes the trace for Request 3?
choices: It succeeds, because neither policy explicitly denies uploading, so nothing blocks it.
It succeeds, because the read permission on scans-archive also covers writing to the same bucket.
It fails, but only because the deny in Policy 2 applies to every action in every bucket.
It fails, because no policy explicitly allows uploading, and IAM denies any action that has no explicit allow.
questions.why: IAM denies everything by default, so an action with no explicit allow fails even when no policy explicitly denies it.

questions.prompt: In IAM, what does the trust policy attached to a role specify?
choices: How long the long-term access key of the role stays valid before rotation.
Which network addresses the role's temporary credentials can be used from.
Which actions the role may perform on which resources.
Who is permitted to assume the role and receive its temporary credentials.
questions.why: A trust policy states who may assume the role, while separate permission policies list the allowed or denied actions on resources.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a nightly job on a virtual server that must send messages to one specific managed queue (a service that holds messages until another program reads them). Which setup best follows least privilege?
choices: Attach a role to the server through an instance profile, with a policy allowing all queue actions on all queues so future jobs do not hit errors.
Create an IAM user for the job, store its access key in the job's configuration file, and allow only the send action on that one queue.
Attach a role to the server through an instance profile, with a trust policy allowing only the compute service and a policy allowing only the send action on that one queue.
Create a role that any identity in the account may assume, with a policy allowing only the send action on that one queue.
questions.why: A role delivered by an instance profile gives temporary, automatically rotating credentials, and the narrow trust and permission policies limit both who can use it and what it can do.

questions.prompt: To get past a permissions error quickly, a developer at a retail startup creates an IAM user for an inventory app, gives it a policy allowing all actions on all resources, and commits its access key to a code repository. The key later leaks. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Little damage, because IAM denies by default and the attacker has no explicit allow.
The attacker can use the long-lived key to take control of the whole account until someone revokes it.
Only the inventory app's own data is exposed, since the user was created for that app.
Little damage, because the access key expires on its own after a few hours.
questions.why: A user's access key is a long-term credential that does not expire on its own, and wildcard actions on all resources turn that single leak into control of the entire account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would give an application an IAM role instead of an IAM user with access keys, and describe one tradeoff or limit of applying least privilege strictly.
lessons.modelAnswer: An IAM role has no permanent credentials. The application assumes it and gets temporary credentials that expire and rotate on their own, so a leak exposes access only for a short window. An IAM user with access keys holds secrets that last until someone rotates them, and those keys tend to end up in code, configuration files, or logs. With either one, least privilege means the attached policy allows only the specific actions and resources the job needs. IAM denies everything else by default, so a compromise stays small. The tradeoff is effort and friction. Narrow policies take time to write, and they break when the application gains a new feature that needs another permission. Teams then feel pressure to add wildcards just to unblock work. You have to keep refining policies using records of which permissions are actually used, and you have to accept some extra access-denied errors during development.
rubricPoints: Defines least privilege as only the needed actions on the needed resources.
Distinguishes long-lived user credentials from temporary role credentials.
Notes that IAM denies by default and allows only what a policy grants.
Explains that narrow permissions limit the damage from a stolen credential.
Names a tradeoff such as maintenance effort, breakage when needs change, or pressure toward wildcards.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner write narrow policies and watch which requests are allowed or denied, which is the core skill of least privilege.

lessons.plain: Every server in a cloud network needs rules saying which traffic may reach it and which traffic it may send. AWS gives you two layers of these rules. A security group is a guard standing at each server's own door: it lets in only what you list, and it remembers who it let in, so replies go back out freely. A network ACL is a checkpoint at the entrance to a whole neighbourhood (a subnet): it checks every packet in both directions, remembers nothing, and can turn specific visitors away. Designing a solution means writing both sets of rules so the right conversations work and nothing else does.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server's guard lets a visitor's request in on port 443. If a second checkpoint further out remembers nothing about earlier traffic, what do you think happens to the web server's reply on its way back out unless you write a rule for it?
lessons.teach:
A security group (SG) is a set of allow rules attached to a network interface, the virtual network card of an instance, load balancer or database. It is stateful: when a connection is allowed in, the reply is allowed out automatically, and vice versa. SGs have no deny rules; anything not allowed is dropped, and all rules are considered together. A rule's source can be another SG instead of an IP range, so you can say "allow port 8080 from whatever carries the load-balancer SG" and it keeps working as instances scale.

A network ACL (NACL) is an ordered, numbered list of allow and deny rules attached to a subnet, a slice of the virtual network. It is stateless: it judges each packet alone, so inbound and outbound must both be written. Rules are checked from lowest number up, and the first match wins. The default NACL allows everything; a newly created custom NACL denies everything until you add rules.

Why two layers: SGs express precise per-tier intent; NACLs give a coarse subnet guardrail and the only place to explicitly block, say, a hostile IP range.

Worked example: users reach a load balancer, which calls app servers on port 8080. Step 1: load-balancer SG allows 443 inbound from 0.0.0.0/0. Step 2: app SG allows 8080 inbound with source = load-balancer SG. Replies need no SG rule because SGs are stateful. Step 3: the app subnet's custom NACL allows 8080 inbound from the load-balancer subnets' address range. Step 4: the same NACL must allow outbound to those ranges on ephemeral ports 1024-65535, the temporary ports the caller used for the connection. Step 5: add a low-numbered deny, e.g. rule 50, for a known bad range so it fires before any allow.

Common mistake: writing the NACL inbound rule but forgetting the outbound ephemeral-port rule. In a running system, connections open and then silently time out, which looks like an application hang rather than a firewall block.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic runs reporting servers in subnet 10.20.4.0/24. They query a PostgreSQL database on port 5432 in a separate database subnet. The database subnet has its own custom network ACL (NACL). A NACL is a numbered, stateless list of allow and deny rules attached to a subnet. Step 1: the database security group (SG), the stateful allow-list on the database's network interface, allows 5432 inbound with source = the reporting servers' SG. Step 2: no SG rule is added for replies, because SGs are stateful. Step 3: the database subnet's NACL gets inbound rule 100, which allows TCP 5432 from 10.20.4.0/24. Step 4: MISSING. Step 5: the NACL gets inbound rule 40, which denies a known hostile range, 198.51.100.0/24, so it is checked before rule 100. What is Step 4?
choices: Add nothing more, because the inbound NACL rule automatically lets the database's replies back out
Add an outbound rule to the database SG that allows replies to the reporting SG on ports 1024-65535
Add a NACL outbound rule that allows TCP to 10.20.4.0/24 on port 5432 only
Add a NACL outbound rule that allows TCP to 10.20.4.0/24 on ephemeral ports 1024-65535
questions.why: The NACL is stateless, so the database's replies need an outbound allow to the callers' range on the ephemeral ports 1024-65535, which are the temporary ports the callers opened, not on 5432.

questions.prompt: A media company wants to stop all traffic from the hostile range 203.0.113.0/24 from reaching every instance in one subnet. That subnet's NACL already has rule 100, which allows HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. Which change achieves the block?
choices: Add a NACL deny rule for 203.0.113.0/24 numbered 150, so it is checked after the allow
Remove 203.0.113.0/24 from the SG source list and rely on the SG to drop it
Add a deny rule for 203.0.113.0/24 to the security groups of the instances in the subnet
Add a NACL deny rule for 203.0.113.0/24 with a number lower than 100, such as rule 60
questions.why: Only NACLs support explicit deny rules, and because NACL rules are checked from the lowest number up with the first match winning, the deny must be numbered below the allow at 100 to fire first.

questions.prompt: A subnet's NACL has two inbound rules. Rule 100 allows TCP 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Rule 200 denies TCP 22 from 192.0.2.0/24. A packet arrives on port 22 from 192.0.2.15. What happens?
choices: It is evaluated against both rules together and dropped because they conflict
It is allowed, because rule 100 is checked first and matches, so rule 200 is never reached
It is denied, because the more specific address range wins over 0.0.0.0/0
It is denied, because deny rules always take priority over allow rules
questions.why: NACL rules are checked in number order from lowest up, and the first matching rule decides, so rule 100 allows the packet before rule 200 is considered.

questions.prompt: An engineer creates a brand-new custom NACL, attaches it to a web subnet, and adds no rules. The web servers' security group allows port 80 inbound from 0.0.0.0/0. What will users see?
choices: Web traffic fails, because a newly created custom NACL denies all traffic until rules are added
Web traffic works inbound, but replies fail because the SG has no outbound rule
Web traffic works, because the SG allow is enough and an empty NACL allows everything
Web traffic works, because SG rules override NACL rules on the same subnet
questions.why: A custom NACL denies everything until you add rules, so it blocks the traffic at the subnet no matter what the SG allows; only the default NACL allows everything.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would specify the rules letting a load balancer reach an app tier on port 8080, covering both security groups and network ACLs, and name one tradeoff or limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd put most intent in security groups. The load balancer's SG allows 443 from the internet, and the app SG allows 8080 only from the load balancer's SG, so it follows instances as they scale. SGs are stateful, so replies flow back without extra rules, but they can only allow, never deny. The subnet's network ACL is stateless and evaluated in number order with first match winning, so I need an inbound allow for 8080 from the load-balancer subnets and an outbound allow on ephemeral ports 1024-65535 back to them, otherwise connections hang. The NACL's strength is explicit denies, like blocking a hostile range with a low rule number; its cost is that rules are per subnet and IP-based, so they are coarse and easy to get wrong.
rubricPoints: Security groups are stateful, allow-only, and attached to network interfaces.
Network ACLs are stateless, attached to subnets, and support allow and deny.
NACL rules are evaluated in number order and the first match wins.
Return traffic through a NACL needs an explicit ephemeral-port rule.
Referencing a security group as a source is more precise than IP ranges.
Names a limit: SGs cannot deny, NACLs are coarse and easy to misconfigure.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet through security group and network ACL rules, and watching a missing ephemeral-port rule break the return path, builds the skill far better than reading.

lessons.plain: Attack mitigation means stopping bad traffic before it hurts a public website, and noticing quickly when something slips through. Picture a busy shop. A crowd-control barrier outside handles stampedes, which is AWS Shield absorbing floods of junk traffic. A door guard checks each visitor against rules, which is AWS WAF filtering web requests. A security camera watches for odd behaviour, which is Amazon GuardDuty spotting threats in activity records. A head-office screen shows every camera and checklist together, which is AWS Security Hub collecting alerts from many accounts. Each layer does a different job, and no single one does them all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A public login page suddenly gets thousands of requests per second from many addresses, each one a valid-looking web request. Would a filter that only blocks oversized network packets stop this? What kind of rule might stop it instead?
lessons.teach:
AWS Shield is managed protection against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, where many machines flood a target to exhaust it. Shield Standard is free and automatic. It absorbs network and transport floods, meaning layer 3 and layer 4 attacks such as SYN floods, in front of services like Amazon CloudFront (a content delivery network) and Route 53 (managed DNS). Shield Advanced is a paid tier. It adds tailored detection, access to an AWS response team, and credits for scaling costs caused by an attack. It also helps against application-layer attacks when it is paired with WAF.

AWS WAF is a web application firewall. It inspects each HTTP request and allows, blocks, or counts it based on rules. You attach it to CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway. A rate-based rule blocks any source address that sends more than a set number of requests in a time window. Managed rule groups block known patterns such as SQL injection.

Amazon GuardDuty is threat detection. It reads activity records such as VPC Flow Logs (network connection records), DNS query logs, and CloudTrail (API call history), and raises findings like a server talking to a known malicious address. It detects. It does not block.

AWS Security Hub gathers findings from GuardDuty, WAF-related tooling, and other sources across all accounts in one place. It also scores your setup against best-practice standards.

Worked example: a login page behind CloudFront and a load balancer is hit by a request flood. First, Shield Standard drops malformed packet floods at the edge. Second, well-formed requests reach WAF, where a rate-based rule of 500 requests per five minutes per address blocks the noisy sources. Third, GuardDuty notices that one compromised instance is now making outbound calls to a command server. Fourth, Security Hub shows that finding beside the others, and an automated rule isolates the instance.

A common mistake is expecting GuardDuty or Security Hub to stop traffic. They only report it. Without WAF rules or automated response, an attack keeps running while an alert sits unread.

questions.prompt: A grocery delivery company runs its checkout API behind Amazon API Gateway, with workloads spread across 12 AWS accounts. The security team traces how its layers handle one bad week. Step 1: a UDP reflection flood (a layer 3/4 attack) hits the public endpoint, and Shield Standard absorbs it automatically at no extra cost. Step 2: attackers send HTTP requests to the product search endpoint containing SQL injection strings, and a WAF managed rule group attached to API Gateway blocks them. Step 3: a container host inside a VPC starts making DNS queries for a domain known to be malicious. ??? Step 4: Security Hub shows that finding next to the WAF-related findings from all 12 accounts, and an automated rule isolates the host. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: GuardDuty reads the DNS query logs and raises a finding that the host is contacting a known malicious domain
Shield Advanced spots the malicious domain lookup and drops the host's outbound traffic
A WAF rate-based rule on API Gateway notices the host sending too many DNS queries and blocks its address
Security Hub reads the DNS query logs directly and blocks the host's outbound traffic
questions.why: GuardDuty is the threat-detection service that reads activity records such as DNS query logs and raises findings, which Security Hub then collects and an automated rule can act on.

questions.prompt: A media company turned on Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub in every account. During an HTTP request flood against its streaming portal, both services show findings, but the flood keeps reaching the servers for hours. What best explains this?
choices: GuardDuty only blocks attacks once Shield Advanced has been purchased
Security Hub blocks traffic only for the account where the attack started, not the others
GuardDuty cannot read VPC Flow Logs, so it missed the flood entirely
GuardDuty and Security Hub only detect and report; nothing such as a WAF rule or automated response was in place to actually stop the traffic
questions.why: GuardDuty detects and Security Hub gathers findings, but neither blocks traffic, so without WAF rules or an automated response the attack continues while alerts wait to be read.

questions.prompt: A news website is served through Amazon CloudFront. A handful of source addresses each send about 3,000 HTTP requests per minute to the comment page, while normal readers send a few. The team wants to automatically block any single address that goes over a set request count in a time window. Which control fits?
choices: Shield Standard, because it absorbs SYN floods at the edge
An AWS WAF rate-based rule attached to the CloudFront distribution
A Security Hub best-practice standard score
A GuardDuty finding about the noisy addresses
questions.why: A WAF rate-based rule inspects HTTP requests and blocks any source address exceeding a set number of requests in a time window, and WAF can attach to CloudFront.

questions.prompt: An online bank needs DDoS (distributed denial of service) protection that goes beyond the free default. It wants tailored attack detection, access to an AWS response team during an attack, and credits for the extra scaling costs an attack causes. Which option meets these needs?
choices: AWS Security Hub
Shield Standard
Shield Advanced
Amazon GuardDuty
questions.why: Shield Advanced is the paid tier that adds tailored detection, response team access, and credits for attack-driven scaling costs, none of which Shield Standard provides.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Shield, WAF, GuardDuty, and Security Hub split the job of protecting a large public web application, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on them.
lessons.modelAnswer: They cover different layers. Shield absorbs volumetric DDoS floods at the network level. The Standard tier is free and automatic. Advanced costs money but adds a response team, cost protection, and better application-layer help. WAF sits on CloudFront, a load balancer, or API Gateway and judges each web request. Rate-based rules stop HTTP floods, and managed rules block things like SQL injection. GuardDuty reads flow logs, DNS logs, and API history to detect threats such as compromised instances. Security Hub pulls those findings together across every account and checks our setup against standards. The big limit is that GuardDuty and Security Hub only detect and report. Nothing gets blocked unless we wire up automated responses or WAF rules. WAF rules also need tuning, because a rate limit set too low blocks real users behind a shared address. Shield Advanced costs money, which only pays off for high-value, internet-facing workloads.
rubricPoints: Shield handles DDoS floods, with a free Standard tier and a paid Advanced tier.
WAF filters individual HTTP requests with rules such as rate limits and injection patterns.
GuardDuty detects threats from logs but does not block anything.
Security Hub aggregates findings across accounts and checks against standards.
Names a tradeoff such as detection needing automation, WAF false positives, or Advanced's cost.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises these services, and the exam tests choosing the right layer for an attack scenario, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so only someone holding the right key can read it. Data at rest is data sitting in storage, such as a disk, a database, or a file bucket. Data in transit is data moving across a network between machines. An encryption strategy decides where data gets scrambled, which keys do it, who may use those keys, and how keys are rotated and audited. Think of a hotel: each room has its own key (the data key), and the front desk keeps a master key locked in a safe (the key management service). Losing a room key is bad; losing control of the safe is a disaster.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you had to encrypt a 50 GB database backup, would you rather send all 50 GB to a central, tightly guarded key service to be encrypted there, or do something else? What might that something else be?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at rest protects stored data; encryption in transit protects data moving over a network. On AWS, AWS Key Management Service (KMS) is a managed key service: it holds master keys, called KMS keys, inside hardened hardware and never lets them leave. A key policy is the authorization document attached to a KMS key that says which identities may use or manage it.

The core technique is envelope encryption. A service asks KMS for a data key, a small key generated for one object. KMS returns the data key twice: once in plaintext and once encrypted under the KMS key. The service encrypts the data locally with the plaintext data key, throws that plaintext copy away, and stores the encrypted data key next to the data. This works because only a few bytes ever travel to KMS, so it stays fast and cheap, while the master key never leaves KMS.

Trace it for a backup file in Amazon S3 (managed object storage). Step one: S3 requests a data key from KMS. Step two: S3 encrypts the file with it. Step three: S3 stores the file plus the wrapped data key. Step four, on read: S3 sends the wrapped key to KMS, which checks the key policy and CloudTrail (the API audit log) records the call, then KMS returns the plaintext key and S3 decrypts.

For transit, use TLS (Transport Layer Security), the protocol behind HTTPS, with certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), a managed certificate service. Terminate TLS at a load balancer, and re-encrypt to backends when a compliance rule demands end-to-end encryption.

Design choices: AWS managed keys are simple but you cannot edit their policy; customer managed keys let you control the policy, rotation, and cross-account sharing; multi-Region keys let replicated data be decrypted in another Region for disaster recovery.

A common mistake is copying encrypted backups to another account or Region without granting that destination use of the key. The copies exist, but nobody can decrypt them, so recovery fails exactly when it is needed.

questions.prompt: A payroll company's application encrypts each monthly salary report with envelope encryption before saving it to a shared file store. Step 1: the application asks AWS KMS for a data key for report 2291 and receives it twice, once in plaintext and once encrypted under the company's KMS key. Step 2: the application encrypts the 40 MB report locally using the plaintext data key. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: months later, when an auditor opens the report, the application sends the encrypted data key to KMS. KMS checks the key policy, CloudTrail records the call, and KMS returns the plaintext data key so the application can decrypt the report. What is step 3?
choices: Throw away the plaintext data key and store the encrypted data key alongside the encrypted report
Ask KMS to export the KMS key to the application so future decryptions can happen entirely on the server
Save the plaintext data key next to the report so the auditor's later read does not need to call KMS at all
Upload the full 40 MB encrypted report to KMS so that KMS can wrap it a second time under the KMS key for extra protection
questions.why: In envelope encryption the plaintext data key is discarded after use and only the wrapped data key is kept with the data, so a later read must go back to KMS, where the key policy is enforced and the call is audited.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company terminates HTTPS at its public load balancer using an ACM certificate. Traffic from the load balancer to the backend servers currently travels unencrypted. A new compliance rule says card data must be encrypted for its whole journey across the network. What should the architect change?
choices: Nothing, because terminating TLS at the load balancer already encrypts the traffic all the way to the backends
Re-encrypt traffic from the load balancer to the backends with TLS so the data stays encrypted end to end
Encrypt the backend servers' disks with a customer managed KMS key instead of changing the network path
Remove the load balancer so that the backends can use an AWS managed key for transit
questions.why: Terminating TLS at the load balancer only protects the client-to-load-balancer leg, so meeting an end-to-end rule requires re-encrypting from the load balancer to the backends; disk encryption protects data at rest, not in transit.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm encrypts its shipment database with a KMS key. The security team needs to write their own rules about which roles may use the key, and they plan to let a separate analytics account decrypt copies of the data. Which type of key fits?
choices: An AWS managed key, with the analytics account added by editing its key policy
A customer managed key, whose key policy the team controls and can use to grant the other account access
An AWS managed key, because AWS keeps its policy up to date automatically
A data key generated once and shared directly with the analytics account
questions.why: Only a customer managed key lets you edit the key policy and share the key across accounts; you cannot edit the policy of an AWS managed key, and data keys are per-object keys, not something you share as a master key.

questions.prompt: A hospital copies its encrypted database snapshots every night into a separate disaster recovery account in another Region. The copies appear successfully. During a recovery drill, the team cannot restore any of them. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The destination account and Region were never granted use of a key that can decrypt the snapshots
CloudTrail blocked the restore because the drill was not logged in advance
TLS was not enabled on the copy, so the snapshots were corrupted in transit
The snapshots were too large for KMS to encrypt, so they were stored without encryption
questions.why: Encrypted copies can exist in another account or Region yet be unreadable if that destination has no permission to use a key that can unwrap their data keys, which is why recovery fails exactly when needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how envelope encryption protects data at rest and how you would protect the same data in transit, naming one tradeoff in choosing customer managed keys over AWS managed keys.
lessons.modelAnswer: Envelope encryption means we never send bulk data to the key service. KMS generates a data key, gives us a plaintext copy and a copy wrapped by a master key that never leaves KMS. We encrypt locally, discard the plaintext key, and store the wrapped key with the data. To read, KMS unwraps the key only if the key policy allows the caller, and CloudTrail logs every use, so we get access control and audit on every decrypt. In transit, we use TLS with ACM certificates at the load balancer and re-encrypt to backends if end-to-end encryption is required. Customer managed keys give us our own key policy, rotation control, and cross-account or multi-Region sharing, which we need for DR copies. The tradeoff is cost and responsibility: a wrong key policy or deleted key can make data permanently unreadable.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes data at rest from data in transit.
Describes envelope encryption: a data key encrypts data and a master key in KMS wraps the data key.
Notes the key policy controls who can decrypt and that use is audited.
Names TLS with managed certificates for transit, including re-encryption to backends when required.
States a tradeoff of customer managed keys, such as operational burden or risk of locking out recovery copies.

suggested.rationale: Generating, wrapping, and unwrapping data keys by hand in an envelope encryption lab makes the key hierarchy and key-policy failures concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: A service endpoint is the address your application calls to reach a cloud service, such as a storage bucket or a message queue. By default that address is public, so traffic leaves your private network and goes out over the internet path. A private endpoint gives the same service a doorway inside your own network instead. Think of a company mailroom: you can drive letters to the public post office, or use the drop box in your own building that the postal service collects from directly. Choosing endpoints well decides whether traffic stays private, what it costs, and what still works if internet access is removed.
lessons.guessPrompt: An application runs on servers with no internet access at all, yet it must save files to a cloud storage service in the same Region. How might it reach that service without opening internet access?
lessons.teach:
A service endpoint is the network address (a DNS name, which resolves to an IP address) that a client uses to call a service API. In AWS each service has a public Regional endpoint, for example the S3 endpoint for us-east-1. Some Regions also offer FIPS endpoints, which use encryption modules validated to a US government standard, for workloads that require them.

A VPC endpoint lets resources in a VPC (your private virtual network) reach a service without an internet gateway or NAT gateway (a managed device that lets private servers make outbound internet connections). There are two kinds. A gateway endpoint, available only for S3 and DynamoDB, adds a route to your subnet route tables pointing that service's address ranges at the endpoint; it has no hourly charge. An interface endpoint, built on AWS PrivateLink (private connectivity to a service), places an elastic network interface with a private IP in your subnets; it costs per hour and per gigabyte, accepts a security group, and with private DNS enabled makes the normal service name resolve to those private IPs, so code needs no changes. Both kinds accept an endpoint policy, a resource-style permission document limiting which actions or resources can be reached through that endpoint.

Worked example: a Lambda function in private subnets must write to S3 and send to SQS, with no NAT. Step one, add an S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables. Step two, add an SQS interface endpoint in each Availability Zone the function uses, with private DNS on. Step three, give the endpoint a security group allowing inbound HTTPS (port 443) from the function's security group. Step four, attach an endpoint policy allowing only the company's buckets, which also blocks copying data to outside buckets.

A common mistake is creating a gateway endpoint but not associating it with the right route tables, or leaving private DNS off. Calls then either time out or quietly flow through the NAT gateway, adding data-processing charges and defeating the private-path requirement. Note also that gateway endpoints reach only services in the same Region.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a nightly batch job on EC2 instances in private subnets across two Availability Zones, with no NAT gateway. The job reads a database password from AWS Secrets Manager (a managed store for secrets) and writes results to a DynamoDB table. The architect's plan: Step one, create a DynamoDB gateway endpoint and associate it with both private subnets' route tables. Step two is missing. Step three, attach a security group to the Secrets Manager endpoint that allows inbound HTTPS (port 443) from the instances' security group. Step four, attach an endpoint policy to the DynamoDB endpoint that allows only the firm's results table. Which choice correctly completes step two?
choices: Create a Secrets Manager gateway endpoint and add its route to both private subnets' route tables
Create a Secrets Manager interface endpoint in each Availability Zone the instances use, with private DNS enabled
Leave Secrets Manager on its public Regional endpoint, because the DynamoDB gateway endpoint already gives the subnets a private path
Create a Secrets Manager interface endpoint in one Availability Zone with private DNS off, and update the code to call the endpoint's own DNS name
questions.why: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, so Secrets Manager needs an interface endpoint in each Availability Zone used, and private DNS makes the normal service name resolve to its private IPs without code changes.

questions.prompt: A media company's servers in private subnets upload large video files to an S3 bucket in the same Region. They want a private path with no internet gateway or NAT gateway, at the lowest ongoing cost. Which option fits best?
choices: An S3 interface endpoint with private DNS enabled in every subnet
A FIPS endpoint for S3 reached through the internet gateway
An S3 gateway endpoint associated with the private subnets' route tables
A NAT gateway in a public subnet with a route from the private subnets
questions.why: A gateway endpoint gives a private route to S3 with no hourly charge, whereas an interface endpoint costs per hour and per gigabyte and a NAT gateway is not a private path.

questions.prompt: A bank's application in private subnets calls AWS KMS (a key management service). The team created a KMS interface endpoint but left private DNS off, and the VPC still has a NAT gateway. Calls succeed, yet the NAT gateway's data-processing charges go up. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Interface endpoints always send traffic through the NAT gateway before reaching the service
The endpoint policy is blocking KMS calls, so they are retried through the internet gateway
KMS supports only gateway endpoints, so the interface endpoint is ignored
The normal KMS name still resolves to the public endpoint, so traffic quietly flows through the NAT gateway instead of the endpoint
questions.why: Without private DNS the standard service name keeps resolving to the public address, so calls take the NAT path, adding charges and defeating the private-path requirement.

questions.prompt: A healthcare company uses an S3 gateway endpoint so its private instances can reach S3. Auditors worry that a compromised instance could copy patient data to a bucket owned by an outside account. Which control applied at the endpoint addresses this most directly?
choices: Remove the gateway endpoint's route from the private subnets' route tables
Move the bucket to another Region so the gateway endpoint cannot reach it
Attach an endpoint policy that allows access only to the company's own buckets
Switch to an interface endpoint so a security group can block outside buckets by name
questions.why: An endpoint policy limits which resources can be reached through the endpoint, so allowing only the company's buckets blocks copying data to outside buckets.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would let private workloads call S3 and SQS without internet access, and name one tradeoff or limit of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every AWS service has a public Regional endpoint, so by default private servers reach it through a NAT gateway. Instead I would add VPC endpoints. For S3 I would use a gateway endpoint: it is just a route-table entry, has no hourly fee, and keeps traffic off the NAT. It only covers S3 and DynamoDB, and only in the same Region. For SQS I would use an interface endpoint, which puts a private network interface in each Availability Zone, with private DNS enabled so the usual SQS name resolves privately and the code does not change. Its security group must allow HTTPS from our app. I would attach endpoint policies limiting access to our own buckets and queues to reduce data-exfiltration risk. The tradeoff: interface endpoints cost per hour per AZ plus per GB, so many services across many VPCs can add up, which is why teams sometimes centralize them in a shared networking VPC.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes public Regional endpoints from VPC endpoints.
Explains gateway endpoints are route-table based, free, and limited to S3 and DynamoDB in the same Region.
Explains interface endpoints use PrivateLink network interfaces with security groups and private DNS.
Mentions endpoint policies to restrict which resources can be reached.
Names a real tradeoff such as interface endpoint cost per AZ or same-Region limits.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from a private subnet through route tables to a gateway or interface endpoint, and seeing where a missing route or DNS setting sends it, is best learned by doing it in a network path tracer.

lessons.plain: Credential management is how a system keeps its passwords, API keys and database logins somewhere safe instead of written into code or config files. Think of a hotel key desk: guests do not carry a master key around. They prove who they are at the desk, get a key that works for now, and the desk can re-cut the locks whenever it likes without anyone rewriting their notes. On AWS, a managed secret store holds the secrets, controls who may read them, encrypts them, and can change them on a schedule. Applications ask for the current value when they need it, and nothing sensitive sits in the code.
lessons.guessPrompt: An application reads its database password once when it starts and keeps it in memory for weeks. The password is now changed automatically every 30 days. What do you expect to happen, and what would you change in the application?
lessons.teach:
A credential management service is a managed store that keeps secrets encrypted, controls who may read them, and can change them automatically. A secret is any value that grants access, such as a password, API key or token. On AWS the main options are AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Secrets Manager is built for secrets. It offers rotation, which means replacing a credential with a new one on a schedule. It also offers cross-Region replication, meaning copies of the secret are kept in other Regions. A resource policy, which is a permission rule attached to the secret itself, lets you share the secret with another account. Parameter Store holds configuration values. Its SecureString type is an encrypted value with no built-in rotation, and it costs less. Both encrypt with AWS KMS, the managed encryption key service. Both let you grant read access through an IAM role, which is an identity a workload assumes to receive temporary credentials. Those credentials are short-lived keys issued by AWS STS, the Security Token Service, so the workload never stores a long-term key.

Why this works: if the secret lives in one guarded place and code only fetches it, then leaking the code leaks nothing. Changing the credential also becomes routine instead of risky.

Worked example. A database password is rotated monthly by a rotation function, which is a small piece of code Secrets Manager runs to perform the change. First, the function creates a new password and stores it with the label AWSPENDING. A staging label is a tag that marks one version of a secret. Second, it sets that password on the database. Third, it tests a login with the new password. Fourth, it moves the AWSCURRENT label to the new version. Applications that ask for AWSCURRENT now receive the new password.

Common mistake: the application reads the secret once at startup, or the secret is baked into an environment variable or machine image. After rotation the old password stops working, logins fail, and you have an outage. Fetch the secret at runtime and cache it only briefly. On an authentication failure, refresh the cached value and retry.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a shipping-quote service in containers. The service calls a carrier's API using an API key stored in AWS Secrets Manager, the managed secret store, and the key is rotated every 30 days. Trace one request across a rotation. Step 1: the container assumes an IAM role (an identity a workload takes on) and receives short-lived credentials from AWS STS, so no long-term key is stored in the image. Step 2: the service fetches the version labelled AWSCURRENT and caches it in memory for 10 minutes. Step 3: at 03:00 rotation moves AWSCURRENT to a new key, and the carrier starts rejecting the old one. A request using the cached old key gets an authentication error. Step 4: ? Step 5: the request succeeds with no outage and no restart. What is Step 4?
choices: Change the service to always request the AWSPENDING version so it gets the newest key before rotation finishes
Restart the container so it reads the key again from the environment variable it was given at launch
Fall back to a backup long-term access key built into the machine image until the cache expires
Discard the cached key, fetch the AWSCURRENT version again from Secrets Manager, and retry the request
questions.why: The recommended pattern is to fetch at runtime, cache briefly, and on an authentication failure refresh the cached value and retry, which picks up the new AWSCURRENT key without downtime.

questions.prompt: A media company is designing a new reporting platform. Its data-warehouse password must change automatically every 60 days, a copy must exist in a second AWS Region for disaster recovery, and a separate analytics account must be allowed to read it. Which design meets all three needs?
choices: Store it in a machine image copied to both Regions and rebuild the image every 60 days
Store it in an environment variable on each server and update the variable with a scheduled script
Store it as a Parameter Store SecureString and rely on its built-in rotation and sharing features
Store it in Secrets Manager with rotation enabled, cross-Region replication, and a resource policy granting the analytics account
questions.why: Secrets Manager offers rotation, cross-Region replication, and resource policies for cross-account sharing, while Parameter Store SecureString has no built-in rotation.

questions.prompt: A ticketing startup enabled monthly rotation on its order database password in Secrets Manager. The morning after the first rotation, every order service instance fails to log in, though the database itself is healthy. The services read the password once at boot and keep it for the life of the instance. What is the cause, and what is the correct fix?
choices: Rotation should never be used with databases; disable rotation and change the password manually once a year
The services still hold the old password; fetch the secret at runtime, cache it only briefly, and on a login failure refresh and retry
The IAM role expired overnight; replace it with a long-term access key stored on each instance
The rotation function forgot to encrypt the password with AWS KMS; turn on KMS encryption for the secret
questions.why: Reading the secret once at startup leaves the old, now-invalid password in use after rotation, so the fix is runtime fetching with short caching and refresh-on-failure.

questions.prompt: A healthcare analytics firm wants a batch job to read a SecureString value from Parameter Store without any long-term credential stored in its code, configuration, or image. How should the job get permission to read the value?
choices: Give the job an IAM role allowed to read the parameter; the job assumes it and receives short-lived credentials from AWS STS
Make the parameter public so the job can read it without any credentials
Embed an IAM user's access key in the job's configuration file and restrict the file's permissions
Copy the decrypted value into the job's source code repository, which is private
questions.why: An IAM role lets the workload obtain temporary credentials from STS, so no long-term key is ever stored, and access can be limited to that parameter.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would store and supply the database password for a new service, why you would pick Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and what tradeoff or limit comes with automatic rotation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the password in Secrets Manager, encrypted with a KMS key. The service would read it through its IAM role, so the code and deploy files never contain it and no long-term access key exists. I would pick Secrets Manager over a Parameter Store SecureString because we need rotation and may need the secret replicated to a second Region for disaster recovery. Parameter Store is cheaper and fine for config values or secrets we rotate by hand. Rotation runs a function that creates a new password, sets it on the database, tests it, then promotes it to AWSCURRENT. The tradeoff is that the application must cope with change. It has to fetch the secret at runtime, cache it only briefly, and refresh it on a login failure. Otherwise rotation causes an outage. Rotation also adds cost and a function we have to keep working.
rubricPoints: Secrets are kept in a managed, KMS-encrypted store, never in code, images or plain environment files.
Workloads read secrets through an IAM role with temporary credentials, not stored access keys.
Secrets Manager is chosen when rotation, cross-Region replication or cross-account sharing is needed, and Parameter Store SecureString when cost matters and rotation is not.
Rotation creates, sets, tests, then promotes a new version using staging labels.
Applications must fetch at runtime with short caching and refresh on auth failure, or rotation causes outages.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner fix how a deploy receives a secret without exposing it, which is the core habit this objective builds.

lessons.plain: Patch management is the routine of keeping every server's operating system and software up to date with security and bug fixes, on a schedule your organization agrees to, with proof that it happened. Think of it like a building's fire-safety inspections: the rules say what must be fixed and how fast, a crew does the work in a quiet hour so tenants are not disturbed, and an inspection report shows which floors pass. In a cloud design, the rules, the quiet hour and the report are all automated, so hundreds of machines stay compliant without anyone logging in to each one.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a critical security fix is released today and you have 200 web servers behind a load balancer, why might you avoid installing it on all 200 at the same moment, even though that would be fastest?
lessons.teach:
Patch management on AWS is mainly done with AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, a service that scans and updates servers through an agent on each machine. Four ideas make it work. A patch baseline is a rule set saying which patches are approved, for example all Critical and Important security updates, auto-approved a set number of days after release so you can test first. A patch group is a tag on instances that links them to one baseline, so production and development can follow different rules. A maintenance window is a recurring time slot when disruptive work such as installs and reboots may run. Compliance reporting records, per instance, whether every approved patch is installed, and can feed AWS Config or AWS Security Hub so auditors see one view.

Why it works: approval rules are written once and applied everywhere, scans run often without changing anything, and installs only happen in agreed windows with rate controls, meaning a cap on how many instances patch at once and how many failures stop the run.

Worked example. The baseline approves critical patches 7 days after release. A fix is published on Monday. The next Monday it becomes approved. A daily Scan operation now marks the prod-web patch group non-compliant. On Sunday at 02:00 the maintenance window runs Install with a 10 percent concurrency limit, so 20 of 200 servers patch and reboot while the load balancer serves from the rest; if more than 5 fail, the run stops. The next scan shows compliant.

Common mistake: patching instances in place inside an Auto Scaling group while its launch image stays old. Every new instance launches unpatched, so compliance drifts the moment the group scales. Pair in-place patching with rebuilding the base image, for example with EC2 Image Builder, or replace instances instead of patching them. In a running system, skipping rate controls or windows turns a security fix into a self-inflicted outage.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs 160 Linux servers tagged with the patch group "orders-api". Their patch baseline (the rule set saying which patches are approved) approves Important security updates 5 days after release. Step 1: A fix is published on a Wednesday. Step 2: The following Monday it becomes approved. Step 3: A daily Scan operation, which checks without changing anything, marks the orders-api group non-compliant. Step 4: On Saturday at 23:00 the maintenance window (the agreed time slot for disruptive work) runs Install with a 25 percent concurrency limit and a failure threshold of 4. ______. Step 5: The next scan shows compliant. Which statement correctly fills the missing step?
choices: All 160 servers install and reboot together, because the maintenance window is the only control that limits disruption.
40 of the 160 servers install and reboot at a time while the other 120 keep serving traffic; if more than 4 fail, the run stops.
The daily Scan installs the fix on the non-compliant servers, since they have already been flagged during the week.
25 servers install at a time, because the concurrency limit is a fixed count of instances rather than a share of the group.
questions.why: A 25 percent concurrency cap on 160 servers means 40 patch at once while the rest serve, and the failure threshold halts the run after more than 4 failures.

questions.prompt: A university wants its research servers to receive patches on a different approval schedule from its student-portal servers, while both are managed by AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager. Which Patch Manager concept links each set of instances to its own rule set?
choices: A patch group, a tag on instances that ties them to one specific patch baseline.
Compliance reporting, which assigns approval rules based on what is already installed.
Rate controls, which set how many servers in each set may patch at the same time.
A maintenance window, which decides which patches each server is allowed to receive.
questions.why: A patch group is the tag that connects instances to one baseline, so different sets of servers can follow different approval rules.

questions.prompt: A retailer's patch baseline approves Critical patches 10 days after release. A Critical fix is published on the 3rd of the month. On the 8th, a Scan runs against a server that does not yet have the fix. What does compliance reporting show for that server regarding this fix?
choices: Compliant only if the next maintenance window has already started.
Compliant, because the fix is not yet approved by the baseline, and compliance only measures approved patches.
Non-compliant, because any published Critical patch counts against compliance immediately.
Non-compliant, and the Scan installs the fix right away to close the gap.
questions.why: Compliance records whether every approved patch is installed, and on the 8th the fix is still inside its 10-day waiting period, so it is not yet approved.

questions.prompt: A media company patches the instances in an Auto Scaling group (a service that adds and removes servers automatically) in place every month, and reports show them compliant. During a traffic spike the group adds 30 new instances, and compliance immediately drops. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
choices: The maintenance window was too short; extend it so new instances are patched as they launch.
The new instances launched from an old, unpatched base image; rebuild the image regularly, for example with EC2 Image Builder, or replace instances instead of patching in place.
The patch baseline auto-approves too slowly; set the approval delay to zero days.
The concurrency limit was too low; raise it so all instances patch at once during the next window.
questions.why: In-place patching does not change the launch image, so every newly launched instance starts unpatched until the base image is rebuilt or instances are replaced.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep a fleet of production servers patched to the company's standard, including how you would prove compliance, and name one tradeoff or limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use Systems Manager Patch Manager. A patch baseline defines what is approved, say critical and important security updates auto-approved after a seven-day delay so we can test them in development first. Instances are tagged into patch groups so production and development follow different baselines. Scans run daily and change nothing; they just report compliance, which flows into AWS Config or Security Hub so auditors see one dashboard. Actual installs run only inside a maintenance window with rate controls, patching a small percentage at a time and stopping if too many fail, so the load balancer keeps serving. For Auto Scaling groups I also rebuild the base image so new instances are not born unpatched. The tradeoff is the approval delay: waiting a week for testing leaves a window of exposure, so an urgent zero-day may need an out-of-band emergency run.
rubricPoints: A patch baseline defines which patches are approved and when, often with an auto-approval delay for testing.
Patch groups (tags) map different environments to different baselines.
Scans report compliance often while installs happen only in maintenance windows.
Rate controls limit concurrency and stop on errors to protect availability.
Compliance results are surfaced centrally as audit evidence.
Names a limit, such as the exposure window from approval delays or unpatched images in Auto Scaling groups.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises patch baselines and windows, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario that balances compliance deadlines against availability adds the most.

lessons.plain: A highly available application keeps working when individual parts break. You start from what the business actually needs: how much downtime per year is tolerable, which features must never stop, and what that protection is worth paying for. Then you design so that no single machine, data center or connection can take the whole service down. Think of a hospital with backup generators, two power feeds and several doctors on shift: any one can fail and patients are still treated. Extra copies cost money, so you add only the redundancy the requirement justifies.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app has two parts that both must work for a request to succeed: a web tier that is up 99.9% of the time and a database that is also up 99.9% of the time. Is the whole app up more than, less than, or exactly 99.9% of the time?
lessons.teach:
Designing for high availability means turning a business target into an architecture with no single point of failure, meaning no one component whose loss stops the service. Availability is the share of time the service works, often written in nines: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, and 99.95% allows about 4.4 hours.

It works because of how probabilities combine. Components in series, where every one must work, multiply their availabilities, so the whole is weaker than any single part. Redundant copies in parallel, where any one is enough, fail only if all fail at once, so the whole is stronger than any single copy.

Worked example. Requirement: 99.95%. Step 1: one web server (99%) feeding one database (99.9%) gives 0.99 x 0.999 = 98.9%, which fails. Step 2: run web servers in two Availability Zones (AZs), which are physically separate data centers with independent power and networking inside one AWS Region (a geographic area). A load balancer, a service that spreads requests across servers and uses health checks (regular probes) to stop sending traffic to broken ones, sits in front. Two independent 99% copies fail together only 1% x 1% = 0.01% of the time, so the tier reaches 99.99%. Step 3: make the database Multi-AZ, meaning a standby copy in another AZ takes over automatically, raising it to roughly 99.95% or better. Step 4: 0.9999 x 0.9995 is about 99.94%, close, so you either strengthen the weakest link or confirm the real figures beat these estimates. An Auto Scaling group, which replaces unhealthy servers and keeps a set count running, holds capacity steady.

A common mistake is making the obvious tiers redundant while missing a hidden single point: user sessions stored on one server, one NAT gateway (the device giving private servers outbound internet access) in one AZ, or all servers launched in the same AZ. In a running system, one AZ outage then logs out every user or cuts outbound calls, and the stated target is silently missed.

Every extra copy adds cost, so the business target, not habit, decides how much redundancy you build.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company needs 99.9% availability for its checkout service. Step 1: one app server (98%) feeding one database (99.5%) gives 0.98 x 0.995 = about 97.5%, which fails. Step 2: run three app servers in three Availability Zones (separate data centers in one Region) behind a load balancer that health-checks them. The three copies fail together only 2% x 2% x 2% = 0.0008% of the time, so the app tier reaches about 99.999%. Step 3: ??? Step 4: make the database Multi-AZ, so a standby in another zone takes over automatically, raising it to about 99.95%. Then 0.99999 x 0.9995 is about 99.95%, which meets the target. Which choice is the missing Step 3?
choices: Take the strongest tier as the system figure. The app tier is at 99.999%, so the whole service is already above 99.9%.
Add a fourth app server in another zone, because more web copies will lift the whole system past 99.9%.
Multiply the tiers in series, 0.99999 x 0.995, which is about 99.5%. That is still below 99.9%, so the single database is now the weakest link.
Add the two tiers' figures together, 99.999% + 99.5%, and since the sum is well above 99.9% the target is met.
questions.why: Tiers that must all work are in series and multiply. That gives about 99.5%, which shows the lone database, not the app tier, is now holding the system below target.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs two identical, independent copies of a tracking API behind a load balancer. Either copy alone can serve all traffic, and each copy is available 95% of the time. About how available is the API tier?
questions.why: Parallel copies fail only if both fail together: 5% x 5% = 0.25% downtime, so the tier is available 99.75% of the time. Multiplying 0.95 x 0.95 = 90.25% would be the series rule, which does not apply here.

questions.prompt: An online furniture shop runs its web servers in two Availability Zones behind a load balancer and uses a Multi-AZ database. Each web server keeps shoppers' carts and login state in its own memory. One zone goes down. What happens, and why?
choices: Nothing visible happens, because the load balancer moves those shoppers' carts to the healthy servers.
Only the database is affected, because web servers in two zones remove every single point of failure.
Shoppers whose sessions lived on servers in the failed zone lose their carts and are logged out. Session storage on individual servers is a hidden single point of failure.
The whole site goes down, because the Multi-AZ database cannot fail over while a zone is out.
questions.why: The obvious tiers are redundant, but each user's session exists on only one server. Losing that server's zone loses those sessions, so the target is silently missed.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm's internal timesheet tool has a business target of 99% availability. It runs on one app server (99.5%) and one database (99.9%). An engineer proposes adding a second app server in another Availability Zone, a load balancer and a Multi-AZ database. What is the best response?
choices: Reject it, because redundant copies lower availability by adding more components in series.
Decline it for now. 0.995 x 0.999 is about 99.4%, which already meets 99%, so the extra copies would add cost without being needed.
Approve it. Every tier should always be redundant, whatever the target.
Approve only the Multi-AZ database, because a database must never be a single copy.
questions.why: The business target decides how much redundancy to build. The current series figure of about 99.4% already beats 99%, so the extra redundancy is spending driven by habit, not by the requirement.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a business request like 'the checkout must be available 99.95% of the time' into an architecture, including the math you would use and one tradeoff you would raise with the business.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I convert 99.95% into a downtime budget, about 4.4 hours a year, so everyone knows what we are promising. Then I list every component a checkout request passes through. Components in series multiply, so a chain of good parts can still miss the target; I find the weakest links. For each one I remove single points of failure: web servers spread across at least two Availability Zones behind a load balancer with health checks, an Auto Scaling group to replace failed servers, sessions kept off individual servers, a Multi-AZ database with automatic failover, and no lone NAT gateway. Parallel copies only fail together, which is what lifts availability. The tradeoff I would raise is cost: each extra copy and zone costs money and some complexity, so if the business accepts 99.9% instead, we may skip some redundancy and save budget.
rubricPoints: Translates the availability percentage into a concrete downtime budget.
States that serial dependencies multiply and lower overall availability.
Explains that redundant parallel copies raise availability because all must fail together.
Spreads tiers across Availability Zones with a load balancer and health checks, plus a failover database.
Looks for hidden single points of failure such as server-held sessions or a single NAT gateway.
Names cost or complexity as the tradeoff to agree with the business.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about reasoning from a stated target to a design and weighing redundancy against cost, which is best practiced by working through exam-style scenarios with availability math.

lessons.plain: Designing for failure means assuming that every part of a system will eventually break, slow down or return garbage, and building so that the whole keeps working, or recovers by itself, when that happens. Think of a ship built with watertight compartments: a hole floods one compartment, not the whole hull, and the crew does not need to rebuild anything mid-voyage to stay afloat. In cloud architecture the same idea shows up as limiting how far a fault spreads, making repeated requests harmless, giving up quickly on slow helpers, and having enough spare capacity already running so recovery needs no emergency action.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout service calls a payment service. When payment slows down, every client immediately retries its request three times. What do you think happens to the payment service's load, and why might that make the outage worse rather than better?
lessons.teach:
Designing for failure is a set of patterns that contain faults and let the system recover without a human. Five matter most.

A timeout is a maximum wait for a reply; without one, slow dependencies tie up threads until everything stalls. A retry repeats a failed call, but it must use exponential backoff (waiting longer after each failure) plus jitter (a random offset so clients do not retry in lockstep). Retries are only safe if the operation is idempotent, meaning doing it twice has the same effect as once, usually enforced with an idempotency key the server remembers. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing and returns a fallback, a reduced but useful answer (graceful degradation). A bulkhead isolates resources so one fault cannot drain all of them; cell-based architecture applies this at scale by splitting customers into independent copies of the stack. Static stability means the system survives a failure without needing to change anything, for example running enough capacity in each Availability Zone (an isolated data-center group in a Region) that losing one zone requires no new launches.

Worked example. Payment latency jumps from 100 ms to 3 s. Step 1: clients time out at 1 s instead of waiting. Step 2: they retry after roughly 200 ms, then 400 ms, then 800 ms, each with jitter, so load rises gently rather than tripling at once. Step 3: each retry carries the same idempotency key, so a request that actually succeeded is not charged twice. Step 4: after repeated failures the breaker opens and checkout shows 'payment pending', queuing orders instead of erroring.

Common mistake: adding retries at every layer. Three layers each retrying three times turn one request into 27, a retry storm that keeps the dependency down. Retry at one layer only.

In a running system, these patterns decide whether a slow dependency causes a brief degradation or a full, self-sustaining outage.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming company's catalogue API needs 600 instances at peak. It runs across three Availability Zones, which are isolated data-center groups within one Region. The team wants static stability: losing any one zone must require no new instance launches and no other changes. Step 1: if one zone fails, the two remaining zones must carry the full peak load of 600 instances' worth of work on their own. Step 2: ______. Step 3: the total provisioned is 900 instances, so the team accepts paying for 50% more capacity than peak as the price of not depending on scaling during an outage. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Run 600 instances in each zone so that any single zone can carry the whole load alone.
Run 300 instances in each zone, because two surviving zones at 300 each already provide 600 with nothing new launched.
Run 200 instances in each zone and put a circuit breaker in front of the API to absorb the lost third of capacity.
Run 200 instances in each zone and set auto scaling to launch 100 more in each surviving zone when a zone fails.
questions.why: Static stability means the surviving zones already hold enough capacity, and 600 divided across the two remaining zones is 300 each, which gives the 900 total in Step 3 with no launches needed.
