questions.prompt: A logistics company's request passes through four layers: mobile app, API gateway, order service and inventory service. Each layer makes up to 4 attempts in total when the layer below it fails. The inventory service goes down. How many calls can one user request generate against the inventory service, and what is the recommended fix?
choices: 16 calls; add jitter at every layer so the attempts spread out.
256 calls; shorten the backoff so the retries finish sooner.
256 calls; retry at only one layer and let the others fail fast.
16 calls; remove timeouts so each layer waits for the reply instead of retrying.
questions.why: Attempts multiply across layers (4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 256), which is a retry storm, so retries should happen at one layer only.

questions.prompt: A grocery-delivery app calls a loyalty service to 'add 5 points' after each order, retrying with exponential backoff and jitter when a call times out. Some customers receive 10 or 15 points for a single order. What is missing from the design?
choices: A longer timeout, so the app never gives up on a slow reply.
A circuit breaker, so the app stops calling the loyalty service after repeated failures.
An idempotency key sent with every retry of the same order, which the loyalty service remembers so a repeated request is applied only once.
A bulkhead, so loyalty calls use a separate pool of threads.
questions.why: A timed-out call may have actually succeeded, so retries are only safe when the operation is made idempotent, typically with an idempotency key the server remembers.

questions.prompt: A software-as-a-service analytics firm runs every customer on one shared stack. One large customer launches a runaway query that exhausts the shared database connections, and all 2,000 customers see errors. Which pattern most directly prevents one customer's fault from reaching every other customer?
choices: Cell-based architecture, splitting customers into independent copies of the stack so a fault stays inside one cell.
A shorter timeout on database queries for all customers.
A circuit breaker that returns a cached dashboard when the database is slow.
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter on every database call.
questions.why: Cell-based architecture applies the bulkhead idea at scale, isolating resources so one customer's fault cannot drain what every other customer depends on.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency and static stability work together to make a service recover from a failing dependency on its own, and name one tradeoff or limit of these techniques.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every call to another service needs a timeout so a slow dependency cannot tie up our threads. When a call fails we retry, but with exponential backoff and random jitter so thousands of clients do not hammer the dependency at the same instant. Retrying is only safe if the operation is idempotent, so we send an idempotency key and the server ignores duplicates; otherwise a retry after a lost reply could charge a customer twice. If failures persist, a circuit breaker stops calling and we serve a degraded fallback. Static stability means we already run enough capacity in each Availability Zone, so losing one needs no new launches. The tradeoffs: retries add latency and load, so we retry at only one layer to avoid a retry storm, and static stability costs money because spare capacity sits idle most of the time.
rubricPoints: Timeouts prevent slow dependencies from exhausting resources.
Retries use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized load spikes.
Idempotency, often via an idempotency key, makes retries safe from duplicate effects.
Circuit breakers or bulkheads contain the fault and allow graceful degradation.
Static stability means surviving a failure without needing new actions or resources.
Names a tradeoff such as retry storms from layered retries or the cost of idle spare capacity.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner implement retries with backoff and idempotency keys, the core mechanics that make recovery from a failing dependency safe and automatic.

lessons.plain: Loose coupling means building a system from parts that talk through a middleman instead of calling each other directly, so one part can be slow, busy or broken without dragging the others down. Think of a restaurant: the waiter pins an order ticket on a rail rather than standing over the cook. The cook takes tickets at their own pace, and if the cook steps out, orders wait on the rail instead of getting lost. On AWS, three managed services act as that middleman. One broadcasts a message to many listeners. One holds messages in a line until a worker takes them. One runs a multi-step process and tracks where each request is.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout service must tell three other systems (billing, shipping, email) that an order was placed, and the email system is sometimes down for maintenance. If checkout calls all three directly and waits for each to answer, what happens to a customer's checkout while email is down, and what kind of middleman would stop that?
lessons.teach:
Loose coupling means components exchange messages through an intermediary, so the sender does not need the receiver to be up, fast, or even known. AWS offers three managed intermediaries for this.

Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a managed publish/subscribe service. A publisher sends one message to a topic, which is a named channel, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber. It is built for fan-out, not storage. If a subscriber is down, delivery retries for a while and then the message can be lost.

Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) is a managed queue. Producers add messages and consumers poll, meaning they repeatedly ask for work, at their own pace. A message being processed is hidden for a visibility timeout, the period a consumer has to finish and delete it. If the consumer does not delete it in time, the message reappears and can be retried. After a set number of failed receives, it moves to a dead-letter queue, a side queue where failing messages are parked for inspection. Standard queues deliver at least once and may deliver out of order. FIFO (first-in, first-out) queues keep order and remove duplicates, but they have lower throughput.

AWS Step Functions is a managed workflow service. You define a state machine, which is a set of named steps with the transitions between them. The service tracks each run and handles retries, branches, waits and compensation, meaning steps that undo earlier work when a later step fails.

Worked example: checkout publishes "order placed" to an SNS topic. The topic fans out to three SQS queues, one each for billing, shipping and email. Email goes down, so its queue simply grows. When email recovers, it drains the backlog, and checkout never noticed. Billing itself needs charge, reserve stock, then refund if reservation fails, so it runs as a Step Functions workflow.

A common mistake is assuming a standard queue delivers each message exactly once. Retries after a timeout can produce double charges unless handlers are idempotent, meaning that processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once.

questions.prompt: A print shop's web store adds each print job to an Amazon SQS standard queue. Several worker servers poll the queue. The visibility timeout is set to 30 seconds, but rendering a large poster takes about 90 seconds. Trace one poster job. Step 1: Worker A receives the job, and the message is hidden from other workers for 30 seconds. Step 2: Worker A starts rendering, which will take about 90 seconds. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The poster is printed twice, so the shop either raises the visibility timeout above the real processing time or makes the print handler idempotent, so a repeated job has no extra effect. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: SQS sees that Worker A is still busy and pauses the 30-second timer until Worker A deletes the message.
When the 30 seconds expire, SQS deletes the message for good because Worker A did not finish in time.
At 30 seconds the message becomes visible again while Worker A is still rendering, so Worker B can receive and process the same job.
When the 30 seconds expire, the message moves straight to the dead-letter queue so that no other worker can pick it up.
questions.why: A message that is not deleted before its visibility timeout ends reappears on the queue, so a second worker can receive it while the first is still working, and that produces the duplicate print in Step 4.

questions.prompt: A travel agency's booking process must reserve a flight, then reserve a hotel, and cancel the flight if the hotel reservation fails. The team wants a managed service to track each booking run, retry failed steps, and run that undo step. Which service fits best?
choices: AWS Step Functions, with the booking defined as a state machine that includes a compensation step
An Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue for failed bookings
An Amazon SQS FIFO queue, so that the steps stay in order
An Amazon SNS topic with one subscriber for each step
questions.why: Step Functions is the managed workflow service. It tracks each run as a state machine and handles retries, branches and compensation, which are steps that undo earlier work, such as cancelling the flight.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain publishes "new delivery scheduled" messages to an Amazon SNS topic. A partner warehouse subscribes directly with its own endpoint. The warehouse system was offline for six hours, and afterwards many delivery messages were simply missing. What change best prevents this loss?
choices: Replace the SNS topic with an AWS Step Functions state machine so that each message becomes a workflow run
Have the bakery send each message to the topic several times so that at least one copy gets through
Subscribe an Amazon SQS queue to the topic and have the warehouse poll that queue, so messages wait in the queue while the warehouse is down
Switch the topic to send each message only once, so retries do not overload the warehouse
questions.why: SNS is built for fan-out, not storage, so messages can be lost after its retries run out. An SQS queue holds the messages until the consumer recovers and polls for them.

questions.prompt: A fitness app sends "workout completed" messages through an Amazon SQS standard queue to a service that adds 50 reward points per workout. Users occasionally receive 100 points for a single workout. What is the most likely cause, and what is the right fix?
choices: The dead-letter queue is sending messages back to the main queue; the fix is to delete the dead-letter queue.
The messages are arriving out of order; the fix is to sort them by timestamp before adding the points.
Standard queues deliver at least once, so a message can be processed twice; the fix is to make the handler idempotent, for example by recording each workout ID and skipping IDs it has already seen.
Standard queues deliver every message exactly once, so the app must be sending each workout twice; the fix belongs only in the app.
questions.why: Standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, so repeats such as retries after a visibility timeout can happen, and an idempotent handler makes processing a message twice have the same effect as processing it once.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would reach for SNS, SQS, or Step Functions to decouple two services, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three let services stop calling each other directly, so a slow or broken part does not stall the rest. SNS is a topic that pushes a copy of each message to every subscriber. It is great for fan-out, but it does not hold messages, so a downed subscriber can miss them. SQS is a queue that holds work until a consumer polls and deletes it. It absorbs spikes and outages, but standard queues are at-least-once and unordered, so handlers must be idempotent. FIFO queues fix ordering but give lower throughput. Step Functions runs a multi-step process as a state machine with retries, branching and compensation. It suits orchestrated business flows, but it adds per-step cost and latency compared with a single queue hop. A common combination is SNS fanning out into one SQS queue per consumer, with Step Functions driving any flow that has several steps.
rubricPoints: Defines loose coupling as communicating through an intermediary so components fail and scale independently.
Identifies SNS as push-based fan-out that does not durably hold messages for an unavailable subscriber.
Identifies SQS as a buffering queue with polling, visibility timeout and dead-letter queue.
Notes at-least-once delivery in standard queues and the need for idempotent handlers, or FIFO with its throughput tradeoff.
Identifies Step Functions as orchestration of multi-step workflows with retries and compensation.
Mentions the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern or another sensible combination.

suggested.rationale: A messaging and events engine would let the learner wire topics to queues, take a consumer offline, and watch backlogs, retries and dead-letter queues behave, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: High availability means a service keeps working when one of its parts breaks. Failover is the act of switching work from a broken part to a healthy spare, ideally automatically and quickly. For the application layer, that usually means a traffic director stops sending users to a dead server and sends them to live ones. For the database, it means a standby copy takes over as the main copy. Think of a relay team with a substitute runner warming up: when one runner falls, the baton passes to the substitute, and the race continues after a short stumble rather than stopping.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database has an up-to-date standby copy in another data center. The main copy crashes and the standby takes over within a minute, yet your application keeps failing for ten more minutes. What on the application side might still be pointing at, or holding on to, the dead database?
lessons.teach:
Failover is automatic switching from a failed component to a healthy one. In AWS, an Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated data center group within a Region, so spreading parts across AZs is the usual starting point.

Application failover: an Application Load Balancer (a managed traffic distributor) sends health checks, small test requests, to each server. A target that fails several checks in a row is removed from rotation. An Auto Scaling group (a managed fleet that keeps a set number of servers running) then replaces the unhealthy server. Across Regions, Amazon Route 53 (managed DNS, the internet's name-to-address directory) can use failover routing: it answers with the primary site's address while its health check passes, and the secondary's address when it fails.

Database failover: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby, meaning every write is confirmed on both copies, in another AZ. On failure, RDS promotes the standby and repoints the database's DNS name, typically in one to two minutes. The classic standby does not serve reads. Amazon Aurora instead uses readable replicas sharing one storage layer, and promotes a replica usually in under a minute. RDS Proxy, a managed connection pool, holds client connections open and shortens the visible interruption.

Worked example: the primary database's AZ loses power. Step one, RDS detects the failure. Step two, it promotes the standby. Step three, it updates the endpoint name to the new address. Step four, the application's next connection attempt resolves the name and connects. Step five, in-flight transactions that were cut off must be retried by the application.

Common mistake: hard-coding the database IP address, or caching DNS for a long time, so the application keeps calling the dead host. Pair this with no retry logic and a one-minute database failover becomes a long outage. Always connect by endpoint name, keep DNS caching short, and retry with backoff.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company runs its full web stack in one AWS Region (primary) and a copy in a second Region (secondary). Amazon Route 53, the managed DNS service, is set up with failover routing and a health check on the primary site. One evening the primary Region's web tier stops responding. Trace what happens. Step one: Route 53's health check sends test requests to the primary site and they start failing. Step two: after several failed checks in a row, the primary is marked unhealthy. Step three: ???. Step four: once a client's short-lived cached DNS answer expires, it looks the name up again, gets the new address, and its requests land on the secondary site. Which choice correctly fills step three?
choices: The Application Load Balancer in the primary Region forwards all incoming traffic over to the secondary Region
Route 53 promotes the secondary Region's database to primary and repoints its endpoint name
Route 53 keeps returning the primary address until an operator edits the DNS record by hand
Route 53 starts answering lookups for the site's name with the secondary site's address instead of the primary's
questions.why: Failover routing means Route 53 answers with the primary's address while its health check passes and switches to answering with the secondary's address once that check fails, with no manual edit needed.

questions.prompt: A fleet-tracking startup is designing a new database tier. It wants a failover target in another Availability Zone (an isolated data center group within a Region), wants that failover usually to finish in under a minute, and wants the failover copies to also handle its dashboard read traffic in normal operation. Which option fits all three needs?
choices: A single-AZ RDS instance placed behind RDS Proxy
A single-AZ RDS instance with frequent backups to restore from
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ with the classic synchronous standby
Amazon Aurora with readable replicas sharing one storage layer
questions.why: Aurora's replicas serve reads and one is usually promoted in under a minute, while the classic Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads and typically takes one to two minutes.

questions.prompt: A payroll service uses Amazon RDS Multi-AZ. During a test, RDS finished failing over to the standby in about 90 seconds, yet the payroll app stayed broken for over an hour until it was restarted. The app caches DNS lookups for 12 hours and does not retry failed queries. What change best fixes this?
choices: Add a Route 53 failover record that points to a second Region's database
Connect by the endpoint name, keep DNS caching short, and retry failed calls with backoff
Configure the app to connect using the database's stored IP address so lookups are skipped
Replace Multi-AZ with a larger single database instance so failover is never needed
questions.why: RDS failover works by repointing the endpoint name, so the app must re-resolve that name soon and retry cut-off work, otherwise it keeps calling the dead host.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore runs its web servers in an Auto Scaling group (a managed fleet that keeps a set number of servers running) of six instances spread across two Availability Zones, behind an Application Load Balancer (a managed traffic distributor). One instance's application process hangs and it begins failing the load balancer's health checks. What is the expected outcome?
choices: The load balancer stops sending it traffic after several failed checks, and the Auto Scaling group replaces it
Route 53 moves the whole site to a secondary Region because one server failed
The load balancer keeps sending it traffic but at a lower rate until the process recovers
The Auto Scaling group adds a seventh instance while the hung one keeps receiving requests
questions.why: A target that fails several health checks in a row is removed from rotation, and the Auto Scaling group then replaces the unhealthy server to keep the set count running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how application failover and database failover work together in a multi-AZ design, and name one limit or tradeoff, such as failover time, read capacity, or cost.
lessons.modelAnswer: Failover means automatically moving work off a broken component onto a healthy one. At the application tier, the load balancer health-checks every server, stops routing to ones that fail, and the Auto Scaling group replaces them, so users barely notice. For whole-site failures, Route 53 failover routing flips DNS to a secondary site when the primary's health check fails. At the database tier, RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and, on failure, promotes it and repoints the endpoint name in roughly one to two minutes; Aurora promotes a readable replica faster. The tradeoff: a classic Multi-AZ standby costs about as much as the primary yet serves no reads, and failover is never instant. The application must connect by endpoint name, avoid long DNS caching, and retry dropped transactions, or a short database switch turns into a long outage.
rubricPoints: Defines failover as automatic switching from a failed component to a healthy one.
Describes load balancer health checks removing unhealthy servers and Auto Scaling replacing them.
Explains database failover as promoting a standby or replica and repointing the endpoint name.
Notes the application must use the endpoint name, short DNS caching, and retries.
Names a real tradeoff such as failover duration, a non-readable standby, or the cost of idle capacity.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between failover mechanisms and spotting client-side gaps in a scenario, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style situations since no existing mission or planned engine exercises failover directly.

lessons.plain: Auto scaling means letting a system add or remove servers by itself as demand changes, instead of a person guessing in advance. Think of a supermarket that opens more checkout lanes when queues grow and closes them when the store empties. A scaling policy is the rule that decides when to open or close lanes: keep each cashier about 60 percent busy, add two lanes at lunchtime every day, or add lanes fast when the queue gets very long. Events are the moments when a server joins or leaves, which you can react to, for example to finish a task before it shuts down.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web servers usually sit at 30 percent CPU, but every weekday at 9:00 a flood of users arrives and new servers take about five minutes to become ready. If you only add servers after CPU climbs, what will users experience at 9:00, and what kind of rule might help?
lessons.teach:
An Auto Scaling group (on AWS, an EC2 Auto Scaling group) is a managed pool of identical virtual servers with three numbers: minimum, maximum, and desired capacity. Desired is how many servers should run now; policies change it, but never outside min and max.

Policy types differ in how they decide. Target tracking keeps one metric near a chosen value, such as average CPU at 50 percent, adding or removing servers like a thermostat. Step scaling reacts to an alarm (a rule that fires when a metric crosses a threshold) with sized steps: add 2 servers at 70 percent, 5 at 90 percent. Simple scaling makes one change per alarm then waits. Scheduled scaling changes capacity at known times. Predictive scaling learns daily and weekly patterns from history and adds capacity before a forecast rise. Warm-up is the time a new server needs before its metrics count, which stops the group overreacting while newcomers boot.

Events are launches and terminations. A lifecycle hook pauses a server in a waiting state during launch or termination so a script can install software, or drain work and copy logs, before it continues. These events can also be sent to an event bus (Amazon EventBridge) or a notification topic for other automation.

Worked example: min 2, max 10, target CPU 50 percent, current 4 servers at 80 percent. The policy estimates 4 times 80 divided by 50, about 6.4, and raises desired to 7. Seven servers launch-hook through setup, warm up, and CPU settles near 46 percent. At night load falls; scale-in removes servers more slowly and never below 2.

Common mistake: relying only on reactive policies for a sharp, predictable spike. Because new servers take minutes to be ready, users see errors during the climb. Combine scheduled or predictive scaling to pre-warm with target tracking for the unexpected, and set max high enough, since a ceiling that is too low turns a traffic surge into an outage while the bill stays deceptively small.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a tracking API in an Auto Scaling group (a managed pool of identical virtual servers) with minimum 2, maximum 8, and a target tracking policy that holds average CPU at 40 percent. During a morning rush, 6 servers are running at 70 percent average CPU.

Step 1: The policy estimates the servers needed as current servers times current CPU divided by target CPU: 6 x 70 / 40 = 10.5.
Step 2: It rounds up to a request of 11 servers.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The new servers launch, warm up, and then their metrics start counting toward the average.

What happens in Step 3?
choices: Desired capacity is set to 11, and the maximum is raised automatically to make room for it
Desired capacity stays at 6 until an operator approves the larger change
Desired capacity is set to 10, because the policy rounds the estimate of 10.5 down
Desired capacity is set to 8, because policies can never push desired above the maximum
questions.why: Policies change desired capacity but never outside the minimum and maximum, so the request for 11 is capped at the maximum of 8.

questions.prompt: A video transcoding firm scales its worker servers in and out all day. When a server is removed, any job it is halfway through is lost, and its log files disappear with it. Which Auto Scaling feature lets each server finish its current work and copy its logs before it is actually terminated?
choices: A scheduled action that lowers the minimum capacity overnight
A step scaling policy with a smaller removal step
A longer warm-up period on the group
A lifecycle hook on termination that holds the server in a waiting state while a script drains work and copies logs
questions.why: A lifecycle hook pauses a terminating server in a waiting state so a script can drain work and copy logs before termination continues.

questions.prompt: A concert ticketing site opens sales every Friday at exactly 10:00, and traffic jumps about tenfold within a minute. Today it uses only a target tracking policy, and customers see errors for the first several minutes of every sale. What design best fixes this?
choices: Lower the maximum capacity so the bill stays under control during the spike
Replace target tracking with simple scaling so each alarm makes one larger change
Add scheduled or predictive scaling to raise capacity before 10:00, keep target tracking for unexpected load, and make sure the maximum is high enough for the peak
Set the target CPU value higher so the policy reacts faster to the jump
questions.why: Reactive policies alone are too slow for a sharp, predictable spike because new servers take minutes to be ready, so capacity should be added ahead of time while target tracking handles the unexpected and the maximum leaves room for the peak.

questions.prompt: A news site's Auto Scaling group sees a moderate rise in traffic. The policy adds servers, but it keeps adding more and more, ending far above what the load needed, and then removes many of them again. Investigation shows that metrics from brand-new servers were counted while those servers were still booting. Which setting most directly addresses this overreaction?
choices: Switch from target tracking to scheduled scaling only
Lower the maximum capacity to stop the group from growing
Set an appropriate warm-up time so new servers' metrics are not counted until they are ready
Raise the minimum capacity so the group starts larger
questions.why: Warm-up is the time a new server needs before its metrics count, and it exists precisely to stop the group from overreacting while newcomers boot.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose scaling policies for a service with a predictable morning spike plus occasional surprise surges, and name one tradeoff or limit of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the servers in an Auto Scaling group with a sensible minimum for availability and a maximum that caps cost but still covers our worst realistic surge. For the morning spike I would use scheduled or predictive scaling so capacity is already running before users arrive, because new servers need minutes to boot and warm up and a purely reactive rule would lag. On top of that, a target tracking policy on average CPU or requests per server handles surprises like a thermostat. I would add a termination lifecycle hook so a server finishes in-flight work before it is removed. The tradeoff is cost versus readiness: pre-warming means paying for idle servers if the forecast is wrong, and a low maximum saves money but turns a big surge into errors.
rubricPoints: Defines the group's minimum, maximum, and desired capacity and that policies move desired within those bounds.
Distinguishes reactive policies (target tracking, step) from proactive ones (scheduled, predictive).
Explains that boot and warm-up time makes reactive-only scaling lag behind sharp spikes.
Mentions lifecycle hooks or scaling events for setup or graceful draining.
Names a tradeoff such as idle cost from pre-warming or outages from a too-low maximum.

suggested.rationale: Tuning policies against simulated load and watching warm-up lag and capacity ceilings is learned best by doing, which the planned autoscaling engine would provide.

lessons.plain: DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's phone book: it turns a name like shop.example.com into the numeric address of a server. A routing policy is the rule a DNS service uses to decide which address to hand back when you have more than one. Simple routing always gives the same answer. Latency-based routing gives each user the server location that has been measured as fastest for them. Geolocation routing gives an answer based on where the user is, such as their country. Think of a receptionist who either always sends you to one office, sends you to the office with the shortest commute, or sends you to the office assigned to your country.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs in one data center in the US and one in Germany. A law says German users' traffic must be handled in Germany. Should DNS pick the server by measured speed or by the user's location, and why?
lessons.teach:
A DNS record maps a name to a value, such as an IP address. A resolver is the server, usually run by an internet provider, that looks names up on a user's behalf and caches answers for the record's TTL (time to live, in seconds). Amazon Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service, and it lets you attach a routing policy to records that share a name.

Simple routing: one record, possibly holding several values. All values come back and the client picks one, with no awareness of health or location. A health check is a probe Route 53 runs against an endpoint, and simple records cannot use one, so a dead server keeps being handed out. Use simple routing for a single resource.

Latency-based routing: you create one record per AWS Region. Route 53 keeps measurements of network delay between user networks and Regions and answers with the Region that is lowest for that user. It optimizes speed, not location, and the winner can change as network conditions shift. Add health checks so an unhealthy Region is skipped.

Geolocation routing: you create records for continents, countries, or US states, plus a default record. Route 53 judges location from the resolver's IP address, or from part of the user's own address when the resolver passes it along. It answers with the most specific match.

Worked example: records exist for Germany pointing to Frankfurt, Europe pointing to Ireland, and a default pointing to Virginia. A user in Berlin matches Germany, so the answer is Frankfurt. A user in Spain has no country match but matches Europe, so the answer is Ireland. A user in Japan matches nothing specific and gets the default, Virginia.

Common mistake: omitting the default record. Users in unlisted locations then get no answer at all, and the site is unreachable for them. A second mistake is using latency routing to meet data-residency rules. Speed measurements can send a German user to another country, which in a running system is a compliance breach, not a slowdown.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming company uses Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing for stream.example.net. Its records are: US state California pointing to the Oregon Region, continent North America pointing to the Ohio Region, continent Asia pointing to the Tokyo Region, and a default record pointing to the Ireland Region. The answers are traced like this. A viewer in Los Angeles matches California, the most specific record, so the answer is Oregon. A viewer in Toronto: [missing step]. A viewer in Nairobi matches no state, country or continent record, so the answer is the default, Ireland. Which choice correctly completes the Toronto step?
choices: Canada has no country record, so Route 53 returns no answer and the site is unreachable for this viewer.
Toronto is closer to California than to Ireland, so Route 53 picks the nearest listed record and answers Oregon.
There is no record for Canada, but Toronto is in North America, so the most specific match is the continent record and the answer is Ohio.
There is no record for Canada, so Route 53 falls straight back to the default record and answers Ireland.
questions.why: Geolocation answers with the most specific record that matches, and when no country record exists the North America continent record still matches Toronto before the default is ever considered.

questions.prompt: A health-records startup must make sure patients in Brazil are always served from its São Paulo Region, because local rules forbid that data leaving the country. Patients elsewhere can use any Region. Which Route 53 routing policy fits this requirement?
choices: Geolocation routing, with a Brazil record pointing to São Paulo plus a default record for everyone else
Latency-based routing, with one record in each Region so Brazilian users reach the fastest one
Simple routing, with one record holding the São Paulo address and the other Regions' addresses
Latency-based routing with health checks, so an unhealthy São Paulo Region is skipped
questions.why: Geolocation routing decides by where the user is, so a Brazil record reliably sends Brazilian users to São Paulo, while latency routing follows network speed and could send them to another country, which would breach the residency rule.

questions.prompt: A small agency points shop.example.org at three web servers using one Route 53 simple routing record that holds all three IP addresses. One server crashes and stays down. What happens to DNS answers for shop.example.org?
choices: Route 53 stops answering for the name until the crashed server is fixed or removed.
All three addresses keep being returned, so some clients will still pick the crashed server.
Route 53 notices the failure and removes the crashed server's address from answers within one TTL.
Route 53 sends every user to the server with the lowest network delay, avoiding the crashed one.
questions.why: Simple routing cannot use health checks, so Route 53 keeps handing out every value in the record, including the dead server's address, and clients choose among them without knowing which one is down.

questions.prompt: A gaming company uses Route 53 latency-based routing with records in the Mumbai, Singapore and Sydney Regions, each with a health check. For players in Jakarta, measured delay is lowest to Singapore, then Sydney, then Mumbai. The Singapore health check starts failing. Which Region will Jakarta players be answered with?
choices: Singapore, because latency routing always returns the lowest-delay Region
Mumbai, because latency routing moves to the Region furthest from the failure
No answer at all, because the best Region for these players is unhealthy
Sydney, because the unhealthy Region is skipped and Sydney is the next lowest delay
questions.why: With health checks attached, latency routing skips the unhealthy Singapore record and answers with the healthy Region that has the lowest measured delay for those players, which is Sydney.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose simple, latency-based, or geolocation routing for a new global application, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Simple routing fits when there is one endpoint. It is easy, but it cannot use health checks, so if I list several addresses, a dead one still gets handed out. Latency-based routing fits when the goal is speed. I put one record per Region, and Route 53 answers with the Region measured as fastest for that user. The tradeoff is that it guarantees nothing about location, and the chosen Region can shift as network conditions change, so it is wrong for legal residency rules. Geolocation routing fits when the user's location must decide the answer, such as for compliance, local content, or licensing. Its limits are that location is inferred from the resolver's IP and may be imprecise. I must also add a default record, or users from unlisted places get no answer. With both latency and geolocation routing, I would attach health checks.
rubricPoints: Simple routing returns fixed values and cannot use health checks.
Latency routing picks the Region measured as fastest, not the closest or the legally required one.
Geolocation routing answers by user location, uses the most specific match, and needs a default record.
Data-residency or compliance needs call for geolocation, not latency routing.
Location is inferred from resolver or client subnet, so it can be imprecise.
Health checks let latency and geolocation records skip unhealthy endpoints.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among routing policies is an exam-style judgment that weighs speed, compliance, and failure behavior, and no current mission or planned engine exercises DNS routing directly.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers split the world into Regions, which are separate geographic areas, and each Region into Availability Zones, which are independent data-center sites a short distance apart. Designing across several zones means a single building losing power does not take your app down. Designing across several Regions protects against a whole area failing and puts servers closer to distant users, but it costs more and makes keeping data in step much harder. Think of a shop with two tills in one store (zones) versus a second store in another city (Regions). The second store survives a citywide blackout, but its stock records lag behind the first store's.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two copies of a database sit in buildings 5 km apart, or in cities 5,000 km apart. For which pair is it practical to confirm every write only after both copies have saved it, and why?
lessons.teach:
A Region is a separate geographic area where AWS runs its services. Each Region contains several Availability Zones (AZs). An AZ is one or more data centers with their own power, cooling and network, placed kilometres apart from the other AZs and linked to them by fast private fiber. A multi-AZ design runs copies of a workload in two or more AZs of one Region. A multi-Region design runs copies in two or more Regions.

Why it works: most failures are local. A power fault or flood hits one AZ, while a broad service outage or a regulatory event can hit a whole Region. AZs are close together, with round trips of a few milliseconds, so data can be replicated synchronously. Synchronous means a write is confirmed only once both copies hold it, so losing an AZ loses no committed data. Regions are far apart, so replication between them is usually asynchronous. The write is confirmed locally and shipped afterwards, which means a Region loss can drop the last few seconds of data. That acceptable loss window is the recovery point objective (RPO). The time allowed to get running again is the recovery time objective (RTO).

Worked example: an order service must lose no orders in a data-center fire and must be fast for US and European users. Step 1: place servers in three AZs behind a load balancer, a service that sends each request to a healthy server. Step 2: use a database with a synchronous standby in a second AZ, which is promoted automatically if the primary fails. Step 3: add a second Region near US users, with an asynchronous read copy, and route each user to the nearer Region. Step 4: state plainly that losing the whole European Region may cost seconds of orders, unless the budget pays for a design that writes to both Regions.

Common mistake: treating multi-Region as free extra availability. It roughly doubles infrastructure, adds cross-Region data transfer charges, and forces you to handle stale reads and conflicting writes. In a running system, failing over to a lagging Region silently loses recent data. Make multi-AZ the default, and add Regions only for a stated need: latency for distant users, Region-level disaster recovery, or data residency.

questions.prompt: A regional ticket-booking company has all its customers in one country. Its requirement: if one data center floods, no confirmed booking may be lost and the site must keep working. There is no data-residency rule and no stated need to survive the loss of a whole Region. The architect's plan so far: Step 1: run the booking web servers in two Availability Zones (AZs) of one Region, behind a load balancer that sends each request only to a healthy server. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: decide not to add a second Region, and write down why: users are local, and nothing in the requirement calls for Region-level recovery, so a second Region would mostly add cost and stale-read problems. Which choice best fills Step 2?
choices: Keep one database in the first AZ and copy a backup of it to a disk in that same AZ every night
Run the database with a synchronous standby in the second AZ that is promoted automatically if the primary fails
Add an asynchronous read copy of the database in a second Region and promote it if the first AZ floods
Run the database with a synchronous standby in a far-away second Region so that a write is confirmed only once both Regions hold it
questions.why: AZs are close enough for synchronous replication, so a write is confirmed only once the standby in the other AZ also holds it, and losing one AZ loses no confirmed bookings.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm writes its recovery targets for a tracking system: "After a disaster we can be offline for up to 45 minutes, and we can afford to lose at most the last 10 seconds of tracking updates." Which statement correctly names these targets?
choices: Both figures describe the RTO, because both are amounts of time
The RPO is 10 seconds, and the 45 minutes is how long replication between AZs is allowed to lag
The RPO is 45 minutes and the RTO is 10 seconds
The recovery point objective (RPO) is 10 seconds and the recovery time objective (RTO) is 45 minutes
questions.why: RPO is the acceptable window of lost data (10 seconds of updates), and RTO is the time allowed to get running again (45 minutes).

questions.prompt: A city council runs a permit-application website used only by its own residents. There is no data-residency rule and no requirement to survive a whole-Region outage. A manager asks for a second Region "just for extra availability." Which response best follows sound multi-AZ and multi-Region design?
choices: Decline any redundancy and run everything in one AZ to keep the budget low
Use a multi-AZ design as the default and add a Region only if a need appears, such as distant users, Region-level disaster recovery or data residency
Agree, because a second Region adds availability at almost no extra cost
Agree, but replicate synchronously between the Regions so no data can ever be lost
questions.why: Multi-Region roughly doubles infrastructure, adds cross-Region transfer charges and brings stale reads and write conflicts, so it should be added only for a stated need, with multi-AZ as the default.

questions.prompt: A payroll company runs its primary database in one Region and keeps an asynchronously replicated copy in a second Region. The whole primary Region suddenly becomes unavailable, and the team immediately switches all traffic to the copy. What is the most likely effect on data?
choices: The last few seconds of writes that had not yet been shipped are lost, often without any obvious error
No data is lost, because every write was confirmed only after the second Region held it
Data is lost only if a single AZ fails; a whole-Region outage never causes data loss
The failover is blocked until the primary Region returns, because asynchronous copies cannot be promoted
questions.why: With asynchronous replication a write is confirmed locally and shipped afterwards, so failing over to a lagging Region silently drops whatever had not arrived yet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would stop at multi-AZ and when you would go multi-Region, naming the main tradeoff you accept with each.
lessons.modelAnswer: An Availability Zone is an independent data-center site inside a Region, close enough to its neighbours to replicate data synchronously. That means a write isn't confirmed until both copies have it. So multi-AZ survives a building or power failure with no lost committed data and little added complexity. It's my default for anything needing high availability. The limit is that it doesn't help if the whole Region has a problem, and it doesn't help users on another continent. I'd go multi-Region only for a stated reason: distant users need low latency, the business needs to survive a Region-level disaster, or data residency rules require it. The tradeoff is real. Regions are far apart, so replication is usually asynchronous and a failover can lose recent writes, a nonzero RPO. I'd also roughly double infrastructure cost, pay cross-Region transfer charges, and have to handle stale or conflicting data.
rubricPoints: Defines Regions and Availability Zones and how they differ in distance and isolation.
Explains that AZ proximity allows synchronous replication with no committed data lost.
Explains that cross-Region replication is usually asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes.
Names concrete reasons to go multi-Region: latency for distant users, Region-level disaster recovery, or data residency.
Names the costs of multi-Region: extra infrastructure, data transfer charges, and data consistency complexity.
Treats multi-AZ as the sensible default for availability.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between multi-AZ and multi-Region is a tradeoff judgment best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios with conflicting latency, continuity and budget requirements.

lessons.plain: A service quota is a ceiling a cloud provider puts on how much of something one account can use in one place: how many virtual servers, how many functions running at once, how many API calls per second. Some ceilings can be raised on request (soft limits) and some cannot (hard limits). Think of a restaurant that only seats forty. A party of sixty needs to book ahead, split across two restaurants, or eat in shifts. Treating quotas as a design constraint means counting the seats before the party arrives, not when the guests are already at the door.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your new service gets 2,000 requests per second at peak, and each request keeps a function busy for about 0.8 seconds. Roughly how many copies of the function must run at the same moment, and what do you think happens if the account only allows 1,000?
lessons.teach:
A service quota (AWS also says service limit) is a maximum the provider enforces on a resource or action. Quotas usually apply per account and per Region, where a Region is a separate geographic set of data centers. A soft quota is a default that you can ask to raise through the Service Quotas tool or a support request. A hard quota is fixed, so you must design around it. Rate quotas cap how often you can call an API, and going over them causes throttling, meaning the provider rejects calls with an error until your rate drops.

Quotas exist to protect shared infrastructure and to stop a runaway script from creating thousands of costly resources. Because of that, a design that ignores them is not finished.

Here is a worked example. AWS Lambda, a managed run-your-code-on-demand service, has a default of 1,000 concurrent executions per account per Region. Concurrency is roughly requests per second multiplied by seconds per request. Step one: 2,000 requests per second multiplied by 0.8 seconds gives 1,600 concurrent executions. Step two: compare 1,600 with 1,000, which leaves a shortfall of 600. Step three: pick a response. You can request an increase with headroom, for example to 2,500. You can also shorten each request's duration, put a queue in front to smooth the bursts, or spread workloads across accounts so they do not share one pool. Step four: reserve concurrency for critical functions so that a noisy neighbor function in the same account cannot starve them.

A common mistake is raising quotas only in the primary Region. When disaster recovery fails over to the second Region, its untouched defaults throttle the recovery exactly when you need full capacity.

In a running system, an exceeded quota shows up as throttling errors, failed launches, or stuck deployments. Increases can take days to approve. So quotas belong in the capacity plan, quota usage should be monitored with alarms before it reaches the ceiling, and increases should be requested well before launch in every Region and account the design depends on.

questions.prompt: A photo-printing startup runs its order-resizing code on AWS Lambda (a managed service that runs your code on demand). It expects a peak of 1,200 requests per second, and each request takes 1.5 seconds. Its account uses the default quota of 1,000 concurrent executions per Region. The architect works through the check. Step 1: [missing]. Step 2: compare that figure with the 1,000 default and note that it exceeds the default. Step 3: request an increase to 2,500 in both the primary Region and the disaster-recovery Region, leaving headroom. Step 4: reserve concurrency for the payment function so the resizing function cannot starve it. What is Step 1?
choices: Multiply 1,200 by 1.5 and add 1,000 for the default pool, giving 2,800 concurrent executions.
Divide 1,200 by 1.5 to get 800 concurrent executions, which fits under the default.
Use the request rate alone, giving 1,200 concurrent executions, because duration does not affect concurrency.
Multiply 1,200 requests per second by 1.5 seconds to get 1,800 concurrent executions.
questions.why: Concurrency is roughly requests per second multiplied by seconds per request, so 1,200 × 1.5 = 1,800, which exceeds 1,000 and fits under the requested 2,500.

questions.prompt: An analytics firm finds that a quota blocking its design is a hard quota, not a soft one. What should the architect do?
choices: Change the design to work within the limit, for example by splitting the workload across several accounts so each stays under the fixed maximum.
Ignore it until production, because hard quotas only apply to test accounts.
Use the Service Quotas tool to raise the value, since that tool handles hard quotas automatically.
Open a support request asking for a larger value, because every quota can be raised if you wait long enough.
questions.why: A hard quota is fixed and cannot be raised on request, so you must design around it, for example by spreading load across accounts that each have their own limit.

questions.prompt: A retailer will launch a new service in 10 days. The service runs in two Regions across three accounts and needs more capacity than several default quotas allow. Quota increases can take days to approve. Which plan is best?
choices: Launch on the defaults and request increases once throttling errors appear in production.
Request increases only in the account with the most traffic, since quotas are shared across an organization.
Request increases now in every Region and account the design depends on, and set alarms on quota usage before it reaches the ceiling.
Request increases only in the primary Region now, and raise the second Region's quotas after a failover happens.
questions.why: Quotas usually apply per account and per Region, and approvals can take days, so you request increases early everywhere the design depends on them and monitor usage with alarms.

questions.prompt: During a large automated deployment, a logistics company's script makes many API calls in quick succession. Some calls fail with an error, then succeed when retried a few seconds later at a slower pace. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A hard quota on the total number of resources, which has been permanently reached.
The second Region's defaults were never raised, so the deployment failed over.
A rate quota was exceeded, so the provider is throttling the calls until the request rate drops.
A noisy neighbor function used up the reserved concurrency of the script.
questions.why: Rate quotas cap how often you can call an API, and going over them causes throttling, which rejects calls with an error until your rate drops, matching calls that succeed when slowed down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why service quotas must be part of the design rather than something fixed after launch. Use one calculation, and name one limit or tradeoff of simply asking for higher quotas.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every account has per-Region ceilings on resources and API rates. Soft ones can be raised, hard ones cannot, and when we hit either we get throttled or launches fail. So we size against them up front. For example, 2,000 requests per second at 0.8 seconds each needs about 1,600 concurrent Lambda executions, which is above the 1,000 default, so we request an increase with headroom before launch. We do it in the DR Region too, or failover will throttle. Asking for more is not a complete answer, though. Approval can take days, hard limits will not move, and a bigger shared pool still lets one noisy function starve another. That is why we also reserve concurrency for critical paths, smooth bursts with a queue, split workloads across accounts, and alarm on quota usage before it reaches the ceiling.
rubricPoints: Defines a quota as a per-account, per-Region ceiling and distinguishes soft from hard limits.
Shows a capacity calculation and compares the result with the quota.
States that exceeding a quota causes throttling or failed provisioning.
Notes that increases take time and must also cover DR Regions and other accounts.
Names a design alternative beyond raising the limit, such as queuing, reserved concurrency, or splitting across accounts.
Mentions monitoring quota usage with alarms.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose a function that is throttling at a concurrency ceiling during a traffic surge, which is exactly the quota constraint this lesson is about.

lessons.plain: An access pattern is the shape of how a system gets used: who reads or writes data, how often, how much at a time, how quickly they need an answer, and whether traffic is steady or arrives in bursts. Designing for access patterns means you write those shapes down first, then pick storage, compute and delivery to fit each one. Think of a restaurant. Takeaway coffee, a sit-down dinner and a wedding banquet all serve food, but each needs a different counter, kitchen layout and staffing. A large system usually has several patterns at once, so it often needs several differently built paths rather than one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fleet app has 50,000 vehicles each sending a small location update every 5 seconds, and 500 dispatchers viewing a live map. Which side do you think puts more load on the database, the writers or the readers, and would you build both sides the same way?
lessons.teach:
Designing for access patterns means describing each way data is used before choosing services. Describe each pattern by five things: read-to-write ratio, request rate, item size, latency need, and the lookup shape (fetch one item by its key, or search and join across many items). Add whether the load is steady or spiky, and whether a reader must see a write immediately (strong consistency) or can accept slightly old data (eventual consistency).

This works because each storage design is cheap for some shapes and expensive for others. A key-value store such as Amazon DynamoDB spreads items across partitions (separate storage slices) by a partition key, so known-key lookups stay fast at any scale, but ad hoc searches are costly. A relational database such as Amazon Aurora handles joins and flexible queries well, but scaling its writes is harder; read replicas (read-only copies) absorb extra reads. An in-memory cache such as Amazon ElastiCache serves repeated reads in under a millisecond. A content delivery network such as Amazon CloudFront serves the same content to many users from locations near them. A stream such as Amazon Kinesis Data Streams takes in a high, continuous flow of small writes in order.

Worked example. Step 1: 50,000 vehicles times one update every 5 seconds is 10,000 small writes per second, steady, keyed by vehicle. Step 2: 500 dispatchers refreshing every 2 seconds is 250 reads per second, each asking for every vehicle in a region, and seconds-old data is acceptable. Step 3: so writes go into a stream, a consumer keeps the latest position per vehicle in a key-value table, and a cache holds a precomputed map per region that readers hit. Two patterns, two paths.

A common mistake is picking the database first and fitting patterns to it later, or choosing a partition key many requests share, such as today's date. In a running system that hot key sends all traffic to one partition, which throttles (rejects excess requests) while the rest sit idle, and the app slows under load.

questions.prompt: A city parking company is designing a system for its street sensors. Step 1: 120,000 sensors each report occupancy once every 4 seconds. That is 120,000 / 4 = 30,000 small writes per second, steady, and each write is keyed by sensor ID. Step 2: A public app shows free spaces per city district. It gets about 2,000 reads per second, mostly asking for the same few district summaries, and data a few seconds old is acceptable. Step 3 is missing. Which design for Step 3 best fits the two patterns described?
choices: Write every reading straight into a relational database such as Aurora, and add read replicas so the app can run a join across sensors per district on each request.
Send writes into a stream such as Kinesis, have a consumer keep the latest state per sensor in a key-value table, and keep a precomputed summary per district in a cache that the app reads.
Store the latest state per sensor in a key-value table, and have the app search the whole table for every sensor in a district each time a user opens it.
Store readings in a key-value table such as DynamoDB with today's date as the partition key, and have the app read that day's items directly.
questions.why: A high, steady flow of small keyed writes suits a stream feeding a key-value table, while many repeated, slightly stale-tolerant reads of the same district summaries suit a precomputed cache, so each pattern gets its own path.

questions.prompt: An online bank requires that after a customer transfers money, the very next balance check must show the new amount, never the old one. Which access-pattern property is this requirement describing?
choices: Strong consistency, because a reader must see the write immediately
The lookup shape, because the balance is fetched by account key
Eventual consistency, because the balance will be correct soon after
A high read-to-write ratio, because balances are read more than written
questions.why: Needing a reader to see a write immediately, rather than accepting slightly old data, is the definition of strong consistency.

questions.prompt: A retail analytics team needs a store for orders, customers and products. Writes are modest, but analysts run many different queries that combine (join) the three kinds of data in ways nobody can predict in advance, and the number of these read queries is growing. Which design fits best?
choices: A key-value store such as DynamoDB keyed by order ID
A content delivery network such as CloudFront in front of the order data
A stream such as Kinesis Data Streams holding all orders in sequence
A relational database such as Aurora, with read replicas to absorb the growing reads
questions.why: Flexible joins and unpredictable queries are what a relational database handles well, and read-only replicas take on extra read load while writes stay modest.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery app stores orders in a key-value table and uses the order's status (such as "pending") as the partition key. During the dinner rush, most requests fail with throttling errors, yet monitoring shows most partitions almost idle. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The table needs more read replicas to spread the load across copies
The table is missing a content delivery network in front of it
The app is using eventual consistency, which causes throttling under load
The partition key is shared by most requests, so traffic piles onto one hot partition that rejects the excess while others sit idle
questions.why: When many requests share the same partition key value, they all land on one partition, which throttles while the remaining partitions go unused.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a new feature's requirements into an architecture by starting from its access patterns, and name one tradeoff that comes from splitting read and write paths.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before picking any service, I list each way the data is used: how many reads versus writes, the request rate, item size, how fast an answer must come back, whether traffic is steady or bursty, and whether readers need the very latest write. I also note the lookup shape, a single item by key or a search across many. Then I match each pattern to a fit: key lookups at huge scale to a key-value table with a well-spread partition key, flexible queries to a relational database with read replicas, repeated hot reads to a cache or CDN, and continuous high-volume writes to a stream. Often that means separate read and write paths. The tradeoff is that readers see eventually consistent, slightly stale data, and I now run and pay for more components, so I only split when the patterns really differ.
rubricPoints: Describes access patterns before choosing services.
Names key dimensions such as read/write ratio, rate, size, latency, burstiness and consistency.
Matches patterns to fitting storage types like key-value, relational with replicas, cache or stream.
Mentions partition key choice and the hot-key throttling risk.
States a tradeoff of split paths, such as staleness or added complexity and cost.

suggested.rationale: This design exercise has the learner build separate write-ingest and map-read paths for very different access patterns, which is exactly this objective.

lessons.plain: An elastic architecture is a system that grows when demand rises and shrinks when demand falls, on its own, so you pay roughly for what you use. It is like a restaurant that can call in extra staff for the Friday rush and send them home at 9 pm, rather than paying a full crew all week. Designing it from business objectives means you start with what the business actually needs. That means how traffic changes over a day or a year, how fast pages must load, and what the budget allows. From that, you pick which parts must stretch, how quickly they must stretch, and how far.
lessons.guessPrompt: A ticket website normally gets a few hundred visitors a minute, but when a big concert goes on sale it gets fifty times that for about half an hour. If you bought enough fixed servers for the peak, what would go wrong for the business the rest of the year, and what would go wrong if you bought only enough for a normal day?
lessons.teach:
Elasticity is a system's ability to add and remove capacity automatically as demand changes, so supply tracks load. You design it backwards from business objectives: the demand pattern (steady, daily cycle, sudden spikes), the performance target (for example, 95% of requests answered under one second), and the budget.

It works through horizontal scaling, meaning adding more identical copies of a component rather than making one copy bigger. Copies are only interchangeable if each tier is stateless: it keeps no user session or data on its own disk, and stores that state in a shared store such as a managed cache or database. A load balancer spreads requests across the copies. An Auto Scaling group is the AWS feature that keeps a fleet of virtual servers between a minimum and maximum size. A managed queue such as Amazon SQS holds work until a worker can take it. Serverless compute such as AWS Lambda runs code per request and can scale to zero.

Worked example: the ticket site has 200 requests per second normally and 10,000 for 30 minutes at an on-sale. The objective is sub-second pages and no lost orders, on a modest budget. Step 1: make the web tier stateless and put sessions in a shared cache, so copies can be added freely. Step 2: set the minimum fleet for normal load and the maximum for the peak. Because the sale time is known, pre-scale before it starts. Step 3: put order submission behind a queue so a burst is absorbed and processed at a steady rate. Step 4: check that the database can handle the peak too, using read replicas or a service that scales on demand. Off-peak, the fleet shrinks back and cost falls.

A common mistake is scaling only the front tier. The extra web servers then overwhelm a fixed-size database, or capacity arrives minutes after a spike has begun. In a running system, that shows up as timeouts and dropped orders at exactly the moment of highest revenue. Elasticity is only as good as the least elastic component in the request path.

questions.prompt:
A university's course-registration portal normally gets about 50 requests per second. When registration opens at 9:00 on a date announced weeks ahead, it jumps to about 6,000 requests per second for roughly 20 minutes. The goals are pages under 1.5 seconds, no lost registrations, and a small budget. The architect works through the design.

Step 1: Move student session data out of each web server's memory and into a managed cache, so every web server copy is interchangeable.

Step 2: ???

Step 3: Put registration submissions into a managed queue, so workers process them at a steady rate instead of all at once.

Step 4: Make sure the student-records database can handle the peak, using read replicas sized for the 9:00 load.

After the rush, the fleet shrinks and cost falls. Which choice is the missing Step 2?
choices: Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum for normal load and its maximum for the peak, and pre-scale before 9:00 because the time is known.
Leave scaling fully reactive, so new servers are added only after CPU load rises once registration has opened.
Replace the web fleet with one much larger virtual server that can handle 6,000 requests per second on its own.
Keep the Auto Scaling group's minimum at the peak size all year, so capacity is always there for the 9:00 rush.
questions.why: Sizing the minimum for normal load and the maximum for the peak keeps costs low off-peak, and pre-scaling for a known start time means capacity is ready before the spike instead of minutes after it begins.

questions.prompt: An online garden-supply shop keeps each customer's shopping cart on the local disk of whichever web server first handled that customer. During a sale, the team adds more servers behind the load balancer. Customers then start reporting carts that empty or change between clicks. Which change best fixes this so the web tier can scale horizontally?
choices: Make each web server larger so fewer servers are needed and carts stay on one machine.
Store cart data in a shared managed cache or database, so each web server copy is stateless and interchangeable.
Remove the load balancer so each customer always connects to the same server directly.
Raise the Auto Scaling group's maximum size so more servers can hold more carts.
questions.why: Horizontal scaling only works when copies are interchangeable, which requires a stateless tier with user state kept in a shared store rather than on one server's disk.

questions.prompt: A small nonprofit runs a feature that resizes photos volunteers upload. Most of the day nothing is uploaded. A few times a week, without warning, hundreds of photos arrive within minutes. The budget is very tight, and resized photos may take a minute or two to appear. Which design best matches these business objectives?
choices: One large virtual server that runs all day and is sized for the biggest burst seen so far.
Upload events placed on a managed queue such as Amazon SQS, processed by serverless functions such as AWS Lambda that scale up during bursts and down to zero when idle.
A fleet of virtual servers in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of four, so capacity is always ready.
A fixed group of servers sized for the average load, with uploads rejected when they are busy.
questions.why: A queue absorbs the unpredictable bursts without losing work, and serverless compute that scales to zero means the nonprofit pays almost nothing during the long idle periods, which fits a tight budget and a relaxed delay target.

questions.prompt: A streaming-sports company configured its web tier to scale from 4 to 40 servers during big matches, and the servers do scale out on time. Yet during the last final, users saw timeouts and failed sign-ins at the peak. The user-accounts database runs on a single fixed-size instance with no replicas. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Auto Scaling group's maximum of 40 servers was too low, so more web servers would have fixed it.
Horizontal scaling only works for steady demand, so a daily-cycle pattern is the wrong fit for it.
The fixed-size database is the least elastic component in the request path, and the extra web servers overwhelmed it.
The web servers scaled out too quickly, and the load balancer cannot handle more than four servers.
questions.why: Elasticity is only as good as the least elastic component, so scaling only the front tier pushes more load onto a fixed-size database, which then causes timeouts at the busiest moment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a business's traffic pattern, latency target and budget into an elastic design, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on elasticity.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the business numbers: what normal load looks like, how high and how sudden the peaks are, the latency we promised, and what we can spend. Then I make every tier that must stretch stateless, so any copy can serve any request. Sessions and data go in shared managed stores, and a load balancer spreads the traffic. I set a minimum capacity that covers baseline load and a maximum that covers the peak. I put a queue in front of slow work so bursts are buffered instead of dropped. Then I walk the whole request path, including the database, to find the piece that cannot grow. The tradeoff is that scaling is not instant. New capacity takes time to arrive, so for sudden or scheduled spikes I either keep extra headroom, which costs money, or scale ahead of time. Elasticity also stops at the least elastic component.
rubricPoints: Starts from business inputs: demand pattern, performance target and budget.
Explains horizontal scaling and why tiers must be stateless, with state in shared stores.
Mentions a load balancer and minimum and maximum capacity sized to baseline and peak.
Uses buffering such as a queue to absorb bursts.
Checks every tier, including the database, for a non-elastic bottleneck.
Names a tradeoff such as scaling lag versus the cost of headroom.

suggested.rationale: The ingest design exercise has the learner shape a read and write path around variable load and stated objectives, which is the core of designing for elasticity.

lessons.plain: Most slow systems are slow because many requests line up for one busy component, usually the database. Three tools move that pressure elsewhere. A cache keeps copies of frequently asked answers close by, so nobody has to fetch them again. A buffer is a waiting line that accepts work instantly and hands it to the slow component at a pace it can manage. A replica is an extra copy of the database that only answers reads. Think of a busy library: a cache is the shelf of popular books by the door, a buffer is the returns bin, and a replica is a second reading room holding the same books.
lessons.guessPrompt: A product page is read 50,000 times a minute but its price changes only once an hour, and every read currently goes to the database. What would you put in front of the database, and what could go wrong with your choice?
lessons.teach:
Caching, buffering, and replicas are three ways to meet a performance objective, a measurable target such as "95% of reads answered in under 50 ms", by keeping load away from a component that cannot keep up.

A cache stores recent results in fast memory. Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache (Redis or Memcached), DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a cache built for DynamoDB, and Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network, a set of edge locations that hold copies of content near users. A cache hit means the answer was found in the cache; a miss means the source had to be asked. The TTL (time to live) is how long a cached copy is trusted before it expires. This works because most traffic asks for a small set of popular items.

A buffer is a queue or stream that absorbs bursts. Amazon SQS is a managed message queue, and Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a managed ordered stream. Producers write quickly; consumers drain at a steady rate, so a spike becomes a backlog instead of an outage. Buffering suits work the caller does not need answered immediately.

A read replica is a copy of a database, for example in Amazon RDS or Aurora, that receives changes from the primary and serves only reads. Replication is usually asynchronous, so replicas trail the primary by some replica lag.

Worked example: a fleet map reads vehicle positions 20,000 times a second while 2,000 vehicles write every 5 seconds. Step one, put writes on a stream so the database sees an even load. Step two, cache each vehicle's latest position with a 2-second TTL, so most map reads become hits. Step three, send heavy reporting queries to a read replica so the primary keeps write capacity.

Common mistake: sending a read that must reflect the user's own write to a replica or a long-TTL cache. The user saves a change, refreshes, and sees the old value. In a running system this looks like data loss, and it triggers duplicate submissions. Route read-after-write paths to the primary, and choose TTLs from how stale the business can tolerate.

questions.prompt: A university is designing its course registration system. Registration opens at 9:00, and requests spike to 30,000 a minute while the database can safely process about 3,000 a minute. Course descriptions change only once per term. A student who has just enrolled expects to see the new course on their 'My schedule' page immediately. Step one: each registration request is written to Amazon SQS (a managed message queue), and the student gets a 'request received' message while workers drain the queue at a steady 3,000 a minute, so the spike becomes a backlog instead of an outage. Step two: course descriptions are cached at the edge with Amazon CloudFront (a content delivery network) using a long TTL, because a stale description for a few hours is acceptable. Step three is missing: where should the 'My schedule' page read from right after the student's enrolment is processed?
choices: From a read replica, so the primary database keeps its capacity for processing registrations
From an ElastiCache copy of the schedule with a one-hour TTL, so repeated refreshes are cheap
From the primary database, because this read must reflect the student's own write
From the SQS queue, by reading the student's registration message back before it is processed
questions.why: A read that must show the user's own change belongs on the primary, because replicas trail by replica lag and a long-TTL cache can serve the old schedule.

questions.prompt: A retailer caches each product's stock count in Amazon ElastiCache (a managed in-memory cache) with a TTL of 10 minutes. What does that TTL setting control?
choices: How many requests per second the cache can answer before it starts missing
How long a cached stock count is trusted before it expires and the source must be asked again
How far the cached value is allowed to trail the primary before replication is paused
How long a request waits for the database before the cache gives up and returns an error
questions.why: TTL (time to live) is the length of time a cached copy is trusted before it expires, after which the next request is a miss that goes to the source.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing app creates thumbnails for every upload. Uploads normally run at 200 a minute but jump to 8,000 a minute after a popular event, and the thumbnail workers can only handle about 1,000 a minute. Users are happy to see thumbnails appear a few minutes later. Which design best keeps the service up during the spikes?
choices: Write each thumbnail job to a managed queue such as Amazon SQS and let workers drain it at a steady rate
Send every upload directly to the workers and return an error when they are busy
Add read replicas to the database so the workers can read the original photos faster
Cache finished thumbnails in Amazon CloudFront with a long TTL so the workers do less work
questions.why: The work does not need an immediate answer, so a buffer absorbs the burst as a backlog that workers drain at their own pace instead of letting the spike cause an outage.

questions.prompt: An architect wants to add a cache in front of a database to lower read latency. For which workload is a cache likely to help the least?
choices: An audit tool where each query looks up a different, randomly chosen old record that is rarely requested twice
A news site where most readers open the same twenty headline stories each hour
A game leaderboard page that thousands of players refresh to view the same top 100 scores
A product catalogue where a few bestsellers receive the large majority of page views
questions.why: Caching works because most traffic asks for a small set of popular items; when nearly every read is for a different item, almost every request is a miss and the source still does the work.
