Route every finding to an email inbox so humans decide each case before anything changes
Keep auto-patch-and-reboot for everything, but only run scans once a month
questions.why: Tiering keeps the exposure window short for dangerous findings without trading them for availability incidents. Emailing everything would bury the critical findings under minor ones.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which vulnerability findings get a fully automatic fix, which get automatic containment plus human approval, and which just get queued. Name one tradeoff of automating too aggressively.
lessons.modelAnswer: I don't sort findings by severity score alone. I combine severity with whether an exploit exists, whether the resource is reachable from the internet, and how critical the workload is. Findings are collected in one place, like Security Hub, and an event rule such as EventBridge routes them by those attributes. Low-impact fixes on non-critical systems, like patching a dev instance, are fully automatic in a maintenance window. Critical, exposed findings on production get immediate automatic containment, for example moving the instance into a locked-down security group and snapshotting it, then a human approves the real patch. Low-risk, unreachable findings just go into a backlog. The tradeoff: automating aggressive actions like reboot-and-patch on production can cause outages, which hurts availability and makes teams switch automation off. Too little automation leaves dangerous holes open longer.
rubricPoints: Risk combines severity, exploitability, exposure, and business criticality, not score alone.
Findings are aggregated centrally and routed by rules to different responses.
Safe, low-impact fixes can be fully automatic.
Critical production findings get automatic containment with human approval for disruptive fixes.
Over-aggressive automation risks outages; too little leaves long exposure windows.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through exam-style scenarios that weigh severity, exposure, and workload criticality to pick the right automated response, which no current mission or planned engine directly exercises.

lessons.plain: A patch and update process is the routine an organization follows to keep every server, machine image and managed database up to date with security fixes and software updates, without breaking what customers use. Think of servicing a fleet of delivery vans. You do not pull every van off the road on the same morning. You service a few at a time, during quiet hours, try any new part on one van first, and keep a logbook showing which vans are done. A good patch process works the same way: it is scheduled, staged, limited in how much changes at once, and recorded.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run 40 identical web servers behind a load balancer, and a critical security update needs a reboot. Would you patch all 40 at once, one at a time, or some other way? What could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
A patch and update process is the repeatable way updates reach every server, image and managed service on a schedule, with proof. In AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager it has four parts. A patch baseline is a rule set naming which updates are approved, such as critical security fixes approved automatically seven days after release. A patch group is a tag that ties instances to a baseline. A maintenance window is a recurring time slot when changes may run. Rate controls cap how many machines change at once (concurrency) and halt the run after too many failures (error threshold). Compliance reporting then lists machines missing approved patches.

Why it works: the approval delay lets an update prove itself in rings, meaning dev first, then staging, then production, so a bad patch is caught before customers see it. Rate controls keep enough healthy capacity serving traffic.

Worked example: 40 web servers tagged web-prod. The baseline approves fixes released seven or more days ago, which dev received last week. The window opens at 02:00. Concurrency of 25% means 10 instances patch and reboot while 30 keep serving. Error threshold 2: if two fail, the run stops. Afterwards compliance shows 40 of 40 compliant.

The alternative is immutable patching. Instead of changing live servers, a pipeline such as EC2 Image Builder builds and tests a new patched machine image each month, and an Auto Scaling group replaces old instances with it. There is no drift between servers, and rollback means launching the previous image. For managed services such as Amazon RDS, a managed database, the provider applies engine patches; your job is choosing its maintenance window and upgrade settings.

Common mistake: patching the whole fleet in one window with no approval delay or rate control, so one faulty kernel update takes every server down together. Patching by hand is the other trap: it leaves no compliance record, so nobody can prove what is still exposed. Unpatched fleets invite known exploits, and uncontrolled patching causes outages; a good process trades a short delay for both safety and proof.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking company runs 60 API servers tagged api-prod. Its patch baseline (the rule set naming which updates are approved) approves security fixes 10 days after release, and the staging servers already received this month's fixes last week. The maintenance window (the recurring time slot when changes may run) opens at 03:00 on Sunday. Step 1: at 03:00, Patch Manager selects every instance whose patch group tag, api-prod, ties it to that baseline. Step 2: concurrency (the cap on how many machines change at once) is set to 20%, so ______. Step 3: the error threshold is 3, so if three servers fail to patch, the run halts. Step 4: afterwards, compliance reporting lists any server still missing an approved fix. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: all 60 servers patch at once, and the run stops if 20% of them fail
20 servers patch and reboot at a time while 40 keep serving traffic
48 servers patch and reboot at a time while 12 keep serving traffic
12 servers patch and reboot at a time while 48 keep serving traffic
questions.why: 20% of 60 is 12, so 12 servers change at once and the other 48 stay healthy to serve traffic.

questions.prompt: In AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, what is a patch group?
choices: A tag that ties a set of instances to a particular patch baseline
A rule set that names which updates are approved and after how long
A limit on how many machines may change at once during a run
A recurring time slot during which patching is allowed to run
questions.why: A patch group is the tag that links instances to a baseline; the other choices describe a maintenance window, a patch baseline and a concurrency rate control.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm patches immutably: each month EC2 Image Builder (a pipeline that builds and tests machine images) produces a new patched image, and an Auto Scaling group (a service that keeps a fleet of instances running) replaces old instances with it. After this month's rollout, the order-tracking app starts throwing errors. What is the quickest correct rollback?
choices: Lower the error threshold and run the same image again
Have the Auto Scaling group launch instances from the previous month's image
Wait for compliance reporting to identify which servers are faulty
Log in to each instance and uninstall this month's updates by hand
questions.why: With immutable patching, servers are never changed in place, so rollback means launching the previous known-good image.

questions.prompt: At an online retailer, administrators log in to each of 70 servers once a month and install updates by hand. An auditor asks which servers are still missing last week's critical security fix. What is the main weakness this exposes?
choices: The servers should be moved to Amazon RDS so the provider patches them
There is no compliance record, so nobody can prove which servers are still exposed
Manual patching always causes more downtime than automated patching
The admins are patching too many servers at once without concurrency limits
questions.why: Hand patching leaves no compliance report, so the team cannot show which machines still lack the approved fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design patching for a production fleet so that it is both safe and provable, and name one tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd define a patch baseline that auto-approves critical and security updates after a short delay, say seven days, and tag instances into patch groups per environment. Dev patches first, staging next, production last, so a bad update shows up in a lower ring. Production runs in a maintenance window during low traffic, with concurrency limited to about a quarter of the fleet and an error threshold that stops the run if a few instances fail, so the load balancer always has healthy servers. Compliance reports prove which machines are patched. Where possible I'd move to immutable images: build and test a patched image monthly, then replace instances, which removes drift and makes rollback simple. For managed databases I'd just set the provider's maintenance window. The tradeoff is time: the approval delay and rings leave a window where a known vulnerability is still unpatched in production, so truly urgent fixes need a faster, approved emergency path.
rubricPoints: Uses a baseline with approval rules and a delay so updates are tested before production.
Stages updates through rings such as dev, staging, then production.
Limits blast radius with maintenance windows, concurrency limits and an error threshold.
Produces compliance reporting as proof of patch status.
Mentions immutable image replacement or provider-managed patching as an alternative.
Names a tradeoff such as exposure time during the delay versus outage risk.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine runs a patch rollout, so reasoning through an exam-style fleet scenario about baselines, rings, rate controls and immutable images builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: A backup process is the routine that makes copies of your data on a schedule, keeps them for as long as the rules say, protects them from people who should not see or delete them, and proves you can get the data back. Think of a law firm's records room. Some files must be kept seven years, some must be shredded after two. Some sit in a locked cabinet, and a copy goes to a second building in case of fire. Designing backups means writing those rules down first and then letting a system follow them automatically, every day.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital must keep patient records backed up for seven years, and nobody, not even an administrator, may delete them early. If an attacker steals an administrator's password, what would you want to be true about where and how those backups are stored?
lessons.teach:
A backup process turns three kinds of requirement into automatic rules. Retention is how long each copy must be kept, and sometimes the latest date it may be kept. Sensitivity is how secret the data is, which decides encryption and who may read or restore it. Regulatory requirements are outside rules, such as finance or health law, that may demand a fixed retention period, copies that cannot be altered, or copies kept in a particular country.

On AWS, the managed service is AWS Backup. A backup plan is a policy saying how often to copy and how long to keep each copy. A backup vault is a protected container that holds the copies, called recovery points, encrypted with a key from AWS KMS, the managed key service. Vault Lock makes a vault write-once. In governance mode, specially permitted users can still change it. In compliance mode, nobody can delete copies early once a short grace period ends, not even the account owner. Through AWS Organizations, a backup policy can push the same plan to every account. Lifecycle rules can move older copies to cheaper cold storage, which has a minimum stay.

Here is a worked example, traced step by step. The rule is that patient data must be kept seven years, must not be alterable, and must survive the loss of a whole region. First, tag the health databases so the plan selects them by tag. Second, schedule daily backups and keep each one for seven years, moving copies to cold storage after 90 days to cut cost. Third, encrypt the vault with a customer-managed key whose key policy limits who can decrypt. Fourth, copy each backup to a vault in a separate backup account in a second region. Fifth, lock that vault in compliance mode. Sixth, run scheduled restore tests and keep the reports as audit evidence.

A common mistake is treating snapshots or replicas in the same account as backups. A compromised administrator or ransomware can delete all of them at once. Another mistake is keeping data longer than the law allows. In a running system, either mistake turns one incident into permanent data loss or a compliance breach.

questions.prompt: An online retailer in the EU stores order records that contain customer home addresses. Privacy law says each record must be kept for at least 1 year and for no longer than 3 years. Only the security team may restore the data, and every copy must stay inside the EU. The architect builds the AWS Backup process like this. Step 1: tag the order databases so the backup plan selects them by tag. Step 2: encrypt the backup vault with a customer-managed AWS KMS key whose key policy lets only the security team's role decrypt. Step 3: copy each backup to a vault in a second region that is also inside the EU. Step 4 is missing: set the retention rule in the backup plan. Which retention rule correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Keep each copy for 3 years and then let it expire, which meets both the minimum and the maximum
Keep every copy forever in a vault locked in compliance mode so that no one can ever delete it
Keep each copy for 7 years, because keeping data longer is always the safer choice for an audit
Keep each copy for 1 year in the vault, but keep same-account snapshots of the databases with no end date
questions.why: A 3-year retention keeps each copy at least the required 1 year and deletes it before the 3-year legal limit, while longer or unlimited retention breaks the rule on the latest date data may be kept.

questions.prompt: A law firm stores case files in a backup vault. Its regulator requires that no one can delete a backup copy before its 10-year retention ends, not even the firm's AWS account owner. Which setting meets this requirement?
choices: A lifecycle rule that moves copies to cold storage after 30 days
Vault Lock in governance mode, so that only specially permitted users can change the vault
Vault Lock in compliance mode, which blocks early deletion by anyone once the grace period ends
A customer-managed KMS key whose key policy limits who can decrypt
questions.why: Compliance mode makes the vault write-once for everyone, including the account owner, after a short grace period, while governance mode still lets permitted users make changes.

questions.prompt: A startup says its customer database is safely backed up. It takes hourly disk snapshots and runs a database replica, all in the same AWS account as production. What is the most serious weakness in this setup?
choices: An attacker or ransomware that gains admin rights in that one account can delete the database, the snapshots and the replica together
A replica in the same account is always encrypted with the wrong kind of key
Hourly snapshots are taken too often, so storage costs will grow faster than the business needs
Snapshots cannot be restored unless they were first moved to cold storage
questions.why: Snapshots and replicas in the same account share one point of failure, so a single compromise can wipe every copy and turn one incident into permanent data loss.

questions.prompt: A media company runs 40 AWS accounts. Each team built its own backup plan, so schedules and retention periods differ between accounts, and an auditor wants one consistent plan everywhere. What is the best way to apply the same plan to every account?
choices: Create a backup policy in AWS Organizations that pushes the same backup plan to all the accounts
Add lifecycle rules in each account to move older copies to cheaper cold storage
Write one KMS key policy that limits who can decrypt backups in each account
Lock each team's vault in governance mode so that the existing plans can no longer change
questions.why: A backup policy set through AWS Organizations applies the same plan across every account, while vault locks, lifecycle rules and key policies do not make the schedules and retention periods match.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design backups for a workload with strict retention and regulatory rules, and name one tradeoff of locking backups so they cannot be deleted.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the rules, not the tools. For each data set I write down how long copies must be kept, any date by which they must be deleted, how sensitive the data is, and what the regulator demands. Then I encode that in an AWS Backup plan that picks resources by tag, sets the schedule and retention, and moves older copies to cold storage. Copies are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key that only a small group can use. I copy them to a vault in a separate backup account in another region, so one compromised account or one failed region cannot wipe everything. I lock that vault in compliance mode for immutability, and I run regular restore tests as proof for auditors. The tradeoff is that a compliance lock really is permanent. If I set retention too long, I pay to store that data and cannot delete it early, even if a privacy rule later requires deletion.
rubricPoints: Starts from retention, sensitivity, and regulatory requirements before choosing tools.
Uses a backup plan with a schedule, retention, and lifecycle, selecting resources by tag or by organization-wide policy.
Encrypts backups with a controlled key and limits who can restore them.
Keeps an isolated copy in another account and region, protected by a vault lock.
Proves recoverability with regular restore tests that serve as audit evidence.
Names a tradeoff, such as a compliance-mode lock being irreversible, or the cost and minimum stay of cold storage.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about mapping stated business and legal rules to the right mix of retention, encryption, isolation, and locking, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: Business people describe what they want in everyday terms: the shop should be fast, the app should never be down, and customers should be happy. Engineers cannot build toward or check words like those. This skill turns those wishes into numbers you can measure. An example is "95 out of 100 checkouts finish in under one second, measured every month." Think of a doctor turning "I feel unwell" into temperature, pulse and blood pressure. Once the goal is a number, everyone can see whether it is being met. They can also see when it is slipping and which fix would matter most.
lessons.guessPrompt: A manager says "our checkout page must feel fast." If you could track only one number to tell whether that promise is kept, what would you measure, and why might the average page load time be a poor choice?
lessons.teach:
A metric is any measured number, such as request count, latency or CPU use. Latency is the time a request takes. A service level indicator (SLI) is a metric chosen because it reflects what users actually experience. Two common SLIs are the share of requests that succeed and the share that finish within a time limit. A service level objective (SLO) is your internal target for an SLI over a time window. A service level agreement (SLA) is a promise to customers, often with penalties such as service credits if it is broken. A key performance indicator (KPI) is a business outcome the organization tracks, such as completed orders per hour or conversion rate.

This chain works because each layer links to the one above it. The business cares about the KPI, users feel the SLI, and engineers can act on the SLI.

Here is a worked example. The requirement is "Checkout must be reliable and fast because lost checkouts lose revenue." Step 1: name the KPI, which is completed checkouts per hour. Step 2: pick SLIs, which are the percentage of checkout requests that return success, and the 99th percentile latency. The 99th percentile is the time that 99% of requests beat. Step 3: set SLOs, which are 99.9% success and p99 under 800 ms over 30 days. Step 4: set the SLA looser than the SLO, for example 99.5%, so you get warned before you owe credits. Step 5: work out the error budget, which is the allowed failure. At 99.9% over 30 days, that is about 43 minutes of bad service. When the budget is nearly spent, reliability work takes priority over new features.

A common mistake is tracking averages or server metrics like CPU instead of user-facing percentiles. An average of 300 ms can hide the 2% of customers who wait 10 seconds. A server at 40% CPU can still be failing requests.

In a running system, a wrong metric means alarms stay quiet while customers leave. It also means improvement work goes to the wrong component.

questions.prompt: A ride-booking company has this requirement: "Riders must be able to book a ride quickly, because failed bookings send riders to competitors." The team works through it. Step 1, the KPI (a business outcome the company tracks): rides booked per hour. Step 2, the SLIs (service level indicators, metrics chosen because they reflect what users feel): the percentage of booking requests that succeed, and p99 booking latency (the time that 99% of requests beat). Step 3, the SLOs (internal targets for each SLI over a time window): 99.95% success and p99 under 1.2 seconds, measured over 30 days. Step 4 is missing: choose the success target for the SLA, the customer promise that carries service credits if broken. Step 5: the error budget at 99.95% over 30 days is about 22 minutes of bad service. Which choice best completes Step 4?
choices: Promise 99.9% success, looser than the SLO, so the team is warned before credits are owed
Promise that average server CPU stays below 70%, since that is easy to measure
Promise 99.95% success, exactly matching the SLO so there is only one number to track
Promise 99.99% success, so customers see a stronger commitment than the internal target
questions.why: An SLA set looser than the SLO means a missed SLO acts as an early warning before the customer promise is broken and credits are owed.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore tracks four numbers. Which one is a KPI (key performance indicator, a business outcome the organization tracks)?
choices: The p99 latency of the search page
Average CPU use on the web servers
Books sold per day
A target of 99.9% successful page loads over 30 days
questions.why: Books sold per day is a business outcome; p99 latency is an SLI, CPU is a plain server metric, and the 99.9% target over a window is an SLO.

questions.prompt: A payments API has an SLO of 99.95% successful requests over a 30-day window. Roughly how large is its error budget, the amount of bad service it may have before missing the SLO? (30 days is 43,200 minutes.)
choices: About 43 minutes
About 22 minutes
About 4 minutes
About 216 minutes
questions.why: The allowed failure is 0.05% of 43,200 minutes, which is about 21.6 minutes, roughly half the 43 minutes allowed at 99.9%.

questions.prompt: A travel site's dashboard shows average page latency of 250 ms and web servers at 35% CPU, and no alarms have fired. Yet completed bookings per hour have dropped and customers complain about slow, failing searches. What is the most likely problem with the monitoring?
choices: The SLA is set looser than the SLO, which hides failures from the team
The average latency target is too strict and should be raised to 500 ms
The servers need more CPU, because 35% is too low to serve traffic well
It watches averages and server metrics instead of user-facing SLIs such as success rate and p99 latency
questions.why: An average can hide a slow minority of customers and a lightly loaded server can still fail requests, so only success-rate and percentile SLIs reveal what users actually feel.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn the requirement "the order API must always be available" into an SLI, SLO, SLA and KPI. Say why "always" cannot literally be the target, and name one tradeoff of setting the target very high.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I would ask what the business actually loses when the API fails. The answer is orders, so the KPI is completed orders per hour. The SLI should reflect what users feel: the percentage of order requests that succeed, measured at the load balancer or client and not from server CPU. "Always" cannot be the target because nothing is 100% available, and chasing 100% leaves no room for deploys or failures. So I would set an internal SLO, say 99.95% success over 30 days. The customer-facing SLA would be looser, perhaps 99.9%, so we notice slipping before credits are owed. The gap between 100% and the SLO is our error budget, roughly 22 minutes a month. The tradeoff is that every extra nine costs much more. It means more redundancy, more regions and slower releases, so the target should match what lost orders actually cost.
rubricPoints: Starts from the business outcome and names a KPI tied to it.
Chooses a user-facing SLI such as success rate or percentile latency, not an average or CPU.
Distinguishes the internal SLO from the looser external SLA with penalties.
Explains that 100% is unrealistic and introduces an error budget.
Names the cost tradeoff of higher targets: more redundancy, money or slower delivery.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning from a vague business statement to defensible numbers, which is best practiced by working through exam-style scenarios and then explaining the choices.

lessons.plain: Imagine a restaurant that can call in extra cooks when the queue grows and send them home when it is quiet. Auto scaling does that for servers: it adds or removes machines automatically as demand changes. An instance fleet is like hiring from several agencies at once, mixing full-price staff with cheap temporary help, so you are never stuck if one agency runs short. A placement group decides where the machines physically sit. You can pack them tightly together so they talk fast, or spread them apart so one broken rack cannot take them all down. Together these choices balance speed, cost and resilience.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run 20 servers that constantly exchange data for a scientific simulation and need the fastest possible connection between them. Would you place them physically close together or spread across separate hardware, and what risk does your choice create?
lessons.teach:
Three tools shape compute performance at scale. An Auto Scaling group (ASG) is a managed set of virtual servers (EC2 instances) that AWS keeps between a minimum and maximum count, built from a launch template, a saved recipe of machine image, size and network settings. A scaling policy says when to resize: target tracking holds a metric, such as average CPU at 50 percent; step scaling adds set amounts as an alarm crosses thresholds; scheduled scaling changes capacity at known times; predictive scaling forecasts from past daily patterns and adds capacity before demand arrives.

An instance fleet, built with a mixed instances policy on the ASG or with EC2 Fleet, lets one group use several instance types and purchase options: On-Demand (full price, reliably available) and Spot (spare capacity at a deep discount that AWS can reclaim with a two-minute warning). Listing many interchangeable types with a capacity-optimized allocation strategy, which picks the Spot pools least likely to be reclaimed, keeps the fleet running when one type runs short.

A placement group controls physical location. Cluster packs instances close inside one Availability Zone (an isolated data center group) for the lowest latency, but they share failure risk. Spread puts each instance on distinct hardware, at most seven per zone, for a few critical servers. Partition splits instances into groups on separate racks, suiting large distributed data stores that track which rack holds each copy.

Worked example: a web tier runs 10 fixed On-Demand servers and slows every day at 09:00. Step one: the CPU graph shows the surge repeats, so add scheduled or predictive scaling to warm capacity before 09:00. Step two: add target tracking at 50 percent CPU for surprise bursts. Step three: keep a base of 4 On-Demand and fill the rest with Spot across six types, cutting cost while protecting the floor.

Common mistake: putting a whole stateless web tier in a cluster placement group for speed. One rack fault then removes every server; cluster belongs to tightly coupled compute jobs, not tiers that need resilience.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company runs its booking API on 6 fixed On-Demand servers. Traffic jumps without warning whenever a popular tour is announced, sometimes at midnight and sometimes mid-afternoon, and the API slows badly each time. An architect works through the fix. Step one: the request graphs show that the surges follow no daily or weekly pattern, so a schedule or a forecast built from past days would not warm capacity in time. Step two: [missing]. Step three: keep a floor of 3 On-Demand servers and fill extra capacity with Spot across five interchangeable instance types using a capacity-optimized allocation strategy, so cost falls while the minimum stays reliable. Which choice best fills step two?
choices: Add predictive scaling so the group learns the announcement times and adds servers before each surge arrives
Move all booking servers into a cluster placement group so they talk to each other with the lowest latency
Add a target tracking policy that holds average CPU near a set value, such as 55 percent, so the group grows during sudden bursts
Replace the fixed servers entirely with Spot capacity of one instance type to cut cost during surges
questions.why: Target tracking reacts to the live metric whenever it rises, which suits surges that have no repeating pattern that a schedule or forecast could use.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a large distributed database of 60 nodes that stores several copies of each record and records which rack holds each copy, so one hardware failure never takes out every copy. Which placement group fits this workload?
choices: Spread, which places every node on its own distinct hardware
No placement group, because placement cannot affect hardware failure
Cluster, which packs the nodes tightly inside one Availability Zone
Partition, which divides the nodes into groups on separate racks
questions.why: Partition placement splits instances into groups on separate racks, which suits large distributed data stores that track which rack holds each copy.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs nightly route calculations on an Auto Scaling group using Spot capacity, but it lists only one instance type. On busy nights that type runs short and AWS reclaims many servers, so the jobs stall. What change most directly keeps the fleet running?
choices: Switch to step scaling so servers are added in larger fixed amounts when alarms fire
Raise the group's maximum count so it can request more of the same instance type
List several interchangeable instance types with a capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Put the servers in a spread placement group so each one sits on distinct hardware
questions.why: A mixed instances policy with many interchangeable types and capacity-optimized allocation picks the Spot pools least likely to be reclaimed, so one short type no longer stalls the fleet.

questions.prompt: A bank wants 12 critical payment-signing servers in a single Availability Zone, each on its own hardware so no single fault hits two of them. An engineer plans to put all 12 in one spread placement group in that zone. What is wrong with the plan?
choices: Spread placement allows at most seven instances per Availability Zone, so 12 will not fit in one zone
Spread placement is meant for tightly coupled compute jobs, not for critical servers
Spread placement packs servers onto one rack, so a single fault would remove all 12
Spread placement only works for Spot capacity, so On-Demand payment servers cannot use it
questions.why: Spread placement puts each instance on distinct hardware but is limited to seven instances per Availability Zone, so 12 servers exceed that limit in one zone.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks how you would make an existing fixed-size server tier both faster under load and cheaper. Explain in your own words how auto scaling, a mixed instance fleet and placement groups each help, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the servers in an Auto Scaling group so the count follows demand instead of being fixed for peak. If load repeats daily, scheduled or predictive scaling adds capacity before the rush; target tracking on something like CPU handles surprises. The tradeoff is that new instances take time to boot, so purely reactive scaling can lag a sudden spike. For cost, a mixed instances policy keeps a base of On-Demand servers and fills the rest with Spot across several instance types. Spot is much cheaper but can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice, so the workload must tolerate losing servers and the base must cover the minimum. Placement groups decide physical layout: cluster gives the fastest networking for tightly coupled jobs but shares failure risk, spread isolates a few critical servers, capped at seven per zone, and partition suits big distributed stores.
rubricPoints: Auto Scaling groups resize between a minimum and maximum using a launch template and scaling policies.
Scheduled or predictive scaling handles known patterns while target tracking handles unexpected load, and scaling has boot-time lag.
A mixed instance fleet combines On-Demand base capacity with Spot across several instance types to cut cost.
Spot capacity can be reclaimed with short notice, so the workload must tolerate interruption.
Cluster placement gives low latency but shared failure; spread isolates few critical instances; partition suits rack-aware distributed systems.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right scaling policy, Spot and On-Demand mix, and placement group type is a scenario judgment best practiced by reasoning through exam-style situations rather than a single hands-on drill.

lessons.plain: Users far from your servers feel slow pages and laggy apps because every request travels a long way over the public internet. AWS offers two main fixes at the edge, meaning the many small AWS sites spread around the world near users. Amazon CloudFront keeps copies of web content close to people, much like a chain store stocking popular items locally instead of shipping each one from the central warehouse. AWS Global Accelerator copies nothing. It gives users a fast on-ramp onto Amazon's private highway to reach your servers. Edge computing runs small pieces of your code at those nearby sites, so simple decisions happen close to the user.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online game sends constant live UDP traffic, not web pages, to servers in two AWS Regions, and players in Asia complain of lag. Would storing copies of content near players help, or would a faster private route to the servers help more? Why?
lessons.teach:
Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN). It is a worldwide set of edge locations, which are small AWS sites near users, that keep cached copies of responses from your origin. The origin is the server or storage bucket that holds the real content. CloudFront speaks HTTP and HTTPS. When a user asks for a file, the nearest edge location answers from its cache if it holds a fresh copy. If not, it fetches the file from the origin once and keeps it for the next users. This works because most web content is requested many times, so both distance and origin load drop.

AWS Global Accelerator caches nothing. It gives you two static anycast IP addresses. Anycast means the same addresses are announced from many edge locations, so each user reaches the closest one. Traffic enters AWS there and travels over the AWS private backbone to healthy endpoints, such as load balancers in one or more Regions, instead of crossing the public internet. It carries any TCP or UDP traffic. When health checks fail, it shifts traffic between Regions within seconds, without waiting for DNS caches to expire.

Edge computing means running your code close to users. CloudFront Functions are tiny, very fast scripts for simple request changes, such as rewriting a header or sending a redirect. Lambda@Edge runs fuller functions that can make network calls, for example an authentication check. Some workloads need extremely low latency near a city, inside a mobile carrier's network, or in your own data center. For those, Local Zones, Wavelength, and Outposts place AWS compute in each of those places.

Worked example: the UDP game above. Step one: is the traffic HTTP and cacheable? No, it is live UDP. Step two: that rules out CloudFront. Step three: Global Accelerator fits, because it gives fixed IPs, backbone routing, and fast failover between Regions.

A common mistake is choosing Global Accelerator to speed up a static website. It shortens the path, but every request still reaches the origin, so origin load and cost stay high. CloudFront would serve most of those requests from cache.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs a card-authorization API behind load balancers in two AWS Regions. Each response is unique to one transaction, so nothing can be reused for another caller. The partner banks' firewalls only allow traffic to a short list of fixed IP addresses. If one Region fails, traffic must move to the other within seconds. Step one: are the responses cacheable? No. Every answer is unique, so a content delivery network (CDN) cache would serve almost nothing and would not reduce origin load. Step two: [missing]. Step three: Global Accelerator health checks move traffic to the healthy Region within seconds. It does not wait for DNS caches to expire. Which statement correctly fills step two?
choices: Lambda@Edge can rewrite each request's destination IP so that it matches the banks' firewall rules.
Global Accelerator caches the last good response at the edge, so the banks keep getting answers while a Region is down.
CloudFront edge locations give each partner bank its own permanent IP address, so the banks can allowlist the CDN instead.
Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IP addresses that the banks can allowlist once. Those addresses stay the same even when traffic shifts between Regions.
questions.why: Global Accelerator provides two fixed anycast IP addresses that stay the same while it routes traffic to healthy endpoints in any Region, which meets the firewall-allowlist requirement.

questions.prompt: A car manufacturer runs robot-control software on its own factory floor. The software needs AWS compute physically inside the company's own building to get extremely low latency. Which offering places AWS compute in that location?
choices: AWS Outposts
CloudFront Functions
AWS Global Accelerator
AWS Wavelength
questions.why: Outposts puts AWS compute in your own data center or facility. Wavelength puts it inside a mobile carrier's network, and the other two do not host general compute on-site.

questions.prompt: An online learning platform serves course videos through CloudFront. It now wants every request checked at the edge before content is returned. The check calls the company's token-validation service over the network to confirm the user's session. Which edge computing option fits this check?
choices: Global Accelerator, because it routes requests over the AWS private backbone
Lambda@Edge, because it runs fuller functions that can make network calls such as an authentication lookup
AWS Local Zones, because they place compute near a city
CloudFront Functions, because they are the fastest option for any request logic
questions.why: The check needs a network call to another service. Lambda@Edge supports that, while CloudFront Functions are limited to simple, fast request changes such as rewriting headers or redirects.

questions.prompt: A recipe website serves the same photos and pages to millions of visitors. The team placed AWS Global Accelerator in front of its web servers to improve speed. Users see slightly faster responses, but origin server load and costs have not dropped at all. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Global Accelerator's health checks are failing, so traffic keeps bouncing between Regions.
Global Accelerator caches nothing, so every request still reaches the origin. A CDN such as CloudFront would answer most of these repeated requests from edge caches.
Global Accelerator only carries UDP traffic, so the HTTP requests skip the AWS backbone.
The static anycast IP addresses send every user to the farthest edge location.
questions.why: Global Accelerator shortens the network path but stores no copies. Repeatedly requested static content therefore still loads the origin, which CloudFront's caching would avoid.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and edge functions when improving a slow global application, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I ask what kind of traffic it is. If it is HTTP content that many users request again and again, such as images, scripts, or pages, I use CloudFront. It caches responses at edge locations near users, which cuts both latency and load on the origin. Its limit is that it only handles HTTP, and dynamic or personalized responses cache poorly. If the traffic is TCP or UDP that cannot be cached, such as games, VoIP, or APIs that need fixed IP addresses, I use Global Accelerator. Its anycast IPs pull users onto the AWS backbone, and it fails over between Regions in seconds. The tradeoff is that every request still hits my servers, because nothing is cached. If I only need small request logic near users, I use CloudFront Functions for simple header or redirect changes, or Lambda@Edge for heavier work. Lambda@Edge is slower and costs more per request than CloudFront Functions.
rubricPoints: CloudFront is a CDN that caches HTTP and HTTPS content at edge locations, cutting latency and origin load.
Global Accelerator caches nothing and routes TCP or UDP traffic over the AWS backbone using static anycast IPs.
Global Accelerator fails over between Regions quickly, without depending on DNS caches expiring.
CloudFront Functions suit tiny request tweaks, while Lambda@Edge suits heavier logic that needs network calls.
Local Zones, Wavelength, and Outposts place compute physically close to users for ultra-low latency.
At least one tradeoff is named, such as no caching in Global Accelerator or poor caching of dynamic content.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right edge service from traffic type, caching potential, and failover needs, so reasoning through realistic scenarios builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: A performance bottleneck is the one part of a system that limits how fast or how much the whole thing can go. Think of a highway that narrows to one lane at a bridge: widening the rest of the road changes nothing, because every car still squeezes through that bridge. In a running application, the narrow point might be a database, a slow outside service, a network link, or a single busy server. Identifying a bottleneck means measuring where requests spend their time and which resource runs out first, so you fix the real constraint instead of upgrading parts that were never the problem.
lessons.guessPrompt: An API's response time has doubled. The web servers show about 20% CPU use, while the single database server shows about 95% CPU use. Would adding more web servers make responses faster? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A bottleneck is the component whose limit caps the whole system's performance. To find it, look at four signals. Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests finish per second. Utilization is how busy a resource is, such as CPU percent. Saturation is work waiting in line, such as a queue or connection pool that is full. Use percentiles rather than averages. The p99, or 99th percentile, is the latency that 99% of requests beat, so it shows the slow tail that users actually complain about.

On AWS, Amazon CloudWatch is the managed metrics service: it collects utilization and latency numbers per resource. AWS X-Ray is distributed tracing, meaning it follows one request across services and shows how long each hop took. Amazon RDS Performance Insights is a database-load view that shows which queries and wait types consume the database's time. This works because a request's total time is the sum of its hops, so the largest, growing hop is where to look.

Here is a worked example. Checkout p99 rises from 300 ms to 2 s. First, CloudWatch shows the web tier at 25% CPU, with no queue building, so the web tier is not the constraint. Second, an X-Ray trace shows 1.7 s of the 2 s spent in the database call. Third, Performance Insights shows one query dominating the load and waiting on disk reads. The cause is a missing index on a newly added filter column. Adding the index brings p99 back to about 320 ms.

A common mistake is scaling whatever is easiest, usually adding web servers. In this example, more web servers would open more database connections, deepen the queue on the real constraint, and make latency worse while also raising cost. Also remember that removing one bottleneck often reveals the next one, so measure again after every fix.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing company's upload API has a p99 that has climbed from 400 ms to 3 s. The team traces the problem step by step. Step 1: CloudWatch, the managed metrics service, shows the API servers at 20% CPU with no request queue building, so the API tier is not the constraint. Step 2: ??? Step 3: The team opens CloudWatch metrics for the image-resizing service and finds its CPU at 97% and its job queue growing steadily, which is saturation. Step 4: They add resizing workers, p99 falls to about 450 ms, and they measure again to check whether a new bottleneck has appeared. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Add more API servers, because the API tier receives every upload request first
Use an X-Ray trace to follow one slow upload and find that 2.6 s of the 3 s is spent in the call to the resizing service
Open RDS Performance Insights first, because the database is nearly always the bottleneck
Check the average upload latency, which is 480 ms, and treat the problem as minor
questions.why: Distributed tracing breaks a request's total time into its hops, so it points the team at the resizing call as the largest hop before they examine that service's own metrics.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site's application keeps a pool of 50 database connections. During a sale, all 50 are in use and 35 more requests are waiting for a free connection. Which of the four performance signals does the waiting line of 35 requests describe most directly?
choices: Throughput, because the number finishing per second is limited
Saturation, because work is waiting in line for a full resource
Latency, because the requests are taking a long time
Utilization, because the pool is 100% busy
questions.why: Saturation is work queued behind a resource that is full, which is exactly what 35 requests waiting on a full connection pool are.

questions.prompt: A bank's balance-lookup service reports an average latency of 140 ms, yet customers complain that lookups sometimes hang. The p99 latency is 2.2 s. Which statement best explains which number the architect should focus on?
choices: The p99, because it shows the slow tail that 1% of requests suffer, which is what users notice and complain about
The average, because it represents the typical request and smooths out rare noise
The average, because a p99 of 2.2 s means 99% of requests take 2.2 s or longer
Neither, because latency matters less than CPU utilization when finding a bottleneck
questions.why: The p99 is the latency that 99% of requests beat, so it exposes the slow tail that an average hides and that users actually experience.

questions.prompt: An online grocery team finds a report query waiting on disk reads, adds an index, and the order page's p99 drops from 2.5 s to 900 ms. Their target is 400 ms. What should they do next?
choices: Add web servers, since the database has already been fixed and the web tier is the easiest to scale
Stop investigating, because a system can only have one bottleneck and it has been removed
Measure again across the request's hops, because removing one bottleneck often reveals the next one
Remove the index, since the fix did not reach the target and probably caused a new problem
questions.why: Fixing one constraint often exposes the next limit, so the team must re-measure to find what now caps performance rather than guess or scale whatever is easiest.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find the bottleneck in a slow production service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach or the tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from what users feel, usually p99 latency, not the average, because averages hide the slow tail. Then I check each tier's utilization and saturation in CloudWatch. A resource that is busy and has work queuing is a suspect; one sitting at 20% is not. Next I follow real requests with X-Ray tracing to see which hop takes most of the time. If it is the database, Performance Insights shows the exact queries and waits. I fix only that constraint, then measure again, because the next bottleneck usually appears behind it. One limit is that tracing typically samples requests and needs code or agent instrumentation, so rare slow paths can be missed. Another tradeoff is effort: guessing and scaling a tier is faster, but it often adds cost and can overload the real bottleneck further.
rubricPoints: Defines a bottleneck as the single component that caps whole-system performance.
Uses percentile latency (such as p99) instead of averages.
Checks both utilization and saturation (queuing) to locate the constrained resource.
Uses tracing to attribute request time per hop and a database-level tool for query-level cause.
Warns that scaling the wrong tier adds cost and can worsen the real constraint.
Re-measures after a fix because the bottleneck moves.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing why the positions API slowed after a deploy has the learner trace latency to the constrained component, which is exactly the bottleneck-finding skill this objective covers.

lessons.plain: Testing a remediation means trying out a proposed fix somewhere safe before you change the real system, and making a recommendation means telling decision-makers which fix to adopt, backed by what the test showed. Think of a doctor choosing between two treatments: rather than guessing, they compare results against how the patient was doing before, weigh side effects and cost, and then advise. In cloud architecture you do the same: measure how the system behaves now, try each candidate fix under realistic conditions, compare the numbers, and recommend the option that solves the business problem with acceptable cost and risk.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app's database is slow at peak hours. Someone proposes three fixes at once: a bigger database server, a cache in front of it, and a code change to queries. If you apply all three together and the app gets faster, what can you not tell?
lessons.teach:
A remediation is a change meant to fix a weakness you found, such as slow responses, a single point of failure, or wasted spend. Testing it means proving the change works before production depends on it.

Start with a baseline: the measured behaviour today, for example p99 latency (the response time that 99 percent of requests beat), error rate, and monthly cost. Then write success criteria tied to the business need, such as "p99 under 300 ms at peak, cost increase under 20 percent." Without both, you cannot say a fix worked.

Next, build a representative test environment. With infrastructure as code (templates that create resources repeatably, like AWS CloudFormation) you can stand up a copy of production and load it with realistic traffic and data volume. Change one variable per trial so you know which change caused the result. For lower-risk changes, a canary, meaning sending a small slice of real traffic to the new version, gives real-world evidence with limited exposure.

Worked example: an order API has p99 of 900 ms at peak, mostly from repeated reads of the same product rows. Option A is a larger database instance; option B is a managed in-memory cache (Amazon ElastiCache) in front of reads; option C adds a read replica, a copy of the database that serves reads. Replaying peak traffic on a cloned stack: A gives 600 ms for +60 percent cost; B gives 180 ms for +15 percent; C gives 400 ms for +45 percent. B meets both criteria, so you recommend B, noting the new risk (stale cached data) and a rollback plan (turn the cache off).

The recommendation itself should state the problem, options tried, evidence, cost, risks, effort, and how to undo it.

A common mistake is testing with tiny data or light load, so a fix looks great in testing and then fails at real peak, leaving production still slow after money and time are spent.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's seat-booking service fails 3 percent of requests during on-sale events. The team works through a remediation test. Step 1, baseline: error rate 3 percent at peak, p99 latency (the response time that 99 percent of requests beat) of 1.8 s, and monthly cost of $8,000. Step 2, success criteria tied to the business need: error rate under 0.5 percent at peak and a cost increase under 25 percent. Step 3: using infrastructure as code (templates that create resources repeatably), they clone production and replay a recorded on-sale traffic spike at full data volume, changing one variable per trial. Option X adds a managed queue (a service that holds requests until workers can process them) in front of the booking workers: 0.4 percent errors for +12 percent cost. Option Y moves to larger servers: 1.1 percent errors for +35 percent cost. Option Z doubles the number of servers: 0.2 percent errors for +30 percent cost. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: write the recommendation with the problem, the options tried, the evidence, cost, risks, effort, and a rollback plan. What is Step 4?
choices: Recommend X, because it is the only option that meets both the error-rate target and the cost limit.
Recommend none yet and rerun all three trials with lighter traffic so the results are more stable.
Recommend Z, because it produced the lowest error rate of all three options.
Recommend Y, because larger servers are the simplest change and need the least effort.
questions.why: X brings errors under 0.5 percent and keeps the cost increase under 25 percent, while Z breaks the cost limit and Y fails both criteria.

questions.prompt: A team wants real-world evidence for a low-risk change to its checkout service, but it does not want every customer exposed if the change misbehaves. Which approach fits, and what is it called?
choices: A canary: sending a small slice of real traffic to the new version while most traffic stays on the old one.
A baseline: recording today's latency, error rate, and cost before making the change.
A cloned stack: a full copy of production built from templates and loaded with replayed traffic only.
A read replica: a copy of the database that serves read requests alongside the main one.
questions.why: A canary limits exposure by routing only a small share of real users to the new version, so it gives real-world evidence with limited risk.

questions.prompt: An analytics firm's report service is slow. In a single test trial, an engineer adds a cache, enlarges the database, and changes the connection settings at the same time. p99 latency drops from 2.4 s to 0.5 s. What is the main problem with this result?
choices: Nothing, because the improvement is large enough that the cause does not matter.
The result proves the cache worked, since caches usually give the biggest gains.
The test should have used a canary on real traffic instead of a cloned environment.
Three variables changed at once, so the team cannot tell which change caused the improvement or whether all three are needed.
questions.why: Changing one variable per trial is what lets you link a result to a specific change; with three changes at once, the cause and the necessary cost are unknown.

questions.prompt: A logistics company tested a new indexing scheme on a copy of its database that held 2 percent of production data, using light test traffic. Latency looked excellent, so the change was deployed. At the next peak, the service was as slow as before. What most likely went wrong?
choices: The team defined success criteria, which made the test too strict for production.
The team should have skipped testing and changed the production database directly.
The change was rolled back too early, before it could take effect at peak.
The test environment was not representative: tiny data and light load hid how the fix behaves at real peak volume.
questions.why: Testing with small data or light load can make a fix look great and then fail at real peak, leaving production slow after time and money are spent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would test candidate fixes for a production weakness and turn the results into a recommendation, and name one limit of testing in a copied environment.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I measure the baseline, so I know today's latency, errors and cost, and I agree success criteria with the business, like a latency target and a cost ceiling. Then I spin up a copy of production from our infrastructure templates and replay realistic peak traffic against it. I try each candidate fix separately, changing one thing at a time, so I know which change caused any improvement. I compare each option to the baseline on performance, cost, risk and effort. My recommendation names the option that meets the criteria, shows the numbers, lists new risks, and includes a rollback plan. The limit is that a copy is never quite production: data shape, traffic mix and dependencies differ, so I may follow up with a canary on a small slice of real traffic to confirm before full rollout.
rubricPoints: Measures a baseline before changing anything.
Defines success criteria tied to business needs, including cost.
Tests in a representative environment with realistic load and data.
Changes one variable at a time so results are attributable.
Recommendation weighs evidence, cost, risk and includes rollback.
Names a limit, such as test environments not fully matching production.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among tested fixes and justifying the pick is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios with competing options, costs and risks.

lessons.plain: Proposing a new technology or managed service means looking at something a team already runs by hand and asking whether a provider-run version would do the same job with less effort and risk. A managed service is one where the cloud provider handles the patching, backups, scaling and failover, and the team keeps only the configuration and the data. It is like switching from maintaining your own office printer to a leasing contract that includes repairs. You still choose the printer and pay for it, but someone else gets called when it jams at 3 a.m. The skill is knowing when that trade is worth making.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team runs its own database on two virtual servers and spends a weekend each month on patching and fixing replication. A provider offers the same database engine as a managed service. Name one thing the team would gain by switching and one thing they might give up.
lessons.teach:
Adopting a managed service means replacing a component your team operates itself with one the provider operates. Operational burden is the recurring human work a component needs: patching, backups, capacity changes and failover. Undifferentiated heavy lifting is the part of that work that gives your business no edge, because every company does it the same way. A managed service removes most of it, and the team keeps configuration, access control and its data. That split is called the shared responsibility model.

This works because the provider runs the same service for thousands of customers, so its automation for failover and patching is better tested than one team's scripts. A good proposal pairs each weakness you find with a service that removes it, then states the cost and the limits.

Worked example. A shop runs MySQL on two Amazon EC2 virtual servers with hand-built replication. Step one: list the pain. Failover is manual and took 40 minutes last quarter, and patching eats a weekend each month. Step two: find a target that keeps the same engine, such as Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ, a managed relational database with a standby copy in a second data center that it promotes automatically. Step three: check compatibility. The app uses standard MySQL with no special plugins, so it fits. Step four: weigh the tradeoffs. The hourly price is higher, but staff time drops, failover becomes automatic in minutes, and the team loses operating-system access. Step five: plan a low-risk cutover, either a replica sync followed by a short switch, or AWS Database Migration Service, a managed copying tool.

A common mistake is proposing the newest, most different service, such as rewriting the app for a serverless key-value store, when a compatible managed version of the same engine solves the actual problem. Rewrites add risk and delay the benefit. Another mistake is skipping the check of service limits and missing features, which can break production after cutover. The best proposal removes the weakness the business feels first, with the smallest change that does it.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its own Redis in-memory cache on four self-managed virtual servers. Over the last two months a cache node crashed three times, and each time an engineer was paged at night to rebuild it by hand. The app uses only standard Redis commands. The architect works through a proposal. First, the pain the business feels: slow pages and night-time pages to staff whenever a node dies, plus monthly patching of the servers. Second, the choice of target: [MISSING STEP]. Third, the cost and limits: the hourly price is higher than the raw servers, and the team loses operating-system access, but nobody rebuilds nodes by hand and failed nodes are replaced automatically. Which choice best fills the missing step?
choices: Keep the four servers and write more failover scripts, because the team already knows the setup and would keep full operating-system control.
Move the cached data into a managed relational database, because a database with a standby copy is more reliable than any cache.
Rewrite the booking app to store sessions in a brand-new serverless key-value database, because it is the newest and most different option available.
Move to a managed cache service that runs the same Redis engine and replaces failed nodes automatically, because the app uses only standard Redis commands.
questions.why: A compatible managed version of the same engine removes the manual node rebuilds and patching with the smallest change, while a rewrite or engine swap adds risk and delays the benefit.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's platform team spends its week on several tasks. Which one is the best example of undifferentiated heavy lifting that a managed service could take over?
choices: Applying operating-system and database patches to the servers that host the order database.
Deciding which employees may read customer shipping addresses.
Choosing which fields the order records should contain.
Designing the route-planning algorithm that lets the firm deliver faster than its rivals.
questions.why: Patching is recurring work every company does the same way and gives no business edge, whereas the algorithm is differentiating and access decisions and data design stay with the team.

questions.prompt: A clinic moves its patient-records database from self-managed virtual servers to a managed relational database service. Under the shared responsibility model, which task does the clinic's team still own after the move?
choices: Promoting the standby copy by hand when the main database fails.
Configuring who can access the database and protecting the patient data stored in it.
Replacing failed disks in the provider's data center.
Applying operating-system patches to the database hosts every month.
questions.why: The provider takes over patching, failover and hardware, while the customer keeps configuration, access control and its data.

questions.prompt: A media company replaced its self-run message queue with a managed queue service. The app worked in testing, but the day after cutover some production messages were rejected because they were larger than the managed service allows. Which part of a good proposal was most likely skipped?
choices: Listing the operational pain the business felt with the self-run queue.
Checking the managed service's limits and missing features against how the app actually uses the queue.
Comparing the hourly price of the managed service against the cost of staff time.
Picking the newest and most different service on the market.
questions.why: Skipping the check of service limits and missing features is the mistake that can break production after cutover, exactly as the size limit did here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether to replace a self-run component with a managed service, and name at least one tradeoff or limit they should weigh before agreeing.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the pain, not the product. I list what the component costs us in human work and risk, such as manual failover, monthly patching and missed backups. Then I look for a managed service that removes that specific work while staying as compatible as possible, ideally the same engine or protocol, so the app barely changes. Under shared responsibility the provider takes over patching, failover and scaling, and we keep configuration, access and data. Before agreeing, we weigh the tradeoffs. The direct bill usually goes up even when total cost including staff time goes down. We lose low-level control like operating-system access or custom plugins. We take on the service's limits and some lock-in. If a compatible managed option fixes the problem, I prefer it over a rewrite to something newer, because a rewrite adds risk and delays the benefit.
rubricPoints: Defines a managed service as one where the provider runs the operational work and the team keeps configuration and data.
Starts from a concrete weakness or burden in the existing system rather than from the new product.
Prefers the smallest compatible change over a rewrite when it fixes the problem.
Names a tradeoff such as higher direct price, loss of low-level control, service limits or lock-in.
Mentions checking compatibility and planning a low-risk cutover.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about judging which replacement fits a given production weakness, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios with competing options.

lessons.plain: Rightsizing means making each piece of a running system the right size for what the business actually needs, no bigger and no smaller. Teams often launch servers, databases, and disks generously sized "to be safe" and never revisit them, so they pay for capacity that sits idle. Others guess too small and users suffer at busy times. Assessing a solution means comparing what is provisioned against the real requirements: how busy it gets at peak, how fast it must respond, and how much spare room it needs. It is like renting a moving truck: measure what you are hauling first, then pick the truck.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server's processor never goes above 18% busy, even at the busiest hour of the month. Before shrinking it to half the size, what else would you want to check, and why?
lessons.teach:
Rightsizing is changing the size or type of a resource (a virtual server, a database instance, a disk) so its capacity matches measured demand plus a safety margin, at the lowest cost that still meets the requirements. Utilization is the share of a resource actually in use, such as CPU percent or memory percent. Headroom is deliberate spare capacity kept for spikes and growth, often 20 to 40 percent. An instance family is a group of server sizes with a fixed balance of processor to memory; on AWS, general purpose (m), compute optimized (c), and memory optimized (r) are examples. AWS Compute Optimizer is a service that reads past utilization and recommends better sizes. Memory use inside a server is not collected by default; you install the CloudWatch agent, a small program that reports operating-system metrics to the monitoring service. p95 latency means 95 percent of requests finish faster than that time.

It works because cost scales with size, so cutting idle capacity cuts cost directly, while requirements tell you where to stop cutting.

Worked example: four m5.2xlarge servers (8 vCPU, 32 GiB each) run a web tier. The requirement is p95 latency under 300 ms with 30% headroom over peak. Over 30 days, peak CPU is 18%, or about 1.4 vCPU, and peak memory is 6 GiB. Try m5.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB): CPU becomes 1.4/4 = 36%, or about 47% with headroom; memory becomes 6/16 = 38%, or about 49% with headroom. Both are safe, so you halve the server cost. You keep four servers across zones because the count protects availability, not just capacity. Then load test to confirm latency.

The common mistake is deciding from average CPU alone, ignoring memory, disk and network throughput, or the monthly peak. In a running system, that shows up as out-of-memory crashes or latency breaches during the busiest hour, exactly when the business notices most.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs its reporting database on one r5.4xlarge instance (16 vCPU, 128 GiB memory). The requirement is query p95 latency under 2 seconds with 25% headroom over peak. Over 30 days, peak CPU is 20% (about 3.2 vCPU) and peak memory use, reported by the CloudWatch agent, is 40 GiB. The team tries r5.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GiB). Step 1: CPU becomes 3.2/8 = 40%, or about 50% with 25% headroom (40 x 1.25). Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: if both checks pass, switch sizes and load test to confirm the 2-second p95 target. What is Step 2?
choices: Memory becomes 40/64 = 62.5%, or about 78% with headroom (62.5 x 1.25), which is still under full capacity, so it fits.
Skip memory, because CPU at 50% with headroom already shows the smaller size is safe.
Memory becomes 40/128 = about 31%, or about 39% with headroom, so the smaller size fits easily.
Memory becomes 40/64 = 62.5%, or about 78% with headroom, which is above the 25% headroom limit, so stay on r5.4xlarge.
questions.why: Peak memory must be divided by the new size's 64 GiB and then scaled up by the 25% headroom, and about 78% still leaves the instance below full capacity, so the smaller size passes the memory check.

questions.prompt: An architect writes that a payments service should be sized to keep 30% headroom. In rightsizing, what does headroom mean?
choices: The share of a resource that is actually in use, such as CPU percent.
Capacity that is idle and should be removed to cut cost.
The latency that 95 percent of requests finish faster than.
Deliberate spare capacity kept above measured peak demand to absorb spikes and growth.
questions.why: Headroom is planned spare capacity on top of peak demand, while utilization is the share in use and p95 is a latency measure.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs six c5.2xlarge servers spread across three Availability Zones (separate data center locations). Peak CPU and memory on each server are low, and analysis shows each server could drop one size and still keep the required headroom. A colleague proposes replacing all six with a single larger server to save more. What is the better rightsizing decision?
choices: Replace them with one large server, because total capacity is what matters.
Keep the servers spread across all three zones and downsize each one, because the server count and spread protect availability, not just capacity.
Cut to two servers in one zone, because the load is low.
Keep six c5.2xlarge servers, because rightsizing should never touch production.
questions.why: Rightsizing changes each resource's size to match demand, but the number and spread of servers protect availability, so you shrink the servers rather than collapse them into one location.

questions.prompt: A media firm downsized its encoding servers after AWS Compute Optimizer (a service that reads past utilization and recommends sizes) showed average CPU of 12%. The CloudWatch agent was never installed. During the month-end rush, the servers crash with out-of-memory errors. What most likely went wrong?
choices: Compute Optimizer only works on database instances, not on servers.
The servers moved to a compute optimized family, which cannot run encoding jobs.
Memory use was never collected, so the decision rested on average CPU alone and missed memory and the monthly peak.
The headroom was set too high, which wasted memory during the rush.
questions.why: Without the CloudWatch agent, memory inside the server is not reported, so a decision based on average CPU ignored memory and the busiest period, leading to out-of-memory crashes at peak.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a production server can be moved to a smaller size, and name one tradeoff or limit of rightsizing.
lessons.modelAnswer: Rightsizing means matching a resource's size to measured demand plus a safety margin. I'd start from the requirements: the latency target, peak load, and how much headroom we want for spikes and growth. Then I'd pull at least a few weeks of metrics covering the busiest periods, not just averages, and look at CPU, memory, disk and network together. Memory needs the CloudWatch agent because it isn't collected by default. Tools like Compute Optimizer can suggest a size, but I'd check its suggestion against our requirements and load test before switching. I'd also keep the number of servers needed for availability across zones, since that's about resilience, not capacity. The tradeoff is that every cut eats into margin: if our data missed an unusual peak or traffic grows, a smaller size can breach latency targets or run out of memory, so we monitor after the change and revisit regularly.
rubricPoints: Defines rightsizing as matching capacity to measured demand plus headroom at lowest cost that meets requirements.
Starts from requirements such as latency targets, peak load, and headroom, not just cost.
Uses peak metrics across CPU, memory, storage and network, noting memory needs an agent.
Separates capacity sizing from server count kept for availability.
Validates with a load test or monitoring after the change.
Names a tradeoff such as reduced margin for unexpected peaks or growth.

suggested.rationale: Rightsizing on this exam is judged through scenarios where you must weigh metrics against stated requirements, so reasoning through exam-style situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Understanding growth and usage trends means looking at how much a running application is used over weeks and months, not just today, so you can see where it is heading before it runs out of room. You separate the steady direction (is use climbing?) from the repeating rhythm (busy Mondays, quiet nights, a December rush). It is like a farmer reading years of rainfall: one wet day tells you little, but the pattern tells you when to build a bigger reservoir. The point is to act early, while there is still time to add capacity calmly.
lessons.guessPrompt: An app's busiest hour handled 400 requests per second last week and 420 this week. If it keeps growing at that rate, roughly how many weeks until it reaches 600, and should you plan from the busiest hour or the daily average?
lessons.teach:
A usage trend is how a demand metric changes over time, and you read it in three layers. The baseline is the normal level of load. The trend is the long-term direction, often compound growth, where each period grows by a percentage of the last, so the curve bends upward. Seasonality is a repeating cycle such as daily, weekly or yearly peaks. Two more terms matter. Headroom is the gap between current peak load and the most the system can safely carry. Lead time is how long it takes to add capacity, such as buying reserved capacity or splitting a database.

This works because past behavior, with its rhythm removed, predicts the near future well enough to plan. In AWS, Amazon CloudWatch, the monitoring service, keeps metric history for up to 15 months at coarser detail. That is enough to see a full yearly cycle. Cost Explorer, the billing analysis tool, can also project spend forward.

Worked example: weekly peak traffic is 400 requests per second and grows 5 percent a week. The safe ceiling is 600. Solve 400 times 1.05 to the power n equals 600. That means 1.05 to the n equals 1.5, so n is about 8.3 weeks. A database change has a 4-week lead time, so the decision must be made by about week 4, not week 8.

The common mistake is planning from averages or from a short window. Averages hide the peak that actually breaks things. A two-week window misses the yearly rush. Drawing a straight line through compound growth also underestimates the future. In a running system, the result is capacity exhaustion during the busiest, most valuable hour, followed by rushed and expensive fixes. Reading trends turns that emergency into a scheduled change.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup stores user uploads on a database volume that now holds 2 TB. Storage grows 10 percent each month, compounding, and the volume can safely hold 4 TB. Moving to a larger storage design has a 3-month lead time, meaning it takes 3 months from decision to finished change. Step 1: Set up the compound growth equation: 2 times 1.10 to the power n equals 4. Step 2: Simplify: 1.10 to the n equals 2. Step 3: Solve for n: n is about 7.3 months until the volume reaches its safe ceiling. Step 4 (missing): By about which month must the team decide to start the storage change?
choices: About month 4, because the 3-month lead time is subtracted from the 7.3 months until the ceiling
About month 10, because the 3-month lead time is added to the 7.3 months until the ceiling
About month 7, because straight-line growth of 0.2 TB a month reaches 4 TB at month 10, minus the 3-month lead time
About month 7, because 7.3 months is when the 4 TB ceiling is reached, so that is when to act
