questions.why: The change takes 3 months to complete, so it must start about 3 months before the ceiling is reached at about month 7.3, which means deciding by roughly month 4.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing platform has an average load of 300 concurrent sessions and a peak load of 900 concurrent sessions during on-sale events. Load testing shows it can safely carry at most 1,200 concurrent sessions. What is the platform's headroom?
choices: 900 sessions, the gap between the safe maximum and the average load
600 sessions, the gap between peak load and average load
1,200 sessions, the most the system can safely carry
300 sessions, the gap between peak load and the safe maximum
questions.why: Headroom is the gap between current peak load and the most the system can safely carry, so 1,200 minus 900 equals 300 sessions.

questions.prompt: In February, a gift retailer's architect reviews the last two weeks of Amazon CloudWatch request metrics and concludes the current web tier has plenty of capacity for the whole year. The retailer's sales spike every November. What is the main weakness in this analysis?
choices: A two-week window cannot show the yearly November peak; the architect should review metric history covering a full year, which CloudWatch can keep for up to 15 months
CloudWatch cannot store request metrics, so Cost Explorer should have been used instead
The architect should have measured the baseline only, since seasonality does not affect capacity
Two weeks of data is too much, because only the most recent day predicts the near future
questions.why: Seasonality such as a yearly rush only appears in a window long enough to include it, and CloudWatch keeps up to 15 months of history, enough to see a full yearly cycle.

questions.prompt: A payroll service's dashboard shows average database CPU at 35 percent across each week, so the team decides no capacity work is needed. A few weeks later, the database overloads every Monday morning when payroll runs. What best explains why the team missed the problem?
choices: The trend was compound growth, which always makes averages higher than peaks
Weekly patterns are not seasonality, so they cannot be seen in metric history
They planned from an average, which hides the recurring weekly peak that actually exceeds capacity
Their lead time was too short, so the database could not be resized in time
questions.why: Averages smooth out peaks, and it is the peak, here the Monday payroll run, that breaks the system, so planning must use peak load rather than the average.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use usage history to decide when to add capacity, and name one limit of trend-based forecasting.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pull at least a year of a demand metric, such as requests per second, so I can see both the long-term growth and any repeating peaks like weekday rushes or a holiday season. I would plan from the peak, not the average, because the peak is what runs out of room. I would estimate the growth rate as a percentage per week or month, because compound growth climbs faster than a straight line. Then I would work out when the peak hits our safe ceiling. Next I would subtract the lead time for the fix, and that gives the real deadline to decide. The limit is that a trend only describes the past. A marketing launch, a new customer or a product change can break the pattern overnight. So I would pair the forecast with alarms on headroom and revisit it regularly.
rubricPoints: Separates baseline, long-term trend and seasonality.
Plans from peak load rather than averages.
Treats growth as compound, not a straight line.
Subtracts capacity lead time from the time-to-ceiling to find the decision date.
Uses enough history, around a year, to capture seasonal cycles.
Names a limit, such as forecasts breaking on sudden business events.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning from metric history and growth math to a timely capacity decision, which an exam-style scenario with numbers exercises best.

lessons.plain: Checking an existing system for reliability means walking through everything it depends on and asking, for each piece, what happens to customers if that piece stops working. Reliability is a system's ability to keep doing its job correctly, and to recover quickly when something breaks. Think of a building inspector who checks wiring, exits and the water supply, not just whether the lights are on today. You are not fixing anything yet. You are producing a ranked list of weak spots, ordered by how much the business would suffer and how likely each failure is.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop runs its web servers in two separate data centers, but all of them talk to one database server in just one of those data centers. If that one data center loses power, what do you think customers will see?
lessons.teach:
Evaluating an architecture for reliability means systematically finding the components whose failure would break the service, then ranking them by business impact. You need a few terms first. A single point of failure is any component that has no working substitute, so its failure stops the service. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more physically separate data centers inside an AWS Region, which is a geographic area containing several AZs. Blast radius is how much of the system one failure takes down. A dependency is anything a request needs to succeed, such as a database, a DNS lookup, a secret store or a network route.

The method works because outages almost always come from a few components that are shared and not duplicated. Tracing a request reveals them. Follow one real user request from entry to exit. At each step, ask three questions. Is there more than one copy? Are the copies in different AZs? What happens to users and data if this step fails?

Here is a worked example. A request enters through a load balancer spread across two AZs, which is fine. It reaches web servers in an auto scaling group, which is a fleet that replaces unhealthy machines and also spans two AZs, which is also fine. The servers reach the internet through one NAT gateway in AZ-a. A NAT gateway is a managed device that lets private servers make outbound connections. If AZ-a fails, the servers in AZ-b lose outbound access. The database is a single instance in AZ-a with nightly backups, so if AZ-a fails, writes stop and up to a day of data could be lost. Rank the risks. The database comes first because it has the largest blast radius and also risks data loss. The NAT gateway comes second.

A common mistake is to treat backups as availability. A backup restores data later. It does not keep the service running during the outage. Another mistake is to inspect only compute and miss shared plumbing such as NAT, DNS or a single queue. In production, these overlooked weak spots turn a small zone failure into a full outage.

questions.prompt:
A concert-ticketing company asks you to check its checkout path for reliability. You follow one checkout request from entry to exit and ask three questions at each step: is there more than one copy, are the copies in different Availability Zones (AZs), and what happens to users and data if this step fails?

Step 1: The request enters through a load balancer spread across AZ-1, AZ-2 and AZ-3. There are several copies in different AZs, so this step is fine.
Step 2: It reaches app servers in an auto scaling group (a fleet that replaces unhealthy machines) that spans all three AZs. This step is also fine.
Step 3: Each order is placed on a message queue that runs on one server in AZ-1. Nothing else can accept orders. There is one copy, in one AZ. If AZ-1 fails: ______
Step 4: Payment records go to a database with a primary copy in AZ-2 and a standby copy in AZ-3. This step is fine.

Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Only the app servers in AZ-1 are affected, because the servers in AZ-2 and AZ-3 still run, so the blast radius is one zone.
The risk is low if the queue is backed up nightly, because the orders can be restored afterward.
Nothing is lost, because the auto scaling group will replace the queue server in another AZ.
No order can be placed from any AZ, so the queue is a single point of failure, and it should rank at the top of the fix list.
questions.why: Every request depends on that one queue copy, and nothing can substitute for it, so losing AZ-1 stops checkout in all zones. That makes it a single point of failure with a system-wide blast radius.

questions.prompt: In reliability terms, which description fits a single point of failure?
choices: Any component that has no recent backup
Any component that runs in only one AWS Region
Any component whose failure affects more than half of the users
Any component with no working substitute, so its failure stops the service
questions.why: A single point of failure is defined by having no working substitute, so the service stops when it fails. Region placement, the share of users affected and backups are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm finds two weak spots. First, its shipment-tracking database is a single instance in one AZ, with snapshots taken every 12 hours. Second, a cache that speeds up a weekly internal report runs on one machine in a different AZ, and without it the report is merely slower. Which should be fixed first, and why?
choices: Both carry equal risk, since each is one copy in one AZ
The cache, because it is the only copy and sits alone in its AZ
The database, because its failure stops shipment tracking for everyone and could lose up to 12 hours of data
Neither, because snapshots and a slow fallback mean both are already recoverable
questions.why: You rank risks by business impact. The database has the larger blast radius and also risks losing data, while losing the cache only slows down a report.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking startup runs app servers across three AZs. It uses a single-instance appointments database in one AZ and backs it up every hour. The team says: "We back up hourly, so the database is highly available." What is wrong with that claim?
choices: The claim fails only because the backups should run every minute instead of every hour.
The claim fails only because the backups are stored in the same AZ as the database.
A backup restores data later but does not keep bookings working while the AZ is down, so the database is still a single point of failure.
Nothing is wrong; hourly backups make the database highly available.
questions.why: Backups protect data for a later restore. They do not provide a running substitute during the outage, so they do not count as availability.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would review an existing production system to find the parts that are not reliable enough, and name one limit or tradeoff of this kind of review.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick a real user request and trace every component it touches, from the load balancer to the servers, network routes like NAT, the database, and any shared services like DNS or secrets. For each step I would ask three things. Is there more than one copy? Are the copies spread across separate Availability Zones? What breaks for users, and what data could be lost, if this step fails? Anything without a working substitute is a single point of failure. I would rank those by blast radius and business impact, so a single-AZ database outranks a single NAT gateway. I would not count backups as availability, because a backup only restores data later. One limit is that a paper review finds the obvious gaps, but it can miss hidden dependencies and slow failovers that only show up under real failure. Also, every redundant copy adds cost, so not every gap is worth closing.
rubricPoints: Traces a real request end to end, including shared plumbing like NAT, DNS and the database.
Defines a single point of failure as a component with no working substitute.
Checks whether copies are spread across separate Availability Zones, not just whether they exist.
Ranks weak spots by blast radius and business impact, including possible data loss.
Distinguishes backups, which restore data later, from availability, which keeps the service running.
Names a limit, such as missed hidden dependencies or the cost of added redundancy.

suggested.rationale: This skill is mainly about reasoning through a given architecture diagram and ranking its weak spots, which an exam-style scenario practices better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: A single point of failure is any one part of a system that, if it breaks, takes the whole service down with it. Think of an old string of holiday lights wired in series: one dead bulb and the entire string goes dark. Remediating it means finding those lone parts and giving each one a backup that can take over automatically, so a single broken piece only dims one bulb instead of the whole string. In cloud architecture this usually means running copies in more than one separate data center and putting something in front that steers traffic away from the broken copy.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs its website on two servers behind a traffic distributor, but both servers sit in the same building and share one internet exit. If that building loses power, what happens to the website, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
A single point of failure (SPOF) is a component with no working substitute, so its failure stops the service. Remediation means adding redundancy, meaning spare copies, plus automatic failover, meaning the system switches to a healthy copy without a human. On AWS the basic unit of separation is the Availability Zone (AZ): one or more physically separate data centers within a Region, with independent power and networking. Copies in different AZs rarely fail together, which is why spreading across AZs works and stacking copies in one AZ does not.

Worked example. A production app has one EC2 virtual server, one Amazon RDS managed database in a single AZ, and one NAT gateway, a managed device that lets private servers reach the internet. Step 1: list every component a request or outbound call touches. Step 2: ask of each, "if this alone dies, does the service stop?" All three answer yes. Step 3: fix in the order the business would feel. The server comes first because it serves every customer request: place an Elastic Load Balancer, a managed traffic distributor that health-checks targets, in front of an Auto Scaling group spanning two or more AZs so failed servers are replaced. Next, turn on RDS Multi-AZ, which keeps a synchronous standby copy in another AZ and promotes it automatically if the primary fails. Then deploy one NAT gateway per AZ, with each AZ's route table pointing to its local gateway.

The common mistake is fixing only the obvious compute tier and missing hidden SPOFs: a single NAT gateway, one VPN tunnel or one Direct Connect link to the office, a self-managed server holding session state, or one hard-coded IP address. A running system with such a gap looks healthy in normal operation, then suffers a full outage the first time that one AZ or link has trouble. Redundancy also costs money, so match the depth of the fix to how much downtime the business can tolerate.

questions.prompt:
A regional bakery chain runs an online ordering app. Every order makes a live call over a VPN tunnel (an encrypted connection across the internet) to the chain's head-office stock system. An engineer reviews it for single points of failure.

Step 1, listing components: an Elastic Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group spread across three Availability Zones, an RDS database with Multi-AZ turned on, and one VPN tunnel to head office.

Step 2, asking of each "if this alone dies, does ordering stop?": the load balancer, the Auto Scaling group and the Multi-AZ database each answer no, because each has a healthy substitute in another AZ. The single VPN tunnel answers yes.

Step 3 is missing. What is the right remediation for the gap found in Step 2?
choices: Keep the one tunnel but add an alarm that pages the on-call engineer, who will rebuild the tunnel by hand when it drops.
Raise the Auto Scaling group's server count from three to six so more servers can share the load of calls to head office.
Move all servers into the single AZ closest to head office so the path to the stock system is shorter and steadier.
Add a second, independent connection to head office, such as another tunnel or link, so traffic switches to it automatically if one fails.
questions.why: The tunnel has no substitute, so the fix is a redundant connection with automatic failover; extra servers, a human-driven alarm, or packing everything into one AZ all leave that one link able to stop every order.

questions.prompt: A ticketing website runs its web servers in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind a load balancer. However, every logged-in user's session is kept on one self-managed server in a single AZ. Which statement best describes that session server?
choices: It counts as redundant because a load balancer health-checks it and replaces it automatically if it fails.
It only matters for cost, since session data can be rebuilt by asking users to log in again with no outage.
It is safe because the web tier is already spread across two AZs, and that redundancy covers the session server too.
It is a single point of failure: it has no working substitute, so if it fails, logged-in users lose their sessions and the service effectively stops.
questions.why: A component with no working substitute whose failure stops the service is a SPOF, and redundancy in the web tier does nothing to protect a separate component that exists only once.

questions.prompt: A media company runs four identical EC2 servers behind a load balancer, all placed in the same Availability Zone. During a power problem in that AZ, the whole site goes down. What is the main reason the four copies did not prevent the outage?
choices: The servers lacked automatic failover, which only RDS Multi-AZ can provide for any type of workload.
Copies in one AZ share the same power and networking, so they fail together; the copies needed to be spread across AZs.
The load balancer was the real single point of failure, so the number of servers made no difference.
Four servers is too few; at least eight copies are needed before redundancy starts to work.
questions.why: An AZ has independent power and networking from other AZs, so spreading copies across AZs works, while stacking copies in one AZ means a single AZ problem takes all of them down at once.

questions.prompt: A payroll company has private servers in two Availability Zones, AZ-a and AZ-b. To fix a NAT gateway (a managed device that lets private servers reach the internet) single point of failure, they deployed one NAT gateway in each AZ. However, both AZs' route tables still send internet traffic to the NAT gateway in AZ-a. What happens if AZ-a has an outage, and what is the fix?
choices: Servers in AZ-b lose outbound internet access; point AZ-b's route table to its own local NAT gateway in AZ-b.
Only inbound customer traffic stops; fix it by adding a second load balancer in AZ-b rather than changing routes.
Nothing happens, because the second NAT gateway in AZ-b takes over automatically no matter what the route tables say.
Servers in AZ-b keep working because NAT gateways share a Region; the fix is to delete the unused gateway to save cost.
questions.why: A spare NAT gateway only helps if traffic is routed to it, so each AZ's route table must point to its local gateway or AZ-b still depends entirely on AZ-a.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find and remove single points of failure in an existing AWS workload, and name one tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd trace every component a request or outbound call passes through and ask whether that piece failing alone would stop the service. Anything that answers yes is a single point of failure. The fix is redundancy plus automatic failover, spread across at least two Availability Zones, because zones have separate power and networking and rarely fail together. Concretely: servers behind a load balancer in a multi-AZ Auto Scaling group, the database on RDS Multi-AZ so a standby is promoted automatically, and one NAT gateway per zone. I'd also hunt for hidden ones like a single VPN tunnel or state kept on one server. I'd fix first whatever customers would feel first. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: standby databases and extra gateways cost money, so the level of redundancy should match how much downtime the business can actually accept.
rubricPoints: Defines a single point of failure as a component whose failure alone stops the service.
Describes redundancy plus automatic failover as the remedy.
Explains spreading copies across Availability Zones rather than within one.
Gives concrete fixes such as load balancer with multi-AZ Auto Scaling, RDS Multi-AZ, or per-AZ NAT gateways.
Mentions hidden SPOFs like a single NAT gateway, network link, or server-held state.
Names a tradeoff such as added cost or complexity weighed against downtime tolerance.

suggested.rationale: Spotting SPOFs in a described production architecture and ordering fixes by business impact is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, which no current mission or planned engine directly covers.

lessons.plain: This objective is about making a running system copy its data, repair itself, and stretch or shrink with demand, without a person stepping in. Data replication means keeping copies of data in more than one place so losing one copy loses nothing. Self-healing means the system notices a broken part and replaces it on its own. Elasticity means capacity grows when traffic rises and shrinks when it falls, so you pay for what you use. Think of a restaurant that keeps a second copy of every order ticket, swaps in a backup cook when one falls ill, and calls in extra staff only on busy nights.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database keeps a copy in a second data center that is updated a few seconds after each write. If the main data center fails suddenly, what might you lose, and why?
lessons.teach:
Data replication is copying data to another location continuously. Synchronous replication confirms a write only after both copies have it, so no confirmed data is lost on failure, but each write waits for the slower copy. Asynchronous replication confirms first and copies afterward, which is faster and works across long distances, but the copy lags behind; that lag is data you can lose. On AWS, Amazon RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby database in another Availability Zone (an isolated data center group within a Region) and fails over automatically. RDS read replicas, S3 cross-Region replication, and DynamoDB global tables (a managed key-value database copied to several Regions) are asynchronous.

Self-healing means health checks find broken parts and automation replaces them. An Auto Scaling group (a managed pool of virtual servers) keeps a set number of instances running; when an instance fails a health check, the group terminates it and launches a new one. A load balancer, which spreads requests across servers, stops sending traffic to unhealthy targets.

Elasticity means capacity follows demand: Auto Scaling adds or removes servers, DynamoDB on-demand mode bills per request, and serverless functions run only when called.

Worked example: an order app runs on one EC2 server with a single-AZ database. Step one, put servers in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind a load balancer. Step two, switch the group to use the load balancer health check, so a server whose app is hung (but whose machine is up) gets replaced. Step three, enable Multi-AZ on the database so a zone outage triggers failover in a minute or two with no confirmed orders lost. Step four, add a read replica to absorb report queries.

Common mistake: treating a read replica as the disaster plan. It is asynchronous, so recent writes can be missing, and promoting it is a separate action. In a running system that means lost orders and a longer outage than the business expected. Match each feature to the recovery point (how much data you may lose) and recovery time the business needs.

questions.prompt: A payroll company runs its ledger on an Amazon RDS database in one Availability Zone (an isolated data center group within a Region). The business rule is: if that zone fails, no confirmed payment may be lost, and the database must be back within a few minutes without anyone stepping in. Today the team's only protection is an RDS read replica in a second zone. Step 1: State the needs. Recovery point (how much data may be lost) is zero confirmed writes, and recovery time is a few minutes with automatic failover. Step 2: Check the replica's replication type. RDS read replicas use asynchronous replication, meaning a write is confirmed first and copied afterward. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Conclusion. Enable RDS Multi-AZ, which keeps a synchronous standby in another zone and fails over on its own. The read replica can stay to serve read-heavy queries. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Because the replica sits in another zone, it already holds every confirmed write, so the rule is met and no change is needed.
Asynchronous copies are slower to write than synchronous ones, so the only problem is performance, not data loss.
The replica lags behind the primary, so recent confirmed payments can be missing, and promoting it is a separate action, so neither need is met.
The replica fails over automatically, but it cannot be used across zones, so it must be moved into the same zone as the primary.
questions.why: An asynchronous replica can be missing the newest confirmed writes and needs a separate promotion step, so it fails both the zero-loss recovery point and the automatic recovery time.

questions.prompt: A team is choosing how to copy a database to a second location. Which statement correctly describes the trade-off between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
choices: Asynchronous replication waits for both copies before confirming, so it never loses data but cannot span Regions.
Both types confirm writes at the same moment, and they differ only in how much storage they cost.
Synchronous replication confirms a write only after both copies have it, so confirmed data survives a failure, but every write waits for the slower copy.
Synchronous replication confirms a write first and copies it later, so it is the faster option for long distances.
questions.why: Synchronous replication protects every confirmed write by waiting for both copies. That waiting is what makes each write slower.

questions.prompt: A media company runs its web app on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group (a managed pool of virtual servers) behind a load balancer. The group uses only the default instance status checks. Twice this week the web process froze while the virtual machine itself stayed up. Users saw errors for hours until someone rebooted the instance by hand. What change makes the system heal itself in this case?
choices: Add an RDS read replica so the frozen server can read from a second copy of the data.
Raise the group's fixed instance count so there are more servers to absorb the errors.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use the load balancer's health check, so an instance whose app stops answering is marked unhealthy, terminated, and replaced.
Turn on DynamoDB on-demand mode so capacity grows when the app slows down.
questions.why: Instance status checks only see that the machine is up. The load balancer health check tests the app itself, so the group can replace a server whose app has frozen.

questions.prompt: A concert ticketing service stores orders in a DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database). Traffic is near zero most days, then jumps about 30 times higher for the hour after a big show goes on sale, and the sale dates are hard to predict. The business wants capacity to follow demand without paying for idle capacity. Which approach fits this goal of elasticity?
choices: Add DynamoDB global tables in three Regions so the extra copies absorb the spike.
Enable RDS Multi-AZ so a standby can take over when traffic rises.
Switch the table to DynamoDB on-demand mode, which bills per request and handles the spikes without capacity being reserved in advance.
Set the table to a fixed high capacity sized for the busiest hour and leave it there all year.
questions.why: Elasticity means capacity follows demand, and on-demand mode charges per request, so the service pays for the spikes only when they happen and nothing for idle capacity.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make an existing single-server, single-database app replicate its data, heal itself, and scale with demand, and name one tradeoff of the replication choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd move the servers into an Auto Scaling group spread over two Availability Zones behind a load balancer, and set the group to use the load balancer's health check so a server whose app has hung gets replaced, not just one whose machine died. That gives self-healing, and scaling policies on the group give elasticity so we add servers at peak and remove them overnight. For data, I'd turn on RDS Multi-AZ: a synchronous standby in another zone that takes over automatically, so we don't lose confirmed writes. The tradeoff is slightly slower writes and paying for a standby that serves no traffic. I would not count on a read replica for recovery; it's asynchronous, so it can be seconds behind and needs a manual promotion. For cross-Region protection I'd accept some lag with asynchronous replication.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes synchronous replication (no confirmed data loss, slower writes) from asynchronous replication (faster, can lag and lose recent data).
Describes self-healing as health checks plus automatic replacement, ideally using the load balancer health check rather than only the instance check.
Explains elasticity as capacity that grows and shrinks with demand, such as an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones.
Notes that a read replica is not an automatic failover target.
Names a concrete tradeoff such as cost of an idle standby, write latency, or replication lag.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose stale data caused by replication lag, which makes the cost of asynchronous replication concrete.

lessons.plain: Every cloud resource you pay for, such as a virtual server or a database, reports how hard it is actually working. A usage report collects those numbers over days or weeks so you can compare what you bought with what you use. Underutilized means you are paying for far more capacity than the workload needs. Overutilized means the resource is running near its limits, so users risk slowdowns or failures. It is like checking a delivery fleet's logbooks: some vans drive empty all week, while others are overloaded every morning. You downsize the first group and upgrade the second.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's processor averaged 8% busy over the last two weeks, but every weekday at 9:00 it hit 95% for twenty minutes. Would you shrink it to save money? What would you want to check first?
lessons.teach:
Analyzing usage reports means reading utilization metrics (measurements of how much CPU, memory, network, disk, or connections a resource consumes) over a lookback period, which is the window of history you examine, and comparing them with the resource's provisioned capacity, the amount you pay for. Underutilized resources sit mostly idle and waste money. Overutilized resources run near saturation, the point where requests start queuing, and harm performance and reliability.

On AWS, the raw numbers come from Amazon CloudWatch, a metrics service. AWS Compute Optimizer is a recommendation service that studies that history and labels servers, disks, and functions as over-provisioned, under-provisioned, or optimized. AWS Cost Explorer, a spending analysis tool, offers rightsizing recommendations tied to dollars, and AWS Trusted Advisor, an account checker, flags low-utilization servers. These tools work because a long, steady pattern predicts future demand better than a single snapshot.

Worked example. A database server has 16 virtual CPUs. Over 14 days, average CPU is 7%, the 99th percentile (the value only 1% of samples exceed) is 22%, and memory peaks at 30%. Step one: check that the window covers a full business cycle, including month-end. Step two: note that even the peak uses under a quarter of capacity. Step three: estimate that a 4-CPU size would run the peak near 88%, too tight, so choose 8 CPUs, keeping peaks near 44% with headroom. Step four: test, then change during a maintenance window. Separately, a burstable server (one that earns CPU credits while idle and spends them under load) that keeps exhausting its credits is overutilized and should move up a size.

The common mistake is deciding from averages alone, or from CPU alone. By default, memory is not reported by the operating system to CloudWatch unless an agent is installed, so a server can look idle while memory is full. Shrinking it then causes swapping, timeouts, and an outage during the next peak, wiping out any savings.

questions.prompt: A logistics company reviews an order-routing server with 8 virtual CPUs and 64 GiB of memory. Only the default CloudWatch metrics are collected; no monitoring agent is installed. Step one: the team confirms the 35-day lookback window includes two month-end shipping peaks. Step two: average CPU is 5% and 99th-percentile CPU is 14%, so CPU stays well below capacity even at peak. Step three: MISSING. Step four: only after that step do they pick a smaller size, test it, and apply the change in a maintenance window. Which action belongs in step three?
choices: Switch to a burstable server so it can earn CPU credits during the long idle stretches
Shorten the lookback window to the last 7 days so the recommendation reflects only recent demand
Install an agent to report memory and review its peaks, because the default metrics do not include memory
Downsize straight to the smallest size, since a 5% CPU average shows the server is mostly idle
questions.why: Memory is not reported to CloudWatch by default, so the server could look idle while its memory is full, and shrinking it blind could cause swapping and an outage at the next peak.

questions.prompt: A media startup runs a small burstable server, one that earns CPU credits while idle and spends them under load, for its video-thumbnail service. Usage reports show it runs out of CPU credits most afternoons, and requests slow down then. How should this server be classified, and what is the right fix?
choices: Optimized; leave it as it is
Underutilized; move it down a size
Overutilized; move it up a size
Underutilized; it only needs a longer lookback window
questions.why: A burstable server that keeps exhausting its credits is running near saturation, so it is overutilized and needs more capacity.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm's claims server has 64 virtual CPUs. Over a 30-day window that covers a full business cycle, its 99th-percentile CPU is 12% and memory, reported by an agent, peaks at 25%. The peak therefore uses about 7.7 CPUs' worth of work. Which new size best balances savings against headroom?
choices: 4 virtual CPUs
8 virtual CPUs
16 virtual CPUs
Keep 64 virtual CPUs
questions.why: At 16 CPUs the peak runs near 48%, leaving headroom, while 8 CPUs would push the peak to about 96%, near saturation, and 4 CPUs could not carry it at all.

questions.prompt: A payroll company's batch server does its heaviest work in the last three days of each month. An engineer pulls a 7-day utilization report from the middle of the month, sees CPU averaging 3%, and proposes shrinking the server by three sizes. What is the main flaw in this analysis?
choices: CPU averages are always enough to size a server, so the flaw is only that the change was not tested first
The lookback window misses the month-end business cycle, so the real peak demand is unseen
Rightsizing tools ignore history and judge only a single current snapshot
Underutilized servers do not waste money, so there is no reason to resize at all
questions.why: Usage history only predicts future demand if the window covers the full business cycle, and this window leaves out the month-end peak the server must handle.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use usage reports to decide whether to resize a server, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on these reports.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pull at least two weeks of utilization history, ideally a full business cycle, for CPU, memory, network, and disk, from CloudWatch or from a recommendation service like Compute Optimizer. I compare peaks and high percentiles, not just averages, against what the server can deliver. If even the peaks use a small fraction of capacity, it is underutilized and I pick a smaller size that still leaves headroom. If it sits near saturation or keeps running out of burst credits, it is overutilized and I size up. The limit is that the reports only know what was measured: memory is invisible without an agent, and a short window can miss month-end or seasonal spikes. The tradeoff is savings versus headroom, so I test the change before rolling it out.
rubricPoints: Defines underutilized as paying for idle capacity and overutilized as running near saturation.
Uses a lookback period long enough to cover a full usage cycle.
Judges by peaks or high percentiles rather than averages alone.
Checks more than CPU, noting memory needs an agent to be reported.
Leaves headroom and tests before resizing.
Names a limit such as missing metrics or seasonal spikes outside the window.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner read usage histories, spot idle and saturated resources, and see the savings-versus-headroom tradeoff of each resize.

lessons.plain: An unused resource is something you are still paying for that no longer does any work. Examples include a disk attached to nothing, a reserved public address pointing nowhere, or a load balancer with no traffic. In a large cloud estate these pile up quietly as projects end and people move on. Finding them is like checking a storage unit you rent every month: half the boxes may belong to someone who left years ago. AWS has tools that scan your accounts and list likely candidates. A person still decides what is truly abandoned and what is only quiet.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team stopped an old virtual server six months ago but never deleted it. Do you think the company is still being charged for anything related to that server, and if so, for what?
lessons.teach:
An unused resource is a billable cloud resource that has no meaningful activity or attachment. Typical cases on AWS are unattached EBS volumes, which are block storage disks connected to no server. Others are unassociated Elastic IPs, which are reserved public addresses mapped to nothing, and load balancers with no healthy targets or requests. Old snapshots, meaning point-in-time disk copies, also count, as do idle NAT gateways, which are managed outbound-internet routers, and databases with zero connections. Each one bills by the hour or by the gigabyte, whether or not it does any work.

Several managed tools find them. AWS Trusted Advisor is an account-checking service that flags idle load balancers, unassociated addresses, and low-use instances and databases. AWS Compute Optimizer studies usage metrics over time and labels some resources as idle. AWS Cost Optimization Hub gathers these recommendations across many accounts in an organization. AWS Config records how resources are configured, so a rule can flag every volume whose state is available, meaning not attached. IAM Access Analyzer reports unused roles and permissions, which cost nothing but widen your security exposure. Tags are key-value labels such as owner or project. They tell you who to ask before you delete anything.

Worked example. Trusted Advisor lists a 500 GB volume that is unattached. You check its tags: project=legacy-reporting, owner=a departed engineer. CloudWatch, the metrics service, shows no input or output activity for 90 days. You take a snapshot as a cheap safety copy and notify the project's cost center. After a waiting period, you delete the volume and keep the snapshot for an agreed retention time.

A common mistake is treating quiet as unused. A disaster-recovery standby, a quarterly batch database, or a stopped instance kept for an audit can all look idle. Deleting them breaks recovery or compliance later, and nobody notices until the day it matters. A related mistake is stopping an instance and assuming the bill ends. Its attached volumes and any reserved addresses keep charging.

questions.prompt: A small analytics firm stops 8 test servers (EC2 instances) on Friday to cut costs. Each server has a 200 GB EBS volume attached, and 3 of them also have an Elastic IP associated. The following month's bill still shows charges for those servers. Trace the reasoning. Step 1: Stopping an instance ends its hourly compute charge. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: For the servers the owners confirm are no longer needed, the team takes a snapshot of each volume, deletes the volumes, and releases the Elastic IPs. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The attached EBS volumes keep billing per gigabyte, and the Elastic IPs keep billing because they are still reserved.
The charges must come from a NAT gateway, because stopping an instance never leaves storage or addresses billable.
Stopped instances keep billing for compute at a reduced idle rate until they are fully terminated.
Charges can only come from snapshots, so the team should delete every snapshot in the account.
questions.why: Stopping an instance ends only the compute charge, while its attached block storage disks and any reserved public addresses keep billing until they are deleted or released.

questions.prompt: A media company wants an automatic, ongoing check that flags every EBS volume (block storage disk) whose state is "available", meaning attached to no server. Which AWS service is built to record resource configuration so that a rule like this can run?
choices: AWS Config
IAM Access Analyzer
Resource tags
AWS Compute Optimizer
questions.why: AWS Config records how resources are configured, so a rule can flag every volume whose state is available, meaning not attached.

questions.prompt: A security review at a logistics company finds 60 IAM roles that have not been used in months. A manager says, "They cost nothing, so leave them." What is the best reason to still review and remove them?
choices: Each unused role bills by the hour until it is deleted.
Unused roles slow down Trusted Advisor's checks on the account.
Unused roles keep EBS volumes and Elastic IPs attached and billing.
They cost nothing, but they widen the account's security exposure.
questions.why: Unused roles and permissions, as reported by IAM Access Analyzer, cost nothing but widen your security exposure, so removing them is a security fix, not a cost fix.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's cost report shows a database that has had zero connections for 80 days. Its tags read purpose=quarterly-claims-close, owner=finance-ops. What should the engineer do first?
choices: Stop it and assume the bill ends, since a stopped database cannot be charged.
Take a snapshot and delete it the same day, because a snapshot makes deletion risk-free.
Delete it right away, because 80 days with zero connections proves it is unused.
Treat it as possibly quiet rather than unused, and confirm with finance-ops before changing anything.
questions.why: A quarterly batch database can look idle between runs, so treating quiet as unused risks breaking a business process, and the owner tag tells you who to ask first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find and safely remove unused resources across your AWS accounts, and name one limit or risk of trusting the tools' findings automatically.
lessons.modelAnswer: Unused resources are things we pay for that do no work, like unattached EBS volumes, Elastic IPs mapped to nothing, load balancers with no traffic, old snapshots, and idle NAT gateways. I would use Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer to flag candidates, Cost Optimization Hub to see them across the organization, and an AWS Config rule to catch new unattached volumes continuously. For each finding, I'd check the tags to find an owner and confirm there has been no activity in CloudWatch over a long window. Then I'd snapshot anything holding data, notify the owner, wait, and delete. The limit is that the tools only see low activity, not intent. A disaster-recovery standby or a quarterly job looks idle but is essential. Automatic deletion trades saved money for the risk of breaking recovery or compliance. Missing tags make the owner check slow.
rubricPoints: Defines unused resources as billable items doing no work and gives concrete examples.
Names at least two AWS tools that surface candidates, such as Trusted Advisor, Compute Optimizer, Cost Optimization Hub, or Config.
Describes verifying with tags, an owner, and activity history before acting.
Mentions a safety step such as a snapshot and a waiting period before deletion.
Explains the risk that quiet but essential resources, like DR standbys or periodic jobs, get removed.
Notes that stopping an instance does not stop charges for its volumes or addresses.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner hunt idle and orphaned resources in a simulated bill and see the saving, and the risk, of removing each one.

lessons.plain: A billing alarm is an automatic warning that tells you when spending on a cloud account is heading somewhere you did not expect. A useful one starts from what normal spending looks like: how much you usually spend, how it rises through the month, and when it is busy, such as month-end batch jobs or holiday traffic. Think of it as a household budget app. 'You spent more than 500' tells you nothing. 'You are on track to spend double your normal grocery bill, and it is only the 10th' tells you something useful early enough to act.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company normally spends about 30,000 dollars a month on cloud, fairly evenly each day. You set one alarm that fires when the month's total passes 30,000. On the 8th, a misconfigured job starts burning an extra 2,000 dollars a day. Roughly when would that alarm fire, and is that early enough?
lessons.teach:
A billing alarm is a rule that watches a cost figure and notifies people, or triggers an action, when that figure crosses a line. On AWS there are three common tools. A CloudWatch billing alarm watches the EstimatedCharges metric, which is a running month-to-date total of the account's charges. Billing alerts must be switched on first, and the metric is published only in the us-east-1 Region. AWS Budgets lets you set an expected amount of cost or usage for a period. It can alert on actual spend or on forecasted spend, meaning where the month will probably end. Budgets can be scoped by account, service, or cost allocation tag, and can run actions such as applying a restrictive policy. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection learns each service's or team's normal spending pattern and flags unusual deviations, so you do not have to guess a fixed line.

Designing from expected usage works because cost has a shape. It may be flat, rise steadily with growth, or spike at month-end. A good alarm compares what is happening with that shape, not with one round number.

Worked example. Expected spend is 30,000 dollars a month, about 1,000 a day. On day 8 a runaway job adds 2,000 a day. A static alarm on EstimatedCharges at 30,000 is reached when 8,000 + 3,000 x days = 30,000, which is about day 15. That is a week of waste, roughly 14,000 dollars extra. A budget with a forecasted alert at 110 percent sees that the projected month-end figure has jumped toward 90,000 within a day or two and fires around day 9. Anomaly detection on that service flags the daily jump at about the same time.

A common mistake is forgetting that EstimatedCharges is cumulative and resets each month. A threshold of 1,000 meant as a daily limit fires on day 1 or 2 every month, and people learn to ignore it. In a running system, noisy or late cost alarms mean real overspend is found on the invoice, after the money is gone.

questions.prompt:
A small analytics firm expects to spend about 9,000 dollars a month, roughly 300 dollars a day, fairly flat. On day 11 a misconfigured logging pipeline starts adding an extra 600 dollars a day, so daily spend becomes 900. They have a static CloudWatch billing alarm on EstimatedCharges (the cumulative month-to-date charges total) set at 9,000.

Step 1: By the end of day 10, month-to-date spend is 10 x 300 = 3,000 dollars.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: An AWS Budgets forecasted alert at 110 percent would see the projected month-end figure jump toward about 21,000 within a day or two and fire around day 12.
Step 4: The static alarm leaves about five extra days of waste, at 600 dollars a day roughly 3,000 dollars, that a forecast or anomaly alert would have caught.

Which line completes Step 2?
choices: 900 x days = 9,000, so the static alarm fires around day 10, as if the higher rate had applied all month.
300 x days = 9,000, so the static alarm fires on day 30, when the normal month's spend is reached.
The static alarm fires on day 11, because it notices the daily jump in spend as soon as it happens.
3,000 + 900 x d = 9,000, so d is about 7 more days and the static alarm fires around day 17.
questions.why: EstimatedCharges keeps adding up from the start of the month, so the 3,000 already spent plus 900 a day reaches 9,000 after about 7 more days, around day 17.

questions.prompt: An engineer is setting up a CloudWatch billing alarm and asks what the EstimatedCharges metric actually measures. Which description is accurate?
choices: The charges for the current day only, which reset to zero every midnight and are published in each Region where you run resources.
A learned baseline of each service's normal spending, used to flag unusual deviations without a fixed threshold.
A forecast of where the month's total spend will probably end, based on the pattern of spending so far.
A running month-to-date total of the account's charges, which resets each month and is published only in us-east-1 once billing alerts are switched on.
questions.why: EstimatedCharges is cumulative month-to-date, resets monthly, requires billing alerts to be enabled, and appears only in us-east-1. Forecasts belong to Budgets and learned baselines to Cost Anomaly Detection.

questions.prompt: A media company plans to spend 50,000 dollars a month on its development accounts. Finance wants a warning partway through the month if spend is on track to exceed that plan, not after it already has. They also want a restrictive policy applied automatically to the development accounts when the plan is exceeded. Which design fits best?
choices: A CloudWatch billing alarm on EstimatedCharges at 50,000 in us-east-1, which notifies finance by email.
A single static alarm at 1,700 dollars on EstimatedCharges, meant as a daily limit that matches 50,000 divided by 30.
An AWS Budgets budget of 50,000 scoped to the development accounts, with a forecasted-spend alert and an action that applies a restrictive policy.
A CloudWatch billing alarm on EstimatedCharges at 50,000, created in the eu-west-1 Region where the workloads run.
questions.why: Budgets can alert on forecasted spend, so the warning comes before the line is crossed, can be scoped by account, and can run actions such as applying a restrictive policy.

questions.prompt: A retail team set a CloudWatch billing alarm on EstimatedCharges at 400 dollars, intending it as a daily spending limit. Their normal spend is about 250 dollars a day. Every month the alarm fires on day 2, and the team now ignores it. What is the underlying problem?
choices: EstimatedCharges is a cumulative month-to-date total, so it passes 400 early every month regardless of any daily spike; a forecast-based budget or anomaly detection would match the intended behaviour.
Billing alerts were not switched on, so the metric is reporting incorrect values early in the month.
The alarm was set too high; lowering it to 250 dollars would make it fire only on days when spend is unusual.
EstimatedCharges only counts one service at a time, so it must be split into separate alarms per service.
questions.why: Because EstimatedCharges keeps adding up and only resets monthly, a threshold meant as a daily limit is crossed within the first days every month, producing noise people learn to ignore.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design cost alerting for a production account whose spend grows each month and spikes at month-end, and name one limitation or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the account's real spending shape, not a round number. First, set an AWS Budget per account and per major team tag, sized to this month's expected spend, with a forecasted alert at around 110 percent. That warns us early in the month if we are on track to overshoot, instead of telling us after the money is spent. Second, turn on Cost Anomaly Detection per service, so an unusual daily jump is flagged even when the monthly total still looks fine. A plain CloudWatch alarm on EstimatedCharges is a useful backstop, but it is a cumulative month-to-date figure, so a static line catches problems late. The tradeoff is upkeep. Budgets must be revised as the business grows, or they become noisy. Anomaly detection needs history, it can mistake the planned month-end spike for an anomaly, and billing data lags by hours.
rubricPoints: Thresholds are derived from the expected spending pattern, including growth and seasonal spikes, not a fixed round number.
EstimatedCharges is cumulative month-to-date and resets monthly, so static alarms on it fire late or misleadingly.
Forecast-based budget alerts warn before the overspend happens.
Anomaly detection catches unusual jumps without hand-tuned thresholds.
Alerts are scoped by account, service, or tag so the right owner is notified.
Names a tradeoff such as data lag, maintenance as baselines change, or false positives.

suggested.rationale: Building alarms against a simulated cumulative spend curve lets the learner see firsthand how static, forecast, and anomaly thresholds fire at very different times.

lessons.plain: A Cost and Usage Report (CUR) is the most detailed bill a cloud provider can give you. A normal invoice says you spent a certain amount on compute this month. The CUR breaks that down into many small rows, often one per resource per hour, each saying what was used, where, by which account, and at what price. Think of the difference between a credit-card statement that says "groceries: 400" and the till receipts that list every item you bought. Investigating the CUR means reading those receipts to find exactly which resource, account or kind of usage is driving the spend, so you can fix the right thing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your monthly cloud bill jumped 30 percent, and the summary only says "compute, other" went up. If you had a spreadsheet with one row per resource per hour, what columns would you want so you could find the culprit?
lessons.teach:
The AWS Cost and Usage Report is a billing dataset delivered as files into an Amazon S3 bucket (S3 is AWS object storage). Its newer form is configured through AWS Data Exports. Each row is a line item: a slice of usage with columns for the account, Region, service, usage type (the specific meter, such as NAT gateway bytes processed), operation (the API action that was billed), the resource ID if you choose to include it, the line item type, cost, and any activated cost allocation tags. Granularity can be hourly or daily. With consolidated billing, the management account's report covers every member account in the organization.

The files are large, so you query them in place with Amazon Athena, a serverless SQL engine that reads files in S3, and you can chart the results in Amazon QuickSight. Summary tools such as Cost Explorer show trends. The CUR answers "which exact resource, and why."

Worked example: the bill rose, and Cost Explorer shows the growth in the EC2-Other bucket, which mixes storage volumes, NAT gateways and data transfer. Step 1: group the CUR by usage type for this month and last month. NatGateway-Bytes tripled. Step 2: group those rows by account. One account, a new analytics team's account, holds almost all of the increase. Step 3: group by resource ID and hour. One NAT gateway, a managed device that lets private servers reach the internet, has been busy every hour since a job began pulling data from S3 through it. The fix is to send that traffic through a gateway endpoint to S3 instead, which avoids the NAT processing charge.

A common mistake is to sum the unblended cost column, which shows usage priced at the rate charged when it happened, without filtering on line item type. When Savings Plans or Reserved Instances apply, that view shows commitment fees as lumps and can double count covered usage. The fix is to use amortized cost, which spreads commitment fees across the usage they cover. If you skip this, you can blame the wrong team, or chase a spike that is really a yearly upfront payment.

questions.prompt: A media company's bill rose sharply in May. Cost Explorer shows the growth sits in the EC2-Other bucket. An engineer works through the Cost and Usage Report (CUR) with Athena. Step 1: she groups May and April rows by usage type and finds that storage-volume usage (the meter for block disks attached to servers) roughly doubled. Step 2: she groups those storage rows by account and finds that one account, used by a video-encoding test team, holds nearly all of the increase. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the results show about 60 volumes that appeared on the same day and have been billed every day since, all named by an automated test pipeline that never deletes its disks. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Group the storage rows in that account by resource ID and by day, which works because resource IDs were included in the report
Group all rows in the organization by service to find out which service grew the most
Sum the unblended cost column for that account to confirm the total size of the increase
Switch to Cost Explorer and filter the EC2-Other bucket by Region to see where the volumes live
questions.why: Once the meter and the account are known, grouping by resource ID over time is what names the exact volumes and shows when they started costing money.

questions.prompt: A finance analyst at a logistics firm wants a cost view in which a three-year Savings Plan fee is spread across the hours of usage it covers, rather than appearing as a lump in one month. Which CUR cost measure gives this?
choices: Amortized cost
Unblended cost with no line item type filter
The total for the EC2-Other bucket in Cost Explorer
Hourly granularity instead of daily granularity
questions.why: Amortized cost spreads commitment fees across the usage they cover, so a prepaid commitment does not appear as a single spike.

questions.prompt: A bank runs 40 accounts under AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. Its platform team wants one CUR dataset covering every account, and it wants to run SQL against those large files without loading them into a database first. What setup fits?
choices: Use only Cost Explorer, because the CUR cannot show account-level detail
Deliver the CUR from the management account to S3 and query it in place with Athena
Turn on a CUR in each member account and read the totals in Cost Explorer
Copy the CUR files from S3 into a spreadsheet and sum the unblended cost column
questions.why: The management account's report covers all member accounts under consolidated billing, and Athena is a serverless SQL engine that reads the files directly in S3.

questions.prompt: At a software company, a manager sums unblended cost by team for January and sees one team's cost jump far above every other month. That team had bought one-year Reserved Instances with an upfront payment in January, and the query did not filter on line item type. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The team's servers really used far more capacity in January and need to be resized
The CUR was set to daily granularity, which inflates monthly totals
Reserved Instances are charged twice in every CUR, so the bill really was doubled
The upfront commitment fee shows as a lump in unblended cost, so the spike may be a payment rather than extra usage
questions.why: Unblended cost without a line item type filter shows commitment fees as lumps and can double count covered usage, so switching to amortized cost shows whether usage actually rose.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use the Cost and Usage Report to find why last month's bill went up, and name one limit or pitfall of working with it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Cost and Usage Report is the itemized version of our bill. It lands in an S3 bucket as rows of line items, hourly if we set it up that way. Each row has the account, Region, service, usage type, operation, resource ID, line item type, cost and our activated tags. I'd query it with Athena and narrow down step by step. First I'd compare this month to last month by usage type. Then I'd break the biggest mover down by account. Then I'd break it down by resource ID and hour, to find the exact resource and when the spend started. The main pitfall is cost columns. If we have Savings Plans or Reserved Instances, summing unblended cost without filtering line item types can double count usage or show upfront fees as false spikes, so I'd use amortized cost. The report is also large and only as useful as the options we enabled, such as resource IDs and tags. It points at the cause, but it doesn't fix anything.
rubricPoints: Describes the CUR as the most granular billing data, with line items per resource and time period, delivered to S3.
Mentions querying it with SQL, for example with Athena, rather than reading it by hand.
Shows a narrowing method: usage type, then account, then resource ID and time.
Names a pitfall such as unblended versus amortized cost, or missing resource IDs or tags.
Ties the finding to a concrete fix or owner.

suggested.rationale: Drilling into itemized charges in a simulated cost dataset, and tracing a spend spike down to the single resource behind it, builds this skill far better than reading about it.

lessons.plain: A tag is a small label you stick on a cloud resource, made of a key and a value, such as Team=Payments or Environment=Production. Cost allocation tagging means using those labels so the monthly bill can be split by team, project, or environment instead of arriving as one big number. Think of a shared office supply cupboard where every item carries a sticker naming the department that ordered it; at month end, accounting adds up the stickers. Without stickers, nobody knows who spent what, and nobody feels responsible for cutting waste.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company tags every server with a Team label, but the finance report still shows 30 percent of spending as unassigned. What kinds of things might be missing the label, or not counted by it?
lessons.teach:
A tag is a key-value pair attached to a cloud resource, for example CostCenter=4410. In AWS, a cost allocation tag is a tag that has been activated in the billing settings, usually from the management account, which is the account that pays for every account in an AWS Organization (a group of accounts managed together). Only activated tags appear as columns or filters in billing tools such as Cost Explorer, a chart-based spending viewer, and the Cost and Usage Report, a detailed line-by-line billing file. There are two kinds: user-defined tags that your teams create, and AWS-generated tags such as aws:createdBy that AWS applies.

This works because billing records each charge against a resource, so a label on the resource travels with its cost. Activation is not automatically retroactive: costs before activation are generally not grouped by the tag, and new tags can take up to about a day to show up.

Worked example: three teams share one account. Step one, agree on a key, CostCenter, with allowed values. Step two, tag resources. Step three, activate CostCenter as a cost allocation tag. Step four, in Cost Explorer, group spending by CostCenter. The report shows 30 percent labelled 'no tag'. Investigating finds untagged storage volumes, data transfer charges that cannot carry tags, and some resources tagged costcenter in lower case.

That last finding is the common mistake: tag keys are case sensitive, so CostCenter and costcenter become two separate report columns. Fix it with enforcement: tag policies in AWS Organizations define allowed keys, capitalization, and values; service control policies, which are guardrails limiting what accounts may do, can deny creating resources without required tags; and an AWS Config rule, which continuously checks resource settings, can flag untagged resources. Cost categories can then group tags and accounts into business units and split shared costs.

In a running system, poor tagging means chargeback to teams is wrong, waste stays hidden, and cost-cutting effort lands on the wrong owners.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs five accounts in one AWS Organization. Its finance lead wants monthly spend broken down by a Project tag. Here is how the team worked it through. Step 1: platform engineers agreed on the key Project with allowed values such as Routing and Billing, and confirmed that the servers and databases in all five accounts now carry it. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: they waited about a day for the new tag to appear in the billing tools. Step 4: in Cost Explorer they grouped spending by Project and saw each project's share, noting that spending from before Step 2 was not grouped. What is Step 2?
choices: Turn on AWS Config in each account so the Project tag gets recorded against costs
From the management account's billing settings, activate Project as a cost allocation tag
Attach a service control policy that denies creating resources without a Project tag
Create a cost category that maps each Project value to a business unit
questions.why: A tag only shows up as a filter or grouping in billing tools such as Cost Explorer after it is activated as a cost allocation tag, usually from the management account, and only costs from after that point are grouped.

questions.prompt: A developer has added the tag Owner=payments-team to forty resources. The finance team says Owner still does not appear as an option in Cost Explorer or in the Cost and Usage Report. Which statement best explains what a cost allocation tag is and why Owner is missing?
choices: It is a tag that has been activated in the billing settings, and Owner has not been activated yet
It is a tag applied by a service control policy, so Owner must be added through one
It is a tag that AWS Config has checked, so Config must be enabled before Owner appears
It is any tag whose key starts with aws:, so Owner must be renamed aws:Owner
questions.why: Only tags activated in the billing settings appear in billing tools. Tagging a resource alone is not enough, and keys starting with aws: are the AWS-generated kind, not something you create.

questions.prompt: A hospital group's cost report shows two separate columns, Environment and environment, and each holds part of its production spend. The cloud team wants to stop this from happening again across all its accounts. Which action targets the root cause most directly?
choices: Activate both keys as cost allocation tags so that every cost is visible in the report
Use a tag policy in AWS Organizations that defines the allowed key and its exact capitalization
Wait about a day, because billing tools combine keys that differ only by capitalization
Delete the Cost and Usage Report and rebuild it, so the two columns merge into one
questions.why: Tag keys are case sensitive, so the two spellings stay as separate columns. A tag policy enforces one allowed key with a fixed capitalization, which stops the split at its source.

questions.prompt: An online retailer activates Team as a cost allocation tag on 15 March. On 1 April a manager opens Cost Explorer, groups the whole of March by Team, and finds that much of early March appears with no Team value, even though those resources were tagged in February. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The resources were tagged in the wrong account, so the tags never reached billing
Activation is generally not retroactive, so costs from before 15 March are not grouped by Team
Cost Explorer cannot group by user-defined tags, only by AWS-generated tags
Tag keys are case sensitive, so the February tags must have used lower-case team
questions.why: Costs from before a tag is activated are generally not grouped by it, so early March shows no Team value even though the resources already carried the tag.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how tagging lets the business see costs per team, and describe one limit of tags that means the report will never be perfectly complete on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: We put key-value labels like CostCenter=4410 on every resource, then activate that key as a cost allocation tag in the billing settings of the management account. After that, Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report can group spending by the tag, so each team sees its own bill. Activation mostly applies going forward, so history before it is not split, and it takes up to about a day to appear. Because keys are case sensitive, we enforce one spelling with Organizations tag policies, block untagged creation with service control policies, and catch drift with a Config rule. The limit: some charges cannot carry tags, such as certain data transfer or shared support fees, and anything people forgot to tag lands in 'no tag'. Those need allocation rules, for example cost categories that split shared costs by a fixed percentage.
rubricPoints: Defines a tag as a key-value label on a resource that travels with its cost.
States that tags must be activated as cost allocation tags before billing tools show them.
Notes activation is not automatically retroactive and has a short delay.
Mentions consistency problems such as case-sensitive keys and the need for enforcement.
Names a concrete enforcement or detection mechanism such as tag policies, SCPs, or Config rules.
Identifies untaggable or shared costs as a limit requiring separate allocation.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing among activation, tag policies, SCPs, Config rules, and cost categories for a given messy scenario, which is best practised by reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: A migration assessment is the homework you do before moving applications to the cloud: list what you run, see how busy each machine really is, decide which servers belong together, and choose how each application should move. AWS Migration Hub is a single dashboard that gathers that homework in one place. It collects the inventory, suggests right-sized cloud machines and a migration approach for each application, then shows progress while other tools do the actual moving. Think of a wedding planner's binder: it moves no furniture itself, but it records every guest, table and supplier and shows what is done.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 300 servers to move to the cloud. Before copying anything, what three questions would you want answered about those servers, and why would you group them by application rather than handle them one by one?
lessons.teach:
An application migration assessment is the step where you turn a raw server inventory into a decision for each application: what it is made of, what size it should be in the cloud, which migration strategy fits, and how you will track it. AWS Migration Hub is the central console for this. It does not copy data or servers itself; it stores and shows information coming from discovery and migration tools.

The flow works in four steps. First, choose a home region, the single AWS Region where Migration Hub stores all your assessment and tracking data; pick it deliberately, because everything reports there. Second, bring in discovery data, meaning the inventory of servers plus their usage (CPU, memory, disk, network connections), either from a discovery tool or by uploading a spreadsheet import file. Third, group servers into applications, so a web, app and database server that serve one business purpose are assessed and tracked as one unit. Fourth, generate recommendations: EC2 instance recommendations suggest a right-sized virtual machine type from observed utilization, and Migration Hub Strategy Recommendations analyzes the application and proposes a strategy such as rehost, replatform or refactor, flagging blockers like an unsupported operating system.

Worked example: a payroll system runs on three servers. You import their data, group them as Payroll, and request instance recommendations. The app server has 8 virtual CPUs but peaks at 15 percent, so the recommendation is a much smaller type. Strategy Recommendations suggests replatforming the database onto a managed database service. Later, as migration tools move each server, Payroll's status in the hub changes from not started to in progress to complete.

A common mistake is treating Migration Hub as the thing that migrates. It only plans and tracks. Another is skipping application grouping: you then size and track servers in isolation, miss dependencies, and can move a database without the servers that call it, breaking the running application during cutover.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is assessing its warehouse tracking application, which runs on four on-premises servers. The team picks one home region so all assessment data reports to a single place. They upload a spreadsheet import file listing the four servers with their CPU, memory, disk and network usage. They group the servers as one application called WarehouseTrack. Next they request EC2 instance recommendations, which suggest virtual machine types for the cloud. The reporting server has 16 virtual CPUs but never goes above 10 percent CPU use over the measured period. Missing step: what will the recommendation for the reporting server most likely be?
choices: A noticeably smaller type, because recommendations are right-sized from observed utilization
No type at all, because Migration Hub first launches the server and then measures it
A type with 16 virtual CPUs, because the cloud server should match the on-premises hardware exactly
A larger type with extra virtual CPUs, so the server has headroom after the move
questions.why: EC2 instance recommendations base the suggested size on observed usage, so a server that peaks at 10 percent of 16 virtual CPUs gets a much smaller type.

questions.prompt: A project manager at an insurance firm says: "Once we load our server inventory into AWS Migration Hub, it will copy the servers to AWS for us." What is the accurate correction?
choices: Migration Hub only plans and tracks; it stores and shows data from discovery and migration tools, while other tools do the actual moving
Correct, Migration Hub copies servers but not databases, which need a separate tool
Migration Hub copies data only if the servers are first grouped into applications
Migration Hub copies the servers only after Strategy Recommendations approves each one
questions.why: Migration Hub is a central console for assessment and tracking; it does not copy data or servers itself.

questions.prompt: A media company has migration teams in Sydney and in Frankfurt, both assessing applications in AWS Migration Hub. What should the company do about the home region, the single AWS Region where Migration Hub stores assessment and tracking data?
choices: Let each team set its own home region so data stays near the team
Skip setting a home region, because Migration Hub picks the closest one per server
Set a home region only for applications that will be refactored
Deliberately choose one home region, since all assessment and tracking data reports there
questions.why: Migration Hub stores everything in one home region, so it should be chosen on purpose and used for all the data.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT team imported discovery data for 30 servers but did not group them into applications. During cutover they moved the database server for the patient booking system, and the booking system stopped working. What most likely caused this?
choices: Strategy Recommendations flagged the database as a blocker and Migration Hub shut it down
EC2 instance recommendations always undersize databases, so it could not handle the load
The home region was set incorrectly, so Migration Hub blocked the database from being reached
Without application grouping, servers were assessed in isolation, so the team missed that the booking web and app servers depended on that database
questions.why: Skipping grouping means dependencies are missed, so a database can be moved without the servers that call it, breaking the application at cutover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what completing an application migration assessment in AWS Migration Hub involves, step by step, and name one thing Migration Hub does not do or one way the assessment can mislead you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Migration Hub is our central place for planning and tracking the move, not the tool that copies anything. First we set a home region, because all assessment and tracking data lives there. Then we load discovery data, either from a discovery tool or an import file, so we have each server's specs and real utilization. Next we group servers into applications, so a web, app and database tier are assessed and tracked together and we do not split dependencies. Then we generate recommendations: right-sized EC2 instance types from observed usage, and Strategy Recommendations proposing rehost, replatform or refactor per application. As other migration tools run, the hub shows each application's status. The limit: recommendations are only as good as the data. If we collected usage during a quiet week, sizing will be too small, and Migration Hub itself never moves a server.
rubricPoints: States that Migration Hub plans and tracks but does not itself migrate data or servers.
Mentions choosing a home region where the data is stored.
Describes loading discovery data from a tool or import file.
Explains grouping servers into applications so dependencies stay together.
Names the recommendations: right-sized instance types and a migration strategy per application.
Names a limit, such as recommendations depending on the quality and timing of collected data.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine walks through a migration assessment, so reasoning through an exam-style portfolio scenario best practises sequencing discovery, grouping, recommendations and tracking.

lessons.plain: Portfolio assessment is taking stock of everything a company runs before deciding what to move to the cloud and how.
