You list every application, the servers and databases behind it, who owns it, how important it is to the business, and what else it depends on. Asset planning then uses that list to decide what each piece needs in its new home. It is like packing for a house move. First you walk every room and note what you own, what is fragile, and what belongs together. Only then do you book the right size truck and decide what to sell, bin, or upgrade.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 400 servers and wants to move to the cloud. Before choosing any tools, what three facts would you want to know about each application running on those servers, and why?
lessons.teach:
Portfolio assessment is the structured inventory and evaluation of an organization's IT estate before a migration. The portfolio is the full set of applications. An asset is any component behind them: a server, a database, a storage share, a license, or a network appliance. Asset planning means deciding, from evidence, what each asset needs in the target environment and whether it should move at all.

A good assessment records several things for each application. The first is business criticality, meaning how badly the business suffers if the application is down. The second is the owner, the person who can approve change. Then come technical facts such as operating system, versions, and end-of-support dates. It also needs measured utilization, meaning the actual CPU, memory, and storage used over weeks, not what was provisioned. Finally it records dependencies, meaning which other systems the application calls or is called by. Licensing terms matter too, because some licenses are tied to specific hardware.

This works because migration decisions are only as good as the facts behind them. Dependencies show which components must move together. Utilization data shows the right size for each target. Criticality and complexity together show which applications to start with.

Worked example: a payroll application runs on two 16-core servers. Step one, group the assets. The two servers plus a shared file server belong to one application. Step two, measure. Over 30 days CPU peaks at 20 percent, so a much smaller target is enough. Step three, map dependencies. Payroll reads nightly from the HR database, so the two should move close together in time. Step four, score it. It has high criticality and moderate complexity, so it is not a first candidate.

A common mistake is to inventory servers instead of applications, or to size targets from provisioned specs. The result in a running system is either an application that breaks after cutover because a hidden dependency was left behind, or a cloud bill inflated by idle, oversized resources.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company is assessing its trip-planning application before a migration. Step one, group the assets: a web server, an application server, a PostgreSQL database and a network load-balancing appliance all serve this one application. Step two, measure: over six weeks, the application server, provisioned with 12 cores, never exceeds 25 percent CPU, so a smaller target will do. Step three, map dependencies: the team finds that the trip planner pulls live vehicle positions every five minutes from a separate fleet-tracking system that is not yet scheduled to move. Step four, score: it has low criticality and low complexity. What is the correct conclusion from step three?
choices: The trip planner and the fleet-tracking system should be planned to move close together in time, or the trip planner may break after cutover.
The trip planner should be retired, because any application with an external dependency cannot be migrated.
The fleet-tracking system should be sized from the trip planner's provisioned 12 cores, because the two share traffic.
The dependency can be ignored, because the trip planner only reads data and never writes to the fleet-tracking system.
questions.why: Dependency mapping shows which components must move together, and leaving behind a system the application calls can break it after cutover, whether the calls read or write.

questions.prompt: A retailer's migration team produces this list: 'online storefront', 'warehouse picking app', a Linux database server, a shared NFS storage volume, and a database license tied to one physical host. Using portfolio-assessment terms, which statement is correct?
choices: All five items are assets, and the portfolio is just the list of servers among them.
The storefront and picking app are part of the portfolio of applications, while the server, storage volume and license are assets behind them.
The license is neither an asset nor part of the portfolio, so it does not belong in the assessment.
The storage volume is an application, because other systems connect to it.
questions.why: The portfolio is the full set of applications, and an asset is any component behind them, including servers, storage shares and licenses.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm is sizing a cloud target for its claims-processing server. The server was bought with 24 cores and 128 GB of memory. A one-afternoon check during a quiet week showed 5 percent CPU. Which sizing approach fits sound asset planning?
choices: Size the target from the one-afternoon reading, because any measured value is better than the provisioned specs.
Match the target to 24 cores and 128 GB, because provisioned specs show what the application was designed to need.
Measure actual CPU, memory and storage use over several weeks, then size the target from those figures.
Double the provisioned specs to leave headroom for growth after cutover.
questions.why: Right-sizing relies on measured utilization over weeks rather than provisioned specs or a single short snapshot, which can miss peaks.

questions.prompt: A university migrated its course-registration application by moving every server it had listed on a spreadsheet of servers. On the first day after cutover, registration fails because it can no longer reach an on-premises identity server that nobody had put on the move list. What assessment mistake most likely caused this?
choices: The team recorded an owner for the application who could approve the change.
The team scored the application's business criticality before choosing when to move it.
The team inventoried servers instead of applications and did not map the application's dependencies.
The team sized targets from measured utilization instead of provisioned specs.
questions.why: Inventorying servers rather than applications, without mapping dependencies, leaves hidden dependencies behind and breaks the application after cutover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a portfolio assessment collects and how it feeds asset planning, and name one limit of relying on the data it produces.
lessons.modelAnswer: A portfolio assessment is our inventory of everything we run, organized by application rather than by server. For each application we capture the owner and business criticality. We also note the technical stack and support dates, real measured utilization, licensing constraints, and above all its dependencies on other systems. Asset planning uses that evidence. Dependencies tell us which components must move together. Utilization tells us how small the target can safely be. Criticality plus complexity tells us which applications are low-risk early movers and which should wait. One limit is that the data is a snapshot. If we measure utilization over a quiet month, we miss quarter-end peaks and undersize things. Automated discovery also misses rare or undocumented connections, such as a yearly batch job. So we confirm findings with application owners, and we accept that collecting enough history costs time before we can plan.
rubricPoints: Defines portfolio assessment as an inventory organized around applications, not just servers.
Names key data collected: owner, criticality, technical stack, utilization, dependencies, licensing.
Explains that dependencies decide which components move together.
Explains that sizing should use measured utilization rather than provisioned capacity.
Names a limit, such as snapshot data missing peaks or undocumented dependencies, and how to mitigate it.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning from a messy inventory to grouping, sizing, and sequencing decisions, which an exam-style scenario exercises better than reading alone, and no existing mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When a company moves its applications from its own data center to the cloud, it does not treat them all the same way. The seven common migration strategies, nicknamed the 7Rs, are seven labels for what to do with each application: switch it off, leave it where it is, copy it across unchanged, move its whole virtual environment, move it with small improvements, replace it with a bought product, or rebuild it properly for the cloud. Think of moving house: some furniture goes to the dump, some stays in storage, most goes on the truck as is, and a few pieces get replaced or rebuilt.
lessons.guessPrompt: An internal reporting tool on your migration list has had no logins for a year. What would you do with it during the move, and why?
lessons.teach:
The 7Rs are seven labels for what to do with each application in a migration portfolio. Retire: switch it off because nobody needs it. Retain: leave it on premises for now, perhaps because of a compliance rule, a recent hardware purchase, or a dependency that is not ready. Rehost (lift and shift): copy the servers as they are onto cloud virtual machines such as Amazon EC2. Relocate: move a whole virtualized platform, for example a VMware cluster, to a cloud-hosted version of that same platform without converting each machine. Replatform (lift, tinker and shift): move with a few targeted changes, such as swapping a self-run database for a managed database service like Amazon RDS, while the code stays mostly the same. Repurchase (drop and shop): replace the application with a different product, usually software as a service (SaaS, software a vendor runs and you rent). Refactor (re-architect): redesign the application around cloud-native features such as serverless functions or queues.

Why it works: the labels run roughly from least to most effort and payoff. Rehost and relocate are fast but carry old inefficiencies along; refactor is slow and costly but unlocks the most scale and agility. You choose by weighing business value, time pressure, team skills and how much the application must change.

Worked example: a company must leave its data center in nine months. An unused reporting tool: retire. A payroll mainframe awaiting regulator sign-off: retain. Fifty stable Windows web servers: rehost to hit the deadline. A self-managed Oracle database eating administrator time: replatform to a managed database. An in-house email server: repurchase a SaaS mail service. The revenue-critical ordering system that crashes at sales peaks: refactor, because its scaling problem is the business problem.

Common mistake: refactoring everything because it sounds modern, or rehosting everything because it is quick. Refactoring a low-value app wastes months; rehosting a core app that cannot scale just moves the outage into the cloud, often at higher cost. A sound plan mixes strategies and may rehost first, then modernize after the deadline.

questions.prompt: A regional university must empty its campus server room within six months. The architect has classified most of the portfolio. First, an old library catalogue has had no users since a new system went live, so it is retired. Second, an exam-proctoring server is retained on premises because a vendor contract requires it there until next year. Third, about 120 virtual machines run on the university's VMware cluster, and the team wants to move the whole cluster at once to a cloud-hosted version of VMware without converting each machine. Fourth, the student portal runs on a self-managed PostgreSQL database that takes up staff time, so it is replatformed to a managed database service. Fifth, the in-house HR system is replaced with a rented SaaS HR product. Which strategy fills the missing third step?
choices: Rehost, copying each of the 120 machines onto its own cloud virtual machine
Refactor, redesigning the cluster's workloads around serverless functions
Relocate, moving the whole virtualized platform to its cloud-hosted equivalent
Retain, keeping the cluster on premises until the deadline has passed
questions.why: Relocate means moving an entire virtualized platform such as a VMware cluster to a cloud-hosted version of the same platform without converting each machine, which is exactly what the team wants.

questions.prompt: A logistics company moves its shipment-tracking application to the cloud. The code stays almost the same, but the team swaps the self-run MySQL database it used to patch and back up for a managed database service. Which of the 7Rs describes this?
choices: Refactor
Repurchase
Rehost
Replatform
questions.why: Replatform (lift, tinker and shift) means moving with a few targeted changes, such as switching to a managed database, while the code stays mostly unchanged.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm is planning its migration. Its claims-archive system runs on storage hardware the firm bought eight months ago, and a national data-residency rule currently requires those archives to stay in its own building. Which strategy fits this system best for now?
choices: Repurchase, replacing it with a SaaS archiving product
Retain, keeping it on premises for the time being
Retire, because archived claims are rarely opened
Rehost, so the archive runs on cloud virtual machines
questions.why: Retain fits when a compliance rule or a recent hardware purchase means an application should stay on premises for now.

questions.prompt: A ticket-selling company's booking platform is its main source of revenue and crashes every time a popular concert goes on sale. Under deadline pressure, the team plans to rehost it unchanged onto cloud virtual machines and call the job done. What is the most likely result?
choices: The scaling problem moves into the cloud, often at higher cost, so the platform should be refactored
Nothing changes, because rehosting and refactoring give the same outcome
The crashes stop, because cloud virtual machines scale automatically on their own
The platform should be retired, since a crashing system has no business value
questions.why: Rehosting a core app that cannot scale just carries the outage into the cloud, so an app whose scaling problem is the business problem is a candidate for refactoring, possibly after an initial rehost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which of the 7Rs fits a given application, and describe the main tradeoff between the fast strategies and refactoring.
lessons.modelAnswer: The 7Rs are retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase and refactor. For each application I ask: is anyone still using it? If not, retire it. Is there a reason it cannot move yet, like compliance or a pending dependency? Then retain it. If it should move, how much does it need to change? Stable apps under deadline pressure get rehosted onto cloud virtual machines, or relocated if the whole virtualized platform can move together. If a small change removes real toil, like moving a database to a managed service, replatform. If a commercial SaaS product does the job, repurchase. I save refactoring for high-value apps whose current design blocks the business, such as one that cannot scale. The tradeoff: rehost and relocate are fast and low risk but keep old inefficiencies and cost; refactoring delivers scale and agility but takes the most time, money and skill.
rubricPoints: Names all seven strategies and what each one means.
Uses business value and usage to decide retire or retain.
Matches rehost or relocate to stable apps under time pressure.
Links replatform to small targeted changes and repurchase to replacing with SaaS.
Reserves refactoring for high-value apps whose design limits the business.
States the speed-versus-benefit tradeoff between lifting and modernizing.

suggested.rationale: Classifying a mixed portfolio against the 7Rs is a judgment skill best built by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine exercises it directly.

lessons.plain: Total cost of ownership, or TCO, is the full price of running something over its whole life, not just the sticker price. Think of buying a car: the purchase price is only the start, because fuel, insurance, repairs and parking add up to more. Comparing an on-premises data center with the cloud works the same way. Servers you already own still cost money for electricity, cooling, floor space, software licences, repairs and the people who look after them. A fair TCO puts every one of those costs on both sides, over the same number of years, before deciding whether moving saves money.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's servers were bought two years ago and are already paid off. Does that make keeping them free compared with moving to the cloud? List any costs you think the company is still paying every month.
lessons.teach:
Total cost of ownership (TCO) is the sum of every cost to run a workload over a fixed time horizon, usually three to five years, compared on equal terms between the current setup and the proposed one. Capital expenditure (capex) is money spent up front on assets such as servers. Operating expenditure (opex) is ongoing spend such as power, rent, licences and cloud bills. Direct costs appear on an invoice; indirect costs, such as staff time patching hardware, often do not.

It works because it forces both sides to include the same categories. Hardware refreshes, facilities, licences, network, staff, and one-time migration costs (tooling, consultants, running both environments in parallel) all go in. Rightsizing, meaning picking cloud capacity based on measured usage rather than on the size of the old server, is the biggest lever. Tools such as AWS Migration Evaluator collect real utilization data to support this, and the AWS Pricing Calculator estimates the cloud side.

Worked example over three years. On-premises: hardware refresh 300k credits, plus per year 30k facilities, 50k licences, 60k staff time. Total 300 + 3 x 140 = 720k. Cloud, mapped one-to-one at old server sizes: compute and storage 180k per year, so already worse. Utilization data shows servers average 30 percent busy, so rightsized compute and storage is 90k per year. Add 50k licences, 10k data transfer out, 10k support, 30k reduced staff time: 190k per year, 570k over three years. Add 80k one-time migration and parallel running: 650k. Cloud wins by 70k, but only after rightsizing.

The common mistake is comparing the monthly cloud bill against zero for already-owned hardware, or lifting servers at their old peak size. The consequence in a real program is a business case that looks wrong later: the first cloud bill exceeds the budget, leadership loses trust, and migration waves get frozen. A credible TCO states its assumptions, time horizon and utilization source so others can check it.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer compares its data centre with a cloud move over a five-year horizon. On-premises: a hardware refresh of 500k credits up front, plus per year 40k facilities, 70k licences and 90k staff time. That is 200k per year, so 500 + 5 x 200 = 1,500k. Cloud, mapped one-to-one at the old server sizes, would need 260k per year for compute and storage. Measured utilization shows the servers average 40 percent busy, so rightsized compute and storage comes to 104k per year. Other cloud costs per year are 70k licences, 15k data transfer out, 15k support and 40k reduced staff time. MISSING STEP: work out the cloud yearly run cost and its five-year total. Finally, add 120k of one-time migration and parallel running, then compare the result with the 1,500k on-premises figure. Which result belongs in the missing step?
choices: 104k per year, 520k over five years, counting only rightsized compute and storage
400k per year, 2,000k over five years, using the one-to-one 260k compute and storage figure
244k per year, but 1,220k minus the 120k migration cost, giving 1,100k over five years
244k per year, 1,220k over five years, with rightsized compute and storage plus licences, transfer, support and staff
questions.why: 104 + 70 + 15 + 15 + 40 = 244k per year, times 5 is 1,220k. Adding the 120k one-time cost gives 1,340k, so the cloud wins by 160k, and only because of rightsizing.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is building a TCO model for its on-premises warehouse system. Which of these is an indirect cost that the model should still include?
choices: The yearly invoice from the colocation provider for rack space and power
The monthly licence fee paid to the database vendor
The up-front purchase price of a new storage array
Hours its own engineers spend replacing failed disks and applying firmware updates
questions.why: Staff time spent maintaining hardware is a real cost that rarely shows up on an invoice, which makes it indirect. The other three are direct costs billed by a supplier.

questions.prompt: A retailer's finance team builds a business case comparing a projected 25k-per-month cloud bill against 0 credits for its existing servers, because the servers are already paid for. What is the main flaw, and what is the likely consequence?
choices: The flaw is only the monthly view; turning 25k per month into 300k per year fixes the comparison
The flaw is that cloud bills should be compared against the original purchase price of the servers
Owned servers still incur facilities, licences, staff time and a future refresh, so the sides are unequal and the case is likely to be challenged and trusted less later
There is no flaw, because owned hardware has no further cost once it is purchased
questions.why: TCO must include the same cost categories on both sides over a fixed horizon. Treating owned hardware as free makes the comparison unequal and leads to a business case that looks wrong later.

questions.prompt: A media firm's draft TCO shows the cloud costing more than its data centre. The architect mapped each server one-to-one to cloud capacity at its old size, but monitoring shows the servers average 25 percent busy. What should change first to make the TCO credible?
choices: Rightsize cloud capacity from measured utilization data, for example collected with a tool like AWS Migration Evaluator, and state that data source in the assumptions
Shorten the time horizon to one year so the hardware refresh can be left out
Remove the one-time migration and parallel-running costs, because they happen only once
Keep the old server sizes but price them again in the AWS Pricing Calculator
questions.why: Rightsizing from measured usage is the biggest lever. Lifting servers at their old size inflates cloud cost, and a credible TCO states its utilization source. Dropping real costs or re-pricing the same oversized capacity does not fix the comparison.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "Our servers are paid off, so the cloud can only cost us more." Explain to them in your own words how a total cost of ownership comparison works, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a TCO estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: Paid-off servers are not free. We still pay for power, cooling, floor space, licences, support contracts, the next hardware refresh and the hours our team spends patching and replacing parts. A TCO comparison adds up every one of those costs over the same period, say three years, for both the current setup and the cloud. On the cloud side we include compute and storage sized from real utilization data, not the old server sizes, plus data transfer, support, licences, and one-time costs like migration tooling and the months we run both environments. Only then do we compare totals. The limit is that a TCO is a forecast built on assumptions: if utilization data is thin, growth is guessed wrong, or we fail to actually rightsize after moving, the real bill can differ a lot from the estimate, so the assumptions should be written down and revisited.
rubricPoints: Defines TCO as all costs over a fixed time horizon, compared on equal terms for both options.
Names hidden on-premises costs such as power, space, licences, refresh and staff time.
Includes one-time migration and parallel-running costs on the cloud side.
Explains that rightsizing from measured utilization drives the cloud figure.
States a limit, such as the estimate depending on assumptions and data quality.

suggested.rationale: Building both sides of a TCO in fictional credits and watching rightsizing and one-time costs change the outcome teaches the comparison better than reading about it.

lessons.plain: Wave planning means deciding which applications move to the cloud together and in what order, instead of moving everything at once. Each group is a wave, and it moves as one batch during a planned window. Think of moving house: you pack the spare room first to learn how the movers work, keep the kitchen together because everything in it is used together, and leave the baby's room until the new house is ready. Early waves are small and low-risk so the team learns. Later waves carry the critical, tangled systems once the process is proven.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has a payroll app that talks to its database hundreds of times per second, plus a simple internal wiki. If you could move only one of them in the first month, which would you pick, and would you ever move the payroll app without its database?
lessons.teach:
A migration wave is a batch of workloads that move to the cloud in the same planned window. Wave planning is the work of grouping workloads into waves and ordering those waves. A move group is a set of servers and applications that must migrate together because they depend on each other. A dependency is any runtime link, such as an app calling a database, a shared file share, or a batch job reading another system's output.

It works because it limits risk and builds skill. Early waves, often called a pilot wave, use simple, low-criticality workloads with few dependencies, so the team rehearses cutover, testing and rollback when mistakes are cheap. Later waves carry complex or business-critical systems, scheduled around business calendars, compliance needs and available maintenance windows.

Worked example. A portfolio has: an internal wiki (no dependencies), an HR portal plus its database, an order system that calls the inventory system and its shared database, and a reporting job reading the order database nightly. Step one: map dependencies, which links order, inventory, shared database and reporting into one move group. Step two: score each group on criticality and complexity. Step three: Wave 1 is the wiki, the pilot. Wave 2 is the HR portal and its database, moderate risk. Wave 3 is the order group, scheduled outside the year-end sales peak. Each wave ends with lessons fed into the next runbook, the written cutover steps.

The common mistake is splitting chatty dependencies across waves, for example moving the order app while its database stays on premises. Every call now crosses the hybrid network link, adding latency, so in a running system pages slow down, timeouts rise, and nightly jobs can overrun. Large tightly coupled groups sometimes cannot be split at all, which forces a bigger, riskier single wave. Good wave plans therefore balance wave size against keeping dependent pieces together.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics company is planning its migration waves. Its portfolio: a public marketing website (no dependencies); a timesheet app with its own database; a dispatch app that calls a fleet-tracking service, where both share one database; and a billing export job that reads that shared database every morning. Step one: map the dependencies and form move groups. [MISSING: which move group does the dependency map produce for the dispatch side of the business?] Step two: score each group on criticality and complexity. Step three: Wave 1 is the marketing site as the pilot, Wave 2 is the timesheet app and its database, and Wave 3 is the dispatch group, scheduled away from the holiday shipping peak. Which choice correctly fills in the missing step?
choices: Dispatch app and fleet-tracking service form one group; the shared database and billing export follow in a later wave
Dispatch app, fleet-tracking service, the shared database and the billing export form one move group
All five workloads, including the marketing site and timesheet app, form one move group
Each server is its own group so every wave stays small and easy to roll back
questions.why: Everything linked by runtime calls or a shared database, including the job that reads it, must migrate together so no chatty link crosses the hybrid network.

questions.prompt: In wave planning, what is a move group?
choices: Any batch of workloads moved in the same planned window, whether or not they are linked
The first, low-risk wave a team uses to rehearse cutover and rollback
A set of servers and applications that must migrate together because they depend on each other at runtime
The written list of cutover steps the team follows on migration night
questions.why: A move group is defined by dependency: its pieces must move together, unlike a wave, which is just a scheduled batch and may hold several move groups.

questions.prompt: A city council is choosing its pilot wave. Which workload is the best pick?
choices: The payroll system, because it is critical and proves the platform early
The permits system that shares a database with three other apps
The tax collection platform, scheduled during the year-end billing run
A staff intranet news page with no dependencies and low business impact
questions.why: A pilot wave uses a simple, low-criticality workload with few dependencies so the team rehearses cutover, testing and rollback while mistakes are cheap.

questions.prompt: A retailer migrates its booking web app in Wave 2 but leaves the app's database on premises until Wave 4. What is the most likely effect on the running system in the meantime?
choices: The database is copied automatically into the cloud, so it simply stops being used on premises
The app cannot start at all, because cloud apps cannot reach on-premises systems
Pages slow down and timeouts rise, because every database call now crosses the hybrid network link
No noticeable effect, because the app and database are still in the same move group
questions.why: Splitting a chatty dependency across waves sends each call over the hybrid link, adding latency that slows pages, raises timeouts and can make nightly jobs overrun.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide what goes in the first migration wave versus a later one, and name one tradeoff you face when a group of systems is tightly connected.
lessons.modelAnswer: Wave planning groups workloads into batches that move together in planned windows, then orders those batches. First I map dependencies so anything that talks constantly, like an app and its database, lands in the same move group. Then I rank groups by business criticality and complexity. The first wave is a pilot: simple, low-risk systems with few links, so we practise cutover, testing and rollback cheaply and improve our runbook. Critical or complex groups come later, timed away from business peaks and inside approved maintenance windows. The tradeoff: if many systems are tightly coupled, keeping them together makes one big, risky wave, but splitting them leaves calls crossing the on-premises-to-cloud link, which adds latency, timeouts and failed batch jobs. I usually accept a larger wave, or decouple first, rather than run a slow hybrid split.
rubricPoints: Defines a wave as a batch of workloads migrated together in a planned window.
Says dependencies are mapped so tightly linked components share a move group.
Explains early pilot waves use simple, low-risk workloads to build skill and refine runbooks.
Places critical or complex workloads later, scheduled around business calendars and maintenance windows.
Names the tradeoff between wave size and splitting dependencies across the hybrid link, with latency as the consequence.

suggested.rationale: Wave planning is a judgement skill best practised by reasoning through an exam-style portfolio scenario, and no current mission or planned engine has the learner sequence migrations.

lessons.plain: Moving data into the cloud is like moving house: what makes sense depends on how much you own and how far you are going. AWS offers four main routes. AWS DataSync is a managed copying service that moves files over your network on a schedule. AWS Transfer Family gives business partners a familiar file-upload doorway (such as SFTP) that drops files straight into cloud storage. AWS Snow Family ships you rugged physical storage devices to fill and mail back when the network is too slow. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance uploads to a storage bucket by routing them through nearby AWS entry points.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 200 TB of files in a data center connected by a 1 Gbps internet link that is already busy during business hours, and the data must be in AWS within two weeks. Would you send it over the network or put it on a shipped device, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS DataSync is a managed online transfer service. You install a small software agent near your file servers, and it copies from file shares (NFS or SMB), Hadoop file systems or other object stores into Amazon S3 (object storage), Amazon EFS (a managed network file system) or Amazon FSx (managed Windows and high-performance file systems). It runs on a schedule, copies only changes after the first run, checks that copies match, encrypts traffic in transit and can cap its bandwidth use.

AWS Transfer Family is a managed file-transfer endpoint that speaks SFTP, FTPS, FTP or AS2 and stores files in S3 or EFS. It suits ongoing exchanges where partners keep their existing scripts; it is not a bulk migration engine.

AWS Snow Family is offline transfer: AWS ships a hardened device (for example Snowball Edge), you load data locally, ship it back, and AWS imports it into S3. It wins when the network cannot move the volume in time, or when a site has little or no connectivity.

Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads to one S3 bucket from far away by entering the AWS global network at a nearby edge location, for an extra per-GB fee.

Worked example: 200 TB, 1 Gbps link. One gigabit per second is about 125 MB per second, roughly 10.8 TB per day at full saturation. At a realistic 80 percent, about 8.6 TB per day, so 200 TB takes around 23 days, and saturating the link starves production. A Snowball Edge round trip of about a week meets a two-week deadline, so ship the bulk on devices, then use DataSync to copy the changes made since loading.

Common mistake: choosing Transfer Acceleration for a data-center migration. It speeds distant uploads to S3 but does not add bandwidth to a thin link or move file-system metadata. Choosing wrongly in a live system means a missed cutover or a business network choked for weeks.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer must move 60 TB of claim archives from its data center to Amazon S3 within 10 days. Its internet link is 500 Mbps, and the network team says the migration can use about 80 percent of it. Step 1: convert bits to bytes. 500 Mbps divided by 8 is 62.5 MB per second. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: 60 TB divided by the daily figure from step 2 is about 14 days. That misses the 10-day deadline and would choke the link for two weeks. So the insurer ships the bulk on Snowball Edge devices, then uses DataSync to copy the files that changed after loading. Which calculation is step 2?
choices: 62.5 MB per second times 3,600 seconds is about 0.225 TB per day
62.5 MB per second times 86,400 seconds is about 5.4 TB per day at full speed, and 80 percent of that is about 4.3 TB per day
62.5 MB per second times 86,400 seconds is about 5.4 TB per day, assuming the link can be run at full saturation
500 MB per second times 86,400 seconds is about 43 TB per day, and 80 percent of that is about 34.6 TB per day
questions.why: A day has 86,400 seconds, so 62.5 MB per second gives about 5.4 TB per day at full speed, and the realistic 80 percent share is about 4.3 TB per day, which leads to the roughly 14 days in step 3.

questions.prompt: A logistics company receives shipping manifests every day from 30 trading partners. The partners upload files with SFTP scripts they have used for years and refuse to change. The company wants to retire its own SFTP server and land the files directly in Amazon S3. Which service fits best?
choices: AWS Snow Family, because a shipped device keeps the files off the internet
AWS DataSync, because it copies only changed files on a schedule
AWS Transfer Family, a managed file-transfer endpoint that speaks SFTP and stores the files in S3
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration, because it speeds up uploads into S3
questions.why: Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 endpoint backed by S3 or EFS, so partners keep their existing scripts for an ongoing exchange.

questions.prompt: A hospital plans to move 40 TB from an on-premises SMB file share to AWS over a congested 100 Mbps link. An engineer proposes turning on Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to make the migration fast enough. What is the main flaw in this plan?
choices: It only speeds distant uploads to an S3 bucket through nearby edge locations, so it adds no bandwidth to the thin link and does not move file-system metadata
Transfer Acceleration works only for SFTP traffic, not for SMB
Transfer Acceleration needs a shipped device before it can start
Transfer Acceleration is free, so it will be throttled during busy hours
questions.why: Transfer Acceleration shortens the path from a far-away client into AWS. It cannot widen a small local link or carry file-share metadata, so the migration would still run long and congest the network.

questions.prompt: A design studio keeps working files on an on-premises NFS share. It wants a nightly copy into Amazon EFS, a managed network file system. Only changed files should be sent after the first run, every copy should be checked against the source, traffic must be encrypted, and bandwidth must be limited so daytime work is not slowed. Which option meets all of these needs?
choices: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration pointed at an S3 bucket
A Snowball Edge device shipped every night
AWS Transfer Family with an FTPS endpoint
AWS DataSync, with an agent installed near the NFS share
questions.why: DataSync is the managed online transfer service that runs on a schedule, sends only changes, verifies copies, encrypts traffic in transit, can cap bandwidth, and writes to EFS.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose among DataSync, Transfer Family, Snow Family and S3 Transfer Acceleration for a given migration, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would reach for most often.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I do the arithmetic: data volume divided by the bandwidth I can actually spare. If the network can move it before the deadline without hurting production, I use DataSync. It is an agent-based managed copier from NFS, SMB or HDFS into S3, EFS or FSx, with scheduling, incremental syncs, verification and bandwidth limits. If the math says weeks or months, or the site is poorly connected, I order Snow Family devices for the bulk and then use DataSync for the changes. Transfer Family is for ongoing partner exchanges over SFTP, FTPS, FTP or AS2 into S3 or EFS, not a one-off move. Transfer Acceleration helps users far from a bucket upload faster through edge locations. The tradeoff with DataSync is that it still rides your link. It needs an agent and network capacity, and a large first copy can take a long time or compete with production traffic.
rubricPoints: Compares data volume against usable bandwidth and deadline to choose online or offline transfer.
Identifies DataSync as agent-based, scheduled, incremental online copying into S3, EFS or FSx.
Identifies Snow Family as shipped physical devices for large volumes or poorly connected sites.
Places Transfer Family as a managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP or AS2 endpoint for ongoing partner exchange.
Places Transfer Acceleration as faster long-distance uploads to S3 via edge locations, not extra bandwidth.
Names a real limit, such as network contention, device shipping time or the per-GB acceleration fee.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine models data transfer, and the core exam skill is reasoning through volume, bandwidth, deadline and protocol scenarios to pick the right service.

lessons.plain: Moving many servers into the cloud happens in two steps: first learn exactly what you have, then copy it across with as little downtime as possible. AWS Application Discovery Service is the inventory step. It records each server's specifications, how busy it is, and which other machines it talks to. AWS Application Migration Service is the moving step. It keeps a live copy of each server in AWS until you switch over. Think of a house move: someone walks every room listing furniture and noting which items must travel together, then a moving crew copies the house so you can step from the old one into the new one.
lessons.guessPrompt: Before you copy a web server into the cloud, why might you want to know which other machines it sends network traffic to, and not just its CPU and memory size?
lessons.teach:
AWS Application Discovery Service (ADS) is an inventory tool. It collects data about servers in your own data centre (on-premises). It does not move anything. It works in two ways. Agentless discovery uses a collector appliance, a small virtual machine you deploy inside your VMware environment. The collector reads server configuration and utilization (how much CPU, memory and disk each server uses) from the virtualization manager. Agent-based discovery installs a Discovery Agent, a small program, on each server. Because it runs inside the server, it also sees running processes and network connections, which reveal dependencies: which servers call which. The results feed the migration tracking dashboard and can be exported for analysis.

AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is a rehost tool. Rehost, also called lift-and-shift, means moving a server unchanged. You install a replication agent on each source server. The agent copies the server's disks block by block (in raw chunks, below the file level) to a staging area. The staging area is a low-cost subnet in AWS holding small replication servers and cheap disks. Replication continues as the source changes. When you are ready, MGN converts the copy so it boots on Amazon EC2 virtual machines. You launch a test instance first, then perform cutover. Cutover is the short final switch to the AWS copy. Downtime is only that final sync.

Worked example: a billing app runs on three servers. You install Discovery Agents on all three. After two weeks the data shows that the app server also calls a fourth server, an old licensing host nobody listed. You add that host to the same move group. Then you install MGN agents on all four, wait for continuous replication, launch test instances, check the app works, and cut over in a short weekend window.

Common mistake: using only agentless discovery and assuming you have the full dependency picture. Agentless data shows sizes and load but not process-level connections. In a running system, the missed licensing host stays on-premises after cutover. The migrated app then stalls or fails on every call across the slow or blocked link.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs 60 virtual machines on VMware and plans to move its shipment-tracking app to AWS. Step 1: the team deploys the agentless collector appliance, a small virtual machine inside VMware, to inventory all 60 machines quickly. Step 2: the collector reports each machine's CPU, memory and disk use, which is enough to size the targets. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the new data shows the tracking app server also connects to an old label-printing server that nobody listed, so the team adds that server to the tracking app's move group. Step 5: the team installs Application Migration Service (MGN) replication agents on every server in the group and lets continuous replication run before testing and cutover. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Install the Discovery Agent on the tracking app's servers so it can record running processes and network connections
Install MGN replication agents on the tracking servers now so the block-level copies show their network connections
Run the collector appliance for two more weeks so it gathers enough utilization history to reveal which servers call which
Export the collector's sizing data to the migration dashboard, which then draws the dependency map from CPU and memory figures
questions.why: Only the Discovery Agent runs inside each server and sees processes and network connections, which is what exposed the unlisted label-printing dependency; the agentless collector only shows sizes and load.

questions.prompt: A project lead at a regional bank writes in the migration plan: "We will use AWS Application Discovery Service to copy our 25 on-premises servers into AWS." What is wrong with this plan?
choices: Application Discovery Service can copy servers, but only when the agentless collector appliance is used inside VMware
Nothing is wrong; Application Discovery Service copies servers and Application Migration Service only tracks progress
Application Discovery Service copies files rather than disk blocks, so it must be paired with a staging subnet
Application Discovery Service only gathers an inventory of servers and their use and dependencies; it does not move anything, so the copying needs a rehost tool such as Application Migration Service
questions.why: Application Discovery Service is an inventory tool that collects data and moves nothing, while Application Migration Service is the tool that copies and rehosts servers.

questions.prompt: A media company uses Application Migration Service (MGN) to rehost a 3 TB file server that changes all day. Continuous replication to the staging area has been running for ten days, and a test instance has been checked. Roughly how long will the file server be unavailable at cutover?
choices: Long enough to copy the full 3 TB, since cutover starts a fresh copy of the disks
Only as long as the short final sync of the most recent changes plus the switch to the AWS copy
Several hours, because MGN must first convert every file into an EC2-compatible format at cutover
Ten days, because replication must be paused for as long as it originally ran
questions.why: Because MGN keeps replicating changes block by block, cutover downtime is only the final sync and switch, not a full copy.

questions.prompt: A retailer inventoried its VMware servers with only the agentless collector appliance, then rehosted its order app with Application Migration Service. Right after cutover, every order request hangs for a long time and then fails. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The test instance was launched before cutover, which locks the production copy
The replication servers in the staging subnet are too small to run the production app
Agentless discovery missed a server the app depends on, so that server stayed on-premises and the app now calls it across a slow or blocked link
The block-level copy skipped the app's files because it works below the file level
questions.why: Agentless discovery shows sizes and load but not process-level connections, so a hidden dependency can be left behind and break the migrated app on every call.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Application Discovery Service and Application Migration Service divide the work in a server migration, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Discovery Service is the inventory step and moves nothing. It records each server's configuration, its utilization, and, with agents installed, its processes and network connections, so we can see which servers depend on each other. The agentless collector is easier to roll out across VMware, but it can't see process-level dependencies, so we could miss a hidden connection. Application Migration Service does the actual move for a lift-and-shift. An agent on each server continuously replicates its disks at block level into a cheap staging subnet in AWS. Then we launch test instances and do a short cutover, so downtime is small. Its limit is that it rehosts the server as-is. It doesn't modernize the app or tune it, and you have to install agents and pay for staging resources while replication runs.
rubricPoints: Discovery Service inventories servers and does not move them.
Agent-based discovery captures processes and network dependencies, and agentless discovery does not.
Application Migration Service rehosts servers through continuous block-level replication to a staging area.
Test launches come before a short cutover, which keeps downtime low.
Names a real limit, such as missed dependencies with agentless discovery or no modernization with a rehost.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine performs server discovery or replication, so reasoning through exam-style portfolio scenarios is the best way to learn which tool and mode fits each case.

lessons.plain: Moving a database to the cloud is like moving a busy shop to a new building while customers keep buying. You need two helpers. One translates the shop's rulebook if the new building uses a different language: that is AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT), which rewrites a database's structure and built-in code for a different database engine. The other carries the stock across and keeps both shops in sync until you switch over: that is AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), a managed service that copies data between databases and keeps copying new changes, so downtime stays short.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you move a company's database from Oracle to PostgreSQL, which do you think must be dealt with first: copying the rows of data, or making sure the tables and stored code make sense to PostgreSQL? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is a managed replication service: AWS runs the machinery that reads data from a source database and writes it to a target. You define a source endpoint and a target endpoint (connection details for each database), a replication instance (the server DMS uses to do the copying), and a task (what to copy and how). A task can run a full load, which copies all existing rows once, then change data capture (CDC), which reads the source's transaction log and replays each new insert, update and delete on the target. Because CDC keeps the target nearly current, the application keeps running on the source until a short cutover.

A homogeneous migration keeps the same engine (MySQL to MySQL), so DMS alone, or the engine's own native tools, is usually enough. A heterogeneous migration changes engine (Oracle to PostgreSQL). Here AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) comes first: it converts the schema (tables, data types, indexes) and code such as stored procedures and functions to the target dialect, and produces an assessment report showing what converted automatically and what needs a human. AWS also offers this conversion as a managed feature inside DMS, called DMS Schema Conversion.

Worked example, Oracle to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL: first, run SCT and read the assessment; it flags, say, ten procedures needing manual rewrite. Second, fix those and apply the converted schema to Aurora. Third, start a DMS task with full load plus CDC. Fourth, when lag is near zero, pause writes, let the final changes apply, validate row counts, and point the application at Aurora.

The common mistake is assuming DMS moves everything. DMS moves data; it creates only basic tables and does not translate stored procedures, triggers or complex logic. Skipping SCT on an engine change leaves an application that connects fine but fails when it calls missing code. Skipping CDC means a full-load-only move, which forces long downtime for a large, busy database.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs a 3 TB Microsoft SQL Server database that takes about 500 bookings per minute. It is moving to Amazon Aurora MySQL, and the business allows at most 20 minutes of downtime. Step 1: The engine changes, so this is a heterogeneous migration. The team runs AWS SCT (the Schema Conversion Tool, which converts schema and database code to the target dialect). Its assessment report flags six triggers for manual rewrite, which the team fixes before applying the converted schema to Aurora. Step 2: In AWS DMS (the managed replication service), they define a source endpoint and a target endpoint (connection details for each database) and a replication instance (the server that does the copying). Step 3: MISSING. Step 4: When replication lag is close to zero, they stop writes, let the last changes apply, compare row counts, and switch the application to Aurora. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Create a DMS task that copies data and also rewrites the triggers, so the earlier SCT work is checked a second time.
Create a DMS task that runs a full load only, scheduled over a quiet weekend, so every existing row is copied in one pass.
Create a DMS task that runs change data capture only, so new bookings flow to Aurora without copying the existing rows first.
Create a DMS task that runs a full load followed by change data capture, so existing rows are copied once and new changes keep replaying.
questions.why: A full load copies the 3 TB of existing rows, and change data capture then replays each new booking from the transaction log, keeping Aurora nearly current so the cutover fits the 20-minute window.

questions.prompt: In AWS DMS, a task copies all existing rows from a source database to its target. What does change data capture (CDC) add after that copy?
choices: It reads the source's transaction log and replays each new insert, update and delete on the target, so the target stays nearly current.
It takes a second full copy of every table at cutover to replace the first copy.
It produces an assessment report listing which parts of the schema need a human to rewrite them.
It converts the source's stored procedures and functions into the target engine's dialect while the copy runs.
questions.why: CDC reads the source's transaction log and applies each new change to the target. Schema and code conversion, and the assessment report, belong to SCT.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm moved its Oracle database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL using only an AWS DMS task with full load plus CDC. After cutover the application connects without errors, but the claims screen fails every time it calls a pricing function that existed in Oracle. What is the most likely cause?
choices: CDC was left running after cutover and overwrote the pricing function.
The source and target endpoints pointed to the wrong databases.
The team skipped schema and code conversion with AWS SCT, and DMS does not translate stored procedures or functions.
The replication instance was too small, so the full load skipped some rows.
questions.why: DMS moves data and creates only basic tables, so on an engine change the code must be converted with SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion). Without that step, the app connects but fails when it calls missing code.

questions.prompt: A media company is moving a self-managed MySQL database on a data-centre server to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Which approach fits this migration best?
choices: Use DMS Schema Conversion to rewrite the stored procedures into PostgreSQL.
Treat it as homogeneous: DMS alone, or MySQL's own native tools, is usually enough, with no schema conversion step.
Run AWS SCT first, because every move into AWS needs its schema and code converted to a new dialect.
Avoid DMS, because DMS only supports moves where the database engine changes.
questions.why: The engine stays MySQL, so the migration is homogeneous, and DMS or the engine's native tools usually handle it without SCT.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how DMS and SCT divide the work in a database migration, when you would need SCT at all, and one limit of DMS they should plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: DMS is the mover and SCT is the translator. DMS is a managed replication service: a replication instance reads from a source endpoint and writes to a target endpoint. A task does a full load of existing rows, then change data capture replays ongoing changes from the source's log, so the app stays live until a brief cutover. If the engine stays the same, like MySQL to MySQL, DMS or native tools are enough. If the engine changes, like Oracle to PostgreSQL, we run SCT first to convert the schema and stored code and to get an assessment report of what needs manual rewriting. The limit: DMS copies data, not logic. It won't translate stored procedures or triggers, so on an engine change we budget human effort for the items SCT flags. Also, a full load without CDC on a big busy database means long downtime.
rubricPoints: DMS replicates data between source and target using a replication instance, endpoints and tasks.
Full load plus change data capture keeps the target current so cutover downtime is short.
SCT converts schema and stored code when the database engine changes, with an assessment report.
Homogeneous migrations usually need no SCT; heterogeneous ones do.
DMS does not translate stored procedures or complex logic, so manual work must be planned.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between DMS alone, SCT plus DMS, and full load versus CDC in migration scenarios, which is best practised by reasoning through situations since no mission or planned engine runs a database migration.

lessons.plain: When a company moves applications from its own data center into AWS, the old and new places must talk to each other for weeks or months, and users must be steered from the old servers to the new ones. Three services handle this. AWS Site-to-Site VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the public internet that you can set up in an hour. AWS Direct Connect is a private, dedicated cable into AWS that is faster and steadier but takes weeks to arrange. Amazon Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, the internet's phone book, which decides which address a name points to. Think of building a bridge between two towns, then changing the road signs.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your migration starts next week, but a dedicated private line from your data center into AWS takes about two months to install. How would you connect the two sites in the meantime, and what would you do with that temporary link once the private line is ready?
lessons.teach:
During a migration you need two things: a hybrid network, meaning a connection between your on-premises data center and your cloud virtual networks (VPCs), and a way to move users from old to new.

AWS Site-to-Site VPN builds two encrypted IPsec tunnels (IPsec is a standard for encrypting traffic between networks) across the public internet, between your router and AWS. It is quick and cheap, but bandwidth per tunnel is limited and speed varies with internet conditions. AWS Direct Connect is a physical, private connection from your site, through a partner location, into AWS. It gives consistent latency and high bandwidth, which suits bulk replication, but ordering it can take weeks, and it is not encrypted by default; you add MACsec (link-level encryption) or run a VPN over it if encryption is required.

Amazon Route 53 is a managed DNS service. DNS translates names like app.example.com into IP addresses. Each answer carries a TTL (time to live), how long resolvers may cache it. Routing policies decide answers: weighted routing splits traffic by percentage, failover routing switches to a backup when a health check fails. Route 53 Resolver endpoints let on-premises servers and VPCs resolve each other's private names.

Worked example: a team needs connectivity now. Step 1, stand up Site-to-Site VPN in a day and start replicating. Step 2, order Direct Connect; when it arrives, make it primary and keep the VPN as a cheaper backup path. Step 3, days before cutover, lower the app record's TTL from 86400 seconds to 60. Step 4, use weighted routing to send 10 percent of users to AWS, then 50, then 100. Step 5, if errors spike, set the weight back to the old site; rollback takes about a minute.

Common mistake: forgetting to lower the TTL in advance. Resolvers keep caching the old address for up to a day, so cutover and rollback both stall, and users hit a decommissioned server.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance company is moving its claims system to AWS. It already has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect link (a physical, private connection into AWS through a partner location), and a regulator requires all data in transit between sites to be encrypted. Their plan: Step 1, confirm the Direct Connect link is up and routing to the claims VPC. Step 2, [missing]. Step 3, start replicating the 30 TB claims database over the link. Step 4, a week before cutover, lower the claims DNS record's TTL from 43200 seconds to 30. Step 5, use Route 53 weighted routing to move 20 percent of users, then 60, then 100. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Nothing extra is needed, because a private Direct Connect link is encrypted by default.
Cancel Direct Connect and replicate only over a Site-to-Site VPN across the internet.
Turn on MACsec on the link, or run a Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect connection.
Create Route 53 Resolver endpoints so that replication traffic stays private and encrypted.
questions.why: Direct Connect is private but not encrypted by default, so meeting the encryption rule means adding MACsec link encryption or an IPsec VPN on top, which keeps the link's consistent high bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A media company's video portal record in Route 53 has a TTL of 7200 seconds, and nobody lowered it before cutover. After moving users to AWS, errors spike, so the team immediately sets the weights back to the on-premises site. For how long might some users still be sent to the AWS address?
choices: No time at all, because changing the weights clears every resolver's cache.
About one minute, because Route 53 applies weight changes almost instantly everywhere.
Up to about two hours, because resolvers may keep the cached answer for the full TTL.
Up to about 24 hours, because DNS resolvers always cache answers for one day.
questions.why: TTL is how long resolvers may cache an answer, so with a 7200-second TTL a cached AWS address can keep being used for up to two hours after the change.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer has a working Site-to-Site VPN between its factory data center and a VPC. Servers in the factory can reach the VPC by IP address, but they fail to look up the private name inventory-db.internal.example of a database inside the VPC. Which addition fixes this?
choices: A Route 53 failover routing policy with a health check on the database.
An AWS Direct Connect link to replace the VPN connection.
A Route 53 weighted routing policy that sends a share of lookups to the VPC.
Route 53 Resolver endpoints so on-premises servers and the VPC can resolve each other's private names.
questions.why: The network path already works; the gap is private name resolution between on-premises and the VPC, which is exactly what Route 53 Resolver endpoints provide.

questions.prompt: A university has migrated its course registration site to AWS but keeps the old on-premises copy running for a month. It wants DNS to send all users to AWS normally, and automatically send them to the on-premises copy if the AWS site stops responding to health checks. Which Route 53 routing policy fits?
choices: Weighted routing with 50 percent to each site
Weighted routing with 100 percent to AWS and a higher TTL
Route 53 Resolver endpoints
Failover routing
questions.why: Failover routing answers with the primary site and switches to the backup when a health check fails, while weighted routing only splits traffic by fixed percentages.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect our data center to AWS and cut users over during a migration, naming at least one limit or tradeoff of the choices you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd start with Site-to-Site VPN because it's an encrypted tunnel over the internet we can have running in a day, so replication can begin immediately. Its limit is bandwidth and unpredictable internet latency, so for large, steady data movement I'd order Direct Connect, a private dedicated link with consistent performance. The tradeoff is it takes weeks to provision and isn't encrypted by default, so we'd add MACsec or a VPN on top if policy demands it, and keep the original VPN as a backup path. For cutover I'd use Route 53. Well before the move I'd drop the record's TTL to about a minute so caches refresh quickly, then use weighted routing to shift traffic gradually, 10 percent first. If something breaks, I flip the weight back. If we skip lowering the TTL, old answers stay cached for hours and rollback is slow.
rubricPoints: Site-to-Site VPN is fast to set up and encrypted but limited and internet-dependent.
Direct Connect is private and consistent but slow to provision and unencrypted by default.
Using VPN first and later as backup to Direct Connect.
Route 53 routing policies such as weighted or failover steer users from old to new.
Lowering the DNS TTL before cutover enables fast switching and rollback.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing among connectivity options and sequencing a DNS cutover under time and security constraints, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style migration scenarios.

lessons.plain: When a company moves applications to the cloud, its people still need to sign in, and many old Windows applications expect a company directory to check who users are. A directory is a central phone book of users, groups and passwords; Microsoft Active Directory is the most common one. AWS Directory Service gives you that phone book in the cloud, either as a full copy or as a relay back to the one in your office. AWS IAM Identity Center is the front door: one sign-in page that lets staff reach every AWS account they are allowed into, like a single building badge that opens only the right floors.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company is moving Windows servers that require users to log in with their existing office usernames. If the cloud servers had to phone the office directory for every single login, what could go wrong on the day the network link to the office goes down?
lessons.teach:
AWS Directory Service runs Microsoft Active Directory (AD), a directory that stores users and groups and lets Windows machines 'domain join', meaning trust the directory to check logins. It has three flavours. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real AD run for you on two domain controllers (the servers that answer login checks); it can form a trust, a relationship where one directory accepts users vouched for by another, with your on-premises AD. AD Connector is only a proxy: it stores nothing and forwards every request to your on-premises AD over a network link. Simple AD is a basic, low-cost AD-compatible directory that cannot form trusts.

AWS IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on (one login for many destinations) across all accounts in an AWS Organization, a grouping of accounts under one management account. You pick an identity source: its own built-in user store, an AD through Directory Service, or an external identity provider such as Okta using SAML (a standard for passing a signed 'this user is authenticated' message) and SCIM (a standard for syncing user lists automatically). Permission sets are templates of permissions that Identity Center turns into roles in each account you assign.

Worked example: a firm lifts 40 Windows application servers to EC2. Step one, the servers must domain join. Step two, the team wants them to keep working if the office link fails, so AD Connector is ruled out. Step three, they deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and create a two-way trust with the on-premises AD, so existing usernames still work. Step four, they point IAM Identity Center at the managed AD and assign a 'ReadOnly' permission set to the auditors group across all accounts.

Common mistake: choosing AD Connector for workloads that must survive a network outage, or Simple AD when a trust is required. In a running system, an AD Connector setup means a dropped VPN or Direct Connect link stops all logins at once.

Identity Center is for people reaching AWS; applications themselves should use IAM roles, not human sign-in.

questions.prompt: A media company already manages its 300 staff in Okta and has 25 AWS accounts grouped in one AWS Organization. It wants each person to sign in once and reach the accounts they need. Step one: enable IAM Identity Center in the Organization's management account. Step two: (missing). Step three: create a 'Developer' permission set and assign the engineering group to 10 development accounts, so Identity Center creates a matching role in each of those accounts. Which step two completes the plan?
choices: Deploy AD Connector and point it at Okta so that every login request is forwarded on to Okta
Create an IAM user for each staff member in all 25 accounts and then group them by team
Deploy Simple AD and create a two-way trust with Okta so the existing usernames still work
Choose Okta as an external identity provider, using SAML for sign-in and SCIM to sync users
questions.why: Identity Center can use an external identity provider such as Okta as its identity source, with SAML passing the signed proof of login and SCIM syncing the user list automatically.

questions.prompt: A bank moved 60 Windows servers to EC2 and domain joined them through AD Connector, which forwards requests to the bank's on-premises AD over a single Direct Connect link. One evening that link fails. What happens to logins on those EC2 servers?
choices: Logins carry on normally, because AD Connector keeps a full copy of every user and group
Logins switch automatically to IAM Identity Center's built-in user store until the link returns
All logins stop, because AD Connector stores no users and cannot reach the on-premises AD
Only new users are blocked, because existing users are still trusted through a two-way trust
questions.why: AD Connector is only a proxy that stores nothing, so when the network link to the on-premises AD drops, it has nowhere to send login checks and all logins fail at once.

questions.prompt: An engineering firm is moving 18 Windows servers to AWS. The servers must domain join, and staff must keep using their existing on-premises AD usernames through a trust between the AWS directory and the on-premises AD. Which AWS Directory Service option meets this?
choices: Simple AD, because it is the lowest-cost directory that Windows servers are able to join
AD Connector, because it creates a trust and stores its own copy of the on-premises users
IAM Identity Center's built-in user store, because it can domain join Windows servers
AWS Managed Microsoft AD, because it is a real AD that can form a trust with on-premises AD
questions.why: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real AD on two domain controllers that can form a trust with on-premises AD, while Simple AD cannot form trusts and AD Connector only forwards requests.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs a nightly reporting program on EC2 that must read files from storage in another AWS account. The team has just set up IAM Identity Center for its staff. How should the reporting program get its AWS permissions?
choices: Assign it a permission set so that it signs in through Identity Center like a staff member
Domain join the EC2 server through AD Connector so the program inherits the AD permissions
Give the program an IAM role, because Identity Center is meant for people, not applications
Give it a staff member's Identity Center login so it can sign in through single sign-on
questions.why: Identity Center provides sign-on for people reaching AWS, while applications themselves should get their permissions through IAM roles rather than a human sign-in.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between AWS Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector and Simple AD for a migration, and where IAM Identity Center fits, including one tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Directory Service gives migrated Windows servers an Active Directory to domain join. If we want a real AD in AWS that keeps working on its own and trusts our on-premises AD so existing usernames still work, we use AWS Managed Microsoft AD; the tradeoff is cost and a second directory to manage. AD Connector is cheaper and simpler because it stores nothing and just forwards login checks to our office AD, but if the network link drops, nobody can log in, and latency adds to every check. Simple AD is cheap and basic but cannot trust another directory, so it is wrong when users must keep corporate accounts. IAM Identity Center sits on top: it gives staff one sign-in across all accounts in our Organization, using AD or an external provider as the identity source, and permission sets define what each group can do in each account.
rubricPoints: Managed Microsoft AD is a real AD in AWS that can trust on-premises AD and works independently.
AD Connector is a proxy that stores nothing and depends on the network link to on-premises AD.
Simple AD is basic and cannot form trusts.
IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on across Organization accounts using a chosen identity source.
Permission sets define what assigned groups can do in each account.
Names a tradeoff such as cost versus resilience to a network outage.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among directory options and wiring Identity Center is an exam-style scenario judgment that no current mission or planned engine exercises directly, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Migration tools are the programs that copy servers, files and databases from your old data centre into the cloud. While they work, they hold passwords to your databases, read every byte of your data and open network paths between old and new environments. That makes them a tempting target. Securing them means giving each tool only the access it needs, keeping its traffic private and encrypted, guarding the credentials it uses, and switching it off when the move is done. Think of hiring movers: you give them a key to specific rooms, lock the truck, track who handled what, and take the key back afterwards.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database migration tool needs a login to your on-premises database. Would you give it the database administrator account, or something narrower? What could go wrong if it kept that login after the migration finished?
lessons.teach:
Securing migration tools means applying normal cloud security controls to the temporary machinery of a migration. Examples are AWS Database Migration Service (DMS, a managed database replication engine), AWS DataSync (a managed file-copy service using an on-premises agent), AWS Application Migration Service (MGN, which replicates whole servers block by block) and the AWS Snow Family (rugged physical devices shipped to you for offline bulk transfer).

Five controls cover most cases. First, least privilege: each tool runs under an IAM role (an identity carrying a permission policy) that allows only the buckets, keys and actions it needs. Second, encryption in transit with TLS, the standard for encrypted network sessions, and at rest with AWS KMS keys (managed encryption keys you control and can audit). Third, private paths: put replication instances in private subnets with tight security groups (instance-level firewalls), and reach AWS through VPC endpoints (private entry points to AWS services), Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect rather than the public internet. Fourth, credential handling: store source database passwords in AWS Secrets Manager (a managed secret store with rotation) instead of typing them into configs. Fifth, logging and cleanup: record tool actions with CloudTrail (an API audit log), then delete agents, replication servers and temporary credentials after cutover. For Snow devices, data is encrypted with your KMS key on the device, and the unlock code should be sent separately from the device's manifest file.

Worked example: migrating an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon RDS with DMS. Step 1, create a read-only replication user on Oracle with only the needed grants. Step 2, put its password in Secrets Manager and let DMS read it through a scoped role. Step 3, launch the replication instance in a private subnet, not publicly accessible, reaching on-premises over VPN. Step 4, require TLS on both endpoints and encrypt storage with a customer-managed KMS key. Step 5, after cutover, delete the instance and drop the Oracle user.

A common mistake is reusing the database admin account and leaving the tooling running. In a live system, that forgotten replication path becomes an always-on, privileged back door into production data.

questions.prompt: A regional dental clinic chain is moving 6 TB of patient X-ray files from an on-premises file server into an Amazon S3 bucket using AWS DataSync, a managed file-copy service that uses an on-premises agent. The team's security plan so far: Step 1, give DataSync an IAM role (an identity carrying a permission policy) that can write only to the one target bucket prefix. Step 2, have the agent reach AWS through a VPC endpoint (a private entry point to an AWS service) over the clinic's existing Direct Connect link instead of the public internet. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, record all DataSync API actions with CloudTrail (an API audit log). Step 5, after cutover, delete the agent and remove the role. Which Step 3 best completes the plan?
choices: Grant the DataSync role full S3 access across the account so it never fails partway through the copy
Turn off encryption during the copy so the 6 TB finishes faster, then enable it on the bucket once the transfer is done
Make the target bucket publicly readable for the migration window so the agent can verify each file it copied
Require TLS for data in transit and encrypt the bucket at rest with a customer-managed AWS KMS key the clinic controls and can audit
questions.why: The plan already covers least privilege, private paths, logging and cleanup, so the missing control is encryption: TLS in transit plus a customer-managed KMS key at rest.

questions.prompt: A logistics company orders an AWS Snowball device (a rugged physical device shipped to you for offline bulk transfer) to move 80 TB of shipment archives. The project lead plans to email the device's manifest file and its unlock code together in one message to the warehouse team. What is the better practice?
choices: Skip the unlock code entirely, because data on the device is already encrypted with a KMS key
Print the unlock code and tape it to the device so the warehouse cannot lose it
Send both in one email but compress them into a single password-protected archive
