Send the unlock code through a separate channel from the manifest file, so one intercepted message cannot unlock the device
questions.why: The manifest and unlock code together open the device, so keeping them apart means one leaked message is not enough to reach the data.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm used AWS Application Migration Service (MGN, which replicates whole servers block by block) to move 40 servers. Cutover finished six weeks ago, but the replication servers, the on-premises agents and a broadly permissioned role are all still in place. What is the main security risk?
choices: AWS will automatically delete the migrated production servers when replication idles
The leftover tooling is an always-on, privileged path into production data that nobody is watching
CloudTrail will stop recording API calls once replication has been idle for a month
The servers will slowly fall out of sync and need to be migrated again
questions.why: Migration tooling that is left running after cutover becomes a forgotten back door with standing access to production data, so it should be deleted.

questions.prompt: A retailer is using AWS Database Migration Service (DMS, a managed database replication engine) to copy a PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS. An engineer proposes typing the database superuser's password directly into the migration task configuration file kept in the team's Git repository. Which approach applies sound credential handling instead?
choices: Create a dedicated read-only replication user, store its password in AWS Secrets Manager, and let DMS read it through a narrowly scoped role
Keep the superuser account but move the password into a private Git branch that only the migration team can view
Use the superuser account but change its password once the migration is complete
Hard-code the password into the replication instance's startup script so it never appears in Git
questions.why: A least-privilege user whose password lives in a managed secret store with rotation avoids both exposed credentials and a reused admin account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would secure the migration tools on an upcoming database and file migration, and name one tradeoff or limit of locking them down.
lessons.modelAnswer: I treat migration tools like any privileged production component, even though they are temporary. Each one, such as DMS or the DataSync agent, gets its own IAM role scoped to the exact buckets, keys and actions it needs, and its source login is a narrow, read-only user whose password lives in Secrets Manager. Traffic uses TLS and travels over VPN or Direct Connect into private subnets, reaching AWS services through VPC endpoints. Data at rest, including on Snow devices, is encrypted with our own KMS key, and CloudTrail logs what the tools do. When cutover is finished, we delete the agents and replication instances and drop the migration users. The tradeoff is setup time and troubleshooting friction: tight security groups, private routing and narrow grants often break the first test run, so we must plan time to fix permissions rather than loosen them out of frustration.
rubricPoints: Gives each migration tool a least-privilege role and a narrow source login rather than admin credentials.
Encrypts data in transit with TLS and at rest with managed KMS keys, including on physical transfer devices.
Keeps tool traffic on private paths such as private subnets, VPC endpoints, VPN or Direct Connect.
Stores tool credentials in a secret store instead of plain configuration.
Logs tool activity and removes agents, instances and credentials after cutover.
Names a real tradeoff, such as extra setup and troubleshooting effort.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios where you must spot the insecure choice among migration designs, so reasoning through a realistic situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: Before moving dozens of applications into the cloud, a company needs house rules: who owns which area, what nobody may do, and where the records are kept. A governance model is that rulebook, applied across many separate cloud accounts. AWS Organizations is the service that groups accounts under one parent, sets limits on them and combines their bills. AWS Control Tower sits on top of it and builds a ready-made, rule-checked starting layout for you. Think of Organizations as the land registry and fencing laws, and Control Tower as a developer who lays out a whole estate to a standard plan.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company wants to stop every team, in every account, from running anything outside two approved regions, would you set that rule separately in each account or once from a central place? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Organizations groups many AWS accounts under one management account, the top account that pays the bill and administers the rest. Accounts sit in organizational units (OUs), which are folders such as Prod or Dev. A service control policy (SCP) is a rule attached to an OU or account that caps the most any user there can do. It never grants access by itself.

AWS Control Tower automates a landing zone, which is a pre-built multi-account starting layout. It creates a log archive account to hold central audit logs and an audit account for security teams. It also adds controls, which are ready-made guardrails. Preventive controls block actions, mostly through SCPs. Detective controls flag rule breaks after the fact, using configuration-checking rules. Its Account Factory creates new accounts that already follow the baseline.

It works because rules attached high in the tree flow down to every account below. A new account therefore starts out compliant.

Worked example: a firm will migrate 40 applications in waves. Step one, it chooses Control Tower because it has no existing multi-account setup and wants a standard result quickly. Step two, Control Tower creates the management, log archive and audit accounts. Step three, the team adds Prod and Dev OUs. Step four, it turns on a control that denies unapproved regions, plus one that stops anyone switching off audit logging. Step five, Account Factory creates one account per application for each wave.

When should you choose plain Organizations instead? Choose it when you already have a large, heavily customized organization, or need layouts Control Tower does not support. An existing organization can also be enrolled into Control Tower later.

Common mistake: assuming an SCP gives people permissions. Users still need their own access policies, and the SCP only limits them. SCPs also do not restrict the management account itself.

In a running system, an SCP that is too tight can block a migration tool partway through a wave. Missing central logging leaves migrated workloads with no audit trail.

questions.prompt: A logistics company already runs an organization of 250 accounts with a heavily customized OU layout that Control Tower does not support. It is preparing to migrate 15 warehouse applications. Step 1: it decides to keep plain AWS Organizations rather than adopt Control Tower, because its existing setup is large and customized. Step 2: it creates a Migration OU (an organizational unit, a folder for accounts) and places 15 new accounts in it. Step 3: it attaches a service control policy (SCP) to the Migration OU that denies every region except two approved ones. Step 4: ??? Step 5: migration engineers in those accounts can now run their migration tools, but only in the two approved regions. Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Attach a second SCP to the Migration OU that allows all migration tool actions, so the engineers receive their permissions from it
Move the engineers' work into the management account, because an SCP there would grant them broader access
Give the engineers their own access policies that allow the migration tool actions they need, inside the limits the SCP sets
Enroll the organization into Control Tower, because only Control Tower can give users permission to act in member accounts
questions.why: An SCP only caps what users can do and never grants access, so the engineers still need their own access policies, and the SCP then limits those policies to the two approved regions.

questions.prompt: A bank uses Control Tower. One of its controls does not stop anyone from making a storage bucket public. Instead, it notices afterwards that a bucket has become public and reports the rule break so the security team can act. What kind of control is this?
choices: A detective control, because it uses configuration-checking rules to flag a rule break after it happens
A management account control, because only the top account can see bucket settings
An Account Factory control, because it is applied when the account is first created
A preventive control, because it is enforced mainly through a service control policy
questions.why: Detective controls flag rule breaks after the fact using configuration-checking rules, whereas preventive controls block the action from happening at all.

questions.prompt: A games studio has never used more than one AWS account. Over the next few months it plans to move 25 workloads, one account per workload. It wants a standard multi-account layout set up quickly, a dedicated account that holds central audit logs, a separate account for its security team, and new accounts that follow its rules from the start. Which approach fits best?
choices: Build a plain AWS Organizations setup by hand and design a custom OU layout before migrating anything
Rely on one account with service control policies attached to each user, since SCPs grant the needed access
Use AWS Control Tower to set up a landing zone, then create the workload accounts with Account Factory
Create all 25 accounts by hand first, then decide on a governance model after the migration finishes
questions.why: With no existing multi-account setup and a need for a quick standard result, Control Tower's landing zone gives a log archive account, an audit account and controls, and Account Factory creates new accounts that already follow the baseline.

questions.prompt: A media company attaches a service control policy (SCP) at the top of its organization that denies turning off audit logging. Later, a logging setting is switched off by an administrator signed in to the management account, the top account that pays the bill and administers the others. Why did the SCP not stop this?
choices: The SCP should have been attached to each user directly, because SCPs only apply to individual people
Rules attached high in the tree only apply to accounts created after the rule, not to the management account's older settings
SCPs do not restrict the management account itself, so actions taken there are not capped by the SCP
SCPs grant permissions rather than limit them, so the administrator was given the right to turn logging off
questions.why: SCPs flow down to member accounts in the organization but never limit the management account, so a guardrail attached there cannot stop actions taken from inside that top account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between using AWS Control Tower and using AWS Organizations on its own to govern the accounts for an upcoming migration. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Organizations is the foundation. It groups accounts under a management account, arranges them into OUs and applies SCPs, which set the maximum anyone in an account can do. Control Tower builds on Organizations and automates a landing zone. It gives us log archive and audit accounts, preventive and detective controls, and Account Factory, so every account we create for a migration wave starts out compliant. For a fresh start or a team that wants a proven standard fast, I would pick Control Tower. The tradeoff is that it is opinionated, so a large, heavily customized existing organization might stay on plain Organizations with hand-built policies, or enroll in Control Tower carefully. Either way, SCPs only cap permissions and never grant them. They also do not apply to the management account, and an over-strict one can break migration tooling, so we test them before each wave.
rubricPoints: Organizations groups accounts into OUs under a management account and applies SCPs.
SCPs cap permissions and never grant them, and they do not restrict the management account.
Control Tower automates a landing zone with log archive and audit accounts, controls and Account Factory.
Control Tower suits a quick, standard setup, while plain Organizations suits heavily customized existing setups.
A tradeoff or risk is named, such as Control Tower being opinionated or a tight SCP blocking migration tools.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a governance model is a judgement call best practiced by reasoning through exam-style company scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine builds multi-account landing zones.

lessons.plain: When you move an application into AWS, it needs somewhere to run. Amazon EC2 gives you rented virtual servers: you choose the operating system, size and software, and you look after them yourself. AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a managed application platform: you hand it your application code, and it builds and runs the servers, load balancer and scaling for you. Think of EC2 as renting an empty kitchen you equip and staff yourself, and Elastic Beanstalk as a catered kitchen where you bring the recipe. The choice depends on how much control the application needs versus how much running work you want to give away.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company is moving two apps: a standard Java web shop, and an old accounting package that needs a special operating system driver and a licence tied to physical server cores. Which one would you put on a platform that manages servers for you, and which on servers you control directly?
lessons.teach:
Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides virtual machines called instances. You pick an instance type (the CPU and memory size), a machine image called an AMI (a template holding the operating system and software), and you patch, configure and scale the instances yourself, often using an Auto Scaling group (a rule set that adds or removes instances as demand changes) behind a load balancer (a service that spreads incoming requests across instances). EC2 is the usual landing place for a rehost, where a server is copied as-is, because almost anything that ran on a physical or virtual server runs there. It also offers Dedicated Hosts, whole physical servers, for licences bound to cores or sockets.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a platform-as-a-service: a managed layer that, given code built for a supported runtime such as Java, .NET, Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, Go or a Docker container, creates the EC2 instances, Auto Scaling group, load balancer and health monitoring, then deploys new versions for you. It still runs on EC2 underneath, but you manage the application, not the servers. It suits a replatform: small changes so the app fits a managed platform.

Worked example: a web shop runs on Tomcat (a Java web server). Step one, it uses a supported runtime, so Beanstalk can host it. Step two, it needs no OS-level customisation. Step three, the team wants less patching work. Result: Elastic Beanstalk. The accounting package needs a custom kernel driver and a core-based licence, so it goes to EC2, possibly on a Dedicated Host.

A common mistake is logging in to a Beanstalk instance and changing it by hand. Beanstalk replaces instances during scaling and deployments, so those changes silently disappear and the fleet drifts; customisation must go into the app bundle or configuration files instead.

questions.prompt:
A veterinary clinic chain is moving two workloads to AWS. The first is its appointment-booking website, a Python app on two on-premises virtual machines. The second is an X-ray imaging server that runs a closed-source vendor service whose licence is counted per physical CPU socket. The architect works it through.

Step 1: Python is a runtime Elastic Beanstalk supports, and the booking site needs no operating-system tweaks.
Step 2: The clinic's two-person IT team wants to stop patching servers, so the booking site goes to Elastic Beanstalk as a replatform.
Step 3: For the imaging server: ______
Step 4: So the imaging server is rehosted, copied as-is onto Amazon EC2.

Which statement best fills Step 3?
choices: The licence is tied to physical sockets, so it needs a Dedicated Host, a whole physical server that EC2 offers.
Because Beanstalk runs on EC2 underneath, socket licences carry over automatically if the app is placed in Beanstalk.
A licence counted per socket does not matter in the cloud, so any ordinary shared EC2 instance works as is.
Beanstalk can host it, and an engineer can log in to the instance afterwards to install the vendor service by hand.
questions.why: A licence bound to physical sockets needs a whole physical server, and EC2 Dedicated Hosts provide exactly that, which is why this server is rehosted on EC2.

questions.prompt: An architect is comparing AWS Elastic Beanstalk with running plain Amazon EC2 instances. Which statement correctly describes what Elastic Beanstalk, a platform-as-a-service, does for you?
choices: It removes the need for EC2 entirely by running the code without any virtual machines underneath.
It creates the EC2 instances, Auto Scaling group, load balancer and health monitoring, then deploys new code versions.
It places every application on Dedicated Hosts so that core-based and socket-based licences are covered.
It rewrites any application, whatever its language, into a supported runtime before deploying it.
questions.why: Elastic Beanstalk builds and runs the EC2-based infrastructure and handles deployments, so you manage the application rather than the servers. It still runs on EC2 underneath.

questions.prompt: An insurance company must move 40 legacy servers in six weeks with no code changes. Several of them run a batch job on a heavily customised Linux build that needs special operating-system settings. Which compute platform fits these servers best?
choices: Elastic Beanstalk, with engineers logging in after launch to apply the operating-system settings.
Elastic Beanstalk, because it automatically creates an Auto Scaling group for every server.
Amazon EC2 as a rehost, because almost anything that ran on a server runs there unchanged.
Dedicated Hosts for all 40 servers, because every rehost requires whole physical servers.
questions.why: A copy-as-is move with deep operating-system customisation is a rehost, and EC2 is the usual landing place for that. Dedicated Hosts are only needed for licences tied to cores or sockets, which these servers do not have.

questions.prompt: A team runs a Go API on Elastic Beanstalk across four instances. An engineer logs in to one instance and edits a file to raise a timeout, and the change works. A week later, after a new version is deployed, the old timeout is back everywhere. What happened, and what is the right fix?
choices: The edit only reached one of four instances. Log in to all four and repeat the change after each deployment.
The Auto Scaling group was missing, so Beanstalk ignored the change. Attach a load balancer and redeploy.
Beanstalk replaced the instances during the deployment, so the change was lost. Put the setting in the app bundle or configuration files.
Go is not a runtime Beanstalk supports, so the deployment fell back to defaults. Move the API to EC2.
questions.why: Beanstalk replaces instances during deployments and scaling, so changes made by hand disappear. Customisation belongs in the app bundle or configuration files so that every new instance gets it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between Amazon EC2 and AWS Elastic Beanstalk for a workload being migrated, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how much control the application needs. EC2 gives us virtual servers where we pick the OS, image and size, so nearly anything runs there, which makes it the default for a rehost and the only fit for custom drivers, unusual software or core-bound licences on Dedicated Hosts. The tradeoff is that we own patching, scaling setup and deployments. Elastic Beanstalk is a managed platform: if the app is a standard web or worker app on a supported runtime like Java, .NET, Node or Docker, we upload code and it builds the EC2 instances, Auto Scaling group and load balancer and handles deployments. That fits a light replatform and cuts operational work. Its limit is less control: it only supports certain runtimes, and manual changes on its instances are lost when it replaces them, so customisation has to live in the app bundle or configuration.
rubricPoints: EC2 is self-managed virtual servers with full OS control and fits rehosting nearly anything.
Elastic Beanstalk is a managed platform that provisions EC2, scaling and load balancing from your code.
Beanstalk needs a supported runtime or container and suits a replatform.
Custom OS needs or core-bound licences point to EC2, possibly Dedicated Hosts.
Tradeoff named: EC2 means more operational work; Beanstalk means less control and lost manual instance changes.

suggested.rationale: The skill is matching an application's runtime, customisation and licensing needs to a platform, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style migration scenarios rather than an existing hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A container is a sealed package holding an application plus everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on any machine. Running many containers needs an orchestrator: a scheduler that decides where each container runs, restarts failed ones and adds more under load. AWS offers two: ECS, its own simpler orchestrator, and EKS, a managed version of Kubernetes, the popular open-source standard. Fargate runs containers without you managing the servers underneath. ECR is a private warehouse for container images. Think of shipping: ECR is the depot, ECS or EKS is the dispatcher, and Fargate is hiring trucks per trip instead of owning a fleet.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team with no Kubernetes experience wants to run ten containerized web services on AWS and never patch a server. Which orchestrator and which kind of compute would you guess fits them best, and why?
lessons.teach:
Choosing a container platform means answering three separate questions: where images live, which orchestrator schedules them, and who manages the machines they run on.

A container image is a built, read-only template; a running copy of it is a container. A registry stores images. Amazon ECR is AWS's managed private registry; access is controlled by IAM (AWS's permission system), and it can scan pushed images for known vulnerabilities. An orchestrator keeps the desired number of containers running. Amazon ECS is AWS's own orchestrator: its unit is a task (one or more containers defined together), and an ECS service keeps a set number of tasks alive, usually behind a load balancer. Amazon EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane (the API and scheduler, the brain) for you; its unit is a pod. Kubernetes is portable across clouds and on-premises and has a huge tool ecosystem, but it is more complex and its versions must be upgraded regularly. The data plane is the compute where containers actually run: either EC2 virtual machines you size, patch and scale, or AWS Fargate, serverless compute that provisions capacity per task or pod and bills for the CPU and memory requested.

These choices are independent: ECR feeds both ECS and EKS, and Fargate works under both.

Worked example. A company is moving twelve services. Step 1: no Kubernetes skills and a requirement for least operational overhead, so ECS. Step 2: spiky traffic and nobody wants to patch hosts, so Fargate. Step 3: the build pipeline pushes images to ECR. A second business unit already runs Kubernetes on-premises and wants the same tooling everywhere, so it gets EKS. Choose an EC2 data plane instead of Fargate when you need GPUs, specific instance types, privileged access to the host, or steady heavy load where reserved EC2 capacity is cheaper.

Common mistake: treating Fargate as a rival to ECS or EKS. It is not an orchestrator; it is a compute option underneath them. In a running system, picking the EC2 option without scaling the cluster leaves new tasks stuck pending when capacity runs out.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm is moving its route-optimisation workload to AWS. The engineering team already maintains Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts on-premises and wants the same tooling in the cloud. The optimiser needs GPUs to run its models. Step 1 (orchestrator): the team wants portable Kubernetes tooling, so it chooses Amazon EKS, where AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane. Step 2 (data plane): ______. Step 3 (registry): the CI pipeline pushes the built images to Amazon ECR, a private registry with access controlled by IAM. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Use AWS Fargate, because serverless compute removes the need to patch any hosts.
Turn on ECR image scanning, because the data plane is where image vulnerabilities are checked.
Switch to Amazon ECS, because AWS's own orchestrator has lower operational overhead.
Use EC2 worker nodes with GPU instance types, because GPU hardware calls for an EC2 data plane.
questions.why: The teaching text says to choose an EC2 data plane rather than Fargate when you need GPUs, and Step 2 is about the compute where containers run, not the orchestrator or registry.

questions.prompt: An architect's slide lists "ECS vs EKS vs Fargate" as three competing options to pick one from. Which statement best corrects the slide?
choices: Fargate is the managed Kubernetes control plane that EKS uses to schedule pods.
Fargate is a lighter orchestrator that replaces ECS for small workloads.
Fargate is a private image registry that ECS and EKS both pull from.
Fargate is serverless compute that runs tasks or pods underneath either ECS or EKS; it is not an orchestrator.
questions.why: Fargate is a data-plane compute option that provisions capacity per task or pod, and it works under both ECS and EKS rather than competing with them.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing site runs its booking service on Amazon ECS using an EC2 data plane of four fixed instances. During a concert on-sale, the ECS service tries to add tasks, but the new tasks sit in a pending state and never start. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The EC2 cluster was not scaled, so there is no spare capacity to place the new tasks.
The Kubernetes control plane version was out of date and needed an upgrade.
Amazon ECR scanning blocked the images because they contained known vulnerabilities.
ECS services can only keep a set number of tasks and cannot add more.
questions.why: With an EC2 data plane you size and scale the machines yourself, so if the cluster is not scaled, new tasks stay pending when capacity runs out.

questions.prompt: A hospital group's security team requires that all container images be stored privately, that access be governed by its existing AWS permissions, and that images be checked for known vulnerabilities when pushed. One department runs workloads on Amazon ECS and another on Amazon EKS. What should the architect recommend for storing images?
choices: Keep images inside the EKS control plane and copy them to ECS when needed.
Use a separate registry type for each orchestrator, because ECR only works with ECS.
Use Amazon ECR as a single private registry, controlled by IAM with push scanning, feeding both ECS and EKS.
Run Fargate, since it stores and scans images for both orchestrators.
questions.why: ECR is AWS's managed private registry, uses IAM for access, can scan pushed images, and serves both ECS and EKS because the registry choice is independent of the orchestrator.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick between ECS, EKS, Fargate and ECR for a migrated workload, and name one tradeoff of the choice you would usually default to.
lessons.modelAnswer: I treat it as three separate decisions. First, images: we store them in ECR, a private registry with IAM access control and image scanning, and it works with either orchestrator. Second, the orchestrator: ECS is AWS's own and simpler, so it fits teams without Kubernetes skills who want low overhead; EKS is managed Kubernetes, worth it when we need portability across clouds or on-premises, already have Kubernetes tooling, or want its ecosystem, at the cost of more complexity and regular version upgrades. Third, compute: Fargate means no servers to patch or scale and billing per task's CPU and memory; EC2 instances suit GPUs, special instance types, host-level access or steady heavy load. My usual default, ECS on Fargate, trades away control over the host and can cost more than well-used reserved EC2 for constant workloads.
rubricPoints: Separates the registry, orchestrator and compute choices as independent decisions.
Describes ECR as a private image registry usable by both ECS and EKS.
Contrasts ECS simplicity with EKS Kubernetes portability and complexity.
States Fargate is serverless compute under ECS or EKS, not an orchestrator.
Names when EC2 compute beats Fargate, such as GPUs, host access or steady load cost.
Names a real tradeoff of the chosen default.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine runs containers, and the exam tests this by reasoning through scenario requirements like skills, overhead and portability, so an exam-style situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: Every application keeps its data somewhere, and different apps expect that data to look different. Some want a private hard disk that only one server uses. Some want a shared network folder that many servers open at once. Some just want a huge, cheap warehouse where each file is stored and fetched by a label. Choosing cloud storage is like choosing between a personal desk drawer, a shared office filing cabinet, and an off-site warehouse. Each works, but only one fits how a given app works. When you move apps to AWS, you match each one to the storage type it already expects. Sometimes you also keep a local box that syncs to the cloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: Ten web servers must all read and write the same folder of uploaded images. Would you give each server its own private disk, one shared network folder, or something else, and why?
lessons.teach:
Picking storage for a migrated workload starts with one question: how does the application expect to reach its data? There are three main shapes. Block storage presents a raw disk that one server formats and mounts. File storage presents a shared folder over a network protocol. On Linux that protocol is usually NFS (Network File System). On Windows it is usually SMB (Server Message Block). Object storage keeps whole files as objects. Each object is addressed by a key and fetched through web (HTTPS) calls.

Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is block storage. It is a network-attached disk for one EC2 virtual machine and lives in a single Availability Zone (AZ, an isolated group of data centers within a Region). It is low-latency and suits boot disks and self-managed databases.

Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed NFS share. Many Linux servers across AZs can mount it at once, and it grows automatically.

Amazon FSx is a family of managed file systems for specific needs. FSx for Windows File Server offers SMB shares with Active Directory permissions. FSx for Lustre gives very high throughput to compute clusters. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS match existing enterprise file-server features.

Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is object storage with near-unlimited capacity and very high durability. It suits backups, media, data lakes and static content, but the app must call its API rather than open file paths.

Storage Gateway Volume Gateway is a hybrid appliance that runs on premises. It offers iSCSI disks (disks reached over a network) to local servers and keeps the data or snapshots in AWS. In cached mode the primary copy lives in AWS and recent data stays local. In stored mode everything stays local and is backed up to AWS asynchronously.

Worked example: take a legacy app with four needs and match each in turn. Its single-server database needs a fast private disk, so it gets EBS. Its Windows shares with AD permissions go to FSx for Windows File Server. Its rarely read invoice archive, fetched by key, goes to S3. A factory server that must stay on site but needs cloud backup of its disks gets Volume Gateway.

A common mistake is choosing EBS for data that several servers share. A standard EBS volume attaches to one instance in one AZ. In a scaled-out tier, each server would then see different files and users would get inconsistent results. Shared access points to EFS or FSx instead.

questions.prompt: A university research lab is moving three workloads to AWS, and each is matched to storage by asking how it reaches its data. Step 1: a genome-analysis cluster of 200 compute nodes needs very high read throughput from a shared scratch file system, so it gets FSx for Lustre. Step 2: four Linux web servers spread across two Availability Zones must all read and write the same uploaded-images folder over NFS, so they get Amazon EFS. Step 3 (missing): a microscope workstation must stay in the on-premises lab and keep all of its disk data on site for fast local use, but the lab wants an asynchronous copy of those disks kept in AWS. Which choice completes Step 3?
choices: An Amazon EBS volume, because it is a fast private disk for one server
Amazon S3 directly, because it is very durable and suits backups
Storage Gateway Volume Gateway in cached mode, because the primary copy lives in AWS
Storage Gateway Volume Gateway in stored mode, because all data stays local and is backed up to AWS
questions.why: Stored mode keeps the full dataset on premises and backs it up to AWS asynchronously, which is exactly what the workstation needs.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup keeps 80 million thumbnail images. Its application already fetches each image by a unique key over HTTPS calls, and it needs near-unlimited capacity with very high durability. Which storage fits best?
choices: Amazon S3
Amazon EBS
FSx for NetApp ONTAP
Amazon EFS
questions.why: The app reaches whole files by key over web calls, which is object storage, and S3 provides near-unlimited, highly durable object storage.

questions.prompt: An engineer puts a shared configuration folder on one standard Amazon EBS volume for a tier of six web servers spread across three Availability Zones. What is the problem, and what is the better choice?
choices: EBS cannot hold configuration files, so the folder should move to Volume Gateway
A standard EBS volume attaches to one instance in one AZ, so servers see different files; a shared file system like EFS fits instead
EBS is too slow for web servers, so the folder should move to FSx for Lustre
Nothing is wrong; EBS is low-latency, so it suits a shared folder for a scaled-out tier
questions.why: A standard EBS volume serves one instance in a single AZ, so shared access across many servers needs a shared file system such as EFS.

questions.prompt: A regional branch office has only 3 TB of local disk space but its servers work with a 50 TB dataset reached as iSCSI disks. The company wants the primary copy of the data held in AWS, with only recently used data kept on site. Which option fits?
choices: Volume Gateway in stored mode
Volume Gateway in cached mode
Amazon EFS mounted over NFS
Amazon EBS attached to the local servers
questions.why: In cached mode the primary copy lives in AWS and only recent data stays local, so a small on-site disk can front a much larger dataset.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between EBS, EFS, FSx, S3 and Volume Gateway for a migrated application, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would most often reach for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how the app touches its data. If one server needs a fast private disk, like a database or boot volume, I use EBS. It is block storage, but it sits in one Availability Zone and normally attaches to one instance, so it can't be a shared folder. If many Linux servers need the same files over NFS, I use EFS, which scales automatically but costs more per gigabyte than S3. If the app needs Windows SMB shares with Active Directory permissions, or a high-performance or enterprise file system, I pick the matching FSx type. For backups, archives, media or data lakes I use S3. It is cheap and durable, but the app must use its API instead of file paths, so a lift-and-shift may need code changes. If servers must stay on premises but want cloud-backed disks, Volume Gateway fits.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes block, file and object storage by how the application accesses data.
Places EBS as a single-instance, single-AZ low-latency disk.
Places EFS as a shared NFS file system for many Linux servers.
Matches FSx variants to Windows SMB/AD, high-performance or enterprise filer needs.
Places S3 as durable object storage that requires API access rather than file paths.
Describes Volume Gateway as a hybrid on-premises block option, and names at least one tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises storage selection, so the skill is best built by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that match each app's access pattern to the right storage service.

lessons.plain: Choosing a database platform means deciding where a moved application's data will live and who looks after it. Think of housing. A managed relational service is a serviced apartment: you bring your furniture (tables and queries) and the landlord fixes the plumbing. A managed key-value store is a huge locker wall where you find anything instantly by its number. A managed search service is a library catalogue built for finding things by words. Running your own database on a rented server is owning a house: total freedom, but every repair is yours. The skill is matching each application's data and needs to the right home.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop needs a search box where customers type 'red waterproof jacket' and get the best matches ranked first. Would you expect an ordinary table-based database or a dedicated search engine to do that job better, and why?
lessons.teach:
Selecting a database platform means matching a workload's data shape, query pattern and operational needs to one of four options.

Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service. Relational means data sits in tables linked by keys, queried with SQL (a query language), with joins (combining tables) and transactions (several changes that succeed or fail together). RDS runs engines such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server, and AWS handles patching, backups and Multi-AZ failover, meaning a standby copy in a second data center takes over if the first fails.

Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document database, a NoSQL store. You fetch items by a key, it scales to very high request rates with steady low latency, and there are no servers to size, but there are no joins and queries must follow the keys you designed.

Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed search and log-analytics engine. It indexes text so it can rank results by relevance and summarize logs quickly. It is a search copy fed from a primary database, not the main record of the data.

Self-managed on Amazon EC2 means installing the database yourself on a virtual server. Choose it only when you need operating-system access, an engine version or plugin the managed service lacks, or licensing tied to specific hosts.

Worked example. A portfolio has four needs. First, an orders system on PostgreSQL using joins: managed relational, so RDS. Second, a shopping-cart store read by user ID with traffic spikes: key lookups at scale, so DynamoDB. Third, a product search box: relevance ranking, so OpenSearch, kept in sync from the orders data. Fourth, an Oracle system needing a custom OS-level agent: managed services block OS access, so EC2.

A common mistake is defaulting everything to EC2 because it feels closest to the old setup. In a running system that means your team now owns patching, backups and failover, and a missed patch or an unhandled failure becomes an outage that RDS would have handled automatically.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company is choosing a database platform for four workloads. Workload 1 is a payments ledger on SQL Server that needs transactions, so that a charge and its receipt are saved together or not at all. Decision: managed relational, so Amazon RDS. Workload 2 holds seat reservations that are read by booking ID and see huge spikes when popular shows go on sale. Decision: key lookups at very high request rates, so Amazon DynamoDB. Workload 3 is a help-center search box where customers type phrases like "refund for cancelled show" and expect the most relevant articles first. Decision: MISSING STEP. Workload 4 is a MySQL database that depends on a plugin the managed service does not offer. Decision: install it yourself on a virtual server, so self-managed on Amazon EC2. Which choice correctly completes the decision for Workload 3?
choices: DynamoDB, because it scales well and can fetch any article by its ID
OpenSearch Service, used as the only and main record of the articles
OpenSearch Service, kept in sync from the primary database as a search copy
Self-managed on EC2, because text search needs operating-system access
questions.why: Ranking text by relevance is what OpenSearch Service is built for, but it is a search copy fed from a primary database, not the main record of the data.

questions.prompt: A city water utility runs a metering system. Each night it records a meter reading and adds the charge to the customer's account, and both changes must succeed or fail together. Analysts also write SQL reports that join the customers table with the readings table. The team wants AWS to handle patching, backups and failover, and it has no special operating-system or licensing needs. Which platform fits best?
choices: Amazon OpenSearch Service, because it summarizes data quickly
Amazon RDS, because it is managed and supports joins and transactions
Self-managed on EC2, because SQL reports need operating-system access
Amazon DynamoDB, because it has no servers to size
questions.why: Joins, transactions and SQL describe a relational workload, and RDS runs relational engines while AWS handles patching, backups and Multi-AZ failover.

questions.prompt: A fitness-tracker maker stores the latest step count for each of its 5 million wearable devices. The app always reads and writes a record by device ID, traffic jumps sharply every morning, and the team needs steady low latency without sizing servers. It never needs to combine this data with other tables. Which platform fits best?
choices: Amazon DynamoDB
PostgreSQL self-managed on EC2
Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
questions.why: Fetching items by a known key at very high, spiky request rates with steady low latency and no servers to size is the case DynamoDB is designed for, and the lack of joins does not matter here.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm migrates a standard PostgreSQL database onto a virtual server it manages itself on EC2, only because that feels closest to its old data center. The database needs no OS access, unusual plugin or host-tied licensing. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: Text search results lose relevance ranking
Queries can no longer use joins, so reports must be rewritten
The team owns patching, backups and failover, so a missed patch can cause an outage
The database can no longer be queried with SQL
questions.why: Self-managing on EC2 moves patching, backups and failover onto the team, so a missed patch or unhandled failure can become an outage that RDS would have handled automatically.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between RDS, DynamoDB, OpenSearch Service and a self-managed database on EC2 for a migrated application, and name one tradeoff of choosing EC2.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the data shape and how the app queries it. If it needs tables, joins and transactions on a standard engine like PostgreSQL or SQL Server, RDS is the default because AWS runs patching, backups and Multi-AZ failover for us. If the app mostly reads and writes items by a known key and must handle huge or spiky traffic, DynamoDB fits, though we lose joins and must design keys around our queries up front. If users need full-text search or we want to analyze logs, OpenSearch Service is right, but only as a search copy fed from the main database, never as the system of record. EC2 is the exception: when we need OS access, an unsupported version or plugin, or host-bound licensing. The tradeoff is control versus toil, since on EC2 we own patching, backups and high availability ourselves.
rubricPoints: Matches relational SQL workloads with joins and transactions to RDS as the managed default.
Matches high-scale key-based access to DynamoDB and notes the lack of joins.
Places OpenSearch as a search or log-analytics copy, not the primary store.
Reserves EC2 for needs like OS access, unsupported engines or plugins, or licensing.
Names the tradeoff that self-managed means owning patching, backups and failover.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning from a workload's requirements to the right database platform, which is best practised through exam-style scenarios rather than any current mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Decoupling means arranging the parts of an application so they do not have to wait on each other or fail together. In a tightly coupled system, one part calls another and stands still until it answers; if the second part is slow or down, the first part breaks too. Decoupling puts something in between, often a waiting line that holds requests until the next part is ready. Think of a restaurant: the waiter pins the order to a rail and goes back to customers instead of standing in the kitchen until the dish is cooked. Spotting where that rail belongs is the skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's checkout page sends the order confirmation email itself before showing 'Thank you'. One morning the email service is slow. What do you think customers experience at checkout, and does the email really need to finish before the page loads?
lessons.teach:
Coupling is how strongly one component depends on another being available and fast at the same moment. A component is one separable piece of an application, such as a web front end, a payment module or an email sender. Tight coupling usually means synchronous calls: the caller sends a request and waits for the reply. Decoupling replaces that wait with an asynchronous hand-off: the producer (the part creating work) drops a message into a buffer, commonly a managed queue such as Amazon SQS, and a consumer (the part doing the work) picks it up when ready.

It works because the buffer absorbs differences in speed and availability. If the consumer is slow, messages wait; if it crashes, they stay in the queue until it recovers. Each side can also scale on its own.

Worked example. A legacy monolith (one deployable unit holding every function) runs checkout like this: save order, charge card, reserve stock, render invoice PDF, send email, then reply. Step one, ask of each task: must the customer see its result before the page returns? Charging the card, yes. The PDF and email, no. Step two, ask whether these tasks fail or scale differently: PDF rendering is CPU heavy and spikes at sales. Step three, redesign: checkout saves the order, charges the card, puts an 'order placed' message on a queue and replies. Separate workers read the queue and build PDFs and emails. A slow mail server now delays emails, not sales.

Signals of an opportunity: work that needs no immediate answer, one failure cascading into others, parts with very different load patterns, and parts owned or released by different teams.

A common mistake is decoupling something the user needs right now, like payment approval, which only adds delay and confusion. Another is forgetting that queues can deliver a message more than once, so consumers must be safe to repeat.

In a running system, if consumers stop, the queue silently grows, so queue depth must be monitored and alarmed.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing site runs its booking flow as one synchronous chain: reserve the seat, confirm payment, generate a QR-code ticket image, add points in a loyalty system run by a separate team, send an SMS, then reply to the buyer. The loyalty system goes down for about 20 minutes each week, and every booking during that window fails. Here is the decoupling analysis, with one step missing. Step 1: The buyer must see the seat reserved and the payment confirmed before the page returns. The QR image, loyalty points and SMS can arrive a little later. Step 2: The loyalty system fails independently and belongs to another team, so its outages currently cascade into lost sales. Step 3: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Put seat reservation, payment confirmation and all follow-up tasks on a queue, so the booking page replies instantly every time.

Have the booking reserve the seat, confirm payment, place a 'ticket sold' message on a queue and reply. Separate consumers then read the queue to build the QR image, add loyalty points and send the SMS.
Move the whole booking chain onto a larger server, so every step finishes faster and the loyalty outage matters less.
Make the loyalty call retry five times in a row inside the booking request, so short outages are covered while the buyer waits.
questions.why: Only the tasks the buyer must see right away stay synchronous, and the queue lets the loyalty outage delay points instead of blocking sales.

questions.prompt: A logistics company decoupled its shipment-label printing. The web app now drops a message on a managed queue, and a fleet of label workers reads from that queue. One night a bad deployment stopped every worker. No errors appeared on the website, and staff only noticed six hours later, when 40,000 labels were missing. What should have been in place to catch this early?
choices: A synchronous call from the web app to the label workers, so the website would show errors
A second queue that copies every message, so no labels could be lost
Monitoring and an alarm on queue depth, the number of messages waiting in the queue
Larger label workers, so they would have processed the backlog faster after restarting
questions.why: When consumers stop, the queue grows silently, so an alarm on queue depth is what reveals the problem quickly.

questions.prompt: A gym chain's sign-up service places a 'member joined' message on a queue. A rewards worker reads each message and credits 500 welcome points. Some new members are found to have 1,000 points instead of 500, even though each signed up only once. What is the most likely cause, and what is the right fix?
choices: The queue delivered some messages more than once; make the rewards worker safe to repeat, for example by skipping members it has already credited.
The queue is too slow; switch the rewards worker to a synchronous call from sign-up.
The sign-up service is sending two messages; add a second queue to filter them.
Queue depth is too high; add an alarm so the extra points stop being credited.
questions.why: Queues can deliver a message more than once, so consumers must be designed so that processing the same message again does no extra harm.

questions.prompt: An insurance web portal is one monolith, a single deployable unit containing every function. Which of its components is the strongest candidate to decouple behind a queue?
choices: Archiving scanned claim documents into a records system that is owned by another team and slows down at month end
Approving the card payment for a new policy before showing a confirmation
Checking the customer's password when they log in
Calculating the price quote that the customer is waiting to see on screen
questions.why: Archiving needs no immediate answer, has its own load pattern and belongs to a different team, while the other three are results the user must see right away.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which parts of a legacy application to decouple with a queue, and name one tradeoff or limit of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: I walk through each step a request triggers and ask whether the user needs that result before we reply. Anything that can finish later, like emails, reports or image processing, is a candidate to hand off through a queue: the front end drops a message and returns, and separate workers process it at their own pace. I also look for parts that drag others down when they fail, parts whose load spikes differently, and parts owned by different teams. The payoff is isolation: a slow downstream service builds a backlog instead of breaking checkout, and each side scales independently. The tradeoff is that work becomes eventually done rather than instant, messages can arrive more than once so handlers must tolerate repeats, and a dead consumer leaves a growing backlog, so we need to watch queue depth.
rubricPoints: Defines decoupling as removing direct synchronous waits between components, often with a queue as a buffer.
Uses 'does the caller need this result now?' as the main test for candidates.
Names other signals such as cascading failure, different scaling needs or separate ownership.
States that async work is delayed and must handle duplicate deliveries.
Mentions monitoring queue backlog because stalled consumers fail silently.

suggested.rationale: The skill is judging, from a described legacy application, which hand-offs can become asynchronous, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios and then explaining the choice.

lessons.plain: Serverless means you hand the provider a small piece of code and say "run this whenever something happens," and you never manage the machine it runs on. AWS Lambda is Amazon's version: a managed function service that starts your code in response to an event, such as a file arriving or a web request, and bills only for the time it actually runs. Think of a taxi instead of owning a car: perfect for occasional trips, costly if you drive all day. Spotting serverless opportunities means finding the parts of an application that behave like occasional, short trips.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has two background jobs: one resizes each photo a few seconds after a user uploads it, and the other converts each uploaded video and takes about two hours per file. If you could move only one of them to code that starts on demand and is billed only while running, which would you pick, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Lambda is a managed function service: you upload code, connect it to an event source, and the platform runs it on demand. An event is any signal that something happened, such as an object landing in storage, a message on a queue, an HTTP request, or a timer firing. Each run is an invocation. You pay per invocation and per millisecond of run time, scaled by the memory you choose, and nothing while idle.

It works well because capacity follows demand. Concurrency, the number of invocations running at the same moment, rises automatically as events arrive, up to an account limit, and falls to zero afterwards. That makes Lambda strong for spiky or intermittent work, short tasks, scheduled jobs, and glue code between services.

The limits tell you where it fits badly. One invocation can run for at most 15 minutes. Functions are stateless, so anything that must survive between runs goes to a database or storage. A cold start, the extra delay when a new copy of the function is first initialized, can hurt very latency-sensitive paths. Steady, high, round-the-clock load is often cheaper on always-on servers or containers.

Worked example: a legacy server polls a folder every minute to resize uploaded images and sits idle most of the day. Step one, the upload goes to object storage. Step two, that upload emits an event. Step three, the event invokes a function that resizes one image in about two seconds and writes the result back. Step four, with no uploads, nothing runs and nothing is billed. The two-hour video job fails the 15-minute limit, so it stays on containers or servers.

A common mistake is lifting a whole monolith into one giant function. It hits timeouts, suffers slow cold starts, and loses the per-event scaling benefit. In a running system, under a surge, concurrency limits can also throttle a function, so the downstream database must handle the burst.

questions.prompt:
A dental clinic runs a small server all day only to send appointment reminder texts. The job runs once each evening at 6 pm, takes about 4 minutes, and the server is idle for the rest of the day. The job must remember which patients were already reminded, so nobody gets a duplicate text. An architect checks whether this job suits AWS Lambda, a managed function service that runs code on demand when an event (a signal that something happened) arrives.

Step 1: A timer event fires at 6 pm each day and starts one invocation (one run of the function).
Step 2: The run takes about 4 minutes, which is well under the 15-minute limit for a single invocation.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The clinic pays only for that one daily run, billed by the millisecond and scaled by the chosen memory, and nothing while the function sits idle.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Keep the list of reminded patients in the function's memory, because the same copy of the function will still hold it at the next evening's run.
Keep the job on the always-on server, because any job that needs to remember data cannot run as a Lambda function.
Raise the function's memory setting so the list of reminded patients persists safely from one invocation to the next.
Write each patient's reminded status to a database after sending, because functions are stateless and keep nothing between runs.
questions.why: Lambda functions are stateless, so anything that must survive between runs, such as which patients were already reminded, belongs in a database or in storage rather than in the function itself.

questions.prompt: In AWS Lambda, what does the term concurrency mean?
choices: The amount of memory chosen for the function, which also scales its per-millisecond price.
The number of invocations running at the same moment, which rises automatically as events arrive, up to an account limit.
The maximum run time allowed for one invocation before the platform stops it.
The extra delay when a new copy of the function is first initialized.
questions.why: Concurrency is the count of invocations running at the same time; it grows with incoming events up to an account limit and falls to zero when the events stop.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is reviewing four legacy workloads for a possible move to AWS Lambda. Which one is the best candidate?
choices: A small handler that receives a few hundred delivery-confirmation webhooks (HTTP requests sent by a partner) at unpredictable times each day and saves each one in under a second.
A pricing engine that serves heavy, steady traffic around the clock and must answer as fast as possible.
A route-optimisation batch that runs for about 50 minutes each night.
A single large monolithic application moved as-is into one function.
questions.why: Short, intermittent, event-driven work fits Lambda because capacity follows demand and nothing is billed while idle; the 50-minute batch breaks the 15-minute limit, the steady latency-sensitive engine suits always-on servers, and a monolith in one function is a known mistake.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site moves its order-confirmation step to an AWS Lambda function that writes each order to a relational database. During a popular concert sale, about 30,000 orders arrive within a few minutes. What risk should the architect plan for?
choices: Lambda will keep one copy of the function running continuously afterwards, so idle billing will rise.
Concurrency limits can throttle the function, and the many parallel invocations can flood the downstream database, so the database must be able to handle the burst.
Each order will run more slowly because invocations share one fixed server whose capacity does not grow.
The function will fail because a single invocation cannot run for longer than a few seconds.
questions.why: Under a surge, concurrency rises until it hits the account limit, which can throttle the function, and the burst of parallel writes lands on the downstream database, which must be able to absorb it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a piece of a legacy application should become an AWS Lambda function, and name at least one limit or tradeoff that would rule it out.
lessons.modelAnswer: I look for work that is triggered by an event, runs briefly, and has uneven or occasional traffic: handling an upload, processing a queue message, a nightly scheduled task, or a lightly used API. Lambda runs that code on demand, scales concurrency up and down by itself, and charges only for invocations and run time, so idle time costs nothing and there is no server to patch. Then I check the limits. Anything that runs longer than 15 minutes per invocation is out. The code must be stateless, keeping data in a database or storage. Cold starts add delay on paths that need consistently low latency. And steady, heavy, all-day load is often cheaper on containers or servers. I also avoid stuffing a whole monolith into one function; I carve off the small event-driven pieces and leave the rest on a fitting platform.
rubricPoints: Defines Lambda as on-demand, event-triggered code with no servers to manage.
Names good fits: event-driven, short, spiky or intermittent, scheduled, or glue work.
States the 15-minute maximum run time per invocation as a hard limit.
Mentions statelessness, cold starts, or concurrency limits as tradeoffs.
Notes that steady high load can be cheaper on servers or containers.
Warns against moving an entire monolith into a single function.

suggested.rationale: The skill is judging which portfolio components suit Lambda, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that weigh run time, traffic shape, state and cost.

lessons.plain: A purpose-built database is a data store designed for one shape of work instead of trying to do everything. Many older applications put every kind of data into a single relational database, a store of tables joined by shared keys. When you migrate, you can spot pieces that would run faster or cheaper elsewhere. Think of a kitchen: one big pot can cook anything, but a kettle boils water faster and a fridge keeps things handy. DynamoDB is the kettle for simple lookups at huge scale. Aurora Serverless is the pot that resizes itself. ElastiCache is the fridge holding things you reach for constantly.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop checks the same popular product details thousands of times a minute, and those details change only once a day. Would you rather read them from the main database every time, or keep a copy somewhere faster? What could go wrong with the copy?
lessons.teach:
Identifying opportunities for purpose-built databases means looking at how each part of an application reads and writes data, then matching that pattern to a store designed for it.

Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document database. Key-value means you fetch an item by its key, like a locker number. It gives fast, steady response times at almost any scale and needs no server management. It works because data is spread across partitions by key, so lookups never scan everything. The tradeoff: you must know your access patterns in advance, and it does not do joins or flexible ad hoc queries well.

Amazon Aurora Serverless is a relational database, compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, whose capacity grows and shrinks automatically, measured in Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs). It suits SQL workloads with spiky, unpredictable or intermittent traffic. For steady, heavy load, fixed provisioned capacity is often cheaper.

Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache running Redis, Valkey or Memcached. In-memory means data lives in RAM, so reads take well under a millisecond. It fits session data, leaderboards and repeated reads of slow-changing data, taking load off the main database.

Worked example: a legacy ticketing app runs on one MySQL server. Step one, list its data uses: user sessions, seat lookups by event ID during sales, and monthly reports with joins. Step two, sessions are short-lived and read constantly, so move them to ElastiCache. Step three, seat lookups are by key and surge at sale time, so DynamoDB fits. Step four, reports need joins and run only monthly, so Aurora Serverless keeps SQL and costs little when idle.

Common mistake: treating the cache as the source of truth. A cache can lose data on restart or eviction, and if nothing durable holds the original, users lose sessions or orders. In a running system, a cold or emptied cache also floods the main database with sudden reads.

questions.prompt:
A city bike-share company runs everything on one PostgreSQL server. A worked analysis, with one step missing:

Step one: list the data uses. Bike unlock records are fetched by bike ID and surge at rush hour. A live 'top riders this week' leaderboard is read thousands of times a minute and is rebuilt from ride history that is stored durably. A yearly planning report joins the rides, stations and maintenance tables.

Step two: unlock records are fetched by a known key and spike at rush hour, so DynamoDB fits.

Step three: [missing]

Step four: the yearly report needs joins and runs rarely, so Aurora Serverless keeps SQL and costs little when idle.

Which statement correctly completes step three?
choices: Keep the leaderboard only in ElastiCache and delete the ride history table to save storage.
Move the leaderboard to Aurora Serverless, because its capacity units scale up with the heavy read rate.
Move the leaderboard into the yearly report so it is rebuilt once a year with joins.
Serve the heavily read leaderboard from ElastiCache, and keep ride history in a durable store.
questions.why: The leaderboard is read constantly, so an in-memory cache such as ElastiCache gives sub-millisecond reads and takes load off the main database, while the ride history it is built from stays in a durable store because a cache can lose data.

questions.prompt: An online game studio stores player profiles in DynamoDB and always fetches a profile by its player ID. Why does DynamoDB keep these lookups fast even as the player count grows into the millions?
choices: Data is spread across partitions by key, so a lookup goes straight to the right partition instead of scanning all of the data.
Its capacity units grow and shrink automatically with a SQL workload.
It joins the profile table to other tables at query time, so related data arrives together.
Every profile is held in RAM, so reads always finish in well under a millisecond.
questions.why: DynamoDB is a key-value store that places items in partitions by key, so a lookup by key never has to scan everything, and response times stay steady at scale.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a MySQL order-processing database that sees heavy, steady load around the clock, every day of the year. A teammate proposes moving it to Aurora Serverless to save money. What is the best response?
choices: Move it to ElastiCache instead, because in-memory storage is cheaper for orders.
Move it to DynamoDB, because order processing never needs SQL.
Be cautious: Aurora Serverless suits spiky or intermittent traffic, and for steady heavy load, fixed provisioned capacity is often cheaper.
Agree, because Aurora Serverless is always the cheapest relational option.
questions.why: Aurora Serverless pays off when capacity can shrink during quiet periods. A steady, heavy workload never shrinks, so fixed provisioned capacity is often cheaper.

questions.prompt: A news website stores shopping-cart contents only in ElastiCache, with no copy anywhere else, to make the carts fast. The cache cluster restarts during a busy evening. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing is lost, because ElastiCache permanently saves every item to disk by design.
DynamoDB automatically rebuilds the carts, because it is linked to every cache.
Carts can vanish, because the cache was treated as the source of truth and nothing durable held the original data.
The carts move into Aurora Serverless, which scales up to hold them.
questions.why: A cache can lose data on restart or eviction. When it is the only copy, users lose their data, so a durable store must hold the original.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether part of a legacy app should move to DynamoDB, Aurora Serverless or ElastiCache, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how each piece of the app actually uses data, not by picking a product. If something is fetched by a known key at high volume, like a cart or a device record, DynamoDB is a good fit because it stays fast at scale with no servers, but I have to design around fixed access patterns since joins and ad hoc queries are weak. If the data really needs SQL and relationships but traffic is spiky or often idle, Aurora Serverless lets capacity scale up and down automatically; for steady heavy load, provisioned capacity is usually cheaper. If the same data is read over and over or is short-lived, like sessions, ElastiCache keeps it in memory for sub-millisecond reads and protects the main database, but it is a cache, so a durable store must still hold the real copy.
rubricPoints: Starts from the access pattern of each data use rather than from a product.
DynamoDB fits known key-based lookups at scale but is weak for joins and ad hoc queries.
Aurora Serverless keeps relational SQL while auto-scaling capacity for variable or intermittent load, and may cost more under steady heavy load.
ElastiCache serves repeated or short-lived reads from memory and offloads the main database.
A cache is not the durable source of truth.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right purpose-built store is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios where a legacy app's data uses must each be matched to DynamoDB, Aurora Serverless or ElastiCache.

lessons.plain: When pieces of an application need to pass work or news to each other, you can wire them together directly, or put a go-between in the middle so each piece can run, fail and scale on its own. AWS offers four such go-betweens. Amazon SQS is a waiting line of jobs. Amazon SNS is a loudspeaker that pushes one message to many listeners. Amazon EventBridge is a mail-sorting room that routes events by their content. AWS Step Functions is a checklist runner that drives a multi-step process in order. Picking well means matching the go-between to the shape of the conversation.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop must email the customer, update stock and notify the warehouse every time an order is placed, and the warehouse system sometimes goes offline for an hour. Would you send each order straight to all three systems, or put something in between, and what should that something do while the warehouse is down?
lessons.teach:
Application integration services sit between a producer (the part that creates a message or event) and a consumer (the part that acts on it), so neither needs to know the other's address or be online at the same moment.

Amazon SQS is a managed queue: a durable list of messages that consumers pull from at their own pace. Each message is normally handled by one consumer, then deleted. It works because the queue absorbs bursts and holds work while consumers are slow or down. A dead-letter queue is a side queue where messages that fail repeatedly are parked for inspection.

Amazon SNS is a managed publish-subscribe topic: a publisher sends one message and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber at once, which is called fan-out. It does not hold messages for a subscriber that is unavailable for a long time.

Amazon EventBridge is a managed event bus: a channel that receives events from your code, AWS services and partner software, and uses rules (filters on the event's fields) to send each event to matching targets. Choose it when routing depends on content or when events come from many sources.

AWS Step Functions is a managed workflow engine: you define a state machine, a diagram of steps with ordering, branches, retries, waits and error handling, and the service runs it and tracks each execution's progress.

Worked example, the order flow. Step one: the order service publishes "order placed" to an SNS topic. Step two: the topic fans out to three SQS queues, one each for email, stock and warehouse. Step three: the warehouse goes offline; its queue simply grows. Step four: it returns and drains the backlog, nothing lost. If routing needed rules such as "only orders over 500 go to fraud review", EventBridge would replace SNS. If payment, then shipping, then refund-on-failure had to happen in order, Step Functions would coordinate it.

A common mistake is subscribing a fragile consumer straight to SNS with no queue behind it; when that consumer is down for long, messages can be dropped, and in a running system orders silently go unprocessed.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company wants every "ticket refunded" event to reach three systems: the accounting ledger, the rider notification service, and an analytics job that only runs between 1 a.m. and 3 a.m. Step one: the ticketing service publishes "ticket refunded" to an SNS topic. Step two: ______. Step three: during the day the analytics job is offline, so the refund messages waiting for it simply pile up. Step four: at 1 a.m. the job starts, works through the backlog, and no refund is lost. Which choice correctly fills step two?
choices: A Step Functions state machine replaces the topic and calls the three systems one after another
The topic sends each refund message straight to the analytics job's endpoint, and SNS keeps it until that job comes back online
All three systems pull from one shared SQS queue, so each refund message reaches all of them
The topic fans out a copy of each message to three separate SQS queues, one for each of the three systems
questions.why: SNS gives every subscriber a copy (fan-out). A separate SQS queue for each system holds that system's copies durably, so the offline analytics job finds its backlog waiting when it starts.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm processes claims in a fixed order. First it verifies the policy. Then it waits up to five days for an adjuster's approval. Then it pays out. If payment fails, it retries twice and then alerts staff. The firm wants a managed service that runs these ordered steps, with their branches, waits and error handling, and tracks where each claim currently stands. Which service fits best?
choices: Amazon SQS, because a queue holds each claim until a consumer is ready
Amazon EventBridge, because rules filter each claim by its fields
Amazon SNS, because a topic pushes each claim to every subscriber at once
AWS Step Functions, because a state machine defines ordered steps, waits, retries and error handling and tracks each run
questions.why: Coordinating ordered steps with waits, retries and failure handling, while tracking each execution's progress, is exactly what a managed workflow engine like Step Functions does.

questions.prompt: A farm-equipment maker receives events from its own apps, from AWS services, and from a partner's sensor platform. It wants only events where the field "soilMoisture" is below 20 to go to an irrigation alert service. All other events should go to an archive. Which service should sit in the middle?
choices: Amazon SQS with a dead-letter queue to separate low-moisture events
AWS Step Functions, because it runs steps in a fixed order
Amazon EventBridge, because its rules filter on event fields and it accepts events from many sources
Amazon SNS, because it fans out every event to all subscribers
questions.why: Routing that depends on an event's content, with events arriving from many sources including partner software, is the case for a managed event bus with rules: EventBridge.

questions.prompt: A ticket-resale startup subscribed its seat-allocation service directly to an SNS topic, with nothing in between. That service is often down for an hour or more during deployments. Afterwards, some resale requests are never processed, and no error appears. What is the most appropriate fix?
choices: Replace the topic with a Step Functions state machine that calls the service directly
Add a dead-letter queue to the SNS topic so that the service's downtime is avoided
Subscribe an SQS queue to the topic and have the seat-allocation service pull from that queue
Publish each request twice to the topic so that at least one copy gets through
questions.why: SNS does not hold messages for a subscriber that is unavailable for a long time. A durable SQS queue behind the topic keeps the messages until the service returns and drains them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between SQS, SNS, EventBridge and Step Functions for a new integration, and name one limit or tradeoff of at least one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what shape the conversation has. If one piece hands work to another and I want a buffer that holds jobs until a worker pulls them, that is SQS, a queue; each message goes to one consumer, and a dead-letter queue catches repeat failures. If one event must reach many receivers at once, that is SNS fan-out, but SNS pushes and does not hold messages long for an absent subscriber, so I put an SQS queue behind each important subscriber. If events come from many sources and need routing by their content, EventBridge rules on an event bus fit better. If I need several steps run in a set order with branches, retries and compensation on failure, Step Functions runs that as a state machine. The tradeoff is that each extra hop adds cost, some latency and another thing to monitor.
rubricPoints: SQS is a pull-based queue that buffers work so one consumer handles each message at its own pace.
SNS pushes one message to many subscribers (fan-out) but does not durably hold it for an unavailable subscriber.
EventBridge routes events from many sources to targets using content-based rules.
Step Functions orchestrates ordered multi-step workflows with branching, retries and error handling.
Combining SNS with SQS gives fan-out plus durable buffering per consumer.
Names a real tradeoff such as added latency, cost, complexity or loss risk without a queue.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing among four services from a scenario's requirements, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations rather than one hands-on lab that covers only part of the set.

scenarios.title: Halvorsen Freight: one network hub, two-way name lookups, and costs per business unit
scenarios.scenario:
Halvorsen Freight is a fictional shipping company moving onto AWS.
