It uses AWS Organizations, a service that groups many AWS accounts under one management account (the account that receives the combined bill and sets rules for the others). Today there are three member accounts, each holding one VPC (virtual private cloud, a private, isolated network inside AWS that you address with your own IP ranges) in the same Region (one geographic area of AWS data centers). The IP ranges are written as CIDR blocks (a starting address plus a size, such as 10.10.0.0/16, which covers 65,536 addresses): Shared-Services VPC 10.10.0.0/16, Payments VPC 10.20.0.0/16, Analytics VPC 10.30.0.0/16. The on-premises data center (the company's own building full of servers) uses 10.0.0.0/16.

The connections were built one at a time. Payments is joined to Shared-Services by VPC peering (a private, direct link between exactly two VPCs). Analytics is also peered to Shared-Services. The data center reaches only the Shared-Services VPC over AWS Direct Connect (a dedicated private network line from the building into AWS, rather than traffic over the public internet), which lands on a virtual private gateway (the AWS-side endpoint that attaches a private line or VPN to a single VPC). Leadership plans to grow to about 30 VPCs within a year.

Three problems have been reported. First, an Analytics job cannot reach a Payments reporting database, even though both VPCs are peered to Shared-Services and the route tables (lists that tell a network where to send traffic for each destination range) in Analytics point 10.20.0.0/16 at the peering link to Shared-Services. A compliance auditor has also said Payments may talk to Shared-Services and the data center, but Analytics must reach Payments only if explicitly allowed. Second, names do not resolve across the boundary. Cloud servers use names in a Route 53 private hosted zone (a DNS zone whose names are visible only inside the VPCs you link it to) called aws.halvorsen.internal, and the data center uses its own DNS servers for corp.halvorsen.internal. On-premises servers cannot look up aws.halvorsen.internal names, and cloud servers cannot look up corp.halvorsen.internal names. Third, Finance wants to see monthly AWS spend for each business unit (Freight Ops, Payments, Data Science), but most resources carry no labels, and the ones that do use mixed spellings such as costcenter, CostCentre and cost-center.

Your tasks:
1. Explain why the Analytics job cannot reach Payments through Shared-Services, then propose a connectivity design that fixes it, scales to about 30 VPCs plus the data center, and still lets you meet the auditor's segmentation rule.
2. Design hybrid DNS so that each side can look up the other's names, and say how the design reaches VPCs in other accounts.
3. Design a tagging strategy that gives Finance spend per business unit, including how you enforce consistent tags and one limitation Finance should be told about.
subParts: Fix transitive routing and scale the network
Tagging for cost per business unit
modelAnswer:
VPC peering is non-transitive: a peering link carries only traffic between the two VPCs at its ends. Traffic from Analytics to 10.20.0.0/16 arrives in Shared-Services, but AWS will not forward it onward across the second peering link to Payments. The route table entry in Analytics does not help, because the hop through the middle VPC is refused no matter what the routes say. The same rule means the data center, landing on a virtual private gateway in Shared-Services, cannot use Shared-Services as a path into Payments or Analytics either. A common mistake is to keep adding routes, or to add more peerings until every VPC is peered to every other. Full mesh grows very fast: 30 VPCs would need 435 peerings, each with its own route entries, which is hard to run and hard to audit.

The fix is AWS Transit Gateway, a managed regional router that acts as a hub. Each VPC attaches to it once, and it does forward traffic between attachments, so it provides the transitive routing that peering lacks. Create it in the Shared-Services account and share it to the other accounts with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM, a service for sharing a resource across accounts in the organization), so each team attaches its own VPC. For the data center, connect Direct Connect to a Direct Connect gateway (a global object that links a private line to AWS networks) over a transit virtual interface (the type of logical connection on the line that is used to reach a Transit Gateway), and associate the Direct Connect gateway with the Transit Gateway. Then remove the old peerings and the virtual private gateway path.

For segmentation, use separate Transit Gateway route tables. Each attachment is associated with one table, and that table decides where its traffic can go. The Payments table holds routes to Shared-Services and on-premises. The Analytics table holds routes to Shared-Services and on-premises but no route to 10.20.0.0/16, so Analytics cannot reach Payments by default. If the auditor approves the reporting database flow, add only that route, and allow only the database port in the Payments database's security group (a stateful firewall on each resource) for the Analytics range. The four ranges do not overlap, which routing through a hub requires. New VPCs must be given non-overlapping ranges too, ideally from a central plan. The consequence for the running system is one place to see and change routing, and segmentation an auditor can check by reading the route tables.

Use Route 53 Resolver, the built-in DNS service in every VPC, together with Resolver endpoints (network interfaces placed in your VPC subnets that let DNS queries cross between AWS and on-premises). Put both endpoint types in the Shared-Services VPC, in at least two Availability Zones (separate data centers within a Region) so one failure does not stop name lookups.

From on-premises to AWS: create an inbound endpoint, which gives fixed private IP addresses that accept DNS queries from outside. Associate the aws.halvorsen.internal private hosted zone with the Shared-Services VPC. On the data center DNS servers, add a conditional forwarder (a rule that sends queries for one domain to particular servers) for aws.halvorsen.internal that points at the inbound endpoint IPs. The traffic travels over Direct Connect.

From AWS to on-premises: create an outbound endpoint, which sends queries out of AWS. Create a Resolver forwarding rule that says queries for corp.halvorsen.internal go through the outbound endpoint to the data center DNS server IPs. Associate the rule with each VPC that needs it.

To reach other accounts, share the forwarding rule with RAM, and have each account associate it with its own VPC. Also associate the private hosted zone with every VPC that needs those names. Those VPCs still send queries to their own built-in resolver. The rule then sends corp names through the central outbound endpoint, which works because the hub network connects the VPCs to the data center.

Traced lookup: a Payments server asks for db1.corp.halvorsen.internal. Its VPC resolver matches the shared rule and sends the query to the outbound endpoint in Shared-Services. The endpoint forwards it over Direct Connect to the on-premises DNS server, and the answer returns the same way. Common mistakes are to point the on-premises forwarder at the VPC's own resolver address (often the VPC base address plus two), which cannot be queried from outside the VPC, and to forget to allow DNS on port 53 over both UDP and TCP in the endpoints' security groups and the firewalls. If the path fails, applications fail at startup or connection time even though the network itself is fine.

Define a small mandatory set of tag keys with exact spelling and allowed values. A tag is a key and value label on a resource. For example, CostCenter with values FreightOps, Payments or DataScience, plus Owner and Environment. Write these down as the company standard.

Enforce the standard in three layers. First, Organizations tag policies, which define the allowed key capitalization and values and report resources that do not comply. Second, a service control policy (SCP, an organization rule that sets the most any account may do) that denies creating key resource types, such as instances and volumes, when the request lacks a CostCenter tag. Third, tags applied automatically by your deployment templates, so people rarely type them by hand. Fix existing resources by retagging the mixed spellings (costcenter, CostCentre, cost-center) to the one standard key.

In the management account, activate CostCenter as a cost allocation tag. This is a tag you have switched on so the billing data groups costs by it. Finance can then use AWS Cost Explorer (a tool that charts and filters spend over time) grouped by CostCenter, and AWS Budgets (spending thresholds that send alerts) per business unit. Because each team also has its own account, grouping by linked account gives a second, reliable split that works even where tags are missing.

Tell Finance about this limitation: cost allocation tags only apply from the time they are activated and the resource is tagged. They do not recolor past bills, so earlier months will show large untagged amounts. Also, some costs are shared and do not belong to a single unit, such as the Transit Gateway, the Resolver endpoints and Direct Connect in Shared-Services. These need an agreed split rule, for example by each unit's share of the traffic. A common mistake is to assume tagging fixes history, which leads Finance to distrust the first reports.

scenarios.title: Month-End Payroll Platform at Larkspur Ledger
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Ledger is a fictional company building a brand-new payroll service on AWS. Small businesses upload timesheets, and the service calculates pay and produces PDF payslips. You are the architect, and the leadership team has given you six requirements that pull against each other.

Continuity: if an entire AWS Region (a separate geographic area of AWS data centers, such as one in Ireland and another in Frankfurt) becomes unavailable, the service must be running again elsewhere within 1 hour. This target is the recovery time objective, or RTO, meaning the longest outage the business accepts. No more than 5 minutes of committed payroll data may be lost. This is the recovery point objective, or RPO, meaning how far back in time you may have to roll. The main database is Amazon Aurora, a managed relational database where AWS handles patching and storage.

Budget: the finance team refuses to pay for a second full-size copy of the whole system running all month just in case.

Performance and reliability: for 27 days a month, payslip requests are light. On the last 3 days of the month they jump about 40 times. Today the design has the web tier call the PDF generator directly. During a load test, the generator ran out of capacity, the web requests timed out, and some payslip jobs were lost with no record.

Deployment: the team releases new code every week using AWS CloudFormation, a service that creates and updates infrastructure from a template file (infrastructure as code, meaning the environment is described in a file that can be versioned and reviewed). A bad release last week reached every customer at once, and rolling it back took 2 hours of manual work.

Security: a review found the database password written in plain text in the application's configuration file. It also found a long-lived IAM access key (a permanent username-and-secret pair for programmatic access in AWS Identity and Access Management, the AWS permissions service) attached to the EC2 servers (Amazon EC2 provides virtual machines), and that key has permission to do anything in the account.

Your tasks:
1. Recommend a disaster recovery approach that meets the 1-hour RTO and 5-minute RPO without paying for a full second copy, name how the database data reaches the second Region, and say how you will prove it actually works.
2. Redesign the link between the web tier and the PDF generator so month-end spikes do not cause timeouts or lost jobs, and say how the generator should scale.
3. Describe a deployment and rollback approach that limits how many customers a bad release reaches and undoes it automatically.
4. Fix the two security findings using least privilege, which means granting only the permissions a component needs and nothing more.
modelAnswer:
Choose a warm standby, or a pilot light that becomes a scaled-down warm standby, in a second Region. A warm standby is a smaller but fully working copy of the system that is always running. A pilot light keeps only the core pieces running, mainly the replicated database, and starts the rest when disaster strikes. Both cost far less than a full-size duplicate, which satisfies finance. A backup-and-restore-only approach is too slow: rebuilding from backups usually misses a 1-hour RTO, and periodic backups can miss a 5-minute RPO.

For the data, use Aurora Global Database. It copies writes asynchronously, meaning in the background a moment after they are saved, from the primary Region to a read-only copy in the second Region. The delay is typically about a second, well inside the 5-minute RPO. In a disaster, you promote the secondary cluster so it accepts writes. The application servers are defined in the same CloudFormation templates and run at minimum size, with Auto Scaling ready to grow them. Amazon Route 53, the AWS DNS service, uses a failover routing policy with health checks to send users to the second Region.

Prove it with scheduled DR tests, for example once a quarter. In a test you actually fail over, time the whole process against the 1-hour RTO, measure any data lost against the 5-minute RPO, write down each manual step, and then automate those steps. The common mistake is assuming the plan works without ever running it. The cost of that mistake is finding missing permissions, quota limits, or stale templates during a real outage.

Put a managed message queue, Amazon SQS, between the web tier and the PDF generator. The web tier writes one message per payslip job to the queue and immediately tells the user the job was accepted. The generator workers pull messages at their own pace. This is loose coupling: the two parts no longer need to be fast at the same moment, and the queue acts as a buffer that absorbs the 40-times spike.

Why no work is lost: a message is deleted only after a worker finishes the job. If a worker crashes, the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout (the period a message stays hidden while one worker handles it) and another worker retries it. Add a dead-letter queue, a separate queue that receives messages that keep failing after a set number of attempts, so bad jobs are kept for investigation rather than retried forever or silently dropped.

Scale the generator with an Auto Scaling group whose target-tracking policy follows queue backlog per worker, meaning messages waiting divided by running instances. For example, aim for 100 messages per worker: 4,000 waiting messages leads to about 40 workers, and the group shrinks again when the queue empties. You can add scheduled scaling just before month-end so capacity is ready early. The common mistake is scaling on CPU alone, which reacts late and ignores how much work is actually waiting.

Use a staged release instead of an all-at-once deployment. A blue/green deployment runs the new version (green) next to the current version (blue) and shifts traffic gradually. A canary sends a small share first, for example 10 percent for 15 minutes, and only then the rest. Services such as AWS CodeDeploy, driven from a CI/CD pipeline (continuous integration and delivery, the automated build-test-release process), can manage this traffic shift.

Connect rollback to Amazon CloudWatch alarms on error rate and latency. If an alarm fires during the canary window, traffic automatically returns to the old version, which is still running, so rollback takes minutes and no one has to act manually. For infrastructure changes, CloudFormation change sets let the team preview exactly what a template update will modify. CloudFormation rollback triggers can also link the stack update to those alarms, so a failing update reverts the stack to its last good state.

Worked example: release 42 goes to 10 percent of traffic, the error alarm passes its threshold after 6 minutes, and traffic shifts back to blue automatically. About 10 percent of users saw errors for a few minutes, instead of every user for 2 hours. The common mistake is having no alarm attached, which turns a canary into a slow all-at-once release.

Remove the database password from the configuration file and store it in AWS Secrets Manager, a credential management service that encrypts secrets and can rotate them, meaning it changes them automatically on a schedule. The application fetches the secret at runtime using its permissions. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is a lower-cost option for configuration values, but Secrets Manager's built-in rotation suits database passwords.

Delete the long-lived access key. Give the EC2 servers an IAM role through an instance profile instead. A role provides temporary credentials that AWS rotates automatically, so there is no permanent key that could leak. Write the role's policy for least privilege: allow reading only this application's secret, sending and receiving only on the payslip SQS queue (for the matching tier), writing only to the payslip storage location, and use KMS (the AWS key management service) to decrypt only with the specific key that protects these resources. Do not grant wildcard admin permissions.

The consequence of leaving things as they are: anyone who reads the config file or steals the key could read all payroll data or take over the entire account. With the fix, a stolen server credential expires soon and can only reach a narrow set of resources.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Bakeries: Fixing an Online Ordering System That Already Runs
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Bakeries is a fictional chain of 40 bakeries. Customers order cakes through a web application that runs on AWS, Amazon's cloud platform. You have just joined as a solutions architect, the person who decides how the system's parts fit together. Your manager asks you to review what already runs in production, meaning the live system customers use, and to suggest improvements.

The application runs on six virtual servers. AWS calls a virtual server an EC2 instance. The six instances sit behind a load balancer, which is a service that spreads incoming web requests across several servers. All six instances are in one Availability Zone. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one of several physically separate data center groups inside an AWS Region, and a Region is a geographic area such as Ireland or Ohio. Orders are stored in Amazon RDS, a managed relational database service, which means AWS runs the database software for you. The database is set up as Single-AZ: there is one database copy in one zone.

The review finds three problems.

First, the database password is typed in plain text inside a configuration file on every instance. The same file is also stored in the team's code repository, the shared place where developers keep their code. The password has not changed in two years.

Second, last month a power problem took one Availability Zone offline for 50 minutes. Because the servers and the database were all in that zone, no customer could place an order. This happened on a Saturday morning, the busiest time of the week.

Third, releases use an all-at-once deployment. In an all-at-once deployment, new code replaces the old code on every server at the same moment. Twice this quarter a bad release broke the site for every customer at once. Each time it took about 40 minutes to put the old version back.

The business has told you that a missed Saturday morning costs more in lost orders than any other incident. It has also said that a leaked database password could expose customer addresses and phone numbers.

Your tasks:
1. Recommend a safer way to store and use the database password, and explain why it is better than the current setup.
2. Explain how to remove the single points of failure that caused the 50-minute outage. A single point of failure is one component whose loss stops the whole system.
3. Recommend a deployment strategy to replace all-at-once, and explain how it limits harm from a bad release.
4. Put the three fixes in order of priority and justify the order using what the business said it would feel first.
modelAnswer:
Move the password into AWS Secrets Manager. Secrets Manager is a managed secrets store: a service that keeps sensitive values such as passwords encrypted and gives them out only to callers that are allowed to read them. Encrypted means scrambled so the value is useless without a key. The application should fetch the password from Secrets Manager when it starts or connects, instead of reading it from a file. Access is granted through an IAM role. IAM (Identity and Access Management) is AWS's permission system, and a role is a set of permissions that an EC2 instance can take on without storing any keys. Give that role only permission to read this one secret. That follows least privilege, the rule that each identity gets only the access it needs.

Turn on automatic rotation. Rotation means Secrets Manager changes the password on a schedule and updates the database to match, so a copy that leaked in the past stops working.

Then remove the password from every config file and from the code repository. Because the old value is already in the repository's history, rotate it immediately. Simply deleting the file does not make the old copy safe.

Why this is better: the secret is no longer sitting in readable copies, access is limited and recorded, and the password changes regularly. Secrets Manager calls are logged by AWS CloudTrail, the service that records who called which AWS action and when, so you can trace who read the secret.

Systems Manager Parameter Store can also hold encrypted values, as SecureString parameters. It is a simpler parameter store inside AWS Systems Manager, the toolset for managing servers. But Secrets Manager is the stronger fit here because it has built-in rotation for RDS database passwords.

Common mistake: copying the secret into an environment variable or a server image. That just puts a plain copy back on every server.

There were two single points of failure, both caused by everything sitting in one Availability Zone.

For the servers: put the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group spread across at least two, ideally three, Availability Zones. An Auto Scaling group is a managed set of instances that keeps a chosen number running and replaces any that fail. That replacement is a self-healing feature. Register the group with the load balancer, and enable the load balancer in the same zones. The load balancer runs health checks, which are regular test requests, and sends traffic only to healthy instances. Size the group so the surviving zones can carry the Saturday peak while one zone is down.

For the database: change RDS from Single-AZ to Multi-AZ. Multi-AZ keeps a standby copy in a second zone and replicates every write to it synchronously. Synchronously means a write is confirmed only after both copies have it. If the main zone fails, RDS fails over automatically: the database name now points to the standby, usually within a minute or two, with no lost committed orders.

Traced step by step: zone A loses power. The load balancer's health checks to the instances in zone A fail, so it stops sending them traffic. Instances in zones B and C keep serving customers. The Auto Scaling group launches replacement instances in B and C. At the same time, RDS promotes the standby in zone B. The application reconnects using the same database name. Customers see a brief pause rather than a 50-minute outage.

Afterwards, prove it works by testing a failure on purpose, for example by forcing an RDS failover or stopping the instances in one zone during a quiet period. Watch it with Amazon CloudWatch, AWS's monitoring service, and set CloudWatch alarms on unhealthy host count and on database failover events.

Common mistake: spreading the servers across zones but leaving the database Single-AZ. The database stays a single point of failure, so the same outage happens again.

Replace all-at-once with blue/green deployment. Blue/green means you run two complete environments. Blue is the current live version. Green is a new copy running the new release. You test green while blue still serves every customer. Then you switch traffic to green, either through the load balancer or through DNS. DNS (the Domain Name System) is the service that turns a web address into a server address. If green misbehaves, you switch traffic back to blue, which is still running. Rollback, meaning returning to the previous version, takes minutes instead of 40.

Traced: version 2 is deployed to green, and smoke tests pass. Smoke tests are quick checks that the main pages work. Traffic moves to green. CloudWatch alarms show the error rate rising. Traffic is moved back to blue. Few customers were affected, and only briefly. Blue is kept until green is proven stable.

A rolling deployment is an acceptable alternative. A rolling deployment updates a few servers at a time while the rest keep serving. It limits how many users a bad release reaches. But rollback is slower, and old and new versions run side by side during the update.

Add automatic rollback by tying the switch to CloudWatch alarms. Also run deployments through an automated pipeline, so every release follows the same tested steps instead of manual ones.

Common mistake: deleting blue the moment traffic moves. That removes the quick way back.

First: secure the credential. The password is already exposed in the code repository, so the risk exists today. A leak would expose customers' personal data. That carries legal and trust damage that cannot be undone, and the fix is quick and cheap. Rotating the password right away closes the open exposure.

Second: remove the single points of failure with multiple Availability Zones and RDS Multi-AZ. The business said a missed Saturday morning is its most costly incident, and a zone failure stops all orders. This is a larger change, so it comes after the urgent security exposure is contained. It should still be done before the next busy period.

Third: move to blue/green deployment. Bad releases have hurt every customer, but the team controls when releases happen. Until blue/green is ready, it can lower the risk by not releasing on Fridays or weekends and by testing more before each release. That makes this risk easier to manage in the meantime than the other two.

The reasoning to show: rank fixes by how soon and how badly the business would feel the failure, how likely it is, and whether a cheap mitigation exists in the meantime. A mitigation is a step that reduces the damage without fully fixing the cause. Ranking by technical interest is the wrong basis. A reasonable alternative order that puts reliability first can earn credit if it is justified, but it must still rotate the exposed password immediately.

scenarios.title: Harbor & Pine Outfitters: sorting a legacy portfolio before the data-center lease ends
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor & Pine Outfitters is a fictional outdoor-gear retailer. Its data-center lease ends in 6 weeks for bulk data and 6 months for everything else, and you are the architect writing the migration plan for AWS (Amazon Web Services, a public cloud provider).

The team sorts every application with the 7Rs, seven common migration strategies. Retire means switch it off because nobody needs it. Retain means leave it where it is for now. Rehost, also called lift-and-shift, means copying the server as-is onto a cloud virtual machine. Relocate means moving a whole virtualization cluster to a cloud-hosted version of the same platform. Replatform means making small changes, such as swapping a self-run database for a managed one, without rewriting code. Repurchase means dropping the custom app and buying a SaaS product (software you rent and use over the internet). Refactor means redesigning the code to use cloud-native services.

The portfolio includes the following.

The Fax Order Gateway turns faxed orders into records. Its logs show the last real order arrived 14 months ago.

The Warehouse Control System drives barcode scanners and conveyor belts in the building next door. The vendor supports it only on local hardware, and it needs replies in under 5 milliseconds.

PayCalc is a home-built payroll app. Leadership has already signed a contract for a commercial SaaS payroll service.

StockView is a Java inventory website on two Windows virtual machines. The business has frozen all code changes for this year.

Checkout is the online order system. When a customer pays, Checkout saves the order, then waits on three other jobs in a row: sending the confirmation email, running a fraud check, and adding loyalty points. When the email server is slow, customers see timeouts. Holiday traffic is about 20 times normal.

There is also an 80 TB archive of product photos and videos (1 TB is about 1,000 GB). It sits on a file server reached through a 100 Mbps internet link (megabits per second, roughly 12.5 megabytes per second at full speed). Only about half of that link can be spared for migration. The archive must be in Amazon S3 (an object storage service that holds files as objects in containers called buckets) within 6 weeks. After that, staff will keep adding a few GB of new files each day until the file server is shut down.

The available tools are these. AWS Snowball Edge, part of the AWS Snow Family, is a rugged storage device AWS ships to you. You copy data onto it locally and ship it back, and AWS loads the data into S3. AWS DataSync is a managed online transfer service. It copies files over the network on a schedule and sends only what changed. AWS Application Migration Service continuously copies running servers block by block onto Amazon EC2, which provides cloud virtual machines. Amazon SQS is a managed message queue: messages wait in the queue until a worker takes them. Amazon SNS is a publish-subscribe topic: one published message is copied to every subscriber. AWS Lambda runs your code in response to events, with no servers for you to manage.

Your sub-tasks:
1. Classify the Fax Order Gateway, Warehouse Control System, PayCalc and StockView against the 7Rs. Give a one-sentence reason for each.
2. Choose how to move the 80 TB archive within 6 weeks, and how to handle the daily new files afterwards. Show the bandwidth arithmetic that drives your choice.
3. Name the tool and target platform for StockView, and say what you would check just before cutover. Cutover is the moment users are switched to the new copy.
4. Checkout is worth modernizing rather than lifting. Name its 7R strategy and describe a decoupled design using the services above. Explain how it fixes the timeout problem, and name one common mistake in this kind of design.
subParts: Move the 80 TB archive and ongoing changes
Rehost StockView: tool, target, cutover check
Refactor Checkout into a decoupled design
modelAnswer: Fax Order Gateway: Retire. Nobody has used it for 14 months, so moving it would only add cost and risk. Switch it off after confirming with the business owner and archiving its data. Warehouse Control System: Retain. The vendor supports it only on local hardware, and its under-5-millisecond reply requirement ties it to the building, so it stays on premises for now. PayCalc: Repurchase. Leadership has already bought a SaaS payroll service, so the job is to move the payroll data into that product, not to move the custom app. StockView: Rehost. Code changes are frozen this year, so copying the Windows servers as-is onto cloud virtual machines is the only strategy that fits. A common mistake is migrating everything by default. Retiring the fax gateway removes a server you would otherwise pay for and patch in the cloud.

The usable bandwidth is about half of 100 Mbps, so 50 Mbps. That is roughly 6.25 megabytes per second. 80 TB is about 80,000,000 MB. Dividing 80,000,000 by 6.25 gives about 12.8 million seconds, which is roughly 148 days. That is far longer than the 6-week deadline, so an online transfer alone cannot work. The answer is an offline transfer with AWS Snowball Edge from the AWS Snow Family. AWS ships the device or devices, staff copy the archive onto them locally at network speed inside the building, ship them back, and AWS loads the data into the S3 bucket. For the few GB of new files added each day, use AWS DataSync over the internet link (or a VPN). On a schedule, it copies only files that are new or changed since the last run into the same bucket, until the file server is shut down. A common mistake is choosing the online tool without doing the arithmetic. The transfer then runs for months and also eats the bandwidth that the business's normal traffic needs.

Use AWS Application Migration Service. Install its agent on both Windows virtual machines. It continuously copies each server's disks to AWS, block by block, so the cloud copy stays almost current while the original keeps running. The target platform is Amazon EC2, which provides cloud virtual machines, launched from the replicated disks with no code changes. This matches the code freeze. Before cutover, launch test instances from the replicated copy and confirm the Java site starts, connects to its database and serves pages correctly. Check that replication is caught up, with no lag. Then stop changes on the old servers briefly, let the final changes replicate, launch the cutover instances and point users at them, for example by updating the DNS (Domain Name System) record. Keep the old servers available briefly as a rollback path. A common mistake is skipping the test launch. The first real launch then becomes the test, and any boot or connection problem turns into a production outage.

Strategy: Refactor, because the design changes from one synchronous chain to independent cloud-native parts. Design: when a customer pays, Checkout saves the order and publishes one 'order placed' message to an Amazon SNS topic, then immediately tells the customer the order succeeded. Three Amazon SQS queues subscribe to the topic, one each for email, fraud check and loyalty points. SNS copies the message into all three. Each queue triggers its own AWS Lambda function, which does that one job. Why it fixes the timeouts: Checkout no longer waits for the email server or the other jobs. If email is slow or down, its messages simply wait in its queue and are processed when it recovers, while fraud checks and loyalty points continue normally. Lambda adds more copies of each worker as messages pile up, so the 20 times holiday peak is absorbed by the queues instead of crashing Checkout. Common mistake: subscribing the Lambda functions directly to the SNS topic with no queue in between. There is then no buffer to hold messages through a long outage or a sudden spike, and failed deliveries can be lost after retries run out. A second mistake is forgetting that a worker may receive the same message twice, so each worker should be safe to repeat (for example, do not award loyalty points twice for one order ID).
